title: ["The Husband's Secret", 'The Uninvited']
cleaned_reviews: the husband's secret may seem like chick lit at first, with its descriptions of school projects, tupperware parties, and perfect housewives -- but give it 20 pages or so, and you'll be completely wowed. in this compelling novel, australian novelist liane moriarty presents the lives of three women whose worlds are all blown apart by secrets kept and uncovered. as the main characters' lives intersect, the impact of their interactions and collisions will have far-reaching consequences for not only themselves, but for everyone they care about. filled with sparkling writing that's deceptively light and humorous, the husband's secret is fast-paced, engaging, and surprisingly moving. highly recommended. (full review posted at bookshelf fantasies.) it's not often that a book so successfully combines a subtle, eerie ghost story with compelling historical fiction, but the uninvited really pulls it off. set during the 1918 flu epidemic in a small illinois town dominated by anti-german, anti-foreigner agitation, the book captures the fear caused by the deaths of so many, on the battlefields overseas and at home from illness. the plot builds, adding tension and complications, until a really stunning final third that ties it all together just marvelously. highly recommended.

title: ['Gifts (Annals of the Western Shore #1)', "Thick as Thieves (The Queen's Thief, #5)"]
cleaned_reviews: orrec is born into a gifted family in the uplands. although his family controls a fey and unsettling gift, they are nevertheless barely able to eke out a life from their sparse and rocky land. the gifted families raid each other for the few resources that remain: livestock, wood, serfs. cut off from the rest of the world by a combination of shunning and pride, the people of the uplands grow more stunted and inbred with every generation. unable to find a wife among his own people, orrec's father rode into lowlands village (he had never seen so many people) and kidnapped a young woman. lovely and cultured, she instilled a love of stories and reading in orrec. but her kindess and memories of art and civilization can only do so much--orrec is still trapped in a claustrophobic society with no choices and no hope. in queen of attolia we were introduced to nahuseresh, nephew of the emperor of the medes and ambassador to attolia. nahusresh is sent back to the mede empire in disgrace, taking his accountant/secretary/major domo kamet with him. kamet has been enslaved since he was young and has entirely bought into the idea that the mede empire is the most civilized place in the world, that its ascendance is only a matter of time (and not that much time), and that enslavement to a royal in mede is better than free life in the barbaric attolia. but then he has to go on the run, and as he journeys with a large and stupidly honest attolian, kamet's certainty is shaken. i loved seeing the change in his mindset over time; it's so gradual one almost doesn't realize, until a particular decision or thought is so contrary to kamet at the start of the novel that the difference is noticeable. it's not that kamet was precisely happy before, but he understood his life, he had certain privileges that he treasured, and being so controlled and choice-less was, in some ways, comfortable. in the attolian's company, he begins to realize how little he paid attention to or understood the common people of the empire, what it feels like to make choices that he has to be solely responsible for, and that qualities like honesty or mischief are not always hindrances. they also develop a great friendship modeled after the tales of what seems like the in-universe versions of gilgamesh and enkidu. i'm so happy to return to this world every time, and every book develops the world and characters all the more.

title: ['Elite (Eagle Elite, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: there is so much wrong with this book... but that didn't stop me from really enjoying it! i'll start with the issues. there's trace - she's ridiculously innocent, and she veers like a crazy yoyo between being strong and standing up for herself, and dissolving into a puddle of tears. there's the insta-love, which i don't have a problem with per se, but i do when the guy, however sexy, is clearly a complete bastard. there's the fact that everyone seems to be insanely gorgeous. and worst of all, there's the trite love triangle which appears to have been stuffed in just for the sake of it. but despite all this, i kind of loved it. it has an addictive mystery and intrigue, it's fast-paced, keeping you turning the pages. the romance, however ill-advised, is hot, and even the farcical situations are entertaining. if i was more of a book snob i'd have to give it two stars, but i'm just a reader who enjoys a good story, so i own up to my guilty pleasures and say i can't wait for the next installment!

title: ['Pivot Point (Pivot Point, #1)', 'Vanishing Girls', 'Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)', 'Siege and Storm (The Grisha, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: initial impressions:this was a really good and interesting concept! didnt totally knock my socks off but definitely interested in reading future books from kasie west!! review originally posted on the book addict's guide: i had been interested in pivot point for a looong time before i got the chance to read it and i admit it, due to my habits of skimming a book summary so as not to encounter any opportunity for spoilers, i wasn't 100% sure how the book played out. turns out that addie is not the only person that has an ability - her whole community is a group of paranormals, each one having a unique ability from using more of the untapped part of their brain. i must say though... i was a bit disappointed in the para community. not because of how it was written but the para community, para high school... it all felt a little cutesy and fortress of solitude-ish and for some reason i wasn't totally sold on it. i kind of loved that the entire book flips back and forth between addie's search of her life if she stays in the para community and her life if she chose to move into the normal world. it was really interesting to see both timelines side-by-side and when we finally reached the end of her search, i felt like she had an impossible choice ahead of her! i loved that after every search, it was like she actually lived both choices so it all felt so real to her - i found that really interesting! - as well as the fact that her ability was a twist on clairvoyance and had a bit more rules & restrictions. overall, i can't say i was really blown away by the book, but i absolutely loved the idea and how it was written as far as the two different paths go and coming full circle to addie making a decision in the end. it was written so well that certain things in each path appear in both, whether addie was directly involved in that event or not. the things i was bothered by were little things like the role that football played in the story (way too much, mostly because i'm so tired of the quarterback/cheerleader roles played out) and sometimes i felt like i was just happy-floating-along instead of really being gripped by the story, if that makes sense. i'm definitely interested to see where the sequel goes and how addie's ability will continue to affect her decisions! i'm actually dying to know where things are going to go and i'm a little mad i have to wait because.... well, when you read it, you'll know!! characters addie: addie is interesting. there were times that i really liked her and other times she was really bothering me. actually, i think i just really liked her when she was with trevor and really bothered when she was with duke. i think i just knew there was something about duke i didn't like and i just didn't want to see her with him! what i did like was seeing how mature she is about her ability and how she's been able to use it to help her grow as a person. when it comes time to decide in the end which path to take, i think we see that trait in addie really shine and i think i'm going to like her a lot more in book two! trevor: i was allllll for addie's time with trevor! there was a point in the book where i had him in my mind as a cross between tim riggins and some kind of prettier-looking guy since she kept talking about his eyelashes. but seriously. cowboy boot and a wool-lined jacket, high school kid in texas? that equals tim riggins. besides the physical aspects, i absolutely loved his interactions with addie, how he treated her, and guys. it's another best-friend-turned-boyfriend romance!!! (kind of.) duke: i just...... never felt like he was trustworthy! probably because of addie's initial reaction to him being a schmoozer. i was on her side! i got a little more comfortable as the book (review to come!) so i was in a very mystery/thriller mood and i had hoped vanishing girls would keep me on that streak! the book was really interesting but i do have to admit that i sort of waffled eaters -- his dedicated followers -- but also the unforgivable curses and so much more about the dark years that preceded voldemort's decline. we've seen the bad guys punished in previous books and we bardugo has developed all feel so real. we definitely see a new alina in the end of shadow & bone and we continue to see how she's changing even more by coming into her power in siege & storm. i felt primary focus is alina's powers and her role as possible savior of ravka. the romance surely does help mold and shape this major plot line and it was wonderful to read, but i was just glad i felt like the powers and the magical elements were still the main focus of this book. you may be happy (or unhappy) to know that the darkling is still a major part of this book! i admit, i was a little concerned because for some reason i felt like he was going to fall into the background in book two, but nope. he is back with a vengeance and it's delightfully wicked. book two is (no pun intended) final opinion of the book is that if you liked shadow & bone, you'll love siege & storm. i guess if you loved the first book, you'll love this one even more (i hope)! i feel even more amazed than i guide 7/12/14: siege and storm was an interesting re-read but ultimately not as exciting as the first time around - don't get me wrong, it was still amazing, but i was in total awe when i first read this book over a year ago. (wow, over a year!?) it was really fun being able to discover everything all over again. some things had lost their surprise, of course, since i already knew the big twists but the best thing about re-reading - like with my re-read of shadow and bone - was that i had forgotten so many of the little details. hell, in siege and storm, i had even forgotten some of the big details and big reveals. it had been so long since i had spent some time in the grishaverse that i had forgotten a lot of the backstories, things like the tales in the book of saints, and how specific events actually transpired. especially re-reading, it's even more apparent how much siege and storm shows off leigh bardugo's writing talent. shadow and bone was so enjoyable (both times) but siege and storm really starts to take the plot to new places, open new doors, and put the characters in even more peril until they learn how to fight their way out of the situation. we learn that not all characters are forever safe. we learn that everyone will be put under much more pressure. i felt like there were so many twists and turns and secrets to discover in this book that even after knowing how it ends, i had forgotten how we even got there. the action was stupendous as well. shadow and bone had its action sequences, but siege and storm really took it up a notch, allowing the characters to roam much more and really develop their strengths, giving them the freedom to find more trouble and conquer it that much better. i really appreciated the intricacy of each situation that much more. this book also offered a lot more in character development. i never felt like i was missing any in shadow and bone, but this was a natural layering of characters as the series progresses. i kind of felt like alina was a bit of a brat in shadow and bone but she really does start to mature in this book. that doesn't mean that she leaves her cheeky attitude or sarcasm behind, which i'm thankful for because i just love the banter that occurs between her and mal and of course, her and sturmhond. she just really comes into her own as a leader, as a grisha, and even just as a young adult. leigh bardugo really stretches her repertoire of characters as well. we all know how much i love sturmhond and his character addition makes me wonder how the series didn't have him from the beginning. he's such a fan-favorite and he really adds a wonderful presence to the story. i just love how he affects the series both in plot and his own effect on other characters. my only issue with the re-read was a personal one and that was that i was reading as an audiobook. since my audiobook time is literally ten minutes at a time to and from work now, it was a hard book to even re-read much less read in short pieces like that. i'm so glad that i really savored it the first time around so even though my re-read was patchy, i still knew how amazing it was and the re-read turned out to be much more of a refresher than a time to sit down and savor. if you need to read or even re-read siege and storm, i highly recommend making sure you allot enough time to really enjoy it and soak it all in!

planned to take a shower, my mom was. so i peeked into the book. and proceeded to spend the next 3 hours reading the story and practically dying at the end. because all the feels oh my god someone save me, my heart.i'm still not sure how the hell i'm supposed to write a review for this book when my heart is still bursting from all the feelings that rutkoski has so rudely shoved into my heart. i have to admit, though, i was a bit surprised with how much i absolutely adored this book. for months before the release, people had been ranting about this book, crying over it, and i was a bit worried that it just wouldn't live up to the hype.oh, but it so did.it's absolutely amazing how marie rutkoski invented and so brilliantly fleshed out this world of the winner's curse. there are so many things about it, tiny details that didn't need to be acknowledged to get five stars, but she just flawlessly weaves them in, making the world as vibrant as the cover. i adored learning more about this world, the history between the two races, the things that sparked their current society, and the feelings between the two. even more than that, rutkoski's writing style is a curious thing. it's different-subtly so and beautifully so. the way she chooses to tell kestrel and arin's story is awe inspiring and just made me love the book all the more. really, there's not much about this book that's not thrilling and amazing, but the writing was definitely one of my favorites.kestrel! kestrel was an amazing character an, perhaps, the most clever character who actually demonstrates how smart and tactical she is. her struggle between not wanting to marry and not wanting to join the military is real, as is her talent for strategy. many times throughout the story we see her come up with brilliant battle plans and tactics that would've worked. it's just stunning how the author comes up with all these battle strategies that sound legit and foolproof and just tweak it to fit kestrel's personality. kestrel is the kind of character you love. she's flawed in so many ways, but she's smart and brave, and she knows what's a good move, and what's not. and that is, perhaps, the best thing about her.we don't really get to explore arin's personality as much as we do kestrel's, but we do know that he's loyal-troubling when he's torn between his people and his love for kestrel. his struggle is just short of heartbreaking, but he's an amazing character and fits kestrel's personality. almost as cunning as her, softer spoken, and as fierce as kestrel is in protecting those he loves.their relationship was a beautiful one that doesn't start out as romance. more of a friendship that you just, well, ship from beginning to end. the loathing arin had for her and watching as she slowly won him and his trust over was another favorite part of mine, and then watching them just fall in love. their love was...enchanting.the plot. oh my god the plot. while in the beginning there isn't much stirring of a heart racing plot, halfway in, it starts. and then you really just can't let go until you get to the end. it's intriguing and it just pushes you on and on until you stare at the acknowledgements and wonder what the heck happened to those last, oh, thousand pages that should be there. the winner's curse is an absoltuely enthralling book that i am officially shoving in peoples' faces. one of my favorites of the year, i need more people to read this and scream with me as i await the second book that will rip out my heart. a gorgeous high fantasy that captures your heart with it's world, romance, and characters, the winner's curse will sweep you off your feet into a world that's as charming and filled with dangers as our own, if not more.

cleaned_reviews: finally we get to read daniel's story! since we first met him when he was a teenager it's a little strange to see him all grown up and finding love himself. but he's actually a wonderful hero even though i felt slightly dissatisfied by the end. daniel meets violet when a man who owes him money takes daniel to see this medium he's hosting in lieu of payment. daniel goes along for the ride but is soon disgusted by his peer and the snooty bunch of young lords that accompany them. he feels sympathy for violet's dependence on the demanding aristocrat while at the same time finding himself intrigued and enthralled by the engineering prowess displayed in her performance. she's got all the other young lords fooled. daniel looks deeper and falls hard for her machines. everybody's got a weakness, right? i loved daniel. i loved violet. so what left me ever-so-slightly disappointed? i felt that some things were not completely resolved, especially on the emotional front. not between daniel and violet, their chemistry was excellent and their friendship to love story was fine for the most part. it's the other family relationships that feel glossed over. i get that they're a messed up family communication-wise, but it seems like years have passed since the ice began to thaw so i'd like to see something a little more relatable. the climax also felt a bit cluttered. i love seeing the mackenzies in all their knock-down/drag-out glory, but it felt like they muddied things. daniel being the four brothers' youngster for so long seems to demand that he get out of the biggest scrape in his story without their help. this family is a team, i know, but story arcs do demand some things and i think this one short-changed daniel as an adult lead in that way. however, ashley writes this family so incredibly well, that my dissatisfaction at the very end was minor. and the excerpt from the next book -- about ainsley's brother sinclair mcbride -- has me anxious to get my hands on that one the moment i can. i'm very loyal to this series, having only been truly disappointed in one of the books. i highly recommend the mackenzie series to anyone who loves historical romance. it begins with "the madness of lord ian mackenzie" which i've seen on sale several times, so look for it. spoilers included but marked i had to think about this one before rating it. there were some really fantastic scenes, but there were also a few things that seemed like they weren't explored well or didn't come to their logical conclusion based on what we know so far. the four stars is actually 3.5 - 3.75 rounded up. mercy's still living in her trailer with samuel and working in her garage. her relationship with adam has progressed to the lovers stage but her relationship with the pack has not improved. in this book samuel's in big trouble and needs mercy's help whether he wants it or not. it's a somewhat heartbreaking as well as infuriating story line with a disappointingly pat conclusion. some in the pack want mercy out, maybe want adam out, too, and are using the whole 'making a coyote part of a wolf pack' upheaval to create a power play. that story line was the most intriguing to me and had a fairly nice conclusion although all the players who deserved punishment didn't quite get their due, imo. there is a nasty fae who wants one of the artifacts mercy has borrowed and there's some real danger for mercy and her friends. this is the story line that i thought was wrapped up and dispensed with too insubstantially. major spoiler: * * * i was particularly bothered by jessie's involvement in the rescue since it didn't provide anything more than a way for ari to find gabriel. mercy said it herself, she could have stopped by sylvia's and gotten something inanimate that ari could use just as well. i mean, sylvia was in the know by that time. mercy did need a human to facilitate communication, but tony couldn't have done it? kyle? in past books in this series, we've gotten to see why certain things that make sense are impossible. this felt like briggs just didn't bother laying the groundwork. and i can't believe adam had absolutely nothing to say about jessie being put in that kind of danger when all these adults were involved. it just doesn't wash. now, if she had followed them and they'd been forced to take her, that would be okay, but that wasn't the case, they chose to take her. and, in any case, her presence was not used for any interesting elements of that story line. she was merely a distraction for me, the reader, because i assumed there would be some real consequences to mercy's tstl decision making. but then there weren't any. it was just kind of brushed away. this was the first book where i saw mercy actually make any tstl decisions. lying to adam, having jessie come along when she wasn't the only option, not talking to adam directly about the pack manipulating her and several others. * * * end spoiler not that this book is bad. far from it. patricia briggs is such a great writer that this is definitely still a "can't put it down" read. i was just disappointed in the follow-through on some of the threads. and briggs has established mercy as this very competent and logical heroine so i just couldn't reconcile some of her decisions with the character i've come to know. it's possible my disappointment is heightened by the fact that i now have to wait months and months for the next installment. but my dissatisfaction is real and i think the elements i've mentioned really weren't in keeping with the high quality i've come to expect. 3.75 stars for excellent writing and partially amazing story telling. and adam. and ben. i do so love those wolves. :d

title: ['Dangerous']
cleaned_reviews: i've been pretty excited about this book. i'm normally excited already about 1) anything from shannon hale; 2) sci-fi; 3) particularly young adult or children's sci-fi because i don't feel like there's a whole lot of it; 4) and books that have a diverse cast without it being a "thing." this book has all of these features. i really enjoyed seeing shannon hale step of out of her usual element in creating a science fiction action-type story. i think that in that area, she should just now consider this part of her element. she did a nice job of putting a lot of science into her sci-fi technology, even though that's not always required, and she created a diverse cast of characters who managed to not constantly slap you in their face going hey i'm latina or look at me, i'm missing a hand, other than when it might naturally come up. those are both difficult tasks and she did them well. there was a lot of action, and there were enough plot twists and turns that i wasn't 100% sure what was going on (and neither was the main character). the book definitely took an arc that i wasn't expecting from how the setup went at the start, which is probably a good thing because it means it wasn't predictable. i also liked that the progressions of the relationships in this book were much more realistic than in most ya. maisie is a strong character who stands up for herself when it counts, and all those people chomping at the bit to tear down the relationship dynamics portrayed between teenage characters should definitely have less to complain about here. i will say, there is some morally shady ground here and it's a sign of the times that hale felt compelled to explain her ending right in the text, almost like she was expecting a huge blowback from the choices maisie ultimately makes and she was trying to head it off at the pass. like, "i'm not condoning this behavior in general but in this one instance it is ok." this is what we've come to? authors have to be so defensive of their stories that it comes out in the text itself? i'm not sure if that's a good thing or not. was it my favorite book ever? no. but i really liked it and would recommend it to others, especially people looking for an entertaining, kick-butt heroine on an alien-tech-fueled wild ride.

cleaned_reviews: i've been looking forward to reading without borders for a while now. there's a lot of repetition going on in new adult, and the premise of amanda heger's debut novel really interested me. and let me tell you, i was not disappointed. annie heads off to a remote area in central america to pad her medical school application, hoping it will get her accepted to the school of her dreams. she knew she'd be roughing it, but she didn't know how much she'd learn, or that she'd meet the man of her dreams. dr. felipe gutierrez has had enough of the spoiled americans who come to his country under the pretense of helping, only to spend the entire time complaining about the dirt and mosquitos. when annie shows up, he's sure she's going to be more of the same, but it doesn't take him long to realize he's never met anyone like her before. from the first page this story pulls you in, and it never lets up. from heger's detailed description of the nicaraguan landscape, to the vivid characters, without borders makes you feel like you are in the middle of the story. this book made me laugh, cry, and had me glued to my ipad all day long. i loved how annie changed throughout the story, and how sweet and caring felipe was to everyone he met. there were times i wanted to reach into the book and slap them both, but that's part of what makes it a good story. they felt real and so did the choices (and mistakes) they made. if you love a good new adult romance, this is the book for you! ***arc provided in exchange for an honest review.

cleaned_reviews: black swan green is a truly enjoyable coming-of-age story. jason taylor is a stammering 13 year old boy who lives in black swan green, a small village in england. he is a bit of a nervous kid, he is frequently bullied, but he somehow copes. he blames his stammer on his inner hangman, who trips him up on his words. jason is a kid that despite wanting to fit in, have a girlfriend, do well in school and please his parents, he still has a strong sense of mischief. his inner voice is entertaining and honest. the extra-foul british slang occasionally had me laughing out loud. (i would never think to call someone piss-flaps!) i wish i had been that self-aware as a 13 year old. i will definitely seek out more of david mitchell's work. as i have said before, i love margaret atwood. her stories are complex and speculative, but only in a way that they reflect our own society's shortcomings in a way that somehow seems scarier if she really went for the sci-fi elements, or the reality of social commentary. this whole trilogy feels impossible, but also somewhat imminent. i didn't get the connection to oryx and crake until about two thirds of the way through the year of the flood, which i preferred for its focus on the female characters. after finishing that one, i needed to find out what happened. maddaddam was the wrap-up i had hoped for, but as i should have learned from the first two books, not at all what i expected. i particularly loved the focus on story-telling and myth-making in this one. toby is a fabulous, if reluctant storyteller and really does an excellent job continuing jimmy's creation myths and almost becomes the preacher adam 1 was. it was fascinating to see how the whole story unfolded and concluded. she kept me surprised at every turn and made me want to know the outcomes for each character. now for her short stories.... i loved this book. i caught my attention immediately and caused me to lose sleep. i couldn't put it down. it owes a lot to jane eyre, which i do not think is hidden in any way. in fact, jane eyre becomes a key detail in the plot. it reads like a 19th century novel, with its ghosts and mansions and strong female characters. it has moments of creepiness, a bit of a mystery and multiple stories within stories. one of the things i loved most about this book though, is it is a book-nerd's book. since the main character/narrator is a rare books dealer, there is a lot of description of the magic of reading, the love of books and the ability of a good book to transport the reader. that is exactly what this one did. the underground railroad is an excellent, yet difficult account of an imagined underground railroad that is an actual railroad. the fantasy elements end there though. it is the story of cora, who upon learning of the railroad escapes the particularly brutal plantation she is on after a bad beating. knowing nothing of her future destinations, she and another slave set out to find freedom and safety. this is not an easy book to read, which i think is an important element of it. it is violent, and brutal, and full of some truly horrifying images i won't easily forget, but i think that is the point. this brutality was real and escaped slaves, even those who managed to get out of the south, were still in danger of being brought by slave catchers. the fear really never subsided, and perceived safety was a danger in itself. colson whitehead has written something important here, and i am very curious to read his other (very different from this) books.

title: ['Binti (Binti, #1)', 'Midwinterblood', 'Saga, Vol. 1 (Saga, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i've been wanting to read this for awhile, but i'm bad at e-books, so i finally just bought myself a paperback because it's been recommended to me enough that i was pretty sure i would like it. and i did! my only real complaint is that okorafor does that thing where suddenly the main character is shouting or shrieking something and it feels...too abrupt and melodramatic, when it comes right in the middle of a conversation where everyone seems to be speaking normally up until then. so that dropped me out of the story a couple of times. and then yeah, a couple of things felt a little...too convenient, i guess. but i loved the main character and i loved the way things develop with okwu, and i'm happy to see a #1 after the title on here because yeah, i want more and am looking forward to a #2! p.s. this paperback weirdly doesn't have anything written on the spine, which i find very disturbing. it's not that tiny! i'm tempted to write the title and author on there myself! i think i've said before that i totally judge books by their covers, even though everyone knows not to do that. there are a couple of nice covers for this book, but the version i've got isn't one of them. the title and the cover art just scream, "hey, this book is all about vampire romance, yay!" and not being so much of a vampire romance fan, i...was not excited to read this, even though i kept seeing reviews about how good it is. i was not excited to read it, that is, until i actually started reading it, and then i was completely hooked by like, page 4. this is totally not a vampire romance, by the way. told backwards through time, from the future back to ancient times, in seven parts, it's kind of an epic love story involving sacrifice and reincarnation, which, i know, sounds horribly cheesy, but totally works beautifully here. it's haunting and brutal and so, so compelling. anyway, i loved it. i'll definitely be checking out other books by sedgwick before too long. i wasn't sure what to make of this at first...it's really weird, you know? but, as usual, brian k. vaughan's storytelling sucked me in quickly, and fiona staples' art is beautifully done. the story is told from the point of view of hazel, looking back on the circumstances surrounding her birth, but we really only see her as an infant here--at this point we're focused on fiona's parents, marko and alana, who are former soldiers from different sides in a never-ending war, with both sides after them and wanting them dead. so there's quite a bit of action, but the fun part for me is discovering who these folks are, and how they got to where they are, and where they're going next. i'm definitely intrigued, and am really looking forward to the second volume of this series!

title: ['First Year (The Black Mage, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i give it a 3.5 officially. ryiah's personality and journey through her first year at the academy reminded me a lot of tamora pierce's alanna and kel which i loved. i'm just looking for more adventure in the next few books (which i'm sure there will be) and for a less hate/like relationship between ryiah and darren (that whole ya bad boy-angsty-relationship thing is getting old in my opinion).

title: ['Article 5 (Article 5, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: 4.5 stars. i would have given it 5 but i just couldn't. let me tell you why... the story was great, the writing well done, and the concept extremely interesting. i liked the characters and saw how they grew, but the main character, ember, annoyed me half the time. i may be old, but i do remember the rashness of youth, but even that doesn't explain some of the stupid decisions ember makes. it was annoying. that was one reason i couldn't give article 5 a 5 star review. the other reason was the lack of explanation regarding the world. the author never fully explains why people live as they do or what exactly happened. it's hinted at, skimmed over, somewhat, but i'm still in the dark. i kept wanting more backstory about the world and less memories about ember and chase. i also wanted more information about the mom. there was no hint about her lifestyle or about why article 5 would relate to them until the 'incident' (hope i'm not giving spoilers). i liked how the book jumped immediately into action, yet more information throughout would have been nice. still, ms. simmons did a great job with and interesting concept and i hope she goes into more detailing in the following books (the end was obviously set up for more books). i'll definitely read them.

title: ['Nowhere But Here (Thunder Road, #1)', 'Opposition (Lux, #5)']
cleaned_reviews: originally posted on city of books nowhere but here is just as riveting and emotional as katie mcgarry's previous books. this new series just proved to me that i will read anything mcgarry writes! i love these characters, i loved the story, and i really cannot wait to see whose story we read next. emily leads a normal life with her mom and adoptive dad, but she meets her real dad once a year - her real dad who is high up in a motorcycle gang. the reign of terror, scary as it sounds, is actually a good, clean gang that goes by the rules. it's more like a family than anything else, and emily finds that out soon enough when she spends the summer with her father and the gang, along the way discovering the truth about her parents and also falling in love - something she never expected to happen in kentucky. it took me a little while to warm to emily, mostly because of her refusal to see what's right in front of her. she wants to stay within her comfort zone, which is acceptable, but she also denies the truth even though everything she knows points towards it. but this is just at first. later on, she opens up to the people around her, especially to her father eli, her grandmother olivia, and oz, a hopeful prospect of the gang who is like family to eli and olivia. i really liked emily later on, though. she has a strong character and her willingness to face her fears really impressed me. emily gets thrown into a pretty bad situation and she adapts well to everything despite the odds. i adored oz too, of course. he's perhaps not on par with mcgarry's previous male protagonists, but still incredibly loveable. like with emily, it took me a while to warm to him. at first he seemed a little shallow, caring only about his chances of getting in the club. everything he did was for that, and when he falls asleep on the job while watching over emily, his first thought is not of emily's safety but what it means for his odds of getting in the club. but i loved seeing the slow and gradual mutual liking of oz and emily. they spend a lot of time together and though at first they dislike each other, they begin to get closer and closer. oz's protectiveness of her is really sweet and his character is impossible to dislike. he's funny and kind and just as stubborn as emily. there are hints of danger throughout the book, which i loved, but i can't say i was too fond of the plot twist towards the end. i won't say much about it, but i just felt like it took away a lot of the danger aspect. regardless, i enjoyed the book a lot. i love the relationship between emily and oz, and i liked that family plays a big role in the plot. the other teenagers we see in this book are all really interesting and quite mysterious, so i'm excited for the next book, whoever it will follow. if you liked mcgarry's other books, or just ya contemporary in general, you have to read nowhere but here! it's intense, amusing, and emotional all at once. *thank you to harlequin teen for providing me with an earc for review* 4.5 stars! this was an awesome end to the series <3

title: ['The Female of the Species', 'Tampa']
cleaned_reviews: 3.5 this is the type of book you can't look away from, and i find myself astonished to say it, because i still can't believe that a book with a cover like that, so unassuming and plain and a seemingly no-strings-attached read, turned out to be such a monster. (it's kinda ironic, in a sense, because i remember reading mcginnis' a madness so discreet last year with its dark, hypnotizing--tantalizing--cover and finding such a drab story as i turned the pages, and here--well, looks like it's rather violently the other way around. my respect for her as a writer has increased tenfold, i warrant you that.) it gives way to not only an unflinching portrayal of suffocating small-town life, but also a gritty, uncompromising rendering of slut-shaming, animal-cruelty, rape and most importantly, girl power. this book basically oozes with an atmosphere of premonition, beginning with the first freaking sentence, i shit you not. you have no idea how complex the characters are. they are so layered and flawed and three-dimensional and so, so utterly human that it kind of hurts to tear your eyes away. straight-talking, sort-of-outcast and oblivious to most of high school's social hierarchy and feuds and trash-talking, living in the world of her books, alex is filled with such fury you'd never expect to see in someone like her. she's a wolf in sheep's clothing, and yet she has never hidden her true nature. yet instead of devouring the flock, she protects; she defends. what i liked about her portrayal was that she could've, very easily, had a god complex, could have been self-righteous in a preachy way, she could've been a female dexter. but she wasn't. her violence is instinctual, unleashed to bring justice and yet she never actively seeks it out--there is something wrong with her head and she might not regret, but she feels guilt, and you see that in every page. she is not a firecracker--she is vengeance personified. and this book is so damn funny, sometimes. i don't know what that says about my personality, but i liked its...somewhat brutal sense of humor. it was so gripping, you don't understand, i ditched my homework to finish this and i did so in one sitting. i can't really believe i did that even now. the cast of the characters was so well-developed, from their insecurities to their douchebaggery, from their highest peaks to their lowest pitfalls, and they came apart layer by layer as the story unraveled. it was not only entertaining, but also cathartic to witness. and the ending felt necessary. it's not how i would've wanted the story to end, but it was necessary. my only complain is that i wasn't very invested in alex and jack's relationship. i felt absolutely nothing about their budding romance and eventual smooching (relax, o fiery readers, this is absolutely not a spoiler). i know people tend to call me an apathetic robot sometimes, but i'm not actually one, you know. i may not cry during movies but that one rare book has made me cry, thank you very much. but you know, screw invested, i didn't even care about them falling in love. i mean, i watched it happen, i was there...but i was sort of...detached to the whole thing??? that's really not a plus point in my book, though i have no idea where and how it went wrong for me. to quote fall out boy, this book may look like seattle, but in reality, in its core, it's the most refreshing, brutal and unapologetic version of l.a. i'm severely uncomfortable but i think it's a good sort of uncomfortable?? say what you will, but this is the type of ghastly you can't look away from. this is the type of story that just won't let you be. it courts you into a strange kind of fascination that's really pseudo-revulsion. celeste is no humbert humbert trying to convince you of her love: she wants, and she takes. cut from an entirely different cloth, she is, and what the synopsis called prose is actually downright vile language (seriously prepare yourself for extensive knowledge of the female anatomy + masturbation techniques. even the metaphors her head cooks up make you grimace in a way you'll never have grimaced before, trust me. and it's a horrifying but necessary type of grimace, if you catch my drift). but it drives the point home. this book and its message would've never been as effective nor as daunting without it. i just can't stop thinking about it and i doubt you'd be able to, either, that's all. also, i'm legitimately tired of society's bullshit. because what happened in the end? it may be fiction but it's still plausible. it's still something that's capable of happening, something that happens and the inside of celeste's mind, no matter what it makes you feel (and trust me on this one: the list is endless), it will make you think very hard for a long, long time. she may not have humbert's charisma that distracts you from the horrors he describes, his rapier wit and skill with words, but she's her own type of ruthless nasty. you'll never understand what i mean when i say that all of it was just so hard to look away from. too hard, in fact. it's both a disillusionment and a horror show, and it will, believe me, no matter what it makes you feel or think, leave a mark.

title: ['Shiver (The Wolves of Mercy Falls, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this was an amazing story. from the first pages whenever people asked what kind of story it was i would say that it's something soft because that was the feeling that i got from it. and then i got to the end with the inevitable and i cried throughout the last thirty pages or something. but it was amazing to read!!

title: ['Wonder']
cleaned_reviews: this is probably a middle grade book, but i'm sure it can be a good read for almost anyone. it was fun, touching, insightful and extremely easy to read. i did google auggie's deformity to help me get an image in my head, and my heart went out to every example that came up. whether mild or severe, i could only imagine the everyday crap some would have to endure from even well meaning people, even more so from taunting kids (and adults, i'm sure) that said, i guess i was expecting a little more in the way of hardships, but then again, middle graders aren't as jaded as i am. most every character was understanding, or eventually came around. the story of them getting there was well told, even if slightly uneventful. i must say i was a little surprised (baffled?) at the movie choice - "the sound of music" - for a group of 10-13 year olds on a camping trip. was it just me? there was a scene at about 75% that had me kinda choked up...ahem...aaanyway... this was a good story for any reader 8 to 80.

title: ['Marrow']
cleaned_reviews: i'm really not sure how i feel about this book. it's different than what i usually read. much darker and pretty disturbing at times. i was left with a lot of questions and i'm not sure what was real versus what wasn't but i have a feeling that tarryn wrote it that way on purpose. i'd recommend if you like psychological, twisted books.

title: ['Something More Than Night']
cleaned_reviews: very different from what i expected, but not in a bad way. really i didn't know what to expect going in to something more than night. it's certainly a departure from the style and substance of the milkweed triptych (which i highly recommend!). i loved the style and character of this book. it's almost dripping with uniqueness which i thought was great. it's poured on a little heavy at times but you come to realize that it just serves to emphasize the plot and setting. there is the temptation to get bogged down in the minutiae of the theological/ontological "laws" being thrown around, but you soon discover to just take it at face value and enjoy the ride, which is quite fun. once you're fully immersed you can appreciate how interesting the world is in smtn. what keeps it from 5 stars is the necessity to gloss over a few plot points and how the plot is advanced in some parts of the novel. i was wondering where the tale would lead and was a little disappointed when characters literally just stated what comes next. also the obtuse feeling you have sometimes while reading can be off-putting but if you stick with it, it grows on you. the characters are great, and there are some touching moments. bayliss is a blast from beginning to end, definitely my favorite, and the ending was satisfying and fitting. worth a read!

title: ['Pure (Pure, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: a world wrecked and filled with hunger and sickness... it was all an accident or a master plan to create a new perfect world? the book is so complex that if i give to you a lot of the plot, i would have to keep going and going until the end and that will be bad (x the book is told from four different points of view, in third person and in present, and even when the book started with a lot of descriptions and explanations about the new world where our characters live, after the first third of the book everything starts moving at a supersonic speed and i had to keep with it, and at some points i had to re-read again and again until it fit into my brain. the scenario of the book, the dome and the deathlands, is so real since it can actually happen that i was almost frightened about it. the characters are so well built and develop, that i can almost keep in touch with them... pressia and partridge, our lead characters, have a lot of issues and emotions that help them to grow and mature in the end of the book. the secondary characters have their importance in the story too, since they helped our leads to face the challenges that the new reality throws at them. this is one of my new favorite dystopian series, since is real and crude, but also adds hope and love in the mix; and as a new twist in the ya genre, the author has change a very well known cliche in this kind of books... i just hope it stays like that until the end. i highly recommend to you this book, it won't let you down!

title: ['The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde', 'Hex Hall (Hex Hall, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i think that everyone has heard of this story but it is always nice to read such a popular book on your own. i was still kind of surprised. i didn't think i was going to enjoy the book that much. but i did! it was a very quick read, enjoyable, mixing harry potter for girls with contemporary ya - and it was a good mixture.for me it was a break between huge and serious fantasy novels and i would like to continue with the series. i really like jenna, so i hope we will see more of her. i would say this book is for younger audience, but i am 22 (not that that age would make me old, i am just not teenager anymore) and i liked it - so if you like witches, boarding schools, easy read - go for it :)

title: ['March']
cleaned_reviews: i approached this particular book with no small measure of trepidation, since it takes place in the world of louisa may alcott's little women. this novel tells what befell the father of the march girls while he was off at war. it's so well done, so richly imagined, and well researched, that it feels to me like a welcome enlargement of my knowledge of that family i thought i knew so well already. i started reading it when i went to bed, and put it down, dazed, sometime after midnight. i recommend it, without reservations.

title: ['Between Friends']
cleaned_reviews: this was sweet and heartbreaking and real. there is something about the voice of the narrirator that i liked. even though it is short it didn't feel incomplete. it's a nice quick read for a cold rainy day.

title: ['Love, Stargirl (Stargirl, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: finally i can say this in one of my reviews. this book would definitely be a hit or miss for fans of the first book. as for me,i wish i hadn't read this book and at the same time, i'm glad that i did. at first i was so scared of reading this book because when i saw that this was going to be in stargirl's point of view, i knew that the girl i saw through leo's eyes will be erased. i knew that by reading this book, i will know who stargirl really is i knew that the image i had left with the first book will be gone. i was scared of that. i was scared of leaving the magical world of leo's stargirl, that i wished i hadn't read this book. but... even though i still wish that i hadn't read this book, i'm still glad because i realized that it would be unfair for stargirl or for anyone, for that matter, to define them or look at them according to how i see them. that, i think is one of the most important lessons this book has imparted on me. this book is not as magical as the first book because the mystery that is stargirl is now gone but it gave me a chance to know the real stargirl, and i'm glad that even for just a short time i met her. i'm glad to know that she's not magical and that she gets sad too but can still do things that only stargirl does. in this book i kind of realized that what makes stargirl, stargirl, is not just her quirky antics but mostly her ability to forget herself and to put others first at most times. i'm glad to have stumbled upon this book and this series. seriously one of the most entertaining and magical series i've read.

title: ['Blackout (Blackout, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: actual rating: 3.5/ 5 before i begin my review, i would like to add that the copy that i own is an arc (advanced reader copy) and, therefore, there are probably going to be some subtle differences from what i've read and what will be on the shelf soon. now that that's been said, let's begin... this is what i felt like is an appropriate synopsis since the copy i own didn't give one on the back of the book: it seems like things are falling apart and it looks like it's all the fault of terrorists- and there are a lot of teenagers caught in the middle of it, willing or not. aubrey just recently discovered that she can turn invisible around the beginning of her high school year and fears that she might have a disease. jack is a close friend of hers that, as far as he knows, isn't infected. laura and alec, however, know they have whatever's been spreading around and they are using it to their advantage. as 'terrorists', it's their job to cause chaos and, what it seems like, to ignite a new world war. and, eventually, these four meet by coincidence... well, first off, right off the bat i get easily annoyed that literally every occurrence is blamed on the assumption that it was all terrorists. that's it. no second guesses, no doing any further research on whether if they were true or not. it was terrorists. this lasted about a quarter of the book and, because of it, it took me a while to even get through the beginning because it felt like every moment i kept reading i just wanted to hit my head against the wall. it was just so frustrating, auuuuugh! and, on top of that, it was very clear how much needed to be edited still with this copy because of the obvious grammar and punctuation mistakes (but, of course, it's just an arc, so obviously that's not being taken accounted for- it's just a personal pet peeve of mine). after the first quarter of the book, however, i ended up finding myself really caught up with the four characters involved. we only get a small glimpse at the other younger teenagers and not many really talk. i didn't like any of the characters at the beginning, to be honest, but as they transformed through the difficult road with the military, i feel like they did grow. even just a little. but part of me still wonder if maybe some more thought into the four characters' would give things a little more oompf. but, with that being said, it is clear that this is simply a starting off point. it gives you what you need to know without putting too much information in your heard, but i'm left craving for the second book for more action (and i can foresee that there will be a lot more action for the sequel). overall, it's an interesting premises and i can't wait to see how the next book will pan out.

title: ['Boomerang (Boomerang, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: although not my usual genre, i have read and enjoyed new adult books from time to time and boomerang is no exception. this is a fun, light and humorous read with characters i can relate too. so what happens when two people hook-up, have differing opinions about what happened the night before, share a taxi ride to their mutual first days as interns, only to find out, they're going to be competing for a job? it's going to be complicated! ethan is a recent graduate from ucla. he wants the job at boomerang to help clear some students loans so he can apply to law school. mia is hoping to graduate soon and become a film-maker. she doesn't have any financial worries because her parents are wealthy and successful in their chosen fields. as an only child of accomplished parents, she wants to achieve her own success, and the internship with boomerang is a springboard opportunity not to be missed. our young protagonists' expectations are crushed when they find out that their internship isn't quite what they expected. add to that a "no-company dating" rule and we end up with a highly amusing romantic comedy which sizzles. the author does a fabulous job at building the sexual tension between ethan and mia as well as convincingly conveying a whole spectrum of emotions that they both have to learn to deal with in the adult world. boomerang is refreshing, entertaining and unputdownable. i'm looking forward to reading rebound, the next installment from this series.

title: ['The Giver (The Giver, #1)']

title: ['Real (Real, #1)', 'Just for Now (Sea Breeze, #4)', 'The Beast (Black Dagger Brotherhood, #14)', 'The Game Plan (Neighbor from Hell, #5)']
cleaned_reviews: okay i have to admit i am torn on this book. i give the first 50% of this book 2 starts but the last 50% 5 stars so really i guess the over all rating would be 3.5 stars. this is the story of brooke who is an ex athlete who has trained to be a rehab therapist. she meets an underground fighter, remy, and finds she is instantly attracted to him. remy hires her for three months to go on the road with him to be his therapist. there is no denying the chemistry between remy and brooke the only question is how far will it go. the first 50% of the book is spent with brooke describing how much she wants remy and what he does to her. it is too much narrative and just seems to go on forever. the saving grace to this book is remy. he is an amazing character. he is hot, damaged, mysterious, loving, tender, and protective. he makes the last 50% so great. i have no doubt i will read the next one just to get more remy. oh abbi you have done it again. abbi has a knack at making bad boys so good! this is another book in abbi's seabreeze series and does not disappoint. i love how this series involves all the characters that you have grown to love but focuses on one couple to give you more detail on them. this is preston and amanda's story and it is hot. it is a story of attraction and love and lots of heat. amanda is the little sister of preston's best friend and she has had a crush on preston since she was 16. preston got to know amanda and has always been attracted to her but kept his distance because he knew she was off limits and he was not good enough for her. preston comes for the wrong side of the tracks and has more responsibility than any of his friends know about. can they fight their attraction for each other and get past all of prestons secrets and baggage? don't go into this thinking preston is a boy scout, he is a man whore, but one waiting for that right someone to make him change. this book is also not pg, it is hot, hot, hot. there is so much chemistry between these two that it leaps off the page. thank you abbi. i am assuming if you are reading this review you have already read some black dagger brotherhood books. if you have not, stop what you are doing and go get books 1-13 and plan on not leaving your rooom for quite a while. the beast is more about rhage and mary. i have to make a confession, rhage is one of my absolute favorite brother, i just love him and i loved his and mary's story so i was very excited to get this one. it did not disappoint. i just love the bdb's and not only do we get more rhage and mary but as always we get to find out more about all the other characters. i really enjoyed this one and cannot wait to see what happens with the developments that are revealed in this installment. this really is one of my favorite series. this is danny and jodi's, aka tinkerbell's story. danny is a cousin of trevor and jason and is like all bradford men, hot male who likes to torment his neighbor while having an appetite that is unreal. i read this book very quickly it is a fun read. i will say it hasn't been my favorite of the series but it was still good. there were a few items that got old for me that just kept repeating (jodi's reaction to medication) it was kind of like a bad pun that just kept getting repeated. however that didn't stop me from enjoying the books. i really liked danny, he is a bradford so just like the rest of them, you can't help but to love him.

title: ['Invitation to a Beheading']
cleaned_reviews: so i can't do what i wanted to do, and smother you with quotes from this novel, shrouding you in a lovely blanket of nabokov's shrewd, simile-dripping observations about the more esoteric subtleties of human behavior and the emotions which inspire such behavior, all circled by and interwoven with the ornate latticework that is his tendency toward purple prose which he frequently hammers to bits with smash-cut asides and stern, terse sentence fragments presented like mantras for emotional yucky stuff. i'm sure that made no sense, but i am currently malnourished and over-coffee'd, so it will have to do for now. you know, it's nabokov. anyway, the reason that i can't quote this book until my fingers bleed is because the austin library system asked for a 'break.' it's not over, but they do want some time alone, so they blocked my account and demanded that i return my million overdue items immediately, which i proceeded to do on my way home from work after finishing this novel. nabokov went with them, the bastard. when i can afford to pay off a few bucks of my debt, they will take me back in their loving arms, but for now i guess i will just have to finish the many 500+ page novels that i own and have read sporadic chunks of. you care about all this, trust me. so, nabokov. i can say this without the book in front of me: this was a deviation from the more edit-heavy nabokov i am used to. there are paragraphs which bleed over pages and pages, predominantly consisting of internal monologues lacking in proper punctuation or breaks in thought, sprawling rambles of collaged paranoid notions and both frightening and hysterical imagery, over-dissections of spiderwebs and furniture and the jailer's jiggly jowls, hallucinations described in vivid detail, surreal imagery presented as hard fact, questions unanswered. pomo kafka, brought to you by vladimir nabokov, inc., via time machine. basically, this is quite an experimental work for the man as i know him from reading just four of his novels, and in such is a rewarding and perception-bending reading experience for someone who already found him to be a voice of reason in a rushing river of nonsense. the best i can gather from this work is that it is a meditation on feeling outside of the society surrounding you, or more specifically, how nabokov felt outside of the society surrounding nabokov, the disparity between how he was expected to behave and create and how he felt he should (and therefore tended to) behave and create. at the risk of feeding that somewhat obnoxious aforementioned 'kafka-esque' notion people are always throwing out there about anyone incorporating magical realism, ambiguity, and metaphor to a fictional work, i must confess that it did remind me, in theme, of a hunger artist: a man doomed to fester away in a cage because he is misunderstood, yet refuses to conform his notions of self and presentation of said self to the more shallow expectations of the world at large. rather than cave to the pressures of the popular appetite for entertainment, he chooses to jump on his sword in the service of both his pride and his integrity. right at this moment, i am guilty of something which always bugs me in reviews and, more commonly, troll-y comments: the assumption that the voice of the narrator or protagonist is necessarily the voice, the mind-frame, opinions, and lifestyle choices of the author, every single time indisputably, but here i feel pretty alright about it. to me at least, this sounds like nabokov discussing what it is to be nabokov. on that note, let me be clear about one thing: he doesn't fuck any children.

really? not buying it, sorry. so how is it that i can still rate it with 4.5 stars and say that i really liked it? come on ladies ... i know you already know the answer here ... his name is christian grey! and i think he is possibly one of the sexiest billionares ever to be written ;) and despite anyone's preferences or complaints about the movie casting ... i really can't picture anyone else but jamie dornan while reading this story ... and quite frankly, don't want to! do wish someone had warned me of that terrible cliffhanger ... but that's ok ... book two just means more jamie ... oops! i mean christian *wink wink 4.5 stars swoon! laugh! cry! this book had my emotions all over the place. i truly loved it. what would you do if the love of your life died? well ... (not so) spoiler alert ... he's alive. very, very alive. being the youngest of the brothers hasn't weakened him in any way - in fact, i'd say just the opposite. this man is crazy deadly. and super freakin' hot. like the rest of the series, this book is full of action and suspense. and sexual tension. lots of sexual tension. the build up to jory & piper's encounter(s) is slow and burning ... maybe a little too slow? the characters for who they really are (instead of all the disguises from book 1) and especially enjoyed seeing how fierce lia is! i really have no idea where the story is going after that ending, but i want more!! ignite me has been one of my most anticipated books of this year. and overall i think it was a wonderful end to the series. i want to talk about juliette's character growth. it's amazing to see a character grow as much as she does throughout the series. i can definitely see her growth, and i love the new stronger juliette. where she's at at the end of the series is incredible, and i "you're my sister. my sister, my blood, my family. i should want to protect you from the sort of boys who want to do with you exactly what i want to do." hashtagcantcantcantcant. as a reader, i so desperately wanted new love interests for both of them that i threw myself behind sebastian wholeheartedly when he first came into the picture. i was desperate for clary to move on so i was too trusting, considering that he turned out to be her real brother. joke's on me. however, i did figure out he was the real jonathan long before it was revealed. a couple of things were predictable, but i will say that jace's background remained a mystery. i felt like his real parents were characters only ever mentioned in this book, which i'm not sure if that was smart of the author to keep all her cards in her hand, or if that was a cheat to bring in new elements to the plot. or maybe i just forgot these people, haha. either way, the answers about everything felt very satisfying. one of the biggest flaws i found with the book was the pacing. i would get really worked up over something only to have a line break and be put into a very slow scene. but at least i was hooked enough to be worked up, that's a good sign. i still have to knock off a star for the sibling thing. although, i will say that them kissing no longer grossed me out after they found out they weren't related. i had thought it would still bother me, that i wouldn't be able to ever get behind them as a couple. will i read the sequel? yes. i'd really like to see clary and jace together now that it's no longer so inappropriate. beautiful and heart-wrenching at the same time. this was not at all what i expected. i was reading along thinking something else had to happen, something to take it from 4.5 stars to that full rounded 5. and it did happen. i can honestly say that this story lacks nothing. it took me through the emotional wringer. starting with the obvious - the romance. it's very sweet. both characters likeable. cute dialogue. it gets downright steamy also. i will admit it pushed my comfort zone because it's a little more intimate than what i prefer in ya books. but, i guess if that's your thing it will deliver? jase is a remarkable guy and he lands a spot in my book boyfriends, where he will be very lonely because i don't often do the whole 'book boyfriend' thing. the characters are all excellent. sam's family, her friends. jase's family. there are a lot of minor characters and i loved every one of them. i felt like i was a part of the family. there is a serious tone toward the end of the book and all i will say about it is that i haven't had a book affect me so emotionally in a long while. this book was more emotional for me than the fault in our stars. now, that may not be saying much because i'm not a big crier and tfios just wasn't my cup of tea. but really, my life next door tugged at my heartstrings. i swooned. i laughed. i sobbed. it made me question the consequences of doing the right thing. like i said, it runs the emotional gamut. read it. everyone. i predict this may be a favorite of 2014 for me. please do yourself 2 favors: 1. do not avoid this book simply because you hated cass's the selection series. the two are nothing, nothing, nothing alike. the characters, the world, the writing tone are all so very different. sure, you may still dislike this one for any number of reasons, but if you're interested in the premise, don't judge it based on a totally separate book series. 2. do not avoid this book simply because mushy romances aren't your thing. yes, there is a romance, and that's very much a big part of the story but there is also so much more. and it's actually more of a tragic tale that i expected. this is a story about many types of love. sisterly love. friendship. parental love. learning to love yourself. (love for cake.) and yes, romantic love too. this is one of the best romances i've read in a long time, which is ironic because the love interest appears in less than a quarter of the book total, but what i really took away from this book was all the other kinds of love. especially the parental love. the parent in this book is the ocean. she is very much a character in this story and the way in which she loves her siren daughters is so reminiscent of a mother trying to hold on to her growing children. i'm struggling with wording this next part (thanks brain), but i also want to point out that although this book in no way felt like it was dealing with religion, i got a sense of some religious symbolism. i believe cass is christian, so i wondered if maybe the ocean was meant to be a personification (naturification?) of god. there are definitely many traits of the ocean that aren't biblical, but it was a parallel that i saw and it hit me on an emotional level. any symbolism you may or may not personally see reflected in the ocean aside, the way in which cass brought to a life a character that in this world was a type of deity and creator full of undying and jealous love was simply astounding. there are a few more things i want readers to know about this story that make it really awesome. -the main characters are college age, which is refreshing. -the fantasy element of this world was very fleshed out. siren mythology is not a backdrop, it's heavily involved in the story. -the love interest was a good guy. a very believable, kind guy. a nice break from the over abundance of bad boys in ya and na. and to be fair, here are some things that might turn you off. -there is a heavy dose of instalove. i can hear most of you groaning. but this was the most convincing case of instalove i have ever seen and the reason for that comes down to the fact that these characters didn't spend every waking moment together with their feelings being clouded by being so wrapped up in each other. for the story being told here, it felt fitting. - i don't even have another point here. but having only one point looked weird. hi. overall, it's a simple and yet very powerful story that i think would appeal to readers young and old alike.

title: ['Brokedown Cowboy (Copper Ridge, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: eta: congratulations to maisey yates for her 2016 rita award for brokedown cowboy!!! if you all haven't read this series, read it! first let me just praise the cover. the guy model? who are you sir and are you single? i mean.... ooof. *fans face* i kept catching myself staring at the cover and wanting to rub my face on it like a lunatic....... aaaaanyways, this is my first book by this author and it won't be my last if the writing is anything to go by. her wordplay is seriously one of a kind and nothing i've seen. i would seriously give a 5 stars just for that. it's so fluid and organic, she manages to go dark and humurous at the same time which i liked and haven't seen before in a cr setting. and by dark i mean dealing with a hero who is still greiving over the death of his wife. the wise cracks and ribbing that bounces off the brothers and group of friends is so much fun and so natural. nothing is trying too hard. there were some lines that really made me lol and re-read and other moments that just made me go yes! i know that feeling exactly. years of fantasies could not have prepared her for the reality of connor's lips on hers. it was new, and it was familiar in the most beautiful way. like christmas. different all the time and somehow the same. with surprises and tradition all wrapped into one. that was kissing connor. ******************************** she wanted a customizable menu of options with boxes she could check. access to his finer feelings? check. awkward self-consciousness? no. a solid, unshakable friendship? check. crippling loneliness and despair? no. consequence-free orgasms on tap? she would double check that. "right," she said. "probably should've just grabbed your penis again instead of trying to talk about feelings." connor sputtered, coffee sloshing over the edge of his mug. "what the hell, liss? you can't just say stuff like that." "now is not really the time to get precious. the horse has left the barn, run across the pasture and trampled the daises. if you go after him now, he'll just get spooked and kick you in the head." the 'i'm in love with my best friend' theme here was executed wonderfully. i liked the fact that the author was conscious of the couple's long standing friendship and the hero's personal struggles to move on from losing his wife. i like that none of it was brushed under the rug and played a big part in the tension between the hero and heroine. it made the dynamic and hea that much more realistic and plausible. the fact that connor could *finally* accept that he will always love his wife and it's ok to move on and love someone else was so simple and honest yet bittersweet. it was a real struggle for this character and it made total sense especially given that the heroine has been his best friends for 18 years. that's a lot of history right there. and i have to say liss, the heroine, really surprised me the most out of the two. her no-filter personality and blurting whatever she thinks was a real hoot and so refreshing. it could have easily turned into an obnoxious quirk but it wasn't here. i loved how she kept connor on his toes and left him speechless. i definitely want to read the next book with playboy jack and connor's little tomboy sister katie. another interesting dynamic with a lot of potential. i really recommend this author because her comedic timing is really great and her wordplay is divine!

title: ['The Goblin Emperor']
cleaned_reviews: wow. if you haven't read this yet, go read it. the goblin emperor has been nominated for a hugo this year, and it's one of few that wasn't on the sad puppies slate. if you don't know what i'm talking about, you must have been completely unplugged from the online sci-fi/fantasy fan community until now. go google "sad puppies hugo awards," then come back. try not to get lost; it's a rabbit hole of delusional extremists, anger, and prejudice. i'll wait. as i was saying, this book made it onto the list of nominees without the assistance of the puppies, and it did so for very, very good reasons. many. all of which can be summed up by the following: it's amazing!!! yes, it merits all caps and three exclamation points. i haven't read all the contenders for the hugo best novel, but i absolutely believe this book deserves its place among them. it even made it onto my favorites list, and i have to really love a book to add it to that. the entire time i was reading this book, i kept thinking (and saying) "nothing's really happening, but i don't want to put it down!" this is definitely in the realm of court intrigues, devoid of the bloody battle scenes that dominate so much of the fantasy genre, but even though there's no physical action, maia alters his government and country to their core. maia is unschooled, but not so naive that he isn't aware of his lack of knowledge and supporters/friends. his experiences as the cast-off son of the emperor made him compassionate, humble, kind, and eager to be the agent of change in a country that both needs and is terrified of change. katherine addison writes characters so varied and so real that you can believe, while you're reading, that their conversations really took place, and you love them and hate them as if they are standing in front of you, affecting your life with their actions. i will re-read this book. multiple times. that's how much i loved it. actually, writing this review, i feel the need to re-read it now, 23 days after finishing it for the first time. i just might go do that. ;)

title: ['Killing Floor (Jack Reacher, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: if i start with later books in a series and then go backwards to find the first, i am usually disappointed with the first effort. generally, it seems to take an author 2-3 books to find his character and style--not so lee child. this was a whiz-bang on target first effort, and he seems to know exactly what he wants from this character and series. i always prefer thrillers told in the first person which seems to put me right into the endangered hero's shoes, and i loved viewing the tense situations through reacher's eye and brain. an amazingly great first novel.

title: ['The Shadow of the Wind (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books,  #1)']
cleaned_reviews: "the shadow of the wind" is everything you would want from a book set in spain about the sense of mystery and wonder that books give us. despite it being a translation, the language inside is absolutely beautiful. once you start, you will be compelled to read until it is finished. this is the story about daniel who wants to know the story of julian carax, the author of a book that he discovers in a place where books go to "die." really, i suppose they come back to life again in the hands of someone who really cares about them. anyway, because he has never heard of carax he wants to know what happened to him. in many ways, daniel and carax's lives reflect each other. it is really exciting how carlos ruiz zafon weaves the different pieces of information, misinformation and action together. the only reason i rated it four stars was because there were times when something didn't quite fit the way i thought it could (always very slight and nothing anyone but nitpicky old me would notice)- and i predicted who the man with no face was from the introduction of him. otherwise, this book was stellar, a-level material. what are you waiting for? go read it!
