title: ['The Shining', 'House of Leaves']
cleaned_reviews: even as a re-read, this book is scary. king is a master at building suspense. the first time i read this i had to take breaks when things got to be too much for me. i'm so glad i finally finished this! more soon. it took me several attempts to finally finish this book. my bookclub selected it for january (while we skipped december) and that finally gave me the motivation to keep going. we had a sort of support group going on through the groups posts here and that seemed to help us all hang in there when things got rough. i know it sounds crazy to talk about about book like this but trust me, this book requires some serious effort. you can't talk about house of leaves without talking about the structure, about how the text layout changes with the events of the book. i really thought i would find the layout stuff gimmicky and annoying but i was surprised at how well it worked. during the part where they are exploring the labyrinth and the footnotes are going vertically up the page from back to front that i literally stopped and thought "how am i going to find my way back?" clearly all i had to do was go back to where i had left off before i started following the footnotes but it was the strangest experience to actually think that while reading a book. i can't even begin to imagine how long it must have taken danielewski to write this book. to create footnotes where the first letter of each word spells his whole name? who does that? in some ways you might think, who the hell cares and i guess that's true, but i am still impressed by the skill and effort it took to make it all come together.

title: ['The Vegetarian']
cleaned_reviews: as children, we are advised by our parents to never judge a book by its cover. in my take on the vegetarian, we ought not to judge one by its title, either. this is not the story of a vegetarian locked up in a korean mental ward for eschewing meat. instead, this three-perspective novel felt more like something penned by sylvia plath or virginia woolf. it is about mental illness and how one young woman's spiral into it impacts those around her. had i known that, despite its recent accolades with the man booker crowd, it would have remained unread for me. regardless the quality of the writing, the topic of unbalanced family members can be painful for me. we don't have mental illness in the family but do have a loved one with serious autism - living with aberrant behaviors is my constant. unless i think the story will be uplifting, i generally need to stay away. if, however, you are okay with novels concerning mental illness and can tolerate reading about abuse, this fantastic work is absolutely worth your while. i will spare you a book report and only share that the young woman around whom this book revolves has been exposed to some violence in her childhood. there is no sexual abuse that we know of, but when her aging father slaps her in the face when she - in her 20s - renounces meat, it is apparent that this type punishment is nothing new for her nuclear family. that said, not everyone whose parent used to slap them around ends up having a nervous breakdown. many former childhood victims often choose life partners that are emotionally unavailable or when preyed upon by others, seem to just acquiesce. but some become fierce instead. when we first encounter yeong-hye, she most decidedly falls into the former camp. when she awakens from a dream - that is never fully described to the reader - yeong-hye has made the decision to be become a vegetarian. she gives up milk, and will not wear shoes made of leather. at an important dinner party with her husband's employer and guests, she abruptly and rudely refuses the proffered dishes. this calm, mild mannered young woman acts strangely detached and nearly militant at the same time, and this is our first hint that it is not vegetarianism that she is embracing. it is mental illness that instead has her in its hands, and it will gradually tighten its grip on her psyche, choking off her desire to eat anything, anything at all. schizophrenia is a cruel master. yeong-hye's desire to eliminate violence from her world is understandable, but as she loses touch with reality, she ironically opens herself up to other attacks as an adult. her victimization is difficult for the reader to witness, yet its catalytic effect on her downward spiral is darkly mesmerizing. i believe that the author wants us to wonder - is yeong-hye truly mad or is she just going to a passive, plant-like extreme? lots of irony here. since finishing the book earlier today, i have been reading various interviews with the author. it turns out that the korean diet does not contain an awful lot of meat, so for one to adopt a vegetarian lifestyle would be very easy - and practically unnoticeable to others. what would be shocking would be to feel the need to make a formal announcement declaring one's vegetarian state. when we read that the hospital has given her a diagnosis of schizophrenia as the root cause for her anorexia and other behaviors, it all clicks into place, even the age she was when the disease began its onset. that her sister questioned her own sanity in the third section of the book was especially poignant. finally, there is some lovely symbolism in the book - dark wings in the artist-husband's video, a white bird that in-hye's little boy dreams of, and the black wings that exited up into the sky at the end. i think the translator did a phenomenal job of bringing images painted in korean into the english language. to whom would i recommend this book? deep and thoughtful readers, those with english degrees or perhaps mfas, those interested in human psychology, or perhaps women who are close with their sisters. i would send up a caution flag to friends who are put off reading about sexual abuse or animal abuse, anorexia, or those who have loved ones suffering from mental or perhaps developmental issues. the latter population of readers may actually love the book because they can relate so well, but it seemed fair to give them a heads-up. this is an incredible, creative novella, and its second section is somewhat surreal with its exploration of fine art and performance art...yet i found it to be a bit pornographic as well. for the right reader, the vegetarian is an exquisite offering. the writing is a solid five stars, but beware the content.

title: ['Perfect Opposite']
cleaned_reviews: 3,5 stars sasha has always just wanted to live a normal life, study art history and forget her ex and his two timing ways as quickly as possible. but of course, her dad has to go and mess things up, as usual. so now her leg is in danger which brings us to part two of the whole mess...alexey, aka the weird mohawk guy who apparently looks like he eats babies for breakfast. alex is sent by sasha's mob-boss dad, to keep her alive, even though at times he is the one wanting to strangle the girl. it's hate at first sight for the two perfect opposites who will have to find a way to not kill each other for the next couple of weeks. i have to say this book positively surprised me. i had the ebook on my laptop for quite some time before is finally manned up and got started on reading it. but once i started, i was hooked. i finished it in one day, seeing as i couldn't put it away. sasha was exactly my kind of protagonist. she's funny, sarcastic and an absolute smart as. i like characters who don't just do whatever everyone tells them to, unless it is absolutely necessary. yes sasha sometimes did stupid things, but hey so would i if someone just bossed me around without giving me a good reason to act the way they want me to. and even then, bit alex and her dad sometimes seemed to forget that she was a 19 year old girl with her own opinion and freedom. she didn't owe them anything and should be allowed to make her own desicions, even if they were stupid ones. then there was alex/oleg or whatever. he was badass. i'm sure this wasn't supposed to happen but because i'd just seen vampire academy last week and alex reminded me of dimitri, the two kind of melted into one person in my head. which is by no means a bad thing, seeing as i love dimitri, plus it helped me forget that awful mohawk! i'm sorry, but what were you thinking zoya tessi? i loved alex to pieces, but every time that mohawk was mentioned i'd cringe and then pretend i hadn't read anything about it. i also really like the cover, but just can't get over alex' hair! anyway, moving on. i really enjoyed the story. the ending however felt a bit rushed. beth and their italian friend (woeps forgot his name) just disappeared halfway and never really came back. they were maybe mentioned in one sentence or something. and mike also kind of dissolved into nothingness. while i like to focus on the main story and couple, i didn't think there were enough small plot lines in the book. to be honest i can't really think of one that was really developed. there were very few minor characters and the ones that did exist we're not really written out. (see above: beth and italian friend). just the fact that i can't remember italian friend's name, even though they were very close, says something about how minor they were. i wish the writer had taken the effort to really think through the minor storylines, because sometimes i like those as much if not more than the main plot. so, perfect opposite was an enjoyable read with good main characters, but sloppy minor characters and storylines. the main storyline was well written and everything was tied very well at the end.

title: ['Then Came You (The Gamblers, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: if i haven't said this before i will now. lisa kleypas is an amazing woman who weaves really sensual, emotional and creative tales of love and adversity. lily lawson, tagged as a decadent woman of the ton because of her eccentric behavior that defy convention is determined that her sister will not be forced into loveless marriage with lord alex raiford. lily is misunderstood and thought to be the mistress of a gaming hell owner while alex is assumed to be rigid and cold ever since his fiance died two years earlier in a riding accident. lily comes armed to alex's house with the sole purpose of thwarting the wedding plans so she goes overboard in her antics to separate the two. the shenanigans she cooks up are really inventive and exciting and it was great to see the rigid alex's reaction to their palpable and undeniable sexual tension. seriously some of their antics were hilarious. lily gets kicked off his estate, knocks alex unconscious, cloths herself as the biblical eve and alex gets kidnapped, tied to a bed, and rescues a barely clothed "eve" from scandal. i swear it was humorous to watch all their crazy interactions. i loved how these two opposites really complimented each other. one more amazing thing about this book is that the hero actually falls in love and acknowledges it first before the heroine. i loved their interaction with alex's emotions in the forefront and lily completely oblivious to his love for her. alex transitioned from the usual regency arrogant, emotionally stunted and tragic hero to a strong, supportive and tender lover. lily is the one who had a lot of growing up to do. she had a lover who jilted her years ago then took their daughter with him. he's been using her daughter as leverage to extract money from her for two years now. so this circumstances makes her wary of men in general and unable to trust herself in an intimate relationship with anyone ever again. she wary of alex's affection toward her because she's scared of his reaction when he learns that she birthed a bastard. she's sure that a man like alex who's a stickler for propriety will resent her and look down on her so she doesn't allow herself to trust him easily because no one has ever come through for her. i loved how kleypas assuages lily's fears by making alex a true knight in shining armor who comes to her rescue both physically and emotionally. he was a man who decided to change his ideal to fit his love and i applauded him for reaching out and holding onto his lady irrespective of society's norm. seriously this couple went on one a hell of a ride and i enjoyed every single moment of it. an absolute delight to read.

title: ['Liesmith (The Wyrd, #1)', 'Black John (Johnnies, #4)']
cleaned_reviews: i received this book as an arc through net galley in exchange for an honest review. i have to admit i have a weakness for a certain kind of main character. all the stories with main characters that start off big, bad, and kick ass are fine. they make sense in a certain context, but i've always found it boring, and anti-climatic to read about someone who you're pretty sure is going to triumph over whatever the plot throws at them. i also understand the books about people who long for adventure, and challenge. i mean most of the time it's that desire for something new, and different that drives the action of the story, and it's usually hard to write about someone who'd rather stay home, and read than slay dragons. this book however found my personal favorite main character: the reluctant, ordinary person. it's probably pretty easy to see this love from my favorites list; from arthur dent who would rather have a nice cup of tea than intergalactic travel to richard mayhew whose act of kindness sends him on an adventure he never wanted, i love the main character who has to almost be dragged into the action of the plot. i think i identify with that kind of person much more easily than the invincible swordsman or the girl who sets off to find her destiny without a backwards glance. i'm a bit of a coward, and i like tea, and reading by the fire. sigmund sussman, for me, fit the bill perfectly. i liked that he was not immediately excited about the prospect of intrigue, and mystery in his life. i liked that he was an ordinary guy, a bit of a nerd, who didn't feel too much like a complete stereotype. he was not defined by his interestes, and i didn't feel like the author overwhelmed the story with references to prove their nerd cred. the relationship between sigmund and lain was well done, and i liked the pace at which it developed. it never felt like instant love, or that they were destined to be together, which all things considered, is a very good thing. another thing i appreciated was that the love story never took over the plot. it wasn't a romance novel thinly disguised as an urban fantasy, but fully fledged urban fantasy with a bit of romance. the plot was nicely developed, and i loved the twists, and turns. it kept me guessing, and i enjoyed that. the mythology fit very nicely into the plot, and story. it was well integrated, so it never felt like awkward information dumps or stilted exposition. i liked how the mythology fit into the modern setting, and how much it added to the plot, the setting, and the characters. i also loved reading an urban fantasy that wasn't set in the united states, or england. it made for a nice change of pace. overall i really loved this book, and am really looking forward to reading more from this author. i love it when a book sweeps me off of my feet. i'm having a hard time reviewing this because the drug problem where i live is pretty serious. no, i'm not kidding. yes, maine is beautiful. we still have drugs. lots of drugs. i don't think i know anyone who hasn't been involved with or affected by someone with a serious drug problem. my younger sister has a friend. they have been friends since they were kids. her friend lost her sister in her early 20's to a drug overdose. i babysat for both girls when they were little. it was awful. so i appreciated the honesty with which the author dealt with john and galen's drug problems. i liked seeing them grow together, and learn to deal with their issues, and face their past. i liked it wasn't about one man saving the other, but about them learning to support each other, and to, in a sense, save themselves. tory's story makes it hard to rate as well. let's just say suicide is a significant issue where i live as well. i'll just close by saying that i appreciate the honesty of this story, and i like the respect the author has for her characters, the work they do, and the situations that they are in. also i still like john better than kane. so much better.

cleaned_reviews: 3.5 out of 5 stars rounded up. i gave hunted this star rating because it was definitely enjoyable, with a captivating plot, dynamic and rounded characters, and wonderful writing, but overall, i am not quite sure that it will really stick with me or leave a long lasting impression. in fact, it wasn't until the last fifty or so pages that i decided to do a round up rather than a round down, but more on that later. hunted is a retelling of beauty and the beast, but certainly not the disney version. this book feels more reminiscent of the brother's grimm and actual fairy tales from centuries ago. it also has a russian flare rather than a french one which served to keep it interesting and separate from the disney classic. however, its release date, and the release of many other novels this march, clearly capitalized on the live action remake (this isn't necessarily a bad thing, i'm just saying). the story is however, very original for a retelling, brining in new and different lessons that the versions i am used to do not discuss. once again, more on that later. beauty (yeva) and the beast as characters were also different from previous versions i have encountered. yeva, is less bookish and more action-heroine, always hunting through the winter woods and never forgetting her bow and arrow. the beast, is also less of a man in a fur suit and more of a man and an animal both trapped inside the same fur suit did that make sense? and both of these were liberties i totally approved of. so why did i round up? and what were the changes in lessons? well they were the same thing. spoilers ahead, but not plot spoilers just like theme/idea spoilers, read at your own risk i guess... title: ['Everything I Never Told You', 'Saga, Vol. 1 (Saga, #1)', 'Slasher Girls & Monster Boys']
cleaned_reviews: you can also read my full review here! this book opens with the line: lydia is dead. but they don't know this yet. everything i never told you is a story about a chinese american family living in 1970s small-town ohio. at the beginning of the book, the favourite daughter of the lee family, lydia, goes missing and turns up dead in a lake. from this synopsis it may sound like a mystery suspense or an investigative novel but that really isn't the case. the book is not plot-driven at all but is a very slow-burning, character-driven read. it's about loss and grief and family dynamics. about secrets and miscommunication, but also gender, race and interracial relationships. rather than having the whole book be about lydia and the way she died, celeste ng uses her death as a catalyst to portray many of the underlying psychological issues going on within this family. the author slowly unravels the family's history for us and explains the events that led up to lydia's death, including how the parents were raised, how their decisions were impacted by their upbringing and how, in turn, that affected the way they raised their own children. "everything i never told you" is the best possible title for this book. it's all about a family that cannot communicate with one another on any level. they are all holding things in, internalising what they're feeling and can't express their fears and desires to each other, or sometimes even themselves. interestingly, the reader often knows more about the characters and their emotions than they know about each other and it is thus up to the reader to put the puzzle pieces together and understand what led to lydia's eventual death. we're switching between different points-of-view as well as different timelines and this adds layers to the book and helps truly bring out the complexity and nuanced nature of these characters. for their own individual reasons both these parents are projecting all their dreams and ambitions onto their kids, especially lydia, and we witness how it hurts her, destroys her. "so every time her mother said do you want -? she had said yes. she knew what her parents had longed for, without them saying a word, and she had wanted them happy. she had kept her promise." so this book really deals with expectations. expectations from society, from your family, from your parents. lydia gets all these expectations placed upon her while her siblings essentially get neglected. both turn out to be predictably harmful. "that long-ago day, sitting in this very spot on the dock, she had already begun to feel it: how hard it would be to inherit their parent's dreams. how suffocating to be so loved. she had felt nath's hands on her shoulders and been almost grateful to fall forward, to let herself sink." this book is incredibly quiet and subtle but full of tension. a tension that builds and builds until you feel like you're going to explode. the characters felt so much like real people: extremely flawed to the point of being almost unlikeable, and yet i could understand where they were coming from, even if i couldn't forgive them for their actions. celeste ng's prose is stunning and the book had such an emotional impact on me. it has stayed with me and i still think about it now, weeks after i finished. if you're looking for a literary fiction novel that is outstandingly written, has rich, well-drawn characters and features diversity, look no further. i can't recommend everything i never told you enough. one of my favourites of the year. tragic in a quiet sort of way, which is always my favourite. verse chorus verse by leigh bardugo 3.5 stars i love leigh bardugo so i had to make sure i didn't go into this one biased. the idea was very interesting and found myself impressed yet again by how quickly and expertly leigh bardugo is able to create believable, distinctive characters that stick in your mind. the story was well-written and definitely hit the mark in terms of creepiness, however, i found myself let down by the ending, which i didn't really grasp and just didn't give me enough to be satisfied. if this story had been longer and things would have been cleared up more, i think it could have been my favourite (or second favourite) in the anthology. hide-and-seek by megan shepherd 3.5 stars if you're going to start a story with a quote from a book of appalachian folktales, you better know that my expectations are going to be high because myths, legends and folktales are always my cup of tea. imagine my disappointment when an enthusiastic google search wielded no results. so apparently, the quote and tale originated from megan shepherd's own mind (please correct if i'm wrong) and i found the idea to be quite intriguing. i don't think the concept was exhausted as much as i would have liked, but i still really enjoyed the story and was taken aback by the ending. the dark, scary parts and all by danielle paige 1.5 stars i really didn't like this one. in my opinion, it's the "rotten egg" in the collection, the only one i can actively remember disliking. it contains all your typical ya tropes with the super-smart but has no friends mary sue protagonist, the drop-dead-gorgeous love interest that suddenly shows interest out of the blue and the high school mean girls that don't go beyond one dimension. lack of originality, annoying characters and unnecessary angst and melodrama made this one hard to get through and it didn't even remotely hit the mark of establishing something scary or creepy. the flicker, the fingers, the beat, the sigh by april genevieve tucholke 2.5 stars although it had some potential, this story fell short for me. i finished it feeling underwhelmed. the concept was unoriginal and because it felt like something i had read before, it never succeeded in scaring me or creeping me out. what should have been a tragic story ended up just being a bit of a rehash with little depth. also, i didn't like the way the story was written; it felt very disjointed and confusing without actually adding anything significant to the story. fat girl with a knife by jonathan maberry 3 stars i really liked dahlia, the main character, for her strong and distinctive voice and appreciated the diversity aspect of the story. dahlia was what made this story so readable. unfortunately, the plot was very predictable and i didn't find it to be even remotely scary. like the story by danielle paige, this one felt quite young and the high school setting didn't really do it for me. sleepless by jay kristoff 5 stars from what i've seen of other people's reviews this one seems to be a favourite and i have to agree. the story was well-written, creepy, unpredictable and had me at the edge of my seat throughout. it was just the right amount of strange and twisted and still remained credible. this is one i would love to see as a full-length novel, although i thought the short story format suited it very well. i really want to read jay kristoff's other works now that are sitting on my shelf. m by stefan bachmann 3.5 stars i love stefan bachmann as an author (i had the fortune of meeting and talking to him in person) but i have yet to be convinced by his storytelling. he has a beautiful, poetic writing-style reminiscent of the period this story is set in, but the overall plot just didn't have me completely hooked. it was interesting, it had potential, but unfortunately, it failed to wow me. the girl without a face by marie lu 4.5 stars another excellent one. it wasn't quite as memorable as jay kristoff's story but i totally loved it. it was creepy and atmospheric and had some important underlying themes. i loved the way the whole thing played out, the characters were interesting and i read it in one go because i couldn't put it down. i adored the ending; it was so gut-wrenching and frightening and really made me think about karma and what guilt can do to people. a girl who dreamed of snow by mccormick templeman 2.5 stars this one left me with a bit of a question mark. i'm not actually sure what this story was trying to achieve and i found it quite boring to be honest. again, the mythology and snowy, unique setting had me excited but mccormick templeman wasn't able to sustain that initial suspense. after a couple of pages i just found myself confused and wanted to know what was going on already. when i lose patience with a story like that, especially a short story, it's not a very good sign. stitches by a.g. howard 4 stars if i'd have to describe this story in one word it would be strange. this story was so disturbing yet calmly told that it really was quite scary. it's the most graphic and gory one of the bunch but i found that to be a strong point. the inspiration of frankenstein was definitely very obvious but i still felt like the author made it her own. the story was engaging and a.g. howard had my attention from the opening line, which perfectly set the tone for the rest of the story. on the i-5 by kendra blake 3.5 stars another interesting one. the author keeps you guessing throughout and i was constantly on my toes. the main character was intriguing and quite badass which made the whole story very enjoyable. unfortunately, i did feel somewhat disconnected to what was happening; this might however, be due to the fact that this is the last story. i think that by the end i had kind of seen it all and twists didn't surprise me as much, which is a shame. also, i'm just not a fan of third person present tense; i find it to be quite jarring at times. regardless, this was still a very creepy story that perfectly combined horror and sadness. on the whole, this is a very enjoyable anthology and i highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys ya and is in the mood for something a little different.

title: ['City of Thieves', 'Station Eleven', 'Broken Harbor (Dublin Murder Squad, #4)', 'The Sympathizer']
cleaned_reviews: set in winter in leningrad in world war ii, this novel follows teenage lev, who is picked up and jailed one night for looting the corpse of a nazi paratrooper. while in jail, fearing he is about to be executed, lev meets kolya, a boy a few years older than him, who has been picked up for deserting his army unit. the next day, lev and kolya are taken to the office of a high-ranking police official, where they are offered a deal: the thief and the deserter will have their crimes forgiven, if they can find a dozen eggs for the official's daughter, to be used in her wedding cake. in a city under siege and blockaded by the germans, where everyone is on the brink of starvation and death, this seems like an impossible task. lev and kolya set out to find the eggs, and the book doesn't shy away from the awful details of life in leningrad during this winter. cannibalism. vendors selling boiled paste from library book bindings. and the cold, - 30 degrees fahrenheit. the book also doesn't shy away from the raunchy talk of lev and kolya. this title received the alex award for adult books suitable for young adults, which caused me to recommend it to a 14-year-old girl and her grandmother, since the girl had recently enjoyed the book thief and between shades of grey. as i started reading the novel a week or so later, i felt some vicarious embarrassment at all the sex talk and masturbation talk and uses of the word 'cock.' maybe for older teenagers, without their grandmothers? "hell is the absence of the people you long for." this book had some weird missteps in pacing and detail for me, but i was still drawn into the world mandel created. i didn't find the symphony, a post-pandemic caravan of orchestra and shakespearean actors traveling with horses pulling old pickup trucks painted with the (star trek) motto "survival is insufficient", nearly as enchanting as the author intended. rather, they bored me. this was because the book opens with a gripping chapter or two featuring jeevan, a paramedic in training trying to get to his wheelchair-bound brother in toronto before the pandemic that will kill 99% of the population hits. to go from that to traveling with the symphony 20 years later was a jolt and it frustrated me. but i liked the world, even though it didn't quite make sense. it was a mainly peaceful, reasonable world - i liked that. taking place in a half-built luxury home development, this novel is about the murder of a family. it has an exciting plot and goes deep into the heads of the characters. it somehow suggests the supernatural horror of the paranormal activity movies without anything paranormal ever happening. the thing about the tournament of books (tob) that keeps me participating is the subtle pressure to read something i wouldn't otherwise make time for in my reading life, which every year leads to at least one great book i would have overlooked. long division by kiese laymon and redeployment by phil klay are two i wouldn't have completed without tob, and now i add this book to that collection. this book is immersive and big and literary and a little difficult to read, but i loved its depiction of the vietnamese american experience. the writing is very good and very original although the paragraphs are looong. i deduct points for the rape depictions and the use of the female body as metaphor. i add points for the narrator and the framing device of the novel. i liked the sendup of apocalypse now.

cleaned_reviews: another excellent book in this trilogy where a young girl's fate is intertwined with that of a nation. this book had so many different little twists and changes that nothing ever quite worked out the way you expected. from the high seas to the unsea, there is travel across the nation as well as ending up right back where everything started. there are machinations going on as each person has a plan for ravka, and all of their plans depend on the sun summoner in some way, either with her alive and at their side, or dead. the relationship for mal and alina goes through a lot in this book and i was surprised that at times it was done in such a mature light. there are realizations about changing for another person, how much you can do it yourself, and what you can expect of others. though it takes time alina comes to see the give and take needed and how sometimes even with love things don't work out. i was impressed that even with that it did not mean that it was an easy thing to give up or move on, but that emotions were complicated and confused as the two still loved each other, but did not love the people they had become. this relationship sits at the core of the book as each decision made for the nation brings them farther apart, while each decision for each other makes them more miserable and threatens a nation. there is a major change a set up for fire in this final book of the trilogy. i don't know which way things will fall for the nation, the grisha, or our mal and alina, but i can't wait to read to find out! woohoo! one of those teen books that swoops in and surprises me- colour me delighted! i really enjoyed reading this book. i liked how the relationships in it have felt pretty natural. heck, it's hilarious because america is actually maxon's wingman. she's not too bad at it either and the frank and open way the two are with each other is enjoyable. there is a sense of this book truly being about america, finding her way to what she wants in the world and in adulthood. it also lets her walk the line between being selfish (wanting to stay in the selection even though she doesn't want to be queen) and selfless (protecting her maids despite the caste difference). i like the picture that has been made of her and i enjoy reading the book through her eyes. it's interesting, because this book has a bit of a sense of watching a television pilot. you know that the groundwork is being laid and sometimes that has to just be put out there. it is clear that this book is supposed to be our world in the future; so why is it like it is? and then there's the background story going on, with castes and rebels that has to be put out. but, like a really good pilot, somehow this information is put out there without being too clunky. it's not just, oh, so that character is saying how the world works because it needs to be said so we understand. there is always further meaning, something else to contemplate, and an intriguing background being built up. some fascinating world building has been done and the story still manages to be about america with it all working rather smoothly. this is a pretty good book to pick up if you're looking for a fun new series! i really enjoyed this new world! fast paced and well imagined, it kept me going and in no time i was finished! vampires have a complicated process of being in this world. it's no little 'bite and go' process. vamps are born, but not by the very vampire they are from. they then live their first few decades as almost completely human, save for an occasional need to drink their vamp parents blood. this human birth, host parent, vamp parent things complicates life for fortitude and is a very interesting new vampire mythos. it gave a self limiter to vamps since they couldn't reproduce easily and it makes them intriguingly weak before they come into powers. we don't learn much about the other supernatural creatures, but it is told that there are many. we get to learn them as fort does because he is just coming more into the supernatural world. there is plenty of potential and i am really excited to learn more! title: ['The Beginning of Everything']
cleaned_reviews: the beginning of everything november 2 after a horrible car accident at the end of junior year, ezra's life turned upside down. no longer school president, captain of the tennis team, nor king of the school, ezra finds himself alone as the new year starts. ezra never thought he would recover from his girlfriend cheating on him until he meets cassidy. vibrant, mysterious, and quirky cassidy walks into ezra's life without any notice and ezra falls hard. as their love blooms, cassidy becomes more and more reclusive until she finds out something that will impact both of their lives forever. i loved this book because it shows the school's golden boy that was thrown off the top of the totem poll and is trying to find his way again. as his wounds heal, so does his mind. cassidy helps him find his way through the tough times by showing him what really matters. as everything starts to fall out of place for ezra, what will he hold on to? what will he let go? what you really come to find out is that cassidy was never the one to get him to open up and express himself, it was ezra himself. their love story, just like the cover art, was a roller coaster of emotions. with so many things left unsaid between the two of them, something was bound to happen, as it did. i really admired ezra from the start because even though his life was at an all time low, he still managed to make the best of it and, isn't that all we can do? tragedies happen to people every second of the day. it is not what happens to you that should define your tragedy, but how you overcome it.

title: ['The Fourth Monkey (A 4MK Thriller, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: why in the world would a civilized person want to read about crazy folks, serial killers and lunatic depravity? i don't have the answer to that but i know that after reading the fourth monkey i certainly do. is it because of the appalling shock effect? i believe that is part of it but come on, we are all slightly curious about what makes those deranged and demented minds work, aren't we? in his disturbing tale mr. barker doesn't fool around or settle for trite effects. he goes straight for the viscera, which is one reason why the story is absolutely enthralling. on the outside the fourth monkey is just another serial killer novel. but on the inside there are many wondrous treasures to behold, if you are brave enough to seek them. the fourth monkey is a great psychological thriller and a police procedural that won't leave you bored with the life of lab technicians and forensics explanations. mr. j.d. barker is an extremely gifted writer and his mind wanders into the darkest of places. he has a magical touch for accurate character psychology and tight scene building. the intricate plot unfolds with what i like to call "the snowball effect". the more you read, the deeper you get into the characters' minds and the scarier it gets. barker spends a good deal of the book presenting us with the diary of the fourth monkey killer, also known as 4mk. his background is rendered so vividly you will be transported to places you wouldn't expect or would want to go. i thought 4mk was your average run of the mill serial killer, but he's much more complex and inscrutable. i won't say more about him and leave you the pleasure of discovering the nooks and crannies of his terrifying mind for yourself. a discussion of the book would not be complete without a thought or two about our hero, detective sam porter. detective porter and 4mk play a cat and mouse game and i found myself rooting for both parties. i hope that detective porter's background is fleshed out a bit more in the next book, i would like to know what makes him tick. overall this book was finely crafted, swiftly plotted, and exquisitely disturbing. more please.

title: ['Lab Rat One (Touchstone, #2)', 'Dragon (Vlad Taltos, #8)']
cleaned_reviews: read my review of the trilogy here. (i must have re-read the ending of this book five or six times. woohoo!) i'm giving this one five stars on re-reading, as an audiobook, in internal chronological order, simply because brust is at the top of his game with the craft of this one. as with taltos, it's really not a good idea to read this out of publication order if you're new to the series, because so much of what happens is layered in with the intent of winking at the reader who's read the other books. dragon takes place in three parts, two of which are woven together so beautifully it's like a master class in how to do transitions. the third is a set of "interludes" that take place much later--after the action of yendi, in fact. it's an interesting way to tell a story, particularly this story. each of the vlad taltos dragaera books (as opposed to the khaavren romances) is titled, with one exception, with one of the seventeen great houses, and there is always an aspect of that house in the plot or structure of the novel. since dragons are proverbially known for being straightforward, brust messing around with time as he tells this story is either unexpected or, more likely, a reference to what one of the characters (i can't remember if it's morrolan or sethra) says about how dragons can be subtle if they have to. but the way this works is similar to the structure of taltos, where each chapter begins with the climactic scene and then transitions to the main body of the story, the part leading up to the climax. the interludes play a part in increasing the tension of the story: (view spoiler)[we learn that sethra the younger stole the sword the whole war is about before the climactic scenes reveal that it was stolen at all, keeping that section from feeling inevitable. (hide spoiler)] the structure is so elegant i have to admire it separately from the plot. the plot, on the other hand, is pretty much as straightforward as a dragon: sword is stolen, morrolan wants it back, morrolan goes to war over it, and vlad is suckered into joining the army so he can help sneakily get the sword back. (view spoiler)[one great throwaway line that, again, you don't get if you've read the books in chronological order is sethra lavode saying "we don't know any thieves." (hide spoiler)] only vlad, who intended to bail before the fighting began, finds he can't abandon these dragonlords who will put their lives on the line because that's what soldiers do. it's an interesting twist for vlad, who started the series (in taltos) hating dragaerans and now finds that not all of them are bigoted jerks. they respect him for fighting with them, they turn loiosh into a mascot for the company, and some of them even come to be friends. brust's grasp of military strategy and tactics is sound, and the story of vlad's time in the army is interesting enough. but i think, if brust hadn't decided to whet our appetites with the climactic scene in between the "main" story, it would have been a very dull book, all that marching and attacking. i'm not sure how i feel about the interludes. they seem to serve the same interweaving purpose, and i think if he'd told the whole story of how the sword finally came to its proper owner at the end, it would have been anticlimactic and maybe tedious. at any rate, it was hugely enjoyable. next up is yendi, one of my favorites because of the romance as well as the highly convoluted plot--worthy of a yendi.

cleaned_reviews: "let the dead bury the dead" i'm going to be 100% completely honest and admit that i went into this story with 0 expectation. seriously, i expected this to be absolutely terrible - a mess. as you can see from my 4 stars, i was more than pleasantly surprised! the main reason this book has received so many stars has to be due to the writing style. on almost every page there were quotes that made realize the beauty of life and blah blah blah. seriously, stunning prose and thought provoking quotes made this book so much more amazing than i thought it would. destefano has this way of making me fall in love with every character included within the novel, even the late daphne, who we never even get to meet. all characters were unique, and despite their mistakes, they were lovable - flawed and beautiful. pen is goals, she is everything i aspire to be in life, this woman made me adore this novel, if pen wasn't here then i don't think i wouldn't loved perfect ruin as much. morgan was harder to like, she was very flawed, and perhaps too naive, but you couldn't help just wanting to take care of her, she became a little sister to me, someone i wanted to protect immensely. you have to give destefano credit for the plot. it is so incredibly hard to write a unique dystopian these days. everything ends up being a spat out version of 1984, or more recently, the hunger games. they may not be exact copies, but they all follow certain tropes, becoming increasingly predictable. although this was definitely the case for perfect ruin, it didn't feel that way. the story felt new, it was refreshing. now this may be because i haven't read a dystopian in god knows how long, however i doubt this is the case. the setting was just so different, it was new, i enjoyed learning about it, the history was rich and wonderful - like fairy tales, woven into historical context. despite the 4 star review, there were obviously some problems that need to be addressed. the world building lacked so much, how did they get there? why did they get there? on a place so small, how can the crazy dictator get away with so much? maybe these questions will be answered within the series, i was just disappointed that i didn't get answers straight away. additionally, morgan has some questionable morals. i couldn't stand the way she blamed pen for what happened, (view spoiler)[hurting the prince (hide spoiler)] the way morgan treated pen afterward was horrific, and totally unnecessary! honestly, i think this novel is definitely worth the read, and i cannot wait to pick up the rest of this series, i hope you all enjoyed it as much as i did!!!

title: ['Still Alice']
cleaned_reviews: still alice is the story of a woman in her early fifties. she is at the peak of success. people reach out to her for advise. she has a successful marriage- a loving husband, with whom she has published a book, three kids who love her with all their hearts and a profession which she loves. her life is as normal as it could be but then suddenly something happens. on her way home, she forgets the route. she starts forgetting words during the lectures she had delivered for past twenty five years. she enters the class and forgets the topic of the day. she blames it all to menopause. during her regular checkup, her doctor attributes memory loss to lack of sleep or depression or tiredness. inside, she knows that none of this is true. she was getting enough sleep and she wasn't depressed or tired. she wants to be in denial. she wants it to be a dream. but alas, it is the reality. she meets a neurologist and is suspected to have been suffering from early onset of alzheimer's. the doctor wants her to be with someone in the next meeting. she can't believe this is happening to her. she breaks the news to her husband who is not ready to believe it and he does his homework on the recent happenings in alzheimer's, trial drugs, tests to check for alzheimer's etc. her life is turned topsy-turvy. the book is the first person account of what alice feels and experiences. right from the onset of alzheimer's her life takes a u turn. when she accost people with the news that she is not depressed or alcoholic, but is suffering from dementia, the attitude of people change. the books doesn't keep you hooked to it, but there are small episodes, which will touch your emotional nerve. alzheimer attacks her memory but not her analytical ability. it decreases her linguistic capability but increases her ability to "feel". she gets emotionally more attached. she even gives an inspirational talk for people suffering from dementia. there are groups for caregivers, but none for actual sufferers. she takes a step forward and creates one. she doesn't know what she wants to drink tea or coffee. but she knows her life is not in ny. there are good days and there are bad. but that is how life is. loved the part of book club and q&a with lisa genova. nicely written lisa.

title: ['The Shadow of the Wind (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books,  #1)']
cleaned_reviews: first reading march-may 2013. i like novels where i change my attitude to characters as more is revealed about them. i like the way the fictive novel became a character and its people and plot appeared in our novel. i will have to think how to say the rest, whether to create a spoiler or if i can say things without spoiling. a group i am in has chosen it for this month, so i am rereading it (march 2016) sometimes plot structure is more clear on a second reading--who is speaking? who is who? what happened before? i am sure i made connections on this reading that i missed on the first. the boy, daniel, is taken by his father to the cemetery of forgotten books to select one to remember and take care of. he chooses the shadow of the wind by julian corax, and he begins a search for information about the author. thus a past story and a present story emerge, stories with many parallels, but not totally parallel--nothing that predictable. one has to read attentively to track which story's background fits the current chapter. the narrator for most is daniel, but there is a surprise section narrated by another with occasional details that seem impossible (or maybe i missed a cue somewhere). however, the lapse, if it is a lapse is minor. it is a first book of a series that inspires reading the next two. another one promised.

title: ['The Elite (The Selection, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: i haven't been this happy since desiree hartsock accepted chris siegfried's proposal in the most dramatic season finale of the bachelorette ever. just kidding. but seriously, i don't mean to be a total fangirl or to sound like i'm 16 years old - but i really can't imagine a better night than sitting down with some wine to watch the bachelorette finale or reading kiera cass' the selection series. okay, hopefully the wine graduated me to at least 21. right? so if it isn't clear, i loved every flipping second of the elite. from the first chapter i was captivated and couldn't put it down until the very last page. and now i'm staring at the expected publication for book #3 in a stupor - may 2014?!?!? i didn't even know there was a 3rd book until i read this one, now i find out i have to wait almost an entire year??? urgh! okay so other than my frustration that i have to wait until 2014 to get my happily ever after with what i anticipate to be a ton of frustration along the way, i cannot say enough amazing things about this book. actually, this is going to be the strangest series of compliments ever - in that they sound like i'm complaining about everything when really kiera cass knows exactly what she's doing. america is enfuriating - but perfect in her own obnoxiously stubborn, blinders up, nearsighted way! she gets so caught up in every little thing that maxon says or does and blows it completely out of proportion, but you know what??? she also cares! like, a lot. about illea, the caste system, the monarchy's role, the responsibility she's undertaking if she marries maxon, everything. i finally opened my eyes and realized that while i might not agree with the way america approaches things or how stressfully long it takes her to give maxon an answer, at least she doesn't just get caught up in the "winning" aspect of the selection process and blindly barrel forward without considering what she's saying yes to. aspen. i kept waiting for him to do something that would allow me to say, see america??? he's not the one! let him get caught kissing a maid or be oblivious to the importance of america's potential role in the country's future, something! but kiera cass wouldn't listen! she just kept writing this great guy that was supportive and understanding, patient and good. and finally, finally, i got it. because it's not that big a deal if america picks maxon over aspen if he's really a jerk. it's only a sign of how true her feelings are if she has two great options and picks maxon. so yah, i was wrong about that too. and maxon? he's not perfect and he's sometimes just a guy needing to be loved or cared for or paid attention to, but he's also endearing and sweet and he has greatness inside of him and he's just smart and quiet enough to know he has to be patient and calculating about how he approaches it. and i fell more in love with him by the minute. (even the novella #0.5 that i complained about because i thought it added nothing to the overall story and if anything just made america look worse in her selfishness, i now realize had its own purpose in allowing the reader to see who maxon is and why, just in case we were as blind as america at the beginning of this book.) i had missed these kisses, so quiet, so sure. i knew that, in my whole life, if i married aspen or someone else, no one would ever make me feel this way. it wasn't like i made his world better. it was like i was his world. it wasn't some explosion; it wasn't fireworks. it was a fire, burning slowly from the inside out. we really didn't see that much of aspen or maxon in the elite; a lot of the book was america's struggles, but honestly, i didn't feel like i was lacking for anything! kiera cass is building something epic and she's doing it one book at a time. i loved the world, the depth of the dystopian society kiera cass has created, and the seamless way she interweaves the dystopian world with the romantic journey and keeps everything in perfect balance. i couldn't be more excited about the one and will most likely be foaming at the mouth by the time it arrives! **reviewed by preppea on i bookie nookie reviews.

title: ['My Not So Perfect Life']
cleaned_reviews: sophie kinsella captured my attention many years ago with the confessions of a shopaholic series. she showed that she had real strength in her writing, being able to balance light topics and mix them with seriousness at the right times, making for a fun combination that doesn't weigh too heavily on the reader. returning to her newest work, my not so perfect life, i was happy to see that the quality of her writing was much the same. after having written over ten novels, i wasn't sure what i would be coming back to. katie brenner, the main character, is totally different from becky bloomwood, the aforementioned shopaholic. while they are a somewhat similar taste for living in the center of it all (london), they are quite different and that's fine. katie's story felt like it might be a bit slow at first. the summary makes much of her losing her job and being forced to return home, so i thought that crucial event was going to take place much sooner than it did. while in the reading it felt a bit slow, upon reflection i think kinsella took just the right amount of time to bring katie's london life into focus, introduce to some major and some minor characters, and then move us to the countryside for the later half of the book where a lot of katie's, and her former boss demeter's, character development takes place. as far as the characters go, i think katie was well rounded and had a good time of things. the one part that i didn't really like was the conclusion of her relationship with alex astalis. it seems like in the end that they'll go their separate ways after having a bit of adult fun and that would have made a lot of sense and been perfectly fine. however, in the last one or two percent of the book, he comes rushing back into her life and she accepts it far too easily. i thought that felt really rushed and it rang of falseness. i would've loved to see katie enjoy their time together, as she said she did, and then move on with her career, as she was doing when alex bumbled back in. then there is there are the interactions that demeter has with the rest of the book's cast. she is quite the villain of the piece for much of the book, or at least made out to be one. it's revealed at the end that a lot of the mad things going on with her (forgetting dates, emails being sent or deleted, etc.) are actually part of a sabotage plot, but that's neither here nor there. some of the actions demeter takes are her own and i'm not sure totally excusing her, letting her apologize and get away totally clear in the end, was all that great. she's a boastful person who doesn't think about what she says half the time and yet this seems to be forgiven once the plot against her is uncovered. it is also mentioned that she might have prosopagnosia (face blindness) to a certain degree. katie knows that there's a rumor about this and through her interactions with demeter it certainly seemed plausible long before demeter confirmed she had a little face recognition problem. on the one hand, katie's treatment of this situation is a bit mean, though. she never acknowledges that this might cause demeter some real trouble with remembering names/faces and lashes out about this both to herself and to demeter's face once things start going down. one the other hand, as i mentioned with regards to demeter's boastful actions being excused earlier, her behavior with not learning to work with her disability doesn't mean that she should get away with being disrespectful to her colleagues. just because you have a disability doesn't mean you get to be disrespectful of the people around you, especially the ones you work with/employ. overall, i think that sophie kinsella's newest novel is a lot of fun to read and the new setting, taking place on a farm with a family that's a bit nutty (a father that goes from project to project until he settles on glamping), was a humorous one to try out. if this was my first kinsella novel, i think it would convince me to try more of her novels. as it is at least my seventh or eighth, i like to think i'll keep reading her future books and make short work of older novels i might have missed. i received a copy of this book from the publisher via netgalley in exchange for an honest review.

title: ['Grave Mercy (His Fair Assassin, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this is not the book you can easily put down. grave mercy is set in 15th century in brittany. at that time, brittany is in complex situation since their disadvantageous treaty with france. anne, the duchess of brittany is not yet crowned and she is only twelve years old. many people try to take advantage of that situation and anne only has a few handful of loyal baron to serve her. the main task is to have anne crowned and marry her to a powerful ruler. ismae was only fourteenth when she was to be married to a pig farmer in a horrible arranged marriage. however, her husband gone berserk when he found out that ismae bears a deep red stain on her back as a proof that she is daughter of god of death. she was in danger to be burnt to death by her husband, but she was saved and brought to a convent in a quiet, remote place. the convent is dedicated to serve st. mortain, the old god of death. the abbes of st. mortain offered her a choice to be the handmaiden of death. ismae was instantly intrigued by the possibility of revenge, to men who have done nothing but hurt her, including her own father. "if you choose to stay, you will be trained in his arts. you will learn more ways to kill a man than you imagined possible. we will train you in stealth and cunning and all manner of skills that will ensure no man is ever again a threat to you." ismae decided to be the handmaiden of death. she will not question the convent or how they pick people she should kill. an unquestioning faith. in three years, ismae quickly learns the art of dagger, bows, and her specialty, poison. she also learns the art of seduction which the sisters said would help her in her missions. she never thought that she would ever use the art of seduction... until circumstance comes and suddenly, she is to act as the mistress of gavriel duval. duval is a breton noble, bastard of the late duke, and the closest advisor of her twelve years old sister, duchess of brittany. he is also being suspected of betrayal by the abbes and her ally, chancellor crunad. ismae is supposed to be the convent's eyes and ears in the court. duval is not a foolish and he knows that ismae is watching his every moves. they're supposed to be ally, but no more than that. still, they can't resist the building attraction between them. is duval really a traitor, as the abbess and chancellor crunad suspected? can ismae trust her own prejudice that duval is not the traitor? will she raise her bow and kill the man she is beginning to trust, if the convent gives her command to do so? as i said earlier, grave mercy is the kind of book that you long to finish in one sit. the story is very engaging and it's easy to slip into the conflict and political play in brittany's court. this book may bore people who don't enjoy court politics, but i find the whole plot very convincing and nicely written. i practically flied through the cleaned_reviews: hands. lips. tighs. devil's kisses. laughter. hope. desperstion. jealousy. poison. totally captivating, a powerful and entertaining read that will make your heart pound. amy lignor's writing style is engaging and full of charm, making it easy to loose yourself in the magical world she created, and connect with all the fabulous characters. dealing with love, duty, destiny, and difficult choices, until the next time is a beautiful book in many ways. matt and emily are angels sent down to earth on a mission to stop bad things from happening, all the while leading a "normal human lives" in their human shells (human bodies they're inhabiting). they've been training for that their whole lives, they have skills and unique angel powers, they're well prepared for anything that could happen. the only problem is once their souls are placed in human bodies, their own memories are wiped clean. they don't remember anything, including each other and their meant-to-be relationship. overwhelmed by human emotions no training could ever have prepared them for, matt and emily will need more than faith to survive their time in human world. what sets until the next time apart from all the other angel books i've read so far, is that the concept behind the story is entirely unique and fresh. and, let's face it, that does not happen very often when it comes to angel books. sure, the general idea remains the same, but at the same time amy lignor puts a very original spin on it, giving us something exciting and new. something that is very hard to dislike. i liked the idea of taking over someone else's body at the exact moment of the person's death, to ensure that their purpose in life is fulfilled. it was fascinating to read about, thought-provoking and very emotional. i found the plot line very interesting and mostly well thought out. i say mostly, because there was a couple of instances when i scratched my head and wondered "hmm.. how did that just happened?" or thought to myself "well, i'm not quite sure if that was entirely necessary". for instance, i wasn't quite sure why all the angel warriors had to train so hard in preparation for their missions, just to have their memories wiped clean before being sent down to earth. and don't get me wrong here, it's not that i don't understand why their angel memories needed to be removed, as amy explained all that very well (they needed to start fresh and go into their missions with open mind), i just didn't see why the extensive training was necessary in the first place. but that's basically all i could possibly complain about. everything else - from the wonderful mythological backdrop that amy so skilfully builds on and expands, to the complex, convincing, likable characters, to the incredible depth of the story and the profound messages it carries - was simply fabulous. i devoured until the next time. touching and thrilling, it's an excellent angel book, and one you should definitely have on your shelf (or ereader).

title: ['Station Eleven']
cleaned_reviews: for some strange reason, i love post-apocalyptic novels even though i love the world. or maybe it's because i love the world that i like to dream of a time when nature will be given the chance to reemerge. while shifting between pre- and post-apocalyptic time periods, station eleven makes the reader realize that no society is perfect and that the current society, with all its complications and problems, might not be so bad after all. there are characters who long for our present day. some weren't old enough to fully remember a time when you could flip a switch to flood an area with light. experiences like that turn into a kind of folklore passed down to the younger generations. they can hardly believe there were ever such things as flying airplanes or refrigeration or electricity. all those things we take for granted. even though they can't bring the old world back, they try to piece it together somehow through magazine articles and objects found in abandoned homes. they want to remember such a miraculous time, to the point where the reader starts to look at the present day with nostalgia. we see the senselessness of the present day too through an actor who fails to connect with others or through lives that are gobbled up by the business world as it turns people into sleepwalkers. one present day character, miranda, tries to live a more artistic life but even she is overtaken by the need for a real job that diverts her energy away from her art. i love her comic book story within the story, and how that parallels the longing felt by so many of the characters.

cleaned_reviews: nora wonders about her former friend that is now getting married and having a pre-marriage get together. she knows she should decline the invite, but she's just too curious. of course we all know what happed to that cat and nora should have known better. but i liked her optimism. i found her trip down memory lane compelling and charming and i rooted for her to find a friendly impasse with her gal pal or at the very least a kick ass party weekend. she found it. partly. i enjoyed the pace of the mystery. ware never gives up too much in the lead up to the big showdown. i liked the nora's inner monologue and her conflicted feelings with herself and everyone in the group. i couldn't help but tense up at ever shift of angle and focus. i thought the suspenseful tension was on point and even though you know something was coming it was plenty emotional and vivid. however, i was a little let down by the whodunit wrap up. it felt rushed and lacked a subtlety that the rest of the book enjoyed. i was equally pleased that ms. ware didn't give us a cookie cutter hea and pissed we don't have a definitive answer of what happened to claire. nonetheless i thoroughly enjoyed it even if i will balk at my next hens' weekend invite. kudos to ware on a climatic and provoking debut. but seriously, claire, matt anything?! 4.5/5 arc kindly provided in exchange for an honest review should you read black lies?

title: ['The God of Small Things']
cleaned_reviews: i'm a person who frequently reads while i eat. this book is not a good choice for that pairing! this is only the second time i've encountered a book i absolutely could not read during lunch. (the first was the cider house rules, if that helps give you a frame of reference.) reading this book was a bit of a journey for me. the first phase involved reading the book almost like a mystery, trying to sort out the clues to figure out what big, terrible thing had happened to these people, and how it had occurred. by the mid-point of the book, i no longer had any desire to know, because i knew enough to know that is would be tragic and sickening. but i still had to keep reading, out of some sort of sense of fairness to the characters i guess. there's no way around the fact that end of the story is depressing. history can't be avoided, and nothings gets better, for anyone. but the end of the book is different from the end of the story. the last chapter of the book is the most beautiful, the most heart-breaking, the most everything. (the second-to-last chapter, incidentally, not a fan. you can see it coming a mile away, but i kept hoping it wasn't going there. i will admit to not understanding why that was necessary.) the things that really sets this book apart, though, has to be the language. roy takes words and twists them, combines them in ways you've ever seen before, to create meanings that are completely her own. the twins like to read words backwards, and have a way of describing things that is completely in tune with their world - their strange family, their bilingual upbringing, their constant feeling of being out of place. overall, i loved this book, even if it was sometimes tough to keep going. terrifying but beautiful, timeless in its treatment of history, this book is stunning.

title: ['Breathe (Sea Breeze, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this book was so sweet. just the perfect amount of sugar. this story is about the gorgeous, self-conscious sadie. she doesn't feel gorgeous; she's 17 years old but lives the life of a parent. she cooks, cleans, sleeps, eats and works to support her deadbeat pregnant mother who she refers to as jessica. fortunately for sadie her mum can't be bothered to drag herself to work so she has to fill in, and this is where it gets juicy. sadie is a maid for the family of jax stone - a major teenage heart throb. they get to know each other and fall head over heels in love. i adored their relationship. *sadie to marcus "i am sure you're right. but no guy i have ever met has made my heart go on a frenzy and my skin tingle just by walking into a room. somehow, he is the only one who has ever been able to touch my soul." sadie is so sweet and insecure and doesn't know how alluring she is and jax is just a boy who wants to be himself and not a pop star. they were the ying to the others yang. i loved them. it wasn't all smooth sailing. *'to live without a daydream or hope for happiness was like walking around dead. there was no future i could see that gave me reason to daydream.' awwww. the despair i felt reading sadie feeling this :( when sam came along, sadie struggled with issues of her heart, being mother to her newborn brother, working to pay the bills and staying awake in school. she really was a machine. i felt for her. truly. she is so kind hearted she put everyone in front of herself and didn't once whine about the cards she was dished. i adored the lyrics throughout and could almost hear the guitar playing in the background. i could imagine the calm feeling surrounding sadie each time she listened. *'he was my air, my soul, and the keeper of my heart.' i felt her love on each and every page. the book had great supporting characters in ms mary (she got me teary), marcus (the best friend) and mr greg the gardener. what a lovely little tight knit group. i am so looking forward to the next of the series "because of low" loving ms glines voice...

title: ['Batman: The Black Mirror']
cleaned_reviews: ** spoiler alert ** gotham's batman, dick grayson, takes on the dealer, a man selling the weapons of supervillains stolen from the gcpd evidence room, gun runners harassing a mob bosses daughter, and possibly the greatest threat of all, commissioner gordon's son... you know, when dc put dick grayson in the bat-costume, we all knew it wouldn't last and while i liked the issues of batman & robin i read, i didn't find anything earth-shattering and thought dick's tenure as the caped crusader would be pretty forgettable. i was wrong! there are epic tales of the bruce wayne batman that everyone mentions: the killing joke, the dark knight, year one, the long halloween, the list goes on and on. this is dick grayson's epic. scott snyder and jock take the reader on a dark journey, following dick grayson as he tries to fill bruce wayne's shoes. while grant morrison made batman fun again when he put dick in the costume, scott snyder made me believe. batman goes up against the dealer, roadrunner, tiger shark, and even the joker, but the most chilling villain in the black mirror is james gordon jr, the commissioner's son. i can't even think of another comic book villain that actually scared me but james was scary because he was so real, so plausible. and i had a batgasm when he finally got what was coming to him. that's about all i can say without giving too much away. i know i clicked the spoilers box but i didn't spoil more than the dust jacket. if i could give this six stars, i would. scott snyder is the real deal and i'm going to continue buying everything of his i can find.

title: ['Pleasure of a Dark Prince (Immortals After Dark #9)']
cleaned_reviews: this review was first posted on http://www.rubysreads.com. i think i'm in love. i fall for kresley cole's lykae heroes every time. i love that they yearn to find life-mates. i love that they're always tall, gorgeous male specimens. i love their protective streak and their single-minded "she will be mine"-ness. in fact, like lucia, i have a thing for jealous alpha males. sigh. but, um, i'm not sure how to say this...well...i hate the way they talk. because all lykae seem to come from scotland, they all speak with a thick brogue. which means that when they're talking to one another, the dialogue reads like this: "i need to follow lousha." "aye, o' course you must go after her. but maybe you could leave after my wedding?" "i canna." garreth took a swig. "no' unless you need me. to help you...acclimate." just, fyi, i deleted some of the extraneous internal dialogue from this passage. anyway, i don't mind the "wees" and the "lasses" so much as the dropped consonants. every time i see them, i want to shout, "it's not, you idiot!" and the "ayes". god save me from the "ayes". but that's just nitpicky niggly stuff and i can mostly ignore it. because kresley cole is wonderful. pleasure of a dark prince is the seventh book in the immortals after dark series. i have to confess that i have not read all of them. this is mostly because i started the second book (no rest for the wicked) and was almost immediately bored by sebastian and kaderin's story. the result was that i did not finish that book, but went straight to bowen's (wicked deeds on a winter's night). i keep telling myself to try another book with a vampire hero, that maybe sebastian was an aberration, but i haven't yet. am i wrong? let me know. pleasure of a dark prince has the same time line as a hunger like no other, but it tells the events of emma and lachlain's story from the perspective of lucia (emma's aunt) and garreth (lachlain's brother). when pleasure of a dark prince begins, everyone who is familiar with the series knows what's going to happen. garreth will recognize lucia as his mate and she will disappear. what we get to learn this time is why lucia runs away, why she refuses to become garreth's mate. i liked that lucia's reasons for rejected garreth are layered, even though they are based on one simple fact. if she sleeps with garreth, she will lose her ability as an unparalleled archer. it is her skill as an archer that is supposed to save her from a long-ago enemy. but it's more than that; being lucia the archer has been lucia's identity for so long that she fears that she'll be nothing without it. and being garreth's mate is not a substitute she is willing to accept. so, to explain a little of the plot: long ago, lucia made a vow of chastity to a goddess in exchange for her extraordinary ability with a bow and arrow. when garreth comes along, he is the first male to challenge that vow. the two are instantaneously attracted to one another. for garreth, that means one thing only: he has to claim lucia and mark her as his own and he has to do it yesterday. it drives him crazy every time she denies him. he can't understand how she can be attracted to him and still say "no." this is the set-up for the first part of the novel: garreth talks big about seducing lucia and lucia talks big about not wanting him. finally, with the help of nucking futs nix (a recurring character who will [yea!] someday have her own novel), garreth tracks lucia down as she's boarded a boat for the far reaches of the amazon basin. lucia is forced to accept garreth's help because it turns out he's the only person ever to return from her ultimate destination (and live). lucia lets garreth know a part of the secret she's keeping, but not everything. she knows that if she tells garreth everything, he will take control out of her hands and solve the problem for her. but the secret that lucia's keeping is big and she knows that hers is a task that no one else can complete. one of the things that i love most about kresley cole's books is that, while her heroes are alpha males, her heroines are not cowering females. they are strong, opinionated, funny and smart. they don't let their men walk all over them. though lucia likes that garreth has an over-protective streak, that doesn't mean she is willing to let him take control of her life or fight her battles for her. it's heroines like cole's that make the alpha male really work. i did love this book. it didn't give me the same delicious afterglow as a hunger like no other, but i did look forward to getting back to reading it and i was always reluctant to put it down. there was one thing that kept pleasure of a dark prince from 6 point status, however. that is, i felt that lucia was able to get out of her deal with skathi (the goddess) much too easily. i was too pat, too easy. i confess i was disappointed. i thought cole's solution would be more clever than it was. i should add that kresley cole did really setting this particular fan up for wanting to read the next books in the series. i can't wait to see what lothaire is up to. and what the deal is with regin and carrow. also, it was nice to catch up with old characters. and, yea!, a baby for lachlain and emma (maybe). i want to end this post with a question. does anyone know of any other books featuring valkyrie? the only other place i've seen them show up is in carrie jones' captivate. i'd like to see some other authors interpretations of this mythical group, so please, please let me know if you can make any recommendations.

title: ['Son (The Giver, #4)']
cleaned_reviews: lois lowry took much from the last three books in the giver world and combined it into what i would like to call an epic of deception, loss, love, and renewal. while it doesn't have quite the same magnitude of epics such as lord of the rings or the faded sun trilogy in terms of world-building and prose, her main focus was on the characters, especially that of claire. all the books from giver to son fascinated me because of their dystopian setting. the readers come to understand in gathering blue that there was a great catastrophe in the world that destroyed much of civilization and even caused one community to create a twisted utopia, from which jonas and claire emerge. like jonas, claire goes on a journey of discovery about the community she was raised in and about herself and her feelings. this book had a wonderfully human touch to it, from human interaction and behavior to the power of the human spirit. it also had some "supernatural" going on; apparently after the great ruin, as they call it, people started gaining special gifts...and along with them rose a great evil with an insatiable hunger. i would recommend the whole quartet to a reader, and would also recommend that the reader read giver, gathering blue, and messenger (in that order) before reading son.
