title: ['Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell']
cleaned_reviews: in his review of donna tartt's the goldfinch, stephen king describes the dickensian novel as "bursting with incident", and while the word-to-word writing style of jonathan strange & mr norrell might tend more towards austen, dickens' influence can certainly be seen in the fact that the book is filled to the brim with side-plots, tangents, digressions, comic interludes, side-characters; it is truly bursting with incident. there's ten novels worth of content (and energy) packed in these pages. one of the basic rules in writing is to "show, don't tell", but i've always thought it ought to be "show what needs to be shown, tell what needs to be told". jonathan strange and mr norrell does a great deal of both, there are lyrical, action-filled passages, and there's proper, almost stuffy periods of telling, where she summarizes a month's worth of work. through this technique, she can, with a paragraph, gloss over what might constitute in a different book, ten chapters, and then spend the next few pages on a critical conversation that develops the characters and moves forwards the plot, then begin 'telling' again, gliding us smoothly through weeks of story which in that different novel might be the 'boring parts'. it allows clarke to always be using her "showing" voice on the interesting, beautiful parts of the book. this is a remarkably realistic book, not because of the spells and the magic, but because of the logic behind the characters. one of the elements that conspires to create this atmosphere of realism is the lack of a driving plot. as anyone will tell you, our own lives are hardly well-plotted, we don't have clear goals like "blow up the death-star" or "destroy the ring". neither do clarke's characters; they long to "restore magic to england" or "aid the war effort" or "modernize magic"; these are abstract, realistic goals, that take months of work. things develop over years; characters don't just change suddenly based off a single scene. this book falls naturally into the rhythm of life, and this serves to make all the magic feel like a regular day-to-day thing. classifying this book as 'fantasy' seems almost like a betrayal. there are so many genres packed into it, the romance, the gothic novel, the war story, the horror novel, the action novel, surrealism... i suppose there isn't a western, although the native americans make an appearance. its one of those books best described by what isn't in it, as opposed to what is. and yet there is so much more to write! what of the witty characters? what of the thrilling plot? what of the beautiful writing? what of the.... i could go on. so perhaps i'll leave the explaining to ms. clarke herself. there is a postmodernist technique known as "mise-en-abyme", wherin an author uses a description to summarize the theme of an entire novel. this might be a description of a tree, of a desk, of a sky. in jonathan strange and mr norrell, the description that ultimately manages to summarize the whole novel comes during a chapter in a peat-bog... i won't be specific lest i give spoilers, but clarke writes. he dreamt that everything in the world - stones and rivers, leaves and fire - had a purpose which it was determined to carry out with the utmost rigour, but he also understood that it was possible sometimes to persuade things to a different purpose. this is a perfect description of both the novel and the things within. all these little side characters and tangential events and minor digressions and incidents all have a clear purpose that they are determined to carry out with the utmost rigour, to move the plot, to facilitate character development, merely to get the heroes from one place or another. even the major characters begin with a clear purpose, the gentleman's was to raise lady pole, norrell's was to restore magic to england, strange's was to merely get married and live a prosperous life. and yet sometimes, things are persuaded to a different purpose... and none of these original aims develop as they were planned. minor characters are thrust into major roles, a magician that hates a certain historical figure might be forced to summon him, a bachelor on his way to his wedding is confronted by a strange vagabond offering him three spells, and a destiny. a gentleman-with-thistle-down-hair grows greedy and mischievous. and thus things are persuaded to a different purpose, a wilder purpose, and this book, this stuffy 19th century drawing-room comedy is itself persuaded to a different purpose, one full of magic, magic worked, if not on the pages, then on the reader...

title: ['Bloodlines (Bloodlines, #1)']

i love how i can tell this series is really going to test sydney's beliefs and tolerances! adrian, by far, is my favorite character in this. even while grieving his broken relationship from rose, he is still witty. combine that with sydney's hidden snark and we get some great dialogue in this book. jill is still the one character i am just not sure about. her character has always been "meh" to me and this book has done little to improve. not to say i dislike her but i can take her or leave her. with a new possible forbidden romance on the horizon, two great, solid lead characters and a new plotline that explores new aspects of the world, richelle mead has done a great job with this!

cleaned_reviews: 3.5/5 stars i'm kind of torn about this book. on one hand, i really liked the setting and how dark it was, as well as most of the characters. it was entertaining and kept my attention all the way through. i was even kind of nervous towards the end. however, it did have some flaws, one being that i figured out the identity of the murderer about halfway through the book without much effort, which was unfortunate since it took away some of the suspense. also, while i definitely appreciate a strong, capable heroine, the repeated mentions of how audrey rose wasn't-like-other-girls, kind of annoyed me, though i guess that's a minor problem. overall an entertaining read if you're looking for a gory sherlock holme-ish, romance-ish story about catching jack the ripper, and don't care too much about historical accuracy. in some ways it reminded me slightly of the monstrumologist by rick yancey, though more in feeling and setting than plot. i can say that i probably will read the sequel if the synopsis sounds interesting. :) i was pleasantly surprised by this book, and will most likely pick up the sequel sooner rather than later. :)

title: ['Lady Midnight (The Dark Artifices, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: cassandra clare is getting really good with this forbidden love thing. tmi was meh for me while i absolutely adored the infernal devices. jace and will herondale were your typical witty hotties with oh-so-much sass @.@ i loved tessa and clary was well..cool..but our characters from lady midnight? so. different. jules is...so perfectly characterized. so complex and yet so very easy to follow. clare did an amazing job capturing what it'd be like to give your all for your family in a parental way. emma on the other hand...i wished so much that she was more like jem.. i do however love that she's the star here, that she's the 'next best shadowhunter after jace' and all that. love how gender isn't in any way limiting in clare's books. sucks that we gotta wait a whole year for the sequel...

title: ['Parasite (Parasitology, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i don't know how she did it, but somehow, grant managed to write yet another zombie series. they may not be the traditional type, but we clearly have mob behavior, shuffling, low mental acuity, menace toward humanity. it's all there. anyway, i still enjoyed it greatly, though it has to be said i spent a great deal of this book annoyed at the main character who i found cowardly and cringing. and look, i even understand a lot of why she was the way she was. i understood it more and more as the book went on. but like her newsflesh series, grant makes some really tough choices in her narrative that (if you are any kind of a reader like i am) will make you want to constantly tear out your hair through 2/3rds of this book. hopefully, it will be much less annoying in the next book, because i genuinely enjoyed this book and its characters. (cue my constant disclaimer: this book is not for everyone) happy reading!

title: ["Crow's Row (Crow's Row, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: for the most part i did enjoy this book. pretty solid writing, i found the character setup really interesting & such a great premise. however...i guess i missed it in the description or something but in light of the setting i was expecting this book to have more of a contemporary/new adult slant on the consummation of their relationship. too young adult for me and i was really disappointed when the time came. i was all "really?! i just went through 200 pages to get to my reward point and 2 lines of nothing is all i get?" also, i have to say emmy really started to bug me. i understand there would be curiosity and then the need for answers when she discovers her connection to the crew, but landsakes i just wanted to throttle her at times when she kept at it, even when she was more entrenched in this new world. it's like, don't you have any sense whatsoever of self-preservation? just shut up! or when she finds herself in peril but isn't able to bring herself to do what she needs to do to save herself. now i'm not saying she should've gave herself to victor but she couldn't even manage a kiss. of course it's the last you'd ever want to do if one found themselves in that situation but if it's at the risk of survival, just conjure up the smoochies. i didn't like how it conveniently worked out for her with the gun despite her "defiance" against his advances. at least we saw some consequence but still and this wasn't the only time where emmy commits a big blunder but still gets an easy-ish way out of the situation. didn't sit right with me. plus, a non-gratifying sort of ending. all in all though it was enough to have me interested in the sequel to see what happens. it's not top of my anticipated list but i'll definitely pick it up. so, to julie, this was a good solid outing, i loved your secondary characters who build this underground world too, but please for the love of god, make emmy a little more grown up and less a petulant child and more of a survivor who's gained some better street intellect and self-possession. please lessen the crying by 70%, i hate criers. ugh.

title: ['These Shallow Graves']
cleaned_reviews: "...stay with me today. and tomorrow. and every day after..." rating: 5 stars "dear eddie, i do not "kid", though on occasion, i jest. this, however, is no such occasion." if you are looking for well-written and engaging historical mystery, look no further. although defying these shallow graves as a simple mystery, does not do this book any justice. "'the truth costs, jo. dearly," he said. "i hope you know that." "lies cost more," she said regretfully." jo's story was thought-provoking and inspiring. "if only she could be bold enough, and brave enough, to claim the things she wanted: love, a purpose, a life. but could she be?" here are a few reason that make this such a great read: *i think the biggest strength of the novel was its main character, jo. donnelly created a vividly realistic girl who i came to appreciate, love and respect throughout the course of her story. her curiosity and naivete are balanced by her often impulsive behaviour and her good-heartedness. her occasional sarcastic remarks made me her even more likeable. i was completely engrossed by her, and more than once, her feelings and actions felt real to me. clever and complex, i wholeheartedly believed in her. " she'd lost faith in him because she had no faith in herself. not in her ability to decide for herself. to choose for herself. or even to be herself. " *the story itself was well crafted. although i figured out soon enough what exactly had happened to jo's father, i think that it was because the reader was meant to understand before jo herself did. the mystery was engaging enough and i could hardly put my copy down. jo's character development accompanied her trough her various leads and investigation, the more i read the more i came to know her and i found myself wanting to see her uncover the truth behind her father's death. "why? jo wondered, mystified. what is she afraid of? whatever it was, jo decided, it would not stop her. she was going to win this battle." *the setting was engrossing and evocative. we get to see new york from all points of view: from fancy parties and esclusive gatherings to poverty-stricken streets. donnelly also addresses various issues pertinent at that time: the limitations of women in both privileged and underprivileged backgrounds, the corruption that ruled over all new york, the unjust treatment of the mentally ill and more... donnelly tackles all of these without reverting to the same old boring ploys. whatever the topic, she incorporated it into the story so it was relevant rather than a forced lecture. moreover there was passion behind her words, i was enraged and mystified by the society she describes so expertly, and saddened by the unfairness jo experiences or is forced to see others endure. "that was what people did when they wanted to stop a girl from doing something-they shamed her." *the cast of characters was not huge, although many different names and faces appear during the story, the focus remains on jo and the people close to her, such as eddie, whom i soon came to adore. his relationship with jo felt grounded and solid. their moments together could be simultaneously cute and bittersweet. i was also pleased to read about fay and oscar. fay's friendship with jo was surprisingly lovely. like jo, their desires and actions felt genuine, and more importantly, just as jo was, they were complex and interesting characters. "for a moment, she forgot her companion was a notorious pick-pocket, devious and dangerous, and that she herself was a proper young society lady. for a moment, they were just two girls heading off on an adventure. " so if you fancy a glimpse into the life of young and brave girl, living in a time which allows her little-to-no freedom, these shallow graves is the book for you. "what is his life like, lived in this small room? she wondered. what would mine be like, living here with him? precarious, exciting, frugal, bohemian-all these words flashed trough her mind, but one flashed more brightly than all the rest: happy. we wouldn't have much, she thought, but we'd have each other." jo's poignant and emotional journey, set in a strikingly evoking new york populated by unique characters, is a must read. the heartfelt and absorbing romance was the cherry on the top. "she picked up his hand, turned it over, and kissed his palm. then she held it against her cheek, eyes closed, wanting to show him how she felt, to show him that maybe there was a way after all. all they had to was find it."

title: ['In a Handful of Dust (Not a Drop to Drink, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: mindy mcginnis' not a drop to drink was my top favorite read for this year, but in a handful of dust collides head first into its companion novel, and i can't decide which one i love more. ten years after the ending of nadtd, the pond where lynn and lucy were living is surrounded by a vibrant community of people. only disease has finally found itself in the center of their community and those in mourning are out to put the blame on someone. from the viewpoint of lucy, now seventeen-years-old, along with lynn, a grown woman and the protector of our young protagonist, in a handful of dust exposes the best and worst of humanity were water is scarce and a long, dry road awaits. to fans of the walking dead, mindy mcginnis's novels are just the harrowing and gritty tales will pull you in and tug at the heart strings of these two strong, independent, and self-sufficient female characters on their way to the western coast, fighting for their own water supply and those who will kill them for just a sip of what they've got. though there are no zombies, the threat of humanity and dehydration turns this post-apocalyptic novel into a daunting realism. the struggle both internally in lynn and lucy's character development and the struggle in the environment with the encounters of other human beings and the encounters with water-bearing areas, the hostility and the caution that brings about an apprehensive air to the readers. and that progressing apprehension into the journey that the two females take into the unknown after being cast away makes in a handful of dust a harrowing and unforgettable novel. final summation: in a handful of dust exceeds all expectations that i had for this second novel in the series. it was just a roller coaster that just kept going up. the gritty journey of survival, the heart-rending relationship between lynn and lucy, and the realistic qualities of a world without water made this series place on my top ten list. a must read for post-apocalyptic readers, and those who enjoy a strong bond between two characters, and the harrowing struggle for survival against the elements and fighting to find humanity in a world where humanity is almost lost.

title: ['Wherever Nina Lies', 'For Keeps', 'Fixing Delilah', 'Summer and the City (The Carrie Diaries, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: almost 4.5 stars....i think this book is unique among recent ya titles i've read because it incorporates drawings and it has some great suspense thrown in. ellie's sister nina disappeared one day two years ago. it wasn't investigated and just assumed that she ran away, especially since she was 18 at the time. but ellie can't believe that her sister would just abandon her and her mom. and she definitely doesn't think she is dead either, or at least chooses not to go there. after two years ellie's best friend is getting tired of ellie not being able to let go of her sister's absence, but then they find one of nina's drawings in some random box of thrift store donations. from there ellie goes on a quest to track nina down, no matter who she leaves behind and what she has to go through. i won't go any further because there are some great twists and turns, but some parts of the story are not appropriate for younger teens. a great read and i will certainly be watching for more from this author. i really enjoyed for keeps by natasha friend. it drew me in right away and i started caring for the characters really quickly. josie has grown up as the only daughter to her single mom kate, who had her at a very young age. josie has also grown up knowing that when her mom was 16 and pregnant, her dad, paul tucci left her and moved to arizona. so when they spot his parents at the grocery store, kate and josie's past comes storming back. is josie's dad back in town too? josie is also a great soccer player and she has a best friend named liv, who has two dads and a ahead-of-her-time fashion sense. the story takes place during josie and liv's junior year and they both have some romantic involvements as well. in particular josie had an encounter of sorts with matt riggs over the summer when he was still with his girlfriend, but now, he's single and making eyes at josie. all in all, i really loved the teen aspects of for keeps, as well as the relationships between josie and her mom, josie and matt and josie and liv. the language of each character was spot on and the writing never got boring or cliched. i felt like i was stepping into the story and the moments in these character's lives. characterizations were great and each person had their own quirks, even josie's grandfather. not too sappy with just the right amount of humor and heart. i read an advance copy of the book (with the title fixing delilah hannaford). delilah and her mom must spend the summer unexpectedly in her mom's childhood home of red falls, vermont after delilah's grandmother passes away. delilah's mom and her aunt have not spoken to her grandmother for 8 years and delilah still does not know why. she also wonders about her aunt stephanie, the one that died at 19 from heart failure. delilah's father is also a mystery. all she has is a newspaper clipping of a man who was killed in an unfortunate accident overseas. once in vermont delilah resigns herself to her mom's silence and finds that some memories come flooding back, but not all are happy or ideal. however, some of the happiest were ones she spent with her childhood friend "little ricky", who just happens to be in vermont as well, but now he is patrick, an intense singer & songwriter who delilah is very happy to get to know again. the story flows nicely, giving away some of the family secrets little by little. it was kind of frustrating though when her mom and rachel were so mysterious as to their family history - i thought that was very unfair of them towards delilah. i really liked her relationship with patrick and all of the imagery of vermont in the summer. i think sarah dessen fans will enjoy this read. 4.5 stars. i think i loved this one better than the first, but that is probably because it appealed more to my "adult" sensibilities. this time around carrie is finally in nyc. she will begin her writer's course and has met samantha. she is rooming with a fellow student and writer in a typical tiny new york apartment where her "room" consists of a small cubicle space cordoned off by dividers. that situation doesn't last long as carrie gets kicked out by the grumpy landlady. carrie also meets miranda, who is immersed in feminist politics and has no qualms about voicing her opinion to everyone. after getting kicked out of her room and board carrie goes to live with samantha who at this point has her own place and is actually engaged. the friendship between carrie, miranda and samantha emerges, as well as other relationships carrie has with her classmates. early on she also begins a romantic relationship with a well known playwright who is at least 10 years older than her. carrie's interest in sex and relationships is a lot more evident in summer and the city and although i really enjoyed reading this aspect of her character, i was left wondering if the portions of the book that went into sexual details were even appropriate for teens. nevertheless, i did enjoy the writing style and characterizations. carrie's wit and charm go a long way, and for fans of the tv series, this is a great way to get to know carrie before she became carrie bradshaw, author of the sex and the city column. again, a note to parents, lots of sex, drinking, and even drugs in this one, so read it or read reviews beforehand.

title: ['The Immortal Rules (Blood of Eden, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: the immortal rules is awesome! has to be one of the best vampire books out there. i'm definitely reading the iron fey series after this, julie kagawa is an amazing writer, and she's so creative. the immortal rules is a vampire dystopian, which is quite a mixture. it was a very good idea. most other dystopians are about some sort of war or apocalypse or something, and a vampire dystopian is a breath of fesh air. the immortal rules is about a girl who gets turned into a vampire. she eventually joins a group of humans, looking for a place called eden. eden apparently has no vampires or hardship, and this group has been searching for it a long time. i loved the rabids in this story. well, not really loved, but i loved the idea. the idea of a red lung virus, and the monsters that are rabids, plus the society in this story equals amazing creativity. the plot is pretty good. i really wanted to see more of kanin in it. i loved kanin. probably more than i liked zeke, actually. man, i hope allie and kanin get together next. :d allison, the main character was pretty awesome. she was very strong, and she was also kind. i liked the way she helped her friend stick so much. she was a great heroine, and she wasn't whiny at all. the secondary characters were good,especially kanin, sarren, and jeb. honestly, the rest kind of melded together. by the end, i couldn't even remember who ruth was. i couldn't tell the difference between most people. i really loved kanin and sarren though. i actually thought that allison would eventually get together with sarren. even though i didn't really like the other secondary characters, nothing was wrong with them. no characters made me want to tear my hair out. they were all just a bit boring. i actually didn't like zeke much. he wasn't a horrible character, but he certainly wasn't very interesting. the immortal rules is a great book. very original and fresh, and definitely worth a read. i don't think it will appeal to everyone, but some people will love it. 4/5 stars.

title: ['Cautious (Disastrous, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: after reading the first book, i thought to myself what else can be thrown at this couple and now book 2 happens!!! wow!! if i hadn't started reading this book so late last night i would have finished it in a day! my oh my!! i love marcus and mia! i think they are such a great couple and work well together, and the secondary characters were amazing in this book, from theresa to jimmy to mia's family. reading the first chapters, my heart stopped for a moment, and i thought this is going to be good!! i knew i had to finish this story! everything in this story was so perfect and so real. especially that it felt like a real relationship. the re-gettting to know each other process, to mia having to worry about exams, and school, and marcus having work, and working together to build their relationship. every day couples have work and school and it was nice seeing the relationship grow in almost real life time. especially seeing each other, and the dates, and the romance really sweet!! completely feel inlove with mia's grandparents, and how sweet and accepting they were of her and marcus. as well as understanding more of marcus' life with jimmie and lou. it was a great insight! the tragedies that happened only strengthen them! not only mia and marcus, but the entire de luca family! perfect ending, yet really sad, and i'm hoping it's not the end ...

title: ['Adaptation (Adaptation, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: really enjoyed the book. i've not read melinda lo before, but now i have to go back and read her other books. by far my favorite thing about her writing was her characters, and her ability to write "wibbly feelings." she had a way of describing awkwardness and emotional tension in a way that i completely relate to (as an adult and as a teenager!) and read very "real" for a teen. i did have to realign my expectations in terms of pacing, about a quarter of the way through the book. the first quarter is fraught with action and tension, and is a quick, engaging read. but once reese and david return home, it becomes more of a simmering character/thriller piece. it works, in its own way, but can be a surprise if you're expecting the same breakneck pace of the beginning. i really loved the treatment of the romance. i totally bought reese's crush on david, and her development of feelings for amber, and then how the two balanced later on. (though every time she showed up with flowers, pushed for dates, showed up at her house, etc. i wanted to shout dude you just met, if this were a guy it would be a stalker, because, seriously: boundaries) i do wish david had had a bit more personality, and i expect that will be developed more in the sequel. just a few quibbles: reese kept posing questions/not getting plot threads that were ridic obvious. i don't know if it was lo's way of hitting the (less astute) reader over the head with it, or her take on "teen's are so wrapped up in feelings that they are slow on the uptake!" but i wanted to shout at reese a few times. specifically, (view spoiler)[: she overhears her girlfriend talking to the scientist who treated reese and blatantly saying that she is keeping an eye on reese/her assignment. yet for the next chapter, and even into the confrontation scene with amber, reese wibbles about what that all meant. she's a spy. duh. then when she and david at kidnapped and are flat out told they are part alien, reese still wibbles "trying to figure it out." she told you you were basically dead and she "adapted" your dna to be part imria. why are you still trying to figure this out in the next scene? (hide spoiler)]

title: ['The Haunting of Hill House', 'Me Before You (Me Before You, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: creepy and satisfying. i loved how the author seemed to turn thoughts around and look deep inside the character's (especially eleanor's head). i've always loved haunted house stories, but there is so much psychological about this one. when louisa clark loses her job at the cafe, she is forced to find other employment. she ends up working for the traynor family has a hired helper for their 35 year old, recently quadriplegic son, will. the two barely get along at first, but as louisa begins to talk back to the moody will, they begin to realize though they have little in common, there is a lot they can do together. but their time together is limited as will has plans of his own and louisa will do anything to change his mind. jojo moyes is a talented writer. i expected this novel to be sappy and maudlin, but to my surprise it was anything but. louisa is a likeable narrator. she is perky and dependable, but everyone always doubts her abilities and her smarts. when she takes the job with the traynors it is eventually her spunky attitude that causes will to treat her with more respect. this isn't an easy book though. it isn't your typical chick lit where everyone lives happily ever after. this is a story complicated by will's disability. moyes keeps it realistic with out finding an easy solution. well developed characters, and fast paced easy writing make this book a great read.

title: ['Room']
cleaned_reviews: this was a heartbreaking but ultimately hopeful book. i really enjoyed it - as much as you can enjoy a subject like this. i know there are some who did not like the author's choice of pov - 5 year old jack - but i thought it was honest and original. maybe that's because i currently have a 5 year old and i can understand his thought process. in my opinion, the best part of this book is the second half where we get to see the "outside" through the eyes of a child who has never been outside of the room. it's confusing and scary and magical all at the same time.

title: ['Vain (The Seven Deadly, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: wow! how do you sum up into a short review how much a book touched you emotionally and spiritually? vain was beautiful and romantic and one of the few books to bring actual tears to my eyes. this book felt real and honest in it's delivery and it was one of the best books i know i will ever read. i am so deeply touched at this moment the only thing i can say is just trust me and read it. it's a beautiful story about a girl finding herself in the most unlikely place and discovering she isn't as bad as she thought. it's about finding love and making real friendships and not letting society dictate how we should live, think, act and be. i absolutely loved watching sophie grow and change, it gave me something to root for during the struggles she faced throughout and after meeting ian in africa the romance was a living thing while reading. you were taken through the emotions of the characters and you loved some and hated others. but the most amazing and beautiful part was the background story which almost became the main character itself, the orphaned children. this book made me fall in love with the orphans that sophie had to help and take care of. it brings an awareness that while sitting in my comfortable living room there are people in the world who are happy with almost nothing. don't mistake what i'm saying though because the delivery of this part of the story was done so well and in a way that makes you yearn to help but doesn't beat you over the head about helping. it just gently tugs at your heart strings enough to want to actually change things. i don't think i will ever be the same after this book and i love when that happens. this will stay deeply rooted in the recesses of my heart for a long time to come and i just can't say enough good things about this book.

title: ['Dreamfever (Fever, #4)', 'Engaging (Alluring, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: 4.5 stars. so good and such an easy fast read 4 stars. i really enjoyed this book! i was excited to be gifted both books by the author in exchange for my review, as they had been mentioned several times from friends and added to my tbr list. this was another simple, but sweet love story with memorable characters and an engaging story line. i really liked both gage and cassie. sarah curtis does a great job of writing strong alpha type heroes that are also very sweet and not jerks to the heroines. i never doubted gage's love for cassie. i enjoyed their love story! it was so refreshingly angst-free. as in the first book in the series, i really enjoyed that the problems they faced were not from each other, but from outside forces, and that they were able to face those problems together head on. i truly felt their connection and am looking forward to reading more from this author!

title: ['Forbidden']
cleaned_reviews: i don't know how to begin this review... because there's so many things that i want to say about this book but i want to say them as coherently as i can so anyone reading will understand. understand that this book is not a happy read. understand that this book is heartbreaking. i want to say them coherently so anyone reading won't get the wrong message and they won't miss out on a book they may have potentially loved but they decided not to read it just because they don't understand what they may get into, so they don't feel like it's worth it. "you can close your eyes to the things you do not want to see, but you cannot close your heart to the things you do not want to feel." this... is one controversial book. it deals with the matter of incest and family abuse and neglect. lochan and maya have never really felt like brother and sister- as said on the excerpt of this book- and as they're taking care of their three younger siblings because their mom has an alcoholic problem and clings to the past of when she never dreamed of having children, so why should she be punished for having them now, lochan and maya develop a relationship bordering beyond the sibling relationship. this book takes place in the uk and taking the descriptions from the book and what i've seen from my good show, just as equally controversial, skins-- the setting of this book was perfect. i imagined gray clouds, heavy air, and rainy days to coalesce with the onerous whitely family life. this book also is read through the perspective of alternating povs between maya and lochan. now given, in the larger chunk of the first half of the book lochan is mentioned more than maya. lochan's distress of being the "man of the house" since he was twelve years old, his painful relationship with younger brother tiffin who disobeys him and runs tensions deeper into the ground, and lochan's problem of engaging in human interaction anywhere outside of his home as his anxiety builds and he tears himself away from friends and relationships. forbidden is definitely about the tragedy of lochan and maya-- but if you are considering reading this book. do not expect to see the author putting effort into developing both maya and lochan's character equally. lochan's chapters are typically longer and then when taking place in maya's chapters- she is usually thinking of lochan. because yes this story is about these two people, but lochan's really the main character. his struggle and his pain is what drives this book to continue as he is the weight sinking in the ocean, and maya is the desperate buoy trying to keep him afloat, farthest away from the bottom as she can. "being together, we harm nobody; being apart, we extinguish ourselves." without spoiling anything though, in the end. it was all sensible to radiate lochan's character over maya's. and for that, tabitha suzuma deserves no less than five stars for this book. "finally, too weak to keep her from my thoughts any longer, i think of maya. maya, maya, maya. i choke her name into my hands, hoping that the sound of her name will bring me some comfort. i never, ever should have taken such terrible risk with her happiness. for her sake, for the children's sakes, i should never have allowed our relationship to develop. i cannot regret it for myself-- there is nothing i wouldn't have endured just for the few months we had together. but i never thought about the danger to her, the horror she would be forced to undergo." her genius and brilliancy in writing and story telling all contribute to how much i loved this book and to how it is one i will never forget easily. incestuous relationships and family abuse are not topics for the light-hearted. and i am the light-hearted. i don't like horror movies, i'm afraid of heights, the vast ocean makes me uncomfortable, and i am able to single-handedly give myself a panic attack by simply psyching myself out and making myself believe that i am not safe and that i am not alone. whenever i am in a hotel and i hear a child crying behind the next door, only to then hear a sudden crash followed by the absence of crying-- i may make the worst possibly scenario in my mind, but i still cringe, panic, and run. because family abuse is something i am uncomfortable confronting. so reading this novel and reading how a mother can neglect her children so selfishly, not acting her age at the expense of young and innocent people she brought into this world, it definitely hit close to my heart. then there's the incest. with the matter of incest- i am less uncomfortable with it. in fact. i am so comfortable with it that it's almost like i can't imagine it. naturally as a human and someone who's grown up in a household with a large set of older brothers and younger sisters, i think it's unimaginable; incest. it's not that i'm offended by it, but by my own upbringing, i can't open myself to it. and that's how i approach it how lots of people approach gay people and lesbians. "they can like whoever they want, as long as it's not me." that statement is probably the most overlooked, misunderstood, and offensive statement i've ever heard. people say "they" referring to gays and lesbians as if they are not normal people, but a completely different race-- deserving them the title of "they", distinguishing difference. people say this statement with smiles and warm glows because it actually is intentional to be welcoming to someone's differences. and people-- people do not realize that with this statement, even though they are claiming they open themselves to this idea of "taboo" and "sin", they are still continuing the trend of ostracizing a group of people because of "socially unacceptable" differences-- the only difference being is that they've tricked themselves into believing that they are welcoming. those people are welcoming to a limited extent and they are hiding behind their warm- hearted claims so they don't have to actually confront the issue and think about it fully. i similarly approach the idea of incest like this because i happily read books about incestuous relationships. and i happily tell everyone that if i actually witnessed an incestuous relationship, then i would be welcoming because they are allowed to love whoever they want to love. but that still doesn't excuse the fact that i have actually not given this topic much thought because it's so foreign to me, and that if i actually did see an incestuous relationship. perhaps i would be welcoming and accepting. but in the initial moments, i would still look upon them like curious kids looking through glass windows at zoos, watching rare specimen. being particularly interested in these beings , naturally, because they are not a generality. and for breaching beyond the borders of generalities with a topic so strong that it's shaken reader's hearts ; that's why this book deserves well above five stars. no matter what opinions you have about the matter of incest, this book makes you fall in love with lochan and maya. hoping with every turn page that things will work out because that's what you desperately hope for and that is what you desperately need. this book is not for the weak= hearted as it's a tear jerker. throwing emotions and events at you until they finally reach it's peak and you are spent and exhausted. but i take it back. this book is not for the weak-hearted. but perhaps for the light-hearted. it's absolutely perfect. happy readings folks -zoe ps. okay. so basically this is what i thought of when thinking of lochan and thinking of maya. :'3 :lochan :maya

title: ['Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter']
cleaned_reviews: wow this was a fun book! i'm really excited now about the movie coming out in june 2012 and can't wait to see the differences and how they built on the characters. my favorite part about this novel was the fact that it read like a true story from the use of all the old photographs and they way the author fit in the historical time line so well to "explain" how vampires have really messed with the world's history throughout the centuries. after being raised in life to view history class as the worst possible thing due to the huge textbooks and never reading past the industrial revolution because we were too busy reading about the greeks and romans, this book made history actually interesting! it was fun to learn about the different battles and what lincoln did during his tenure as president along with the fun fictional vampire storyline. overall highly recommended it to my friends who were looking for a fun but different kind of book to read this summer.

title: ['The Fixer (The Fixer, #1)']

title: ['Soulless (Parasol Protectorate, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this book was recommended to me by a woman at the farmer's market i work at, and i wish i could find her again and hug her. i loved this so much. mixing victorian england with the supernatural is just the tip of the iceburg, here. i love alexia tarabotti. she's got so much spirit. how can you not love a heroine like that? then, conall maccon is impossible not to fall madly in love with. he's hot. he's charming in the way that only a hot grumpy man can be. he's a werewolf. hell yeah. their love story is charming and, even though i totally saw it coming, it was adorable to watch it happen. plus, how much fun is it to see the 26 year-old spinster get married to a high society earl with her family, that finds her mostly a nuisance, watching. in your faces! i love the outrageous and flamboyant vampire. the sterotypical, society concerned mother and step-sisters. the kind and efficient side kick. the silly and concerned best friend. the evil scientists! ah! this was just such a kick ass book!

title: ['Redshirts']
cleaned_reviews: i'm a huge meta-fic fan. when it's done well, there's nothing quite like it. and this was done well. very well done. extremely well done. done right up there with fforde's thursday series. the first half of the book is enjoyable and even laugh out loud funny at times--it even has a head-bomb explosion. you've gotta love a book that features a head-bomb! the second half is not so funny, but still a good solid meta-fic read. the come the last codas. i was a bit concerned that the first, second, and third person conceit was going to be little more than that--a conceit. the first was ok. the second a bit better. but the third. my oh my! the book was worth reading if for nothing more than getting to the last coda. i rarely give 5-stars*, but this ending definitely deserves it. brilliant! *after letting this simmer for a few days, i've decided to demote it to 4-stars. five stars should be reserved for something along the lines of "remains of the day", and although this is good...it's not rotd good.

title: ["Rosemary's Baby"]

title: ["Lament: The Faerie Queen's Deception (Books of Faerie, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: well, it feels like the dagger on the front cover pierced through my heart. this book was so much more than i expected it to be. i expected it to be stiefvater's worst novel, considering it's her first and this series is her least popular. no. i actually liked this more than the wolves of mercy falls, because i feel like there was so much romance (not that there is necessarily anything wrong with romance) in wolves of mercy falls that it didn't balance out the fantasy aspects of it very well. lament balanced romance and fantasy beautifully. luke wasn't nearly as creepy as i expected. of course, i didn't like this nearly as much as the raven boys series, and remember loving the scorpio races more than this. i love how stiefvater has a common theme in her books of something paranormal getting in the way of a very passionate romance (even though it kills me every time) and there are parts in her writing that are just so her.. like it's wonderful how unique she is. i did have problems with the love triangle, and thought it was super cliche how james loved deirdre, and not only that, but ballad is apparently though james's perspective, which makes me so mad because i didn't like him. i loved deirdre so much and could really relate to her. i would have savored this book more if i realized the next one wouldn't be through her perspective. the ending killed me. i didn't cry or anything, but it killed me. maggie stiefvater has really grown as an author too, and it's cool to see how she started. there are some flaws of course, like the beginning of the book was really rushed and there were some things described that could get confusing. but the celtic lore was so great, because whenever i read anything with authentic celtic mythology, i feel so.... at home somehow. i feel in touch with my celtic ancestors. the fantasy aspect of this novel was very neat, not anything spectacular, but i really appreciated the celtic mythology. i did like this book a lot, though, and don't at all regret picking it up.

title: ['Cinder (The Lunar Chronicles, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i really loved this series. the way the author adapts the different fairy tales to a dystopian science-fiction story involving moon colonization and cyborgs is seamless and clever. the nods to the original stories are subtle and never pulled me out of the story, and the characters are far more than fairy tale stand-ins. there is a richness to the world-building especially-i want to learn more about the history of how our version of earth becomes the version in this series-but also in terms of theme. just the fact that all of the books are titled after the woman each book is focused on, except for fairest, which contains levana's backstory, is incredibly telling. (and i love how fairest creates such a complex character in levana, without demanding that we pity her, and without using her experiences to justify her actions. someone can be mistreated and take responsibility for her actions-and make better choices-and the series overall takes that position. i think that is far more complex than a lot of other "villain's point of view" books, which i feel tend to excuse the villain's actions.) despite the large cast of characters-many of whom are protagonists in their own rights-and how much is going on in terms of plot, none of the books feel bloated. in fact, i actually found the writing to be pretty effective, and the pacing works really well. there could be a little more subtext, but that is a personal preference, and there is already a lot of symbolism. if you're looking for female-led science-fiction (so many female characters) with poc characters, read this series. this is a series i would have loved in 4th or 5th grade, when i started reading more science-fiction and had a hard time finding books in the genre that were about women (and that also appealed to a kid that age).

title: ['The Faerie Guardian (Creepy Hollow, #1)']

title: ['Tiger Lily']
cleaned_reviews: i really have to give some heavy props to jodi lynn anderson. tiger lily was an excellent read. i loved how she brought these fantastical characters down to earth and made the plot so much more realistic. the idea that neverland was an actual island somewhere of the coast of god knows where instead of some distant star made the story that much more believable to me. the characterizations were absolutely flawless. i loved how stoic tiger lily was from the very beginning and that it made her tribe look at her as almost an outsider. the idea that she was some kind of crow goddess and that it terrified them was especially funny. and it made the fact that being with peter made her laugh just that more significant. tik tok and pine sap were great additions to the tribe. i just wished i could have seen more of moon eye and what her reaction was to giant's "mysterious" death. peter was perfectly executed from the get-go. all of his layers of bravado, cockiness, charm, and deep seated fear are all beautifully rendered. he's a boy who wants to be a man, but needs someone who will encourage him, the way wendy is portrayed to. i loved anderson's explanation to peter's secret of flight. the lost boys were the perfect companions for him. i especially loved nibs. the point of view through tinker bell was very well done. i loved all of the little nuances, like her love for peter, but knowing he'll never love her back and putting her ear to his chest just to hear his heart beat. so sweet. and i loved that she wasn't torturing wendy for her own sake but to protect tiger lily. the little moments like how she drinks water from the rose petal or how she explains how her father left for another fairy were so lovely. the only problem i had was that the third person/first person shifts threw me off from time to time. the plot was very well paced for the length of the book, but i felt like i was missing some of the peter/tiger lily relationship because of the limited point of view. i didn't see how their relationship could have developed so fast. and if she felt so strongly, even if he did fall for wendy, i didn't believe she would betray peter the way she does. thus, the 4 star rating. but overall, i thoroughly enjoyed anderson's storytelling and i would absolutely recommend this one to my friends and fellow peter pan fanatics.

title: ['The Bone Season (The Bone Season, #1)']

title: ['Moonraker (James Bond, #3)']

title: ['Wolf Hall (Thomas Cromwell, #1)', 'The Sense of an Ending']
cleaned_reviews: this one takes close concentration and effort. mantel's writing here is so dense that you have to constantly pay attention to figure out who is speaking and being described. when in doubt, it's the protagonist, cromwell. that being said, this is worth the effort. it is slow at times and the pacing does seem a bit too drawn out occasionally, but it's still highly worth the read. it not only defuses formerly-held beliefs you may have had about the reign of henry viii (thomas more was not the sympathetic objector portrayed in "a man for all seasons" and he certainly was no saint), but it also presents an interesting portrait of a man who is somewhat in the shadows of history but was front and center at the time. i read this almost in one sitting, so it's quite engrossing and very readable. its unique meditation on the nature of memory, aging, and life's tricky subtext make it clear why it won the booker prize. i've tried to read barnes in the past and haven't been successful, but this is one that was mostly a joy to read.

title: ['The Carnivorous Carnival (A Series of Unfortunate Events, #9)']
cleaned_reviews: and so the plot thickens. "the carnivorous carnival" was everything i had hoped and waited for since i began reading the series. lemony snicket finally fulfills the great potential of these books, and they rise to become something entirely extraordinary. finally the story evolves into something darker, bending into an extreme degree of absurdism and morbidity. and suddenly the story ceases to be a tale of three sad orphans running from an evil count with only one eyebrow - somehow the story evolves to become an exploration of dysfunctional adults in a world that is ruled by bloodlust and a greedy desire to watch other people's failures in order to feel comfortable about oneself. and what i loved most of all, was the point which explained how suppressed, lonely and neglected outcasts will do just about anything to be accepted into society. even if it means killing an innocent woman.

title: ['Dark Places', 'Veronika Decides to Die']

title: ['This is Not a Test (This is Not a Test #1)', 'Forever Mine (The Moreno Brothers, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: life is not a test. you only have one and it's the only one you get. this is not a test is, by far, the best courtney summers book i have read, it was amazing in a way i cannot even describe. it had the signature courtney summers writing, with troubled characters that go far beyond your average in ya books, and she always goes beyond the surface. this is not a test is the story of six students that are trapped inside their school while the zombie apocalypse happens outside - wow, what a way to destroy a story, i just made it sound like some cheap friday night movie. i swear to you the story is way better that i just made it sound. it's funny though, because these characters are finding it hard to hold on to something when they are just stuck inside their school. they are never going anywhere, not really. they're just waiting for their death. but when you really think about it, you're stuck in this planet, with really nowhere to go, except around the sun, over and over, waiting to die. funny, huh? maybe they are not exactly living, they are waiting, surviving. they say you can be alive but not living, and i fully understand what that means; but, again, if you give a lot of thought to it, we're always waiting, waiting to finish college and start our lives, waiting for christmas, waiting in line in mcdonald's so they can take our order. we're constantly waiting, and, in fact, we are surviving. in a different way, but we are. and once we start getting all philosophical you realize that pretty much nothing has a point. why do my homework if i'm gonna die one day? why follow the rules of society to end 6 feet under ground? in fact, why do anything? everything looses it's value when you start with this train of though, and really, if you dwell too much on it, it'll simply drive you insane. but why? why do we go to school? why do we fight for good jobs and to get a new car, to get the tv, the ipad, why do we bother to try and fit in? why? and that, ladies and gentleman, is what this is not a test is about, courtney summers portrays a character that is done with why's, that cannot find the answers she is looking for and it's completely hopeless, until she's surrounded by people that have nothing else to cling to expect that - hope. and just how far would you go for your own survival? would you sacrifice yourself for someone? or would you sacrifice someone else in order to save yourself? and who decides? all of this is not answered until the very last page of this book, and, like all courtney summer's books, it left me breathless. her stories all come in a nice white box, that once opened, whatever they bring inside, hits you with an incredible force that it simply rocks your world, then, like a friend of mine said, they are closed and neatly tied with a pink ribbon. one word to describe this book: flawless. a satisfying ending. the story was everything i hoped for and more. hard-core courtney summers fan right here. if i could go around the streets shoving this book down people's throats, i would. a must read. http://inbetweenwritingandreading.blo... oh my god i loved this book!!! it was amazing!! i'll stop gushing and go to the point: reading the plot you can immediately associate it with the perfect chemistry novels by simone elkeles. good girl falls in love with trouble mexican boy. yes, they do share this in common but they also could have not been more different. angel - main character of forever mine - is a mexican boy that doesn't know spanish xd and he is a good guy, just a little bit of a don juan - he goes out with a few lotta girls - but when a girl with sad green eyes enters his life, everything changes. meet sarah, who just came to live to la jolla in san diego - i spend most of my time there :d!! - because of some problems her mother's in, she's determined not to get too attached to things because as soon as she can she goes back to arizona to live with his best friend sydney. but obviously things never go as planned. she's soon completely and hopelessly in love with angel moreno. but still, there are things both have to work out and discover that it is not easy to come clean and also to forgive. angel and sarah's relationship goes really quick, too quick i'd say. i wasn't buying it, but then they date more and more and more and some more and you just can't help but thing they are perfect for each other. the story is predictable - you can tell how things are going just by the summary - but it still takes some twist and turns you just don't see coming and how things unraveled is just beautiful. but i really think that what makes this novel so strong and powerful is the support characters. they are all just so beautiful and unique that they all make a chain. you take one out, everything breaks. eric, the voice of reason and - in angel's words - dumb. romero, the one that always gets drunk and says stupid yet hilarious things - in angel's words - dumber. alex, moreno bother number 2, total flirt, hot 'till the ends, sparks definitely fly. sydney, sarah's bff and her voice of reason, he'll always have her back. valerie, fearless and she's part of sarah's straight. sofia, she adds the spark and also becomes your best friend. and of course there's sarah, she's so much worth than what she gives credit to herself and angel, whom is determined to show her her beauty and also he's afraid of what he feel, but is still giving it all to sarah; he can be sometimes possessive and goes into "macho" mode, but he learns to loosen up. if you love romance, some romance, a little bit of romance and some more romance, this is the book for you. i loved it. i recommend it. i gush about it. i loved it. :dd! title: ['Being Jazz: My Life as a (Transgender) Teen', 'The Name of the Wind (The Kingkiller Chronicle, #1)', 'Landline', 'Brideshead Revisited: The Sacred and Profane Memories of Captain Charles Ryder']
cleaned_reviews: not sure i'm going to write a full review of this, but it's definitely a good (quick) read. definitely a young adult memoir (meaning adults might find it simplistic). and though it is ghostwritten, jazz's voice comes through really clear (she's so young! i do not miss being a teenager). she's honest and confident about what her life has been like. this book would be a great way for younger readers to learn about transgender issues, and to develop empathy for people who are gender non-conforming or who identify on the lgtbqia spectrum (not to mention, of course, it's a great resource for transgender children themselves). i hope jazz writes another book, though, when she's older. i was obviously not the target audience for this book. it would be really interesting to see what kind of book she would write after she's got a few more decades in her. i have a feeling it would be great. march 2011: after re-reading it in preparation for the wise man's fear, there are five things i want to say about the name of the wind: 1. it was just as engrossing [?] if not more so [?] the second time. i found myself eagerly looking forward to parts i didn't even know were coming the first time around. 2. it struck me this time through how young kvothe is. the first time, as soon as he hit the university, i began picturing him as a young man of seventeen or eighteen, and all of his actions were colored through that lens, but he was still just fifteen. he just speaks so much older than that, that my mind automatically pictures this confident, handsome redhead. picturing him accurately really affected the way that i saw the rest of the book unfold (not in a bad way, mind you). more like, wow. you're just a kid. wow. 3. this in turn led me to a whole new realization that there is so much more story for me to read, and some of it is currently sitting on top of my bookshelf. (you guys: don't let me start that book until next friday at 4 pm. otherwise i will fail my master's exams.) 4. i like to randomly capitalize things like kirstie alley. 5. number five is something i'm surprised i didn't mention in my first review, although i kind of mentioned it when i talked about running around and screaming and throwing up and such (i cringe whenever i re-read that first review, btw . . . you guys don't even know how many times i've almost deleted it; there's just something about it i'm not happy with). number five is about music. simply put, the name of the wind is the one and only book i've ever read (and i have read so many fucking books, you guys), that has ever portrayed in words the way that i feel about music. i don't know how rothfuss did it, that fucker. even if you don't like fantasy or magic or love stories or revenge stories or growing up stories or school stories . . . read this book for the music. capiche? march 2009: this is a hard review to write for such an easy-to-read book. i'm going to preface this review by saying that i haven't read a book this fast or this hard (that's what she said) since harry potter and the deathly hallows. i'm also going to say that i only have one criteria for how many stars i give a book: how many feelings it can make me feel. and not bad feelings, mind you, like anger or frustration, good feelings like suspense and nervousness and love and, well, everything the characters are feeling. no book is perfect, this one certainly isn't, but i loved it, and that's enough for me. por ejemplo, there's this scene in the middle of the book when kvothe is attempting to prove himself, and i had to put down the book and run around my room screaming for a little because the scene was making me so nervous i was getting sick to my stomach. that's how you know it's the good shit. let me explain even further. pat rothfuss was doing something different in writing this book. he has broken all the rules, or rather, he doesn't care about them and he admits as much in the book itself. "we have all the groundwork now. a foundation of a story to build upon," says kvothe, our hero, at the end of 653 pages. that's something you'd expect to hear around page 100 if this were a normal book. but no, this book doesn't follow the traditional story arc. it is a rambling biography of a man who is lost, told in his own voice. it is subjective and flawed. it is also only the beginning of the story. there are two more (yet-to-be-published) books in the kingkiller chronicle, so instead of thinking of this as one book, you should more accurately be thinking of it as part one in a giant big ass novel. if you're not feeling closure after you finish this book, that's okay, he's only just begun. if that doesn't sound like something you're interested in, then stay away, but if you feel like pulling the stick out of your butt and trying something new, this comes highly recommended. [also, i would like to state that i wish i hadn't read it so soon because now i have to wait for books two and three. dammit.:] updated september 6, 2014: ugh, trying to write about each successive rainbow rowell novel gets more and more difficult. how many different ways are there to say this was so good. her words are so good. her characters so good. everything good. relate so much. help. that's pretty much all i feel like saying, because even over a month later, my feelings about this book are so jumbly wumbly it's hard to get them to sit still long enough to make them cohesive enough to write about. granted, having never been married and never had a serious vocation like our main character georgie mccool does, i don't relate quite as much to this book as i have in her previous efforts (fangirl and attachments in particular). but there's just something about the way rainbow rowell writes about emotions that makes me instantly think yes i recognize that. it's like her books are the story versions of falling in love or making an instant connection with a person. like, those rare instances where you meet someone and you just instantly know them. i've only had that happen a couple of times in my life, which is probably part of why i love reading her so much. just completely disregard the silly sounding plot with the time traveling phone. it's not important. it's just another way to explore the dynamics between people we care about, and how relationships can change and evolve, how we lose and find each other over and over again, how we have to commit to the relationships that are important to us. (although, honestly, i think that kind of silly shit is incredibly cool.) definitely glad i own this in hardcover, and i'm sure i will be revisiting it over and over in years to come, just like i plan to do with all her other books. rainbow rowell, why can't i quit you!?!? (also, please don't stop writing these wonderful books. please don't ever stop.) updated july 30, 2014: guh. why is she so good at writing books i love. full review later. june 2013: this doesn't sound like something i would necessarily pick up on my own, but i will read anything rainbow rowell writes, regardless of topic or genre. the list of authors i will do that for is not very large. i have lots of favorite books by authors i like, books i would probably stab people over (not really, just metaphorical stabbing), but a lot of those authors have also written books i will never read. but these authors? i love them and their words so much i don't even care. it goes like this: rowling, gaiman, dahl, sanderson, green, rothfuss, rowell. that? is trust. i can see how this would be a five star book for a lot of people, i'm just not one of them. me and waugh, we're not on the same wavelength. he was a pessimist who thought human society was basically doomed to artifice and meaninglessness, and i'm . . . not.

title: ['Catching Fire (The Hunger Games, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: why i read this trilogy: i was part of the small group of people who had yet to read these books. i don't know what i was waiting for exactly but once the movie came out, i knew i had to jump on them. so i did. finally. now i can proudly shout from the rooftops that i have read the hunger games! and i have totally book bullied my in-laws into reading these books. what i liked: from the moment we meet katniss, i connected with her. i was on her side and will forever be in her corner. she's put in one helluva position and comes out a winner, in more ways than one. the premise for this trilogy is pretty disturbing. it's kids killing kids in a 'fight to the death' tournament. if that, in itself, isn't an indicator of how dark and dreary these books are, i don't know what is. but as disturbing as it sounds, the author did a good job of not overwhelming the reader with blood, guts, and gore. the shock value is that this, the actual hunger games itself, is considered to be a form of 'entertainment' for the people in the capitol. and that blows me away. the world building was phenomenal. it was so rich in detail and the author has mastered the craft of showing this world she created without an overuse of words. here's an example of this clear and concise word magic i'm speaking of: the stew doesn't taste bad, but there's a certain sliminess that's hard to get around. like you have to swallow every bite three times before it really goes down. these books were fascinating and occupied all my spare time. sure, there were parts that made me raging mad - like when the hunger games officials added a new rule only to later retract it - and made me want to throw my kindle against the wall. it was infuriating but i was totally engrossed in the story. what i didn't like: am i the only one who finds peeta's name amusing? he's a baker, he bakes bread. peeta. bread. peeta (pita) bread. i had some issues with mockingjay. it's not that i didn't like that book, because i did, but i had some problems with it. three specific problems to be precise. i'm going to be vague to avoid spoilers. 1. the character who dies at the capitol - are you freaking kidding me?!! after all that has happened, after all everyone has been through, and that character dies?!! this, i wasn't prepared for. at all. i was prepared for (and expecting) other characters to die (whom end up surviving the entire ordeal) but i wasn't prepared for this death. i cried and i was pissed. 2. the way the [important event that takes place but shall not be named to prevent spoilers] ends is ... inadequate, to say the least. there was a huge void there for me. 3. the ultimate ending. there's a decision that's made and i feel like that the person who should have made that decision was robbed of that. it felt like the character robbed of that decision settled with what was decided. memorable moments: gale is mine. i am his. anything else is unthinkable. --- "real or not real?" --- "katniss will pick whoever she thinks she can't survive without." overall impression: the hunger games trilogy was an emotionally draining read but an incredible one at that. i had dreams about these books and the characters from the moment i began reading it. it just has that haunting affect that bleeds into your mind and lingers there. even weeks after i finished reading the trilogy, my mind was still abuzz. i couldn't get it out of my head. i give 5 stars for the hunger games, 4 stars for catching fire, and 3 stars for mockingjay. and just for the record, i'm team katniss because at the end of the day, it's all about her.

title: ['On Broken Wings (Wild Aces, #3)']

title: ['1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus']
cleaned_reviews: there is a lot of good stuff in this book, and i'm afraid i'm going to forget most of it. (i'll remember the gist, of course, but i want to remember the supporting evidence, too!) the gist: - there were many, many more indigenous people in north and south america than early colonists thought. - indigenous americans had large, complex societies. - despite how different these societies were, what they all have in common is obliteration by european disease. the diseases raced ahead of the europeans themselves, so by the time europeans and their descendants reached certain parts of the americas, there were few native people left. - native people sculpted the land they lived on. the "pristine, untouched" wilderness we think existed did not exist. if anything, europeans created it when their diseases removed native americans and their control of the landscape. - the concept of liberty in the american constitution may be the result of native influence (the haudenosaunee in particular; indigenous societies were quite diverse in their cultural practices). this is a well-written book overall. it meandered at times, but i enjoyed it.

title: ['What You Left Behind', "All the Truth That's in Me"]
cleaned_reviews: so... this book was one of the rare few that have really pulled me in lately. in the beginning, it was anger and irritation. how could our protagonist repeatedly wish his child hadn't been born? how could he continuously insist that he would've preferred his child be aborted? how could he swear that if he could go back and change things, he wouldn't miss a beat? i'm so spoiled by the feel-good ya that is so popular recently that i didn't even realize that this is a very real reaction to a less than wonderful situation; 17 year old ryden has become a teen father, and on the same day that his girlfriend and mother of his child, meg, dies due to cancer. his dreams of going to ucla on a soccer scholarship and going pro seem shattered; he's got to go to high school, attend regular soccer practices, work part time, and raise an infant as a single dad. this is not to say he had to go it alone; he had help from his mother (more on her later) and alan, meg's best friend. regardless, it's no wonder he is resentful and bitter. however, the book does show a great example of character development with ryden. so i won't complain too much about that. what i will complain about is this: joni is a manic pixie dream girl. she has quirks and is different than the other girls and shows ryden the better side of life. in the beginning, i found her to be incredibly childish and inappropriate. i hated that this would be his love interest. over the course of the book, i didn't have her so much but let it be known that i still don't like her all that much. i also didn't like meg like i should've at the end; i think she was insane. she had unjust motives and was selfish. she was obsessive and she lied. so boo for her. what i loved? the relationship between ryden and his mother. she was there for him as a mother and a friend, whenever each was needed. she was a shoulder to cry and the foot when someone had to put their foot down. she was stern but supportive, kind and understanding, and really made me connect. so the beginning of this book, i give a three. the end is a five. averaged, this book deserves a 4 star rating. i can't explain it. with the first few pages i was sure i was going to hate it. i wasn't used to the more mature and proper vocabulary, and second person pov, and all the sections. and it takes place sometime around 1850-1870 i imagine? so many things working against it but my god if i didn't absolutely love it. it was so refreshing from what i usually read. very good.

title: ['A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: it took me long enough to jump on the game of thrones bandwagon. i never thought i would read this book. i always said i wasn't the kind of person who read fantasy. it was never my style. then i watched the hbo series and loved it. i loved the drama and how so many of the episodes left me with a "wtf?!?!" reaction at the end of each show. it was watching that first season that made me want to start reading the books. this is one of the few books that i'm glad i read after seeing the movie/tv show. having a basis for the plot helped me keep the characters straight and remember what was happening. it also made me all the more appreciative how well the show captured the overall feeling of the book and stuck to the plot so well. there are things that bothered me about the book, of course. martin can be a little long winded at times, writes really awkward sex scenes, and doesn't seem to know any synonyms for joke other than "jape". even so, the book is an enjoyable read. can't wait to read the second book and watch the second season of the show.

title: ["The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: i don't usually read fictional comedies. i like movie and tv comedies, i like funny biographies and listening to hours of podcasts. i like novels that have funny characters mixing up the pace and making me burst into laughter. but not novels that are centered around being a comedy. for whatever reason it's hard for me to get swept into the fictional world if the narration isn't taking itself seriously, constantly giving me a wink and a nudge. even so, i rather enjoyed this. inventive, insightful, and made me chuckle aloud more than a few times. a fair amount of quotable lines to be found in here, for sure. if you're a fan of comedic novels and cheeky humor and sci-fi, you will probably love this book. 3.5 stars. would have given it a full 4 if it was longer. it ended a bit abruptly, to my taste. maybe i'll check out the sequel one of these days.

title: ['Point of Retreat (Slammed, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: will and lake's story is just so real. although it should be hard to believe all that tragic stuff could happen to the same two people, the author accomplishes to write it in a simple but beautiful way, so that it is as real as it's written. my favorite details about this book are the way their relationship evolves with the hardships, as every human relationship does. it's incredible to find a story that i love so much as this one. i began reading it today, just after i finished slammed, and i can tell i was really enthusiast after reading the first one. i knew i would love this one too. i'm not sure if there is really a need for another book. point of retreat's ending seems like a great finale for the story, but i know i will begin reading this girl tomorrow. what i highlight about this one, though, should be that it mantained the reality factor which made me fall for slammed, that it surprised me from the beggining, and how colleen manages to change the perspective of the story so perfectly. pd: i think i'll do an origami-star advice vase, such a good idea!

title: ['Sandman Slim (Sandman Slim, #1)']
