this girl, phoebe, is basically someone i know. i've been her, and i know a few other girls like her. the author did a really good job capturing the life of a serious bookworm, or excuse me, a book dragon. i'm guessing isabel bandeira is one herself. phoebe's book-influenced hobbies, the arts and crafts at school, the can't-talk-about-anything-else-but-no-one-wants-to-hear-it, the attending book signings and events in costume, and of course, the too distracted reading all the time. she is spot on. then there's the story. it it definitely interesting. phoebe lives her life, first and foremost. the purely high school events come slowly (timewise, not plotwise), as in real life. phoebe struggles through her attraction to two different boys, her mistakes, and the awkward situations she walks into. phoebe is phoebe, a teen with her head in the clouds. dev is pretty longsuffering, though he has his own set of flaws and mistakes. there isn't much else to say. the book is as it sounds - the story of a girl looking for her happily ever after in books rather than real life but finding it in the latter. i enjoyed it, and i think that anyone who enjoys books as much as phoebe (and i) do, will appreciate this take. i received a complementary copy of this book. all opinions are my own. cute story! i love mermaids, and i can't seem to find many good mermaid books. this one was pretty good, and i'll read the rest of the series soon. <3 but i want more mermaid books! maybe i should write one... any ideas?

title: ['The Bro-Magnet (Nice Guy, #1)', 'Waiting for the Flood']
cleaned_reviews: i started this with some trepidation, because humor based on gender stereotypes is rarely my thing. it sounded fun though, so i gave it a try -- and it turned out to be a lot of fun, as well as sweet and unexpectedly wise. johnny is a really good guy, who somehow rarely gets credit for his stellar qualities from women. the traits that other men love in him, like being good at sports and able to fix junker cars, always seem to lead women to one conclusion: "asshole. " they rarely notice that he's considerate, generous, warm-hearted, chivalrous and at least makes an effort to remember to put the seat back down. when johnny meets a woman who seems like she might just possibly like him, he's determined not to mess it up this time. and seeking advice from pretty much anyone who'll give it, he performs a make-over, becoming "john" (because "y" ending names are too little-boyish) who likes wine instead of beer and opera instead of sports. what happens next is partially incredibly obvious and partially a real surprise. this is a light story -- lighthearted, lightly characterized, lightly over-the-top. the beginning description of johnny's adolescence, in his first-person narrative, made me feel like i was reading ya -- and actually i think young adults could love this story. (there's some swearing but no graphic sex.) it's very funny in a wry sort of way, and though there is some ridiculous situational humor, it's not what entirely drives the book: in one memorable scene, john takes his date to an opera that turns out to be put on by a farm family in a hayloft, but they just go with it and have a really good time. i think what i liked best about the story is that it's essentially non-judgmental. although johnny's "manly," low-brow tastes are embraced, he discovers he actually likes some of the new things he's tried -- but more importantly, he discovers that "things like who loves sports and who loves gh (general hospital) and who loves both... none of that stuff mattered so long as, somehow, you saw down into the essence of the other person and they saw you." it's hard to categorize this book: it's not traditional romance, not exactly ya, certainly not realistic fiction. its most obvious category is humor. but i think romance readers will also enjoy it; i certainly did. (reviewed from e-arc provided by netgalley) disclosure: the author and i are friendly online. e-arc provided by netgalley. i think this novella is hall's first contemporary romance since glitterland, and i'm happy for the return, being more into serious contemporaries than fantasy. it's not a sequel, though there's a small hint that it's set in the same world. edwin has a complicated relationship with his home. he loves the house, but his love stemmed from the life he envisioned sharing in it: "from the moment i saw it, i saw us. i saw us in every room: talking, touching, sharing. i saw it all, but as it turned out, i saw only my dreams." since his lover left him, he's been marking time -- leaving the holes left by the things marius took with him, staying out of spaces that are too painful to be in. but now a flood threatens him and his neighbors, and edwin is forced out of passivity. this is a quiet, tender story about rebirth after grief, with the flood providing poignant symbolism -- as well as an opportunity for edwin to meet a charming civil engineer named adam. i empathized with the domestic homebody edwin, who has to learn to appreciate himself again. though my favorite character may be his former sort-of mother-in-law, who still regards him as a son, telling him, "family is really just whoever sticks around." (curiously enough, my main quibble with the book also involves this character, who is described as indiscriminately using lol in texts, including "uncle teddy dead lol." it irks me when urban legends/jokes are incorporated into fiction.) i like adam and the romance too, but i think it was the atmosphere and elegant prose that really won me over.

cleaned_reviews: i'm usually either overwhelmed or bored by science (even popular science), but that didn't happen with this book. the blend of science, history, and human interest was compelling (i couldn't put the book down) and thought-provoking. i've heard complaints that the author put herself too much into the story, but i actually think that was one of the book's strengths. skloot's perspective mirrors that of the readers - outsiders who unearth the story little by little. a more removed narration would've diminished the extent to which henrietta's story has been hidden and the arduous research necessary to uncover and share it. highly recommended.

its pages, its slower pacing lets you explore the dark, grimy world of this bleak future. the atmosphere, love triangle, the kisses, the unexpected twists--all these things kept me turning the pages and left me craving the sequel. while the end seemed a bit anti-climatic, the book overall worked its magic and cast a spell over my whole reading experience. i will definitely be first in line for the sequel next april. last year, eve was one of my favorite dystopian stories. something about eve's fierce nature combined with her "girly" one worked for me and created a character that i felt like i connected with. i enjoyed her adventures and gradual "awakening" (of sorts) to the realities of the world that she lived in. in my review last year, i ended saying "this book is a fabulous combination of action and sweet romance with an ending that will leave you speechless (and if you're like me, in tears)." obviously once was high on my list of sequels to read in 2012 and i'm happy to say that (thankfully) it lived up to all of my expectations. picking up a few months later, once begins with eve living in califia. while it's not the haven that she expected, she's safe there and when arden shows up unexpectedly, things are looking up. however, a series of events leads to eve and arden running away from califia--but the escape doesn't go well and they end up separated: arden back to the "trade school" and eve carted off to the city. the unexpected twists that happen from then on out are something for you to discover on your own but suffice it to say that i was surprised and blown away by the events that ms. carey threw my way. while eve is still a bit naive in her understanding of the world, i felt like she developed a lot through this story (both in eve and continuing in once). the world has thrown her a lot of curve balls and she's still standing--still fighting. she has a strength of character that i sort of admired. she's fiercely loyal to her friends (her real friends) and she's most definitely a survivor. i loved watching her relationship with caleb develop in little bits and pieces (my only regret being that we didn't get to see more of him) and her exploration of the things that the school told her were wrong and forbidden. ms. carey crafted this sequel with utmost care and the ending (once again) left my speechless. my connection with this story and these characters was so intense that at times i had to put the book down because the emotions were too overwhelming for me (generally the sad and angry emotions!). the ending leaves you begging for the sequel, not just because it's an intense cliffhanger (which it is), but because i honestly don't know where the story is going to go next! the twists and turns of once have left me with ideas about the many ways it could go but not a solid idea of what my dear eve is going to do next! if you enjoyed eve, once is a must read that you should pick up as soon as it releases!

cleaned_reviews: sign me up as scared. i've had this book since it came out, i'm very proud of myself for lasting this long without reading it. busy and expectant, not a good combination, so i wanted to wait for when i had the time and was a little bit more calm to read it. this book was as dark and interesting as i'd hoped, and adelina's journey was sad to witness as well as powerful. for some reason i still find myself alined to adelina, she is broken, sad and angry but in all her evilness i can't help but be on her side. her rapid descend into madness made me realize that i still think she can turn back; magiano's introduction proved at least that she still has some light inside her. i'm scared for what the next book will bring because, i want her to recover but there is still so much about her darkness that has not been fully developed and that i hope we get to see unfold. this book, though not perfect, was so interesting to read. i honestly kept thinking that at some point i would get bored but i never did, which just proves the power of marie lu's writing. the world she has created is so complex, i'm almost sure we are not going to be able to completely understand it even if we get more than 3 books. as for the plot, it was never boring but it was also always predictable and that is both good and bad; good because there is always a sense of accomplishment when you know what is going to happen, bad because i also love being surprised by something unexpected. as for the character's i still feel like i don't know them at all, which is also good and bad. as i've stated above i'm on team adelina, so obviously, i love her. i still don't know how i feel about violetta though she has proven that she cares about adelina and that puts her on my you're good for now -list. sergio is a complete mystery to me so hopefully we will get to see more of him in the next book. as for super-sweet-and cuddly magiano, i just love him, i think there is so much more to him and i just want to know it all. stepping away from the rose society there is pain in the neck -teren who, though wicked as he is, i still find to be an awesome character, and the dagger's who i still love and hate, but i guess that's the point. this book is dark but, is not as dark as i think the next book will be. so i'll hold on to my reins very tightly. if you've read the young elites and haven't read the rose society: what are you doing with your life? and if you haven't read the young elites: what are you doing with your life? just read this book and/or the previous one. do it. you'll like it, trust me. this seriously getting bizarre. this is like the 5th book that i have had to re-add to my read books. what is happening? also i love this book!

cleaned_reviews: so i thought this might be another story about rolex, but i wasn't certain. it's not though. if you're wondering about the red tie on the cover, it's because the rentboys refer to him as red tie. the driver, callum, thinks his boss, james, might be self-medicating with the rentboys he sees. he'd much rather be the one his boss needs. but cal is fairly certain those needs are special and seeks help from one of james's ex-rentboys, nick, who is known for being a sexual sadist. this story is told from callum's point of view as he is learning to become a dom and fulfill james's needs. cal is believable as a new dom, instinctive enough to make it work for james, but still insecure about reading his cues and getting it right, not losing control of himself in the scenes. these guys are private, so they're bedroom/home scenes, not dungeon scenes. but what makes this story special is the navigation of their employer/employee relationship outside of sex. because the sex is instinctual and natural between them. figuring out how to act around each other the rest of the time is the hard part for james and cal. by the end, you get the feeling that they'll manage to navigate the rocky patches and come out strong together. not my absolute favorite of the series, but a very strong addition to it. i love the rentboys, so i'm hoping there are more stories to come. this was a short epilogue follow-up to ash and darian's quick ending in glitterland and immediately follows those events. it was a lovely revisit of the two when darian discovers ash's tattoo of darian's name. quite satisfying.

title: ['Ink and Bone (The Great Library, #1)', 'The Nightmare Affair (The Arkwell Academy, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this was simply an amazingly well written book, and now i'm going to suffer the cursed wait for the next book in the series. but the good thing is i can read all the other books rachel caine has as i wait. review to come. this was the first novel i have read by the author rachel caine, and i was thoroughly amazed by her skill in creating a world and characters that had both depth and individuality. i really enjoyed reading about the world jess brightwell lives in, also the way it was presented to the reader. rejoice, for there is no info dumping but rather a very natural and gradual buildup of information pertaining to the world of the great library. it was artfully done through jess's thoughts and through the interaction and speech of other characters, where it was actually relevant and did not have a big glaring sign that said "info dump here". a major reason as to why i thought that the world building was done well is because of the essence of the world itself. because the story revolves around people who value knowledge above all else (and i mean all else), and because jess our main protagonist, becomes a one of the few postulents that are selected to train in order to have a chance of obtaining a position at the great library, it is not surprising or out of place for the characters to regurgitate history every so often to prove their knowledge whilst provide us readers more insight on the world that they live in. considering that this novel is a dystopian, it's not surprising that the library is not as caring or great as it seems. besides being revealed through the happenings of jess, the corruption of the higher ups and the overall lack of concern for life is shown through the brief messages sporadically spread in-between chapters. these snippets also provided a more in depth view of some characters that were more prominent in the storyline as well as a preview of those that were not. (or will be in future installments is my guess) usually i don't have much thoughts or feelings for these small interludes, but i enjoyed reading these ones because they were well placed and did not have that overly subliminal message feeling to it that some authors do which i don't really like. on the topic of characters...oh the characters. caine successfully created real life human beings that you loved, ones that you hated but eventually came to love because they had depth and were not your typical stock characters. for example, dario the cocky b***- i mean spaniard jess has to room with. at first he was the typical a-class jerk who looked down his nose at everyone, was a brat and just plain annoying in everything he did. but by the end of the book i couldn't help but like him because he grew as a character/person over the course of the book and was no longer that annoying brat at the beginning but someone that could be admired. plus the frenemy status between him and jess was just plain adorable. i don't want to say more about other characters because it would be a spoiler, but in conclusion the characters have a way of worming into your hearts. as for the plot, i found that it was well paced and balanced. although there were no giant surprises that stole your breath away or sent your mind reeling, there was no lack of excitement in the novel either. right from the start caine has you running along with jess trying to survive in a world where knowledge and books are sacred, and jess comes from a family that deals in the black market. technically none of the real excitement/plot starts until and around a good 60-70 pages into the book, however the world building, introduction of important characters, and the buildup to the plot was done so well that i did not mind or realize that so many pages had already gone by before the heart of the plot was even revealed. having the story begin with jess in his home turf also helped, giving you a taste of excitement and dread that comes with living an illicit lifestyle. another aspect about the book that i really enjoyed was the imagery of all the places that jess goes to. it's really interesting because he practically visits all the possible types of environments, from the pristine castle that is the home ground of the great library, to the dark and bloody grounds of war and chaos, and of course the tightly packed backstreets of london. this was one of those books where images automatically popped up in my mind as i read, which just helped enhance the aesthetics of this book. really nicely written, i thoroughly enjoyed unfolding the mystery in this book. i really enjoyed the world that she built, it's definitively going to be interesting to see that world change in the next book considering what happens at the end of this book. which also nicely sets up the next book, most likely centering the plot on the consequences from the first book judging by the little snippet that was provided at the end of book 1. something else that i really enjoyed about this book is how mindee arnett kept the identity of the true criminal hidden until the end. which i thought was a nice change since most of the time many authors drop tiny hints that can help you connect the dots before the big reveal. in any case it makes sense as well, since if you're the big evil boss why would you be stuck doing the dirty work that could get you caught? anyways i'm looking forward to the next book, and to see some legit eli and dusty interaction kkk

"parting is such sweet sorrow - juliet from shakespeare's romeo and juliet. that is the phrase that came to mind as i read the very last page in the very last installment of the 'burg series. oh my goodness. i will say, that no matter how i felt about the individual stories in this series, the way it wraps up in this book made me love them all. i read the other books before i started blogging so this is the only one i have a review for. but i would recommend that you read all of the stories and that you read them in order. and if you start a book and are not feeling one of the characters or one of the story lines, trust me, stick with it!! you will not be sorry because the couple in each story has a compelling and heartwarming story that you will enjoy reading. i was surprised when i saw that cher (aka cheryl) was the main female character in this book. she was a significant character in book one- for you and a minor one in the other books (she worked at j&js), but somehow it never occurred to me that she might have an interesting story waiting to be told. merry is also in the other stories. he is mike haine's partner ( games of the heart) and rocky lane's brother ( golden trail). whatever i thought of the pairing, i am so glad that their story got told. it was beautiful. merry is on the rebound from a five year back and forth with his ex-wife and cher is on a permanent rebound from the crap life has dealt her --her son ethan being the exception to that - and they are good friends. what starts a fling ends up being the start of something profound for both of them. of course, this wouldn't be the 'burg without murder, mayhem, kidnapping, crazy jealous exes and great kids thrown in for good measure. this book has all of that and then some because it as the most epic epilogue that gives you everything you could need to know about the how life has played out for the 5 couples we met in this series. it's awesome and i am so sad there is no more. cher and merry have issues. cher gave me moments where i was literally yelling at her. merry- not so much- but he had a whole other book and his sister's experience to help him work out his issues. also, in golden trail we were introduced to ryker who , even though he didn't have his own book, is a huge part of the 'burg storylines and who is one of my favorite ka characters. and that is saying a lot because i tend to love her characters. you'll read some negative reviews that talk about the way ka's dialogue is written and her use of the same phrases, etc...but hey, it's not for everyone. and i happen to love it and so do a lot of other people. if you can't get the rhythm of the speech in the books, i would recommend listening to the audio versions. the narrators do a great job. the first book i read of hers was knight and i was struggling with the dialogue so i bought the audio and i totally got how they sounded and it it totally made sense and brought the characters to life. i love the descriptive narratives and i love the multiple points of view that often exist in her novels. so, yes, parting is such sweet sorrow. but what a way to end on a high!

cleaned_reviews: i genuinely like urban fantasy. it is one of my favourite sub-genres. however, it is one that is in my opinion extremely over-emphasized in today's market. it has gotten to the extent that i have intentionally culled my reading, and unfortunately, this means that there are a number of authors who i like who i don't get read anymore). there are some whom i have read and stopped either because they straddled the paranormal romance/urban fantasy line too much on the paranormal romance side of things or because they straddled the urban fantasy/superhero line too much on the superhero side of things. however, i also have culled where two authors are both writing excellent books but the books are a bit similar in topic or theme (hmmm, a fascinating were-x series, but i'm also reading this amazing were-y series... which one do i keep). now here is my conundrum. i enjoy ben aaronovitch rivers of london series which is a police procedural urban fantasy that takes place in london. i have just finished london falling which is also a police procedural urban fantasy that takes place in london. do i keep both or cull one? well, the answer my friends is that i will keep both!! london falling is just too good to not keep reading. if aaronovitch's rivers of london is midsommer murders and justin gustainis's scranton pd novels are law and order, london falling is the wire or the shield - a dark, realistic police procedural where the culprits just happen to be supernatural. the characters, while starting from somewhat stereotyped archetypes, are fulling realized fascinating figures who are thrown into the deep end of the supernatural pool and are still trying to figure out how to swim. my favourite character is the undercover cop who had been undercover a bit too long and was/is in desperate need of redemption. it wasn't an easy book to read but it was definitely worth it. i am looking forward to the sequel. one last comment, you have to love an urban fantasy that includes a glossary at the back which mostly about policing.

cleaned_reviews: perhaps because i already had the phrase, "balm of gilead" in my head when i started this fine novel, i was so happy that it had religious overtones. reverend john ames is a preacher for the congrationalists in gilead, iowa and dying from a heart condition. re-married much later in life, after his young wife dies in childbirth along with their infant, he writes his history and thoughts to leave with his young son, who, at seven to his seventy-six, will have few memories of him and none of him as a younger man. after finishing gilead, i think it should be everyone's charge in life to leave a written history including sentiments, stories and wandering thoughts for posterity. of course, most of us won't put words on a page like marilynne robison has john ames put words on a page (so pleasantly meaningful), but the value will come from the experience. i couldn't help but feel the pleasure ames had in his memories. of course, because death loomed in his future, it was tinged with sadness too. after a lifetime of baptizing babies, counseling individuals and feeding his flock, ames appreciates the treasure that is his family. the pride and joy he feels as a father is palpable and that father/son bond, as distant their ages may be, brings to mind other father/son relationships: his and his athiest brother's with their own father, his best friend, old boughton, with his son and namesake, john ames boughton, his abolitionist grandfather and his pacifict father, and several well-known examples from the bible. in reality, this story is a re-telling, in many ways, of the prodigal son parable only with a lot more digression. but, it's more than that too. filled with symbolism, quotes you'll want to remember and a message of love and forgiveness, gilead is exactly the kind of book i love to read. i am no eccentric. i like shopping at old navy. i tap my toes to most top 40 songs. halloween tries my patience with its weirdness. so, i wasn't really expecting to enjoy my second neil gaiman book as much as i did. the ocean at the end of the lane reminds me of roald dahl's book. while i tend to appreciate dahl's books, rather than like them, gaiman got past my preference for normal by sandwiching his bizarre with brilliant meaning. in spite of my inability to imagine some of his more intangible descriptions, like the ratty fabric in the sky with teeth, i absolutely engaged in both the fear felt by the memories of a 7 year old child and protection provided by the wise and calm hempstock sisters. how it all came to be, hinging on memories rekindled by setting, with my comfortable normal just within reach in the background, is believable, even though i know it can't be. vivid and unique, this is a great read.

title: ['Kindred: A Graphic Novel Adaptation', "Babylon's Ashes (The Expanse, #6)", 'Lovecraft Country']
cleaned_reviews: a harrowing and timely sci-fi, time travel tale that is at once deeply personal and chillingly universal. when a modern black woman finds herself mysteriously transported to an antebellum plantation, she must carefully navigate her outrage and horror in order to ensure her own ancestor's birth. but her fate--and her road back and forth through time--is inextricably linked to the volatile young slave owner who both loves and distrusts her. this frightening and gripping story is effectively told via curt, matter-of-fact first-person narration. it gives an appropriate sense of a trauma victim verbally working through memories that would drive anyone mad if bottled up. the writer, deftly adapting butler's sci-fi classic, conveys the chilling need for this modern woman to make accommodations with our country's awful heritage. nevertheless, her strength and resistance shine through, as she endures beatings and demoralization, and never stops using her wits and intellect to find the surest path through danger and insanity. unfortunately, it's never easy for her, as both whites and blacks alike view her as an "uppity," distrusted outsider. the most tragic thing this story exposes, in fact, may be the ways that the institution of slavery pitted the african people on our shores against one another. the art is sketchy and dynamic and serves well to convey the violence and misery of the era it depicts. it doesn't do a great job of distinguishing between characters, though, which can be confusing, and the figures have an overall cartoonish quality that sometimes detracts from the drama and thrills on the page. if ever there was a time to delve into unflinching depictions of our nation's ignoble past--and to think on how it has shaped a no less compromised present--this is it. this graphic novel--and the book it's based on--would make a good start. possibly the weakest in the series, or possibly just the most philosophical, which is not at all the same thing. i need to think about that some more. but a weak expanse book is still a contender for one of my favorite reads of the past few months. this volume is all about war and its consequences and the seemingly hopeless human impulse we have to destroy ourselves by proxy--to repeat the social and political cycles that get us all at each others' throats. and then the flashes of goodness and beauty and virtue that make it seem like we might end up okay after all. but maybe not, because maybe an exotic alien entity will come kill us all. who knows. this also marks the first major break in the series' narrative structure. not sure how i feel about it yet, and i'm not 100% sure i think it was necessary; one could argue that this is a "bigger" story than what's gone before, but, i mean, the battles and conspiracies and half-alien ghosts and ambulatory moons and huge freaking disasters of all the other books have been pretty big. regardless, i don't mind the increased amount of voices heard in this volume; it just makes it hard to tell who the focus is on, and some of the subplots come across as vaguely staccato. finally, i don't know if i'm just going to see this in every book i read forever, but there are disturbing echoes of the 2016 election cycle here. particularly in the charismatic megalomaniac obsessed with making space great again. ugh, save us. at least marco inaros actually believes in something--the fine folks of the expanse may be better off with him than we are with our guy. sort of a series of interlinking stories, but sort of a novel that works as a whole, this book evokes the feeling of reading a bunch of lovecraft tales but with much more of a through-line in the form of re-appearing characters and much more human themes. now, of course, i love my lovecraft, in spite of all his warts. we know them all: overblown vocabulary, underdeveloped characters, and most of all, his horrible awful no food very bad racism, ethnocentrism and misogyny. this book takes the best of lovecraft--the sense of impending doom, the creeping terror, the remarkable ideas about powers beyond our control and the cultish human beings who seek to harness them--and grounds it in a much more real world, with real people, and consequences beyond "ok, the narrator is insane, transformed, and/or dead now." the brilliant thing about this novel is that it takes famous racist lovecraft's supernatural milieu and ties it in with a group of african-americans living in mid-century chicago. author ruff makes full use of the attendant ironies and dramatic potential. we have proud men struggling with their status as sort of magical "house negroes;" we have characters given the opportunity to change their race, and struggling with the temptation it provides; we have children haunted by dreams of lynching and white caricatures of actual black people, tinged with a hint of scrabbling lovecraftian terror. what it all does is show that institutional racism is just as weird, terrifying, and, yes, cyclopean as anything h.p. dreamed up. my favorite thing about this, though, is that there's this whole, truly lovecraftian story going on in the background, a contest of wills between lodges of power-hungry white cultists who are trying to use these black characters as pawns in their struggles--but they're not the focus. this focus is on atticus and letitia and harold and montrose and all the rest of these really well-drawn african-american characters; they resist the cultists' influence on their lives, and yes, that makes for interesting horror stories, but they also just go on living, looking for work, buying homes, pursuing their family lives. and when lovecraftian weirdness arrives, they accept it and deal with it as just another messed-up facet of the messed-up world they live in, and they try to make the best of it, and they endure. it's pretty neat.

title: ['Four Seconds to Lose (Ten Tiny Breaths, #3)', 'Gone Girl']
cleaned_reviews: review originally published at love literature art and reason if i'm honest, i can admit that i didn't really want to read this. i didn't like cain very much and i'm not sure why. so when i say that it was probably the best book in the series so far, it's obvious how much my opinion turned around. which is my absolute favorite thing about k.a. tucker. she gives me this pov i swear i'm gonna hate and i love it. cain's story ended up being amazing. i gained so much respect and admiration for the type of person he was, especially when i realized that owning a strip club isn't something he did for money, power, or sex. he kept it open even when he didn't want to because he knew he was giving the girls a decent place to work and keeping them off of the streets and out of the seedy clubs he knew about. i think i expected him to be a creepy strip club owner, even when i saw how much the other characters liked him in the earlier books, so i'm happy that he ended up being one of my favorite characters. charlie was an interesting character, too. she was full of secrets and couldn't trust anyone. she wanted out of her lifestyle, but knew there was no way she could just quit doing what she was doing. so she thought, away from the eye of her stepdad, she could work at cain's club and try to save up enough money to disappear. i liked her, but i also felt weirdly protective of cain and the other characters i've grown to love, so i had hoped that she wouldn't ruin their lives. i wanted her to stay, to go, to do the right thing, to disappear, and i couldn't make up my mind the whole time. four seconds to lose was really amazing. i was so set on not reading it for so long and i'm glad i decided to. i love that k.a. tucker is somehow able to make me care about characters i'm not so sure about by giving them a narration and putting them in the spotlight. and when they fall in love, i'm on the edge of my seat trying to figure out how on earth the relationship is possibly going to work out with such insane conflicts. i fall with them and i end up caring so much! i highly recommend this series. i know my previous review of five ways to fall said that i was glad i didn't read the rest of the series because i didn't have to, but i was wrong. i should have kept reading in order because the series is all the more amazing having done so. i swear, k.a. tucker can't write books as fast as i'd like them! these books are must reads for any fan of contemporary romance with a bit of suspense, conflict, and characters that aren't cookie cutter perfect people. each character has their own set of issues, but their stories are moving and heartwarming without being wholesome or preachy and i like that the author takes the seedy strip club setting and makes us love the characters without taking them away from that setting. gone girl was incredible. truly. but perhaps in order for me to explain how much i loved it without ruining the plot, i have to explain my reading habits. i hate suspense fiction. crime dramas, mysteries, thrillers, and romantic suspense are genres i avoid 99% of the time. especially popular ones that everyone is talking about. because i'm always disappointed. for a long time, suspense fiction was all i read and watched. james patterson, sandra brown, csi, law & order, and tons of lifetime movies were my first choice in entertainment. and then, one day, suddenly and completely, i was done. burned out. from time to time, i will pick up a book in these genres, but typically off beat and weird ones that deal more with human nature, with more grit and complex themes than the run of the mill who-dun-it plot and typically shelved with literary fiction than mystery fiction. so, when gone girl was the hot book, i didn't expect to read it. after awhile, i started hearing praise from people who, like me, don't typically read suspense novels. but even after i added myself to the library waiting list, i wasn't sold on it. when the book became available for checkout right before my vacation, in the middle of me packing for my move, i removed myself from the waiting list because i just didn't have the time. i was on the waiting list for months, but it wasn't that important to me. when i got to the hotel room with my grandmother in ireland, what was she reading?! gone girl. and seriously, if you watch anyone's reactions while reading gone girl, you know that you just have to read it. books that make people react like that are must reads for most of us. my grandmother reads great books and although our tastes differ greatly, we read many of the same novels, like the book thief, hunger games, etc. so when she told me i had to read gone girl, i finally caved and bought a copy while in ireland. and of course, i had the same kinds of reactions. i've never read a book that made me feel so conflicted while reading it. i wanted to scream at the end of every chapter in frustration, but for different reasons in each chapter and not in a bad way. i wanted to know what would happen next, but i needed to put it down and take in everything i just read. while reading, i would abruptly set the book down because i just couldn't take it anymore, only to stare at it a moment later, needing to continue because i needed to find out what would happen next. it was an insane ride. "seriously?" "what the...?" "but.." "what?!" were all things i said out loud while reading. my grandmother thought it was hilarious because she knew exactly what i was talking about, having just read the book herself. unpredictable, clever, brilliant, fast paced, gritty, twisted, and incredible are just a handful of words i could use to describe gone girl. it was worth the hype, worth my time, and an absolute must read. it's brilliant while also being an easy read, fast paced while also being precise and intricate. and, unfortunately, i refuse to explain why. the plot is amazing, but it's one that i refuse to spoil, even if the tiniest way. a few people have mentioned that it's a bit hard to get into the story. i suppose i could agree with that. you're not sure what you're reading yet and neither person is all that likable. in fact, i hated amy and distrusted nick for awhile. but keep reading. it gets better and more involved as the book goes on. it's not just an episode on a crime show, even though it kind of starts out that way. i promise. "i've literally seen it all and the worst thing, the thing that makes me want to blow my brains out, is: the secondhand experience is always better. the image is crisper, the view is keener, the camera angle and the soundtrack manipulate my emotions in a way reality can't anymore. i don't know that we are actually human at this point, those of us who are like most of us, who grew up with tv and movies and now the internet. if we are betrayed, we know the words to say... we are all working from the same dog-eared script." title: ['White Hot Kiss (The Dark Elements, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: a quick feel good read jennifer l. armentrout has quickly become one of my go to authors when it comes to needing a quick trashy good read and white hot kiss did not disappoint. immediately dropping you in on the action and not letting go white hot kiss follows layla, a half demon half gargoyle girl who sort of has an inner battle going on between the different parts of herself. still, she is a strong, steady and fearless heroine despite not really being a hundred percent okay with who she is. the other characters roth, prince of hell and zayne, sexy gargoyle extraordinaire along with a slew of other demon and gargoyle characters all managed to seem fairly three dimensional despite their sometimes infrequent appearances. and god were the scenes with layla and roth swoon worthy as were the ones with her and zayne for albeit entirely different reasons. jennifer l. armentrout managed not only to make a love triangle that i was actually a fan of but she also pulled off a fantastically paced story that kept me going and broke me out of my slump. you go queen j! can't wait to get to the next book.

title: ['Departure']
cleaned_reviews: a truly great novel you must read good novels, like movies, are amazing things; their design and purpose are solely to entertain, to transport, to allow you (the reader) to play in a new world, one that you wouldn't have imagined on your own before. great novels, however, leave you after words longing for more. great novels make you feel more intelligent about a subject. but, even these are just the side benefits. great novels coax out from you a full range of emotions; sad or happy, anxious or relieved, empty or fulfilled. regardless, you close the book fully invested, still pondering your journey and its impact on you. departure is that kind of great novel. after reading it, i completely understood why it's been such a blockbuster which commanded a seven-figure auction by publishers and a major motion-picture deal. i too am an author and i'm very familiar with a.g. riddle and his work, even having corresponded with him. this is a name you will read a lot about in the coming years. he reminds me of michael crichton in so many ways, offering a wonderful blend of science and fiction, on subjects and technologies that are as big as the human imagination. departure is a perfect mix of tv's lost and riddle's own vision of atlas shrugged. you'll see this when you read it. it's a fun journey that will make you think about yourself, our world, and your place in it. so, please take your seat, fasten your seat belts, stow your baggage, and get ready for a bumpy flight that you'll remember for years to come. oh, and don't forget to buy your ticket.

title: ['City of Heavenly Fire (The Mortal Instruments, #6)']

title: ['No One Belongs Here More Than You']
cleaned_reviews: excerpt from my full review at seattlebooks.tumblr.com: over turmeric curry and sauteed broccoli the other day, my friend told me about this great "new-old" film she'd seen called me and you and everyone we know. it won a sundance award for best vision or something, and roger ebert loved it, and the trailer made it difficult to pin down a plot or even a general feel, but what i liked was that it was a sort of one-woman project, written, directed, and featuring miranda july. four days later, i stood in city lights books and picked up this short story collection without realizing the connection between the two. from the get-go, july's character development gripped me completely. oftentimes characters are the least arresting part of literature (in my personal experience), taking a backseat to an intricate plot twist or phenomenal use of metaphors. here, july introduced me to women deeply flawed and terribly funny in an off-putting way. i don't know that, had these been real women, i would be able to stand being in the same room with them for more than an hour. at various intervals, they are falling asleep on the shoulders of unconscious men and lusting for underage students and teaching 80-year-olds how to swim across vast expanses of carpet. this could very easily have been an unlikeable book, full of unlikeable people who do inexplicably awful things to each other. but july redeems her characters, baring their thoughts and neuroses in a way that makes them almost relatable and undeniably fascinating.

title: ['Mockingjay (The Hunger Games, #3)']
cleaned_reviews: ** spoiler alert ** 8/10 it takes ten times as long to put yourself back together as it does to fall apart. i read these books almost six years ago, not long after mockingjay was released, and i kind of forgot about them. i mean, i knew they were on my shelf. i remembered devouring them with the single-minded awe that i think all of us book lovers have known at least once in our lives. i remembered admiring katniss and falling a little in love with peeta and not wanting the series to end. but i also remembered how the movies ruined it for me. after the movies, i never really looked at them the same, but this summer, i got ahold of a matching set of the books. yesterday, i was looking through my endless piles of books, hoping to find something that would make me feel... something. you can never really rely on a book that you've never read to give you that. i thought maybe i could recapture some of that childish wonder that i had at thirteen, even just a snag of that desperation that makes you forget you're reading a book. after all, i've changed a lot in six years. apparently, i haven't changed enough to forget the gripping magic of the hunger games trilogy and all of it's twisted, gruesome turns. it is truly a story about war and the depravity of humanity. plenty of people have their complaints about mockingjay in particular--all entirely valid complaints--but i disagree with most of them. the senseless deaths, the layers of conspiracy and distrust, the non-fatal casualties (such as katniss and gale's lost friendship and peeta as he was in the first two books), the unanswered questions, these are all things that force us to experience the worst of us. the last book, to me, was the most realistic of them all. it left me raw and crying, aching for the people who died and, more so, the people who didn't. these characters are the kind so real that you can't help but fall in love with them. they don't leap off the page, but rather, you fall into the book and land next to them. you have to watch them grow up too fast and cling to the last dregs of their youth in the form of defiance and naivety surrounding love. when rue dies, you cry because she could be your little sister or your daughter or your cousin, and when finnick dies, you weep because you could be his lover in thirteen, waiting for him to come back to you. i'm so thankful that collins chose to explore so many of the characters' stories because her loyalty to showing their depth is what makes them real. i know i'm ages behind the rest of you, only posting my review now, but these books left me with as much feeling tonight as they did six years ago. not sitting down and pouring out at least some of them would have driven me a little bit insane. i could talk about these books for ages and not touch on everything i could say--the theme of personal tragedy and my appreciation for the fact that there was a well-portrayed demiromantic main character among others. i've also realized that i'm apparently incapable of writing actual book reviews and i usually stray towards something along the lines of discussing my experience reading the book as opposed to actually praising the merits and pointing out the flaws, so sorry about that.

title: ['Dune (Dune Chronicles #1)']
cleaned_reviews: dune is one of the essential science fiction books, and since this is my third time reading it, i can honestly say, it still impresses time and time again. the core of dune is a story about a series of great houses in the future who have rules that permits vendettas and fighting between the houses. the two core houses are the atreides and the harkonnen. house harkonnen is losing the desert planet arrakis also known as dune to house atreides. with in the first three chapters herbert sets up everything, how house atreides knows arrakis is a trip, how house harkonnen's full trap works (including flat out naming the betrayers) and the book starts. what works is that the betrayals and plans all play out simultaneously. the one thing i noticed when reading the book is the fact there is almost no filler in dune at least for the first two thirds of the book. every scene has a purpose and a use if not multiple uses. out of the major characters (ten or so of them) their mentality and thought process is exposed whether it be in exposition, or their direct thoughts. the main characters are well fleshed out but so many minor characters that most books would throw away are well developed. in fact dune does something that few books seem to do. it heavily develops the "bad guys" and in fact goes so far as making them pseudo heroes. their plans are well developed and makes sense. in fact almost everyone of their plans should work. there's no obvious flaw in their logic, their no true hubris, there's just a solid well organized villain (or groups of villains, and a solid well organized hero. often times the reader thinks the villains are going to win, they have solid well thought out plans, well other times it's clear their ignoring intel that they would have if they didn't have a big blind spot, a blind spot that has been cultivated for decades. on the other side of the equation it seems that on this time reading the ending of the book is short. shockingly short. major actions and themes, and how the book plays out happens in only a scant few pages at the end of the book. a number of these are clearly planned out, but few parts and reveals seem to stack up. the sheer amount of cleaning up the loose ends falls a bit flat. but the fact is at over 800 pages, there could be another 100 to tie up some of these loose endings, and most wouldn't have the true impact as the finale of the book has with everything stacked up. the end result though is dune is a fantastic book, if you like sci fi, it's a must read, it is one of the essential books in the title: ['Persuasion']
cleaned_reviews: i hadn't re-read this book in a while, and i'd forgotten just how wonderful it is. it's definitely one of my favorite austen novels. anne elliot is a quieter but tremendously appealing heroine; we can empathize with her and feel what she feels. she is a sensitive person who experiences a great deal of emotion, both painful and pleasurable, yet is called upon to conceal most of it. i think there is a heightened sense of characters' feeling and emotions in general in persuasion, compared to austen's other novels. there are also much clearer and detailed physical descriptions of people and places, though i don't think austen ever goes so far as to tell us what color hair someone has! another thing that particularly struck me on this reading is that persuasion seems to contain a much larger number of happy and pleasant people--the crofts, the harvilles, the musgroves, mrs. smith. the crofts are some of the most charming characters in all of austen, and probably the nicest example of a happy married couple in all her books. even lady russell, though she can be regarded as an antagonist for the role her advice has played in anne's initial unhappiness, is depicted as a woman of sense and kindness, who in spite of her shortcomings is still a true friend to anne, and is willing to admit her misjudgment of both captain wentworth and mr. elliot.

title: ['A Mad, Wicked Folly', 'The One (The Selection, #3)', 'The Pledge (The Pledge, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: something about a mad, wicked folly was just so appealing to me from the very beginning. yes, the cover is pretty in that stereotypical pretty dress cover way. that and the synopsis are what enticed me to begin with, but i quickly knew there was a whole lot more to this book than pretty (though it is so pretty, in every way--it starts with the cover and goes all the way through the book's design). we're treated to a whip-smart and kick-butt heroine who doesn't take no for an answer, an adorable, swoony love interest, and a great setting (i mean, who writes about suffragettes?) y'all. vicky is a firecracker. in her time, women are expected to be demure, quiet, and perfectly obedient to their parents/husband. vicky is none of those things, and it's awesome. she takes her clothes off in front of a bunch of other artists to model. she mouths off to her future father-in-law at their first meeting--because she's drunk. she expressly goes against the wishes of her parents by continuing to draw, pursue art school, and sneaking out. not to mention she's outspoken and quick-witted. she's a teenage girl, and she's bound to make rash, ill-advised decisions, but she's trying to fight for her right to choose her own life. so what if she's been kicked out of her prestigious and proper french boarding school? so what if her parents forbid her from drawing and take away all of her art supplies? nothing can stop this girl, and it's fantastic. while vicky is being her rebellious self, she comes into contact with some people (i am a master of vague.) some of these people are suffragettes (more on them in a second, but first...) can i just mention how swoony our male lead, will, is? i mean, it's really kind of unfair. the boy is as sweet as can be, totally supportive of everything vicky wants to do (totally supportive of the suffragettes, as well!), and clearly is the best kind of person. i was even seething with jealousy a couple of times, remembering that he's fictional. he's progressive but respectful of old values and chivalry--perfect mix. he also encourages vicky to become a better version of herself, urging her to fight for what she wants. now, the suffragette angle of this book is what makes it stand out. had the book had vicky, her art, and will, it would've been fun and i still would have enjoyed it. but, the suffragettes are what pushed me into love for this one. first, we're treated to lots of information about how the suffragettes fought for their rights and how they were treated unjustly (learning!). but, their fight for the vote also ties so perfectly into vicky's fight for her freedom to make her own choices. the strong, wonderful women she meets while helping their cause are what spur her movement from just a headstrong girl into a powerful woman of conviction. yes, she fights it and doesn't think she wants to be a part of something so large and dangerous, but she learns that there's a big difference between wishing for change for yourself and fighting for change for everyone and that you have to make a choice whether or not to stand up for that change. i also want to mention how pretty this thing is. i said it before, and i'll say it again. i absolutely can't wait to see this book in hardcover. the arc has all these pretty little flourishes and details that just made it so pleasurable to look at, and i imagine the finished copy will be even better. ooh! and there are some fun things in the back, like lots more historical information on the suffragette movement, info on the art mentioned, and a recipe (yes, cooking!) do not be deceived by a mad, wicked folly's pretty appearance. there's substance and heart to this book, and it's an absolute joy and pleasure to read vicky's story. you can find this review and many more fun things on my blog: paper cuts. despite any flaws, i found the one to be the perfect series-ender. i got it in the mail this afternoon and finished it in one sitting. it's both emotionally satisfying, no matter which guy you rooted for, and deals with the political parts (which, admittedly, had been pretty neglected in the first two books) well. i cried several times (always a mark of a book i love) and i will unabashedly admit that i love this series, flaws and all. i didn't quite know what to expect coming into the pledge. i read the body finder, but just liked it, and never read the other books in the series. i thought the premise of the pledge sounded super intriguing but wasn't sure if she could pull off the task that is a well-written and developed dystopian. while it isn't perfect, the pledge is certainly an entertaining and original addition to her work. a couple of things struck me at the start of the book. first, i didn't feel like the languages were differentiated well enough. i loved that the classes were divided by language, because it truly would be a perfect way to divide people into castes. charlie's big important talent is that she understands all languages, even though she's not supposed to know but two. there were only a couple of times where it felt like her friends and family were truly excluded from what was going on, and they spent a decent amount of time around people not of their class. language is the great divider in charlie's world, and it just didn't feel all that divisive, though i'm a big fan of the idea. the other thing that hit me, in a good way, was that ludania was ruled by a monarch. i haven't seen this in dystopians much, if at all, and it was an interesting view. this made the government's motives very different and more human, though the queen didn't seen to have much humanity left in her. i enjoyed the romance a lot, and the "pledge" set me to swooning. i appreciated charlie's reluctance to engage in any sort of relationship with max at first. it was realistic. sure, she was a little bit of a rebel at first, but it was normal teenage rebellion. an instant relationship and trust just wouldn't have fit. at her heart, charlie was trying her best for her family. eventually, max does earn her trust and their relationship grows from there. i did feel like the situation set up in the end--in terms of their relationship--was odd. it didn't mesh with how they'd been up until that point, but we'll see. i also really loved the ending. there was a very satisfying conclusion to the problems charlie had faced, but new problems arose. we had closure, but we're still left wanting more without a cheap cliffhanger. the pledge is filled with thrilling and breathtaking moments of action and romance. it explores the ties of romantic, familial, and societal love and the heart of friendship. kimberly derting has written an individual and exciting dystopian that definitely exceeded my expectations. more reviews and other exciting things on my blog: paper cuts.

same day (cupid day) every time with all the little details intact and fixed. that knowledge in itself can become miserable before adding in the fact that everything she does is ultimately in vain. i can't explain how afraid i was of the end. instead of just reading the book and finding out how it ended i stressed about the end being terrible. my thought process was basically "if it ends this way cleaned_reviews: alas, another review i started writing and then abandoned until so long after i'd read the book that i don't remember what i wanted to say! i'll see what i can do. ellen hopkins wrote a grown-up book! even before i started freaking out about being 25 (shut up), i never really read books about middle-aged women (except for anything by kate chopin, etc.) because i just didn't relate to it. i've never enjoyed reading about those middle-aged women's sex lives, either, because a) i don't relate to it on a personal level at all; b) it reminds me of my mother, ick; and c) it freaks me out to think someday i will be able to relate to it on a personal level. i read triangles in the throes of my turning-25-trauma, over the two days before my birthday. just like her ya books, hopkins wrote this one in verse. i loved the poems she used as breaks between points of view (interludes? intermissions?), how they would spell out a second message if you read certain words and how the last line always tied into the next woman's story. i was sucked in from page one and kept finding reasons to be reading instead of working. the characters aren't sympathetic. marissa is probably the most pitiable, but that doesn't mean i didn't want to shake her. i can only imagine how difficult it would be to juggle a terminally ill daughter, a son whose lifestyle is nothing like the one you want for him, and an absent husband. holly is having the midlife crisis to end all midlife crises, and andrea is sleeping with her best friend's husband. but these women love their children and are trying to hold themselves and their families together while seeking satisfaction and it is so interesting to see the different ways in which they seek it. and ellen hopkins is just good.

title: ['The Martian']
cleaned_reviews: this is a great book for any space/nasa nerds out there. it is very sciency science fiction, and seems extremely well researched. for once, the glib "x meets y" publisher description seems pretty apt (the blurb says "apollo 13 meets castaway"), at least plot-wise. this is a book about a much nerdier, astronaut version of robinson crusoe, stranded on mars by an extreme mixture of bad and good luck. this book goes into a lot of technical detail, which is one of its biggest strengths, but also a little bit of a problem, early on especially. on the positive side, it makes the whole thing seem really plausible. even though the technologies being discussed don't all exist yet, and we're not sending astronauts to mars, there's so much detail included, in such a matter of fact, straightforward way, that it feels like all the things being discussed are real. the downside of this is that it can be a bit dry, especially in the early parts. i'll admit, i skimmed a bit, because i was starting to get a little bored of all that technical description. once we started seeing the perspective of the folks back at nasa and had a few more characters in the mix it picked up, but until then it was starting to be too much of a good thing. the variety of narrative perspectives after that helped. i'm generally a very character-driven reader, so the fact that mark watney (our stranded astronaut) is a pretty fun narrator helps move things along. of course, the fact that he stays in such good spirits isn't remotely authentic - he's incredibly isolated and under a huge amount of stress, and that doesn't really show in the writing. he might curse, or express frustration/fear/etc, but his narrative voice never changes to show the strain. this makes the whole thing slightly less authentic, but for me was actually a good thing, because i think something that was authentically narrated would be pretty harrowing, really, and this made the book a more fun read. i think maybe a bit more depth, character-wise, might have been nice. as it was, i never fully connected with mark. so, great technical content, and a fun story, but you have to really be a space nerd in order to love this book, i think. and, that's a good thing - this is a book written by a space nerd, for space nerds.

(hide spoiler)] there are very few times when i read a book and i feel absolutely gutted. i went into this book completely blindsided about the actual plot. i had it on my 'to read' shelf and just proceeded to read it after seeing it on my shelf for so long. it started out exactly like most of hoover's novels do, beautiful and human in the best way. ryle and lily form a connection of 'naked truths' from the beginning of the novel. they are different people, with different needs and wants, who are just trying to make their lives work together. it seems earnest, it seems real. their characters are written in the way most of hoover's protagonists are, they yearn for each other and they burn bright and strong. ryle and lily call to you because of their intense connection with each other, and it leaps off the page. and this is why this book hit me so hard. for the first time in my life, i felt what lily was feeling. as the book proceeds and the inevitable destruction arises, as a reader you're left just as shell shocked as lily is. there is disbelief, strong and pulling at your core. there is unadulterated fear accompanied by the resounding thought of how did i let it get this far?. how did this happen? why didn't i see the signs? what's happening? how is this happening? a million questions hit you at once and that's when you realize that the power hoover has a writer, is that she makes the experience of her characters so real, that you're compelled to feel exactly what happens when events like the ones in this novel unfold. you see a relationship you've been warned about a thousand times, swore up and down you'd protect yourself from, unleash in the way that it would in real life, and you try to find all the signs where things went wrong. for the first time, in a very long time, i was able to journey through with a mc in a way that left me completely vulnerable. this book is very heavy, and as someone who went into this not knowing what it would be about, i am so unbelievably humbled by the journey it gave me. this book is an extremely powerful narrative on a subject most don't delve into, and one that's so important to talk about. thank you for this book colleen hoover, and thank you for writing it in such a smart and incredibly complex narrative.

cleaned_reviews: another fantastic read in a sea of books! there are layers that many people overlook, expecting instant gratification which is where this world is stuck on. life is meant to be enjoyed, experienced - the good and the bad - it's how we learn who we are, what we want to do and where we want to go. regardless if this is a fable as some people classify it, it contains many truths about us as a species and us as individuals. you can and will learn a lot about yourself when you read this book. are you the shepard? are you the alchemist? are you the crystal shop owner? are you any other character in the book? how would you handle the obstacles . . . how would you respond to the ending when you've found your treasure, especially when it's been right where you've been all along and need to take the journey to not just understand it, but appreciate it as well? embark on your own journey with the alchemist to find out.

title: ['The Countess Conspiracy (Brothers Sinister, #3)']
cleaned_reviews: this was one of the first romances i read. i'm sure if i had reviewed it then i would've given it five stars, because milan was such a revelation and it was so different to anything else i'd read at that point. that said, this was my first full reread and i'm not sure it holds up to a five star rating, hence me dropping it to 4.5 stars. fantastic book though. i love the plot here. it's very victorian - a story occurring up and down the country at the time - men taking credit for women's work in the sciences. in this case it's not coercive but agreed between our h/h, sebastian and violet. layered onto to that, milan manages to capture the victorian moral panic about progression in the sciences and the fear that it might be corrosive to traditional social structures. it makes for a great premise to the book. you can feel sebastian's frustration with the arrangement and i'm still enamoured of the opening - the first exchange between them includes sebastian telling violet to fuck off, it's a helluva way to start. i think there are a few too many things going on in the plot. the marbles, violet's sister, sebastian's brother, the trip to the seaside, the journey at the end. elements could have been taken away and the book would lose nothing. at its centre, my favourite type of heroine: prickly and brilliant. violet has a tragic background and it's made her fold in on herself. science is her life and as far as she's concerned she's done with love and romance after her tragic first marriage. her characterisation is deeply complicated and multi-layered. and here i pause for a criticism - perhaps too much. there are the issues with her marriage, her mother, her father, her sister and those with her mother and the deportment book, really felt like too much. i think taking an element away here makes the characterisation clearer and stronger. still: she's awesome. and anyone who disputes romance can be feminist need look no further than violet (and, indeed, this whole book). then there's sebastian. an affable rake, meandering his way through life, happy to play the part of gentleman scientist because he's in love with violet. until he's not. responsibility comes knocking and he sees that he cannot live the lie anymore. sebastian is kind of a beta hero. he's sort of perfect and now i consider it his real role is to midwife violet through the changes in her character. his characterisation is actually a little inconsistent. the whole thing with his brother felt rather unresolved - i didn't buy that violet could simply convince him out of his opinion. but i still adore sebastian because of how he loves violet and how he treats her. on which note, i love that these two talk to one another. it would be easy for sebastian to hang back and let his unrequited love go unrequited whilst we the reader waited for violet to figure it out and fall into his arms. none of that. sebastian just tells her and then puts absolutely no pressure on her. the sex is hawt as hell and super duper consent centric. perhaps most importantly, the romance is wonderful. i cannot explain how much you are rooting for these two. there is serious chemistry between them, even with violet's issues and the sexual tension winds up to an extreme level by the time they have their first sexual encounter. again, one might imagine that would be removed by a mutual declaration of feelings, but it's not, it's amped up. as i said, i have some criticisms here, but i'm grading on a milan curve, and i still think anyone who enjoys romance should definitely read this book, it's great.

title: ['The Ghost of Graylock', 'Murder of Crows (The Others, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: packed with thrills and chills to keep you in suspense and quickly turning pages! the ghost of graylock was such a pleasant surprise! i enjoy a good bone chilling ghost story and this one definitely delivered. young neil and bree are staying the summer with their aunts in hedston because their mother is having a hard time coping with their father having left them all to "follow his dream" of being an actor. neil is our main character and though it never outright says it i believe he is 12 - as it was mentioned he's 4 years younger than his 16 year old sister bree. neil is such an interesting young character, he is a thinker and its so fascinating to read how his mind works. he occasionally thinks about his mother's behavior over the past few months in response to their father leaving and he thinks about this new mom that they've been seeing as a "shadow person." he wanders if we all have a shadow person that is inside of us. i love how the author put this in because the way he works it out in his dead really seems like how i would imagine a young teen thinking. we get to the main plot because neil likes to think of himself as a paranormal investigator, trying to emulate his favorite tv show ghostly investigators. so when he meets a local kid in town and hears about the closed mental hospital graylock that is out in the woods and the ghost story tied to it - he simply must investigate and try to gather evidence. so off he goes to have a look, along with his sister, friend wesley and his brother eric. while there, neil and bree have a close encounter and the tale takes off from there and the momentum barely slows down right up til the end. i thought because of how young the characters were that this wouldn't be as suspenseful as it was but i have to admit there were points where i really was on the edge of my seat. there is a great mystery aspect to the book where the kids are trying to figure out who the ghost is and why it is haunting neil and bree. i couldn't guess it right! - to me that's a good thing. seeing them work through the mystery and trying to figure it out along with them was a treat. i didn't figure it out until they did and i absolutely loved that. if you fancy a good quick ghost story this is for you - i devoured it in one night! murder of crows, how you could you make me love the others more than i already do? with strong themes, necessary violence and tension that makes my heart ache - oh yes, anne bishop you hurt me so good. plus the title is a double entendre. *smirk* every little cut i make brings me closer to you... - have you ever heard of a 'cutter'? if you haven't then go watch that movie the secretary (a favorite of mine) and you'll learn about what it means to be a cutter. essentially its a disorder where a person cuts themselves, it isn't suicidal attempts. so take that disorder and combine and twist it for the purposes of urban fantasy and you have the cassandra sangue aka blood prophet. never before have i run across a blood prophet in fiction i've read. so the fact that this fresh new series gives me something new mixed with something i already love (urban fantasy) made both written in red and murder of crows un-put-down-able! these girls see the future when their skin is cut, as they speak their visions they are given orgasmic type ecstasy, but if they don't speak them they are wracked with extreme bodily pain. one can see why these girls would become addicted to the cutting euphoria. we humans are strange... - come, come now, you know it's true! humans overall are destructive creatures. for as much as we invent and create we also reek havoc on the world and destroy it's resources. i only wish there were such a race of others in existence that would keep humanity in check from destroying the planet. there are some harsh things that happen in these books and i think by reading from the perspective of simon worlfgard (the wolf other) you really come to sympathize with the harsh methods they have in place over humans. then it makes you wonder who is really the enemy - because i know whose side i was on in these books. that's right i'm a wolf lover. we women are even stranger... - women, bah, we complicate thing, misunderstand things, read too much into things. ladies don't tell me i'm alone in this! but hey that is what makes things all the more interesting. men can't live with us and certainly don't want to live without us. alright they really couldn't live without us - who would make sure everything got done? anyways, meg corbyn is even more confusing because she grew up locked in an institution with only the images and people there that she was exposed to. simple social interactions are new to her, so imagine how she might react to possibly intimate ones? there is a whole lot of tension in murder of crows due to meg's and simon's confusion and i loved it. the feelings that are growing between these two cannot be denied even if they both fight it. nothing like a hot splash of blood to get this party started... - if you're expecting fairy farts and rainbows this is not the series for you. there are strong themes of rape, sexual abuse, child abuse and no shortage of blood and violence. there isn't a ton of violence, indeed i thought it was just the right amount. though we see the darker side of human nature we also see some really wonderful things. for me, murder of crows toes the perfect line of gritty urban fantasy with marvelous splashes of humor and compassion. read it and i dare you not to love it!

apologies but i don't want to spoil it! russell built the structure of the space system and the planets so that it was easy to create a picture in my mind of the world these characters live in. i loved the space travel and the differences between each of the twelve houses...and the mystery surrounding the mythical 13th house. rho is an interesting character and i liked her. i have to admit, i was frustrated with some of the decisions she made but she made those decisions with the right intentions...in most cases, i think. as she is thrown into a life she never imagined she jumps right in and embraces all aspects. the thing that stands out for me about rho is the fact that she never changes her point of view on what is really going on regardless of what people are telling her. this is most evident when she is trying to figure out if she should hide her belief of ophiuchus and the fact that he is the one attacking the houses. i thought that both mathias and dysan were solid characters as well. they were almost complete opposites of each other but when it came to rho, they both cared a lot about her and were willing to do whatever they could to keep her safe. i'm not going to say too much about these two as i don't want to give anything away but i will warn you, if it isn't clear, there is a bit of a love triangle. with that said, it doesn't take over the story but it does flow through the book and plays a part in some of the decisions made. as rho tries to navigate the politics of being guardian of house cancer as well as figuring out how to get everyone to see how much danger they are in, she is also faced with the potential loss of her family and has to figure out how to keep going without know where they are or if they are safe. i can't really say too much about the rest of the story as i don't want to give anything away but i think the bigger mysteries still exist around ophiuchus and rho's mother. i felt like we - whether anyone will help her or not. depending upon how you look at it, she meets wolf. although she suspects he has had a hand in her grandmother's disappearance, she decides she is going to trust him and they begin their journey. where cinder's character was shy and nervous in the first book, scarlet is the exact opposite. she is tough, opinionated, and independent. i really liked her and i honestly really liked seeing her relationship with wolf evolve. the entire time i was reading, i was thinking...wait, the wolf is bad in the fairytale but i kept wishing for it not to be true. i don't want to give anything away so i won't but i was cautiously optimistic that i would get what i wanted. i loved how meyer brought all of the different pieces of the story together. at first i wasn't sure how it was going to flow but she did it well by rotating the different pieces in and out. this was a well done second book and if how much i liked this one compared to the first book is any indication, goodreads better come up with a way to give more than 5 stars. another good book in the series. we pick up with violet as part of the team now and helping to find bodies left by the collector. i won't do a plot summary -
