title: ['Her Darkest Nightmare (The Evelyn Talbot Chronicles, #1)', 'The Deal (Off-Campus, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this review was originally posted on latte nights reviews. 3.5 stars rounded up to 4. when i read the prequel, hanover house , last year and really loved it, i was so eager for her darkest nightmare! evelyn is a psychiatrist who has dedicated her life to studying psychopath's behavior since her ex-boyfriend was one and left her for dead. she runs hanover house in hilltop, alaska, a place that has over more than 100 inmates who have psychopathic behavior. it's been three months since hh has been opened and now, evelyn faces a nightmare when a dismembered body appears. she had to keep some distance between her emotions and what she encountered every day or she would never survive this job. to be honest, i had no idea what to fully expect. hanover house was such a thrilling read. i felt so creeped out by everything! sadly, it wasn't the case with her darkest nightmare. while the hunt for the killer was thrilling, it still was lacking something. i loved the hunt and trying to figure out who the heck was the killer, if it really was evelyn's ex or if there was someone else. my mind was reeling with the possibilities of who it could be. i never guessed right. i was completely blind-sided and i loved that! i questioned so many people in this novel and i was wrong on all of them. novak did a great job with the element of surprise on this one. something that i loved of hanover house was the point of view from the killer. it gave so much depth to the story and it added to the creepy feel of it. in her darkest nightmare, the killer's point of view appeared less than five times. i was definitely missing it. even with the killer's pov, i still couldn't guess who it was! "these aren't people who hear voices that tell them to kill or don't know the difference between good and evil. they simply have no real understanding of emotion, can't truly connect with other humans. they do whatever benefits them, whatever interests them, and they feel perfectly justified. the real problem is that psychopaths are more common than most people think." evelyn had some character development in this novel. she has been so tormented by her past that she can't enjoy life anymore, not even the company of a man. when amarok met evelyn, he disliked her for bringing hh to his town, but after meeting her, he was hung up on her. he knew all the nightmares that evelyn had faced so he gave her space. we finally see this couple worming their way into a relationship very slowly. amarok is always there for evelyn no matter what. when evelyn is ready to take a new step in their relationship, amarok lets her go at her own pace. it was so sweet to read how much he cared for her. i can't wait to see more of them in the next novel. what i didn't like was evelyn's back-and-forth thing with amarok when it came to his age since he was seven years younger. i wish she had surpassed that early in the story, but it wasn't until much later that she kind of gave it a rest. there's an inmate in this story that i actually liked a lot. don't ask me how or why since he's a psychopath, but i had really liked his appearance in the prequel so having him back in this story had me excited. i really don't know why i like him. i think it's because he makes the story much more interesting, and i'm sure he will be even better in the next installment! overall, her darkest nightmare was an intense mystery novel that i enjoyed quite a lot. the way it ended had me gasping out loud and so very excited for the next novel and what it will bring. i received an earc from the publisher for free in exchange for an honest review. this does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review.this review was originally posted on latte nights reviews. this review was first published on latte nights reviews. one of my friends and fellow blogger nicole from books and starlight recommended me this book a while ago. she knows i adore the rusk university series by cora carmack and she said since i loved this series so much, that i would love the deal. i have to say that this book has made it's way into my 2015 favorite reads list and i have a new #1 book boyfriend. garrett was fighting mathias from never too late for a while...a long while but eventually garrett won. i know, i know! i love mathias, i adore the guy and i will always fight for him but garrett.... hot damn... *fans face while standing in front of very cold a/c* not exactly working.. garrett is... it is impossible to describe this perfect and extremely hot specimen! i was expecting a high class jerk but what i got was so much more! garrett is smart (has a's on all of this college classes while being captain of the hockey team), he is hot, he is sweet, very caring, amazing personality, funny, driven, goes after what he wants, has a great sense of humor, the guy has a body that will leave you drooling so much it would fill a bucket entirely. "look, i'm the dd tonight, but i'm offering to be more than just your driver. i'll be your bodyguard, and your bartender, and most importantly, your friend. i promise to look out for you tonight, wellsy." the female protagonist of this book is hannah, whom i found to be a very judgmental person but let's face it. even if we say we don't judge, we always do so i honestly let that part slide. on a side note of this character, i loved that the author didn't hide what had happened to hannah. some female characters are even afraid of thinking that word so they just don't say it or stumble while saying it. hannah would do the contrary--she would think it and say the word in her mind without a thought and i actually liked that because, to me it showed a sense of maturity, knowing that thinking that word won't kill you. i'm not being insensitive, i promise. if it were someone in real life, i wouldn't be thinking these things but it's just that the girls in books are always so scared of thinking that word that it just frustrates me. again, not how i would think if it were real life. anyways, hannah is a very strong girl and one who definitely doesn't take bullshit. she will call you off on it and be on her way. what i also loved about hannah is that the girl didn't swoon immediately over garrett. it took a long time for her to actually think of him as someone to date or kiss and this rarely happens in books. also, hannah was so funny and i have to say, a mood-killer but garrett would brush it off and just laugh. he's such a good sport *sighs dreamily* the chemistry these two characters come to have is sizzling hot. i'm pretty sure volcanoes would erupt with this kind of chemistry (it is 1:54 am while i'm writing this review so if stuff doesn't make sense, do ignore it). anyway, the sex scenes were definitely steamy. "are you taking human growth hormones or something? i snatch my hand back, fighting another rush of nervousness. "there's no way that huge man monster is fitting inside me!" [...] i might have big boobs and a grabbable ass, but have you seen my hips? tiny and narrow! which stands to reason that my lady canal is narrow too. you're going to rip me in half." he raises his head and there are honest-to-god tears in his eyes. "i think that's the nicest thing a girl has ever said to me," he chokes out. what you just read above? yeah, there's a whole lot where that came from. i read on a few reviews that this book was filled with cliches but i honestly didn't find a single one. yeah, there's the hockey player and the girl who helps him study for a class he's failing but that's pretty much it. i actually related to hannah in one part. i won't say because it is very personal but let's just say there's an experience she goes through with garrett that happened to me recently and my eyes opened up to a new world (don't laugh, please). anyways, the supporting characters were a great addition to the story, especially the hockey team. i had so much fun reading about these crazy guys with hearts that i just couldn't deal. the only reason i would put this book down would be because i either had to study, work or eat. other than that, i would read until my eyes would drift off and whatever i was reading would start to not make sense at all (yeah, this actually happened). my point is you have to read this book. do you want another reason to read this book? how about the fact that this book has a 4.40 average rating on goodreads with 54% being 5 stars and 33% being 4 stars... you guys know that it is nearly impossible for a book to have such high ratings on goodreads. so if that's not enough reason, i don't like you. just kidding but seriously you have to read this book. you won't be disappointed. i'm recommending this book to everyone i can find because it must be read!

title: ['Bloodstream']
cleaned_reviews: tess gerritsen is definitely the queen of the medical thriller, at least in my eyes. her background in medicine helps create very believable and readable medical situations, which are the basis for the thriller aspect of the stories. in this case, teenagers in an otherwise sleepy maine town are becoming unexplainably violent and turning on friends and family members. when a historically similar situation is uncovered, the town is divided between those who want to hide the information because it could kill tourism income (most of the town), and those who want to discover the cause and save the kids (the police chief and the new doctor in town)! while some aspects of the plot are easily figured out, there are plenty of twists and turns to keep you surprised and guessing, and i was gratified at times when i, and the townspeople, were wrong about someone (altho of course the townspeople were wrong more often than the reader!) i am somewhat chagrined to have to admit that i was surprised by the ultimate ending - she caught me on that! this took me two days to read only because it's not the kind of book i can read right before bedtime!

title: ['The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon', "The Cuckoo's Calling (Cormoran Strike, #1)", 'Full Dark, No Stars']
cleaned_reviews: the girl who loved tom gordon by stephen king is not typical king horror. instead, it is king at his story-telling best. this may have been a scary to the little girl in the book, but it is pure pleasure to read. trisha mcfarland is 9 years old. she is on a hike along the appalachian trail with her mom and brother pete. since their parents divorce, her mom has been trying to spend a lot of time with the kids, much to the dismay of everyone. pete, however, is very vocal about his displeasure, and he and his mom are constantly arguing. to get a little peace from the bickering (and she sort of has to pee), trisha steps off the trail and into the forest. that was an unfortunate decision, the first of many. the second was deciding to go a little deeper into the woods, and then to take a short-cut and meet up with the trail and her family further along. it is a long time before they even notice her missing. then there is a tip called into the police station that derails the search. meanwhile poor trisha is battling the rain, the bugs, the hunger, the swamp, the darkness, illness and something else that seems to be following her. but trisha is not really alone. she has baseball on her radio, and her favorite closer for the red sox, tom gordon, who walks with her, and talks with her, and "mostly" gives her encouragement. but she is in those woods a long time, and even tom gets discouraged. this is a story of a brave little girl, who finds a way to handle her fears. through tears, anger, tenacity and a touch of insanity, as well as imagination, faith and acceptance, trisha keeps going. the reader loves trisha from the first page, and you will root for her til the end. really good book. the cuckoo's calling by robert galbraith is the 1st in the cormoran strike detective series. note that it didn't take long for these books to be recognized as actually being written by jk rowlings. you can't really blame her for using a pseudonym. after harry potter's success, if you want to change genre, taking a new name was necessary. this series is different for rowlings. an adult based pi series. after losing his leg to a land mine in afghanistan, cormoran strike needed a new career. as a private investigator, he is barely scraping by, and he has just broken up with his girlfriend. living in his office, things are not looking good. when john bristow comes calling with doubts about the suicide of his legendary supermodel adopted sister lula landry known as cuckoo), cormoran is skeptical. the case was thoroughly investigated at the time, but since he needs the money... when he interviews a neighbour who had heard an argument from lula's apartment just before she fell to her death, more questions arise. meanwhile, his new secretary robin (who he hired for a week), is proving worth her weight in gold. i liked this book very much, definitely worth the read. full dark, no stars by stephen king contains 4 short stories. classic stephen king stories, but a little "more" believable, and thus more intense. "1922" is the tale of a man who is confessing to killing his wife because she wouldn't let him have her 100 acres of farmland. sounds a little extreme, but he lives to regret this. "big driver" is the story of tessa, who is an author and travels around speaking to little old ladies about the books she has written. one night on the way home, she takes a different route, and is savagely beaten, raped and left for dead. but she gets her own revenge. i loved this one. "fair extension" is about dave, who is dying of cancer. he meets a man who tells him he can "extend" his life. but at what cost... "a good marriage" is a story about darcy, who finds out that perhaps she has not known her accountant husband as well as she thought. -- loved this one too!

title: ['Girl in Pieces']
cleaned_reviews: 4/5 stars. when i initially heard about this book from jacqueline (jbooklover) on yt before this novel came out i knew i would fall in love with it. i knew i wanted to read the story of a girl who harmed herself in a way that the media often skews as a "cry for attention." i knew i wanted to read a story that had an accurate representation of how damn hard it is to recover. and by golly, i got that story. girl in pieces by kathleen glasgow is about a girl named charlie. charlie has been on the streets since her mother kicked her out and her best friend attempted suicide; this girl has been through hell and back. she's lived on the streets and been pimped out. she's sliced her body to numb the pain of her best friend's addiction to drugs and a boy who is bad news. she's fallen for a guy who will never love her the way she wants to be loved. charlie is truly a girl in pieces when she finds herself in a rehabilitation center, but this is not the end of her story only a chapter of it. this book is hard to read, i won't sugar coat that. this book made me cry hard in the best way possible. glasgow has a way with words; they are strong yet easy to comprehend for readers who don't constantly research mental illnesses *like i do.* girl in pieces is beautiful in the way it makes you feel after setting it down; you feel like you've gained knowledge. yet, that does not mean this book is perfect, i found myself skipping pages because scenes were longer than i felt necessary and i wasn't learning anything about the characters in those pages, but glasgow's writing is beautiful - there is no doubt about that. we'll talk more in depth about characters once we get into the spoiler section, but, damn, charlie is a hard character's perspective to read from. charlie is hurting; she has lost everything that matters to her, yet she is still fighting to stay alive and overcome her mental illness - which is so admirable. she is a fighter, an overcomer, and i respect her for that. she is recovering, and she relapses, and she is real, which i needed to read about because i could relate to it. as a girl who has been recovering from an eating disorder for years, i know that it is not easy to recover, and you never truly will. you don't just magically get better, you have scars to show for it. you have battle wounds because you are a fighter, and it is hard to get better, but if you take every day step by step it will be easier to cope with. i really hope you pick up this book if you haven't already because it is worth your while. title: ['School Spirits']
cleaned_reviews: with this spin-off of her hex hall series, rachel hawkins' books hold their place on my shelves as some of my favorite books. in her distinctive style, she gives us one more story that is so entertaining and just plain fun to read. from the moment we meet izzy brannick in spellbound (book 3 of the hex hall series) i was so taken by this spunky youngest member of the tough brannick family, so you can imagine my excitement when i first heard she would be the main character in this new spinoff series. i was not disappointed. she has a fresh voice, so different from sophia's hilarious constant snarkiness, but still bright and sure of herself, tough in a way that shows the no-nonsense way that she was raised as a brannick, and sweetly naive to the ways of the outside world. she's still so funny (how could any character written by hawkins not be?), but with the fear and sorrow that she feels for her missing sister, we get to see her vulnerable side as well. she's faced with some major challenges---both in proving herself as a creature hunter and in facing down the hallways of her new high school. the story weaves around and keeps you guessing as izzy works to discover the mystery of the ghost haunting the school and who is behind it. she makes some great friends for the first time in her life and discovers that being normal definitely has it's up and downs, but she learns to love it and knows she will miss it when it's time for her to move on. more mysteries pop up when she meets a very unique guy named dex who she comes to suspect of packing some pretty deep secrets...just one more thing to investigate, all while trying to figure out her growing feelings for him. romy is another super quirky character---leader of the school's "ghost hunting club" and the one to give izzy her first experience of having a best friend. the ending was exciting and pretty surprising! some might disagree, but i certainly didn't see it coming. the twists kept coming and, for me, even as the ending neared, the guilty party could have been anyone! i really enjoyed this one all the way through---another fast-paced and incredibly fun read from rachel hawkins. i hope it continues (though sadly i've heard that this will be a stand-alone).

even through this discovery snake still pursues reggie, but reggies not so sure she can risk her heart once again even if he is the reason she starting to feel again. it was refreshing to see two characters openly talking about depression and not acting like it's such a taboo. at least for them it wasn't. i always hear about depression but don't really think about it to much, but after reading this book i understand what depression can be more clearly now. reggies sarcastic and slightly mean attitude were definitely high points for me. i don't know why but i love a sassy mc and reggie was definitely sassy (aka scary). snake was another really good character. yes he was a scumbag for not telling reggie about carla but it was easy to forgive him when you could see he was making a difference in reggies life. i actually liked carla too. she became a mature and humbled version of herself when she became pregnant and i respected her attitude and i have respect for anyone who can put up with reggie and snake. definitions of indefinable things had lots of whit, lots of laughs, even some crying and a lot of honesty. ms. taylor is a very talented author and i look forward to more of her books.

cleaned_reviews: i will admit i don't remember all of this book. my teacher read it to my class when i was about seven, so it's been a while. but i remember that i was mesmerized by the story at that age, looking forward to each new chapter and i definitely remember the last half. great characters, though the plot in it's self is fairly cliche (from what i can remember.) this is exactly the kind of fantasy book i love! the world building is fascinating, the internal logic is consistent and the characters are lovable and interesting. we follow moon, a young man unsure of his own species and with no sure place in the world, as he finds out more about what kind of people it is he shares genes with. sadly culture shock isn' the only thing he'll have to deal with - "his" people prove to have plenty of trouble on their own to deal with. when i'd finished this book i immediately wanted to read the next - not because the ending was unsatisfactory or because i felt there were pieces missing of the story told in the book, but simply because i wanted more. more knowledge about raksura culture, more situations involving these characters, and more adventures in this very interesting, huge setting. the set-up of a orphaned loner without knowledge of who or what he is cliche, but cliches are cliches for a reason. you relate to moon and all that he's going through; plus with such interesting world- and species-building, finding out more is exciting! the only parts that took me out of the book were some of the dialogue that just didn't click with me. not sure i can say it sounded "stilted" or anything, it just brought me out of the moment a little. other than that there's nothing i didn't love about this. favorite part, i think, is the internal consistency of the world - every time the plot does something that "breaks the rules" that the characters have come to accept, they will be questioning what happened before you as a reader has time to feel disgruntled. and not only will they question the rule-breaking, said rule-breaking will be explained. no hand-waving here, no. love stuff like that. need to read the next book in this series a-sap! a very entertaining read! i love how complex a person kamala and the people she interacts with are. her family and friends feel very real, especially her. the way she got her power and the challenges she faces are both interesting and entertaining. will definitely be keeping up with this series!

title: ['Gone with the Wind']
cleaned_reviews: gone with the wind is most definitely a problematic read. i took quite a lot of time reading this novel, and when i was about halfway in, i began questioning why i was reading it at all. this happened mostly because at this point of the novel it becomes clear that the novel undeniably, unarguably has a racist element to it. reading through this was frustrating. however, it had had its moments, i had begun to quite like the characters, and i loathed giving up when i was already halfway in. i was willing to see if there were something more to it that would appease me. being racist, i thought, didn't invalidate its importance entirely. if not anything else, i realized, as much as it is fiction, it is also history. this line of thought, as i continued reading, proved to be helpful. i began warming up to the novel, and began to think that it wasn't particularly racist, which is not to say that it does not convey the racist mindset of the southerners (and for that matter, the northerners, too, who, while they emancipated the blacks, did not much care to do anything for them except use them as political tools). but while portraying this mindset, it also shows how this was, for most people, just something that they had inherited, and never thought to question. slavery didn't exist just because they (not true for all, of course) hated or even consciously inferiorized the blacks, but because they (and even the black characters, who draw distinct class lines between themselves) were complicit with it. the novel is trying to elucidate how the civil war wasn't just the north standing up for what's right. it's not black and white. it never is. it's very clear that the white characters cared for the black characters. it is the class difference which seems to matter more. it is, therefore, obviously a brilliant account of the civil war, showing that while the war was probably a necessary evil, as slavery probably wouldn't have ended otherwise, there was much, much more to it, too. that said, i loved the novel because of scarlett. she is so flawed a character and hence so real you cannot help but love her. of course, her being a fiery independent and empowered woman helps. she definitely doesn't change a lot throughout the novel, but i can't say i hate that; she is who she is. which brings me to rhett. i loved rhett so very much in the beginning when he seemed the only voice of reason, and the dynamic between him and scarlett was brilliant as well. by the end of the novel, though, rhett gave me really mixed feelings. i'm still not sure how to feel about him, but i can't say i love him anymore. i finished this book at around 4 in the morning today, and despite the sleep deprivation, and the endless tears i had shed while reading it, i was so, so happy because i loved this novel despite having been sure that i wouldn't. that says it all, i think.

title: ['The Witness']
cleaned_reviews: it's been awhile since i've picked anything up by la nora, and it was clear by a couple of pages in that i was reading the work of a polished, established author. (yet another reason i have got to stop picking up those kindle freebies on amazon!) she is sticking to a formula that works for her - the laid back, laconic wit of the handsome small-town cop (of course, he used to be a big-city cop until something brought him back home), the danger trailing the heroine to his backyard, instant attraction between the two with the heroine fighting it every step of the way...she's pulled it off for, what is it, 200 books now? even if you don't like nora roberts, you have to admit she's built a pretty good widget. anyway, the fresh take on the trope she's pulled out of her hat this time is that the heroine is, shall we say, different. i struggled to put my finger on it for the first 1/3 of the book, and bazinga! it hit me. nr has created a female version of sheldon cooper. that gave my enjoyment of the book a completely different perspective, and one that ms. roberts would probably not appreciate. all in all, a great lawn chair read - nothing particularly new or memorable (other than the hero and his way with words), but better than a lot of what is currently out there. especially for free on amazon. 3.5 stars

title: ['Wither (The Chemical Garden, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: wither is haunting, beautiful, sinister, and at times, even disturbing. i actually devoured it in one sitting, which was surprising, because there were a couple of things that actually turned me off about the novel. nonetheless, something kept me going until the wee hours of the morning, just to know what happens at the end of it all. i even had a bizarre sister-wife dream of my own after finishing! the world lauren destefano has created is scary in the fact that it seems so plausible. genetic engineering happens already today, girls are snatched off the streets and sold in today's society. though, if i'm being perfectly honest, if a third world war did break out, i don't know if i'd believe america would be the last place standing. (china has my vote!) rhine as the main character wasn't irritating, though i almost felt a lack of...something. emotion maybe? her pull in either direction wasn't strong enough, her hatred wasn't fierce enough, she wasn't as sympathetic as i expected, and she wasn't as determined as i wanted. she had elements of all these traits, enough for me to like her and sympathize with her, but not enough for me to admire her. i wanted more of a forbidden romance out of her and gabriel - more than a couple of stolen kisses. though i did like the bit about him hiding june beans in her breakfast, and the fact that they actually talked. a conversation is so rare in young adult romances these days! however, as usual, i'm in love with the secondary characters. especially the sister-wives. i loved the deep relationship between all of the girls, the strange combination of being sisters and friends and wives. i enjoyed jenna's character, though i wish we'd seen more of her. i loved little cecily, though she was one of the parts that disturbed me the most. the whole concept of a thirteen-year-old being completely obsessed with marriage, sex, and pregnancy is a little nauseating. i tried to get in the mindset that, really, in their society, she's pretty much ready for it, given their lifespan is so short, but my modern sensibilities just wanted to grab a black marker and black it all out. i can also understand why rhine could become so easily frustrated with her, but i also found myself wanting to tell her to lay off, the cecily is only a child. by the end of the novel, i'm so drawn to cecily and totally scared for her that i hope she makes appearances in the rest of the series. i need to know what happens to that poor, vivacious little redhead. as for the men of the story, i appreciated all three for what they were. gabriel is the (obviously) gorgeous servant who connects with rhine over the simple desperation of being trapped. i can't wait to find out more about him, because i felt he was a little bland in this one. linden was also incredibly sympathetic. i was left at the end really wishing that, you know, someone had told him the truth. he's such a naive, sweet man, he deserves to know the truth about the people he loves. i appreciate that he never forces himself on any of his wives, and that he was actually so head-over-heels in love with his first wife. it made him extremely likable. his father on the other hand? total creepster! i foresee him being a huge problem in the series - or at least i hope so, because he's such a fantastic antagonist. as mentioned, there were a couple of things i didn't quite like about wither. the pacing was a major one. even though i read it in one day, it just felt so, so, so slow. like nothing was really happening until the last couple of pages. i've been wondering if it's a deliberate choice though, to reflect the monotonous lives of the sister-wives, stuck in an endless, unbreakable routine inside the mansion. if it was, i understand it, but i could've used a few little pick-me-up scenes to keep the ball rolling. i also didn't like the repetitiveness of a couple of things. saying over and over where she hid gabriel's handkerchief, repeatedly letting us know exactly what ages men and women die. little details, certainly, but when they're repeated every couple of chapters, it starts feeling a little redundant. however, the ending was so deliciously hopeful, i'm begging for more! i can't wait to see what comes next in rhine's life. do they make it out ok? are they hunted? is a cure discovered? i am definitely looking forward to an amp up in the action and romance in the sequel! the final word: while slow, and a bit repetitive, there is definitely enough to keep you going. the world in wither is haunting, beautiful, and terrifying. while maybe not the strongest of the future series, it lays a lot of necessary groundwork, and i think the series will only improve from here. definitely a must-read of 2011! (originally from http://thetealeafreview.blogspot.com)

cleaned_reviews: 4.5 stars. full review to come. this was absolutely adorable. i couldn't help but love the story and the characters. i don't read a lot of contemporary romance, but this is the kind of story i hope for when i do. a combination of serious topics with a cute romance and lovable characters... where can you go wrong? caymen is a fabulous main character. she is by no means perfect but she does so much growing throughout the novel that it's impossible not to root for her. she totally deserves a good guy, which is what she finds in xander, thank goodness. caymen dismantles her prejudices despite her family history and allows xander into her life, and what comes of it was so wonderful to read. they were so much fun together, and xander worked so well with caymen's sarcastic nature. they genuinely appreciated each other, which i loved. one of the things that had me most excited about this novel was the pretty in pink comparison, on which it completely delivered. the parallels were obvious to me (a big fangirl of that movie) and they were really well done. i absolutely adored that part because it was an excellent tribute, in a way. such an enjoyable read. for the first middle grade novel to be reviewed on my blog, this was a fantastic choice! it clearly had promise, and on that it absolutely delivered. i was definitely pleasantly surprised by this one. this is a wonderfully written novel. with middle grade, i think it's very important to have a narrative voice that a younger reader can connect to. this was absolutely present with the main character and narrator, jack. his narrative voice is so friendly and easy to follow, especially at the beginning, and i think it is perfect for younger readers. at the same time though, it did not feel juvenile at all. as an older teenager reading an mg novel, i did not feel spoken down to, or like it was too young for me. that can be a hard balance for mg authors to find, but i think peter lerangis has done an excellent job writing in a voice that can appeal to people of any age. if i had to describe this novel in two words, i'd say action-packed. there is always something happening. this is the perfect book for a reader who gets bored quickly because there is no time to get bored. it jumps from some wild event to a daring escape to an unbelievable rescue, and so on. this was done extremely well because while it is definitely exciting and always moving, the transition is still there. it moves at a fast pace but not at the expense of important information. this is another area in which i feel lerangis' experience in this field really comes through. you cannot dispute that he knows how to write for his audience. while the plot was certainly the highlight of the novel, you can't forget the characters. the main character, jack, is smart, entertaining, and, what i especially enjoyed: skeptical. when he is told a bunch of wild, unimaginable things about himself, he doesn't just accept them; he thinks the man who told him is absolutely nuts and tries to run away. he thinks logically, which in a story with such wild happenings, helps make a lot of things more understandable. as for the friends he makes, cass, marco, and aly; they're all a little strange and they each have their quirks that sometimes make you want to grab them by the shoulders and shake them, but these things make them feel like real 13 year olds. what real 13 year old doesn't have some annoying quirk or habit? you really grow to enjoy them despite the occasionally irritating behaviour, because really, it's normal. overall this was a fun, exciting novel for my first foray into middle grade fiction on the blog and i loved the mythology/history aspect! can't wait to see which wonder they tackle next! i will absolutely be keeping my eye out for the next novel in the series. 4 stars!

title: ['Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - Parts One and Two (Harry Potter, #8)']
cleaned_reviews: spoiler free: as much as i love harry potter i wasn't really sure we needed this story and i was nervous about it, especially since i don't really like reading plays - they are meant to be seen after all. but...i really really liked this. except that i am now going to have to rename my cat now that we know moaning myrtle's full name. we named her myrtle because she was meowing outside our house whilst we were watching hp and we took her in. could definitely have done without that bit. it was weird adjusting to a perspective that wasn't harry's, but i think that's also what made this work. it's not the 8th hp book - it's the next generation. thinking of it like that helped me just enjoy it. i connected with it enough that it made me cry due to nostalgia and also because i may have a wee crush on neville. which feels less gross here since it's more clear that they are my age. :) i was born two days after the fight in godric's hollow. i liked that this showed the more positive side of slytherin, considering that is the house pottermore sorted me into (even though i'm obviously a ravenclaw). i liked that the next generation weren't just duplicates of their parents. i liked that harry was flawed. i liked seeing life go on. i liked harry struggling with parenting because he had no good example of parenting. i liked the plot but won't give any details. :) i liked the format - this isn't harry's story and that made it feel different. i hope i get to see it performed at some point, although i do think it would be hard seeing different actors in the roles. i have seen some people say it was poorly written and i didn't feel that way. it's just different from the novels because it's all dialogue, which isn't as rich as what we got in the novels. i also don't think calling it fan fiction is fair since rowling came up with the story and worked with the playwright - it's not like she wasn't involved. is it as magical as the novels? nope. but it's still an enthralling story and a new chapter in the hp universe and it made me happy.

title: ['An Exaltation of Larks (Venery, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i'm finding it hard to write a review for this book, but i'll have a go while it's still fresh in my mind. it's certainly not my usual fare. i'm not really sure what category or genre it fits into. it's not a cr, it's not a hr (although it begins in the 1970s). in fact although it has elements of romance, i wouldn't call it a romance at all. it's not chick lit. maybe it's should simply be classified as 'fiction'. kind of a big, sprawling saga, not quite a 'family saga' as the mcs aren't all related, although it does centre on the lark family. i didn't read the book straight through, finding i had to keep taking breaks from it. not sure why. the plot was unpredictable (in a good way), but perhaps i kept fearing the angst i was worried was around the corner. and sometimes it was..... yes, i shed a few tears during the reading of this book. the story itself turned out to be quite labyrinthine and fascinating. the connection to (relatively) recent historical events added extra interest. i liked the characters and thought they were pretty well-fleshed out, although i was uncomfortable with jav's occupation the whole way through. you could see inside his head and see why his life turned out that way, and you loved him, but still...... i would never knowingly read a book about an mc with that occupation. tacky. there were moments in the book that felt a bit too contrived to me e.g. when jav was saying goodbye to flip. i could feel the fell hand of the author intervening in their story. it didn't flow in the effortless way a reading experience should. however this wasn't true for the whole book - just some parts. i did like that the characters were from different cultures and backgrounds. this made for a great and interesting mix. i also liked the way that the writer explored the varieties of sexuality the characters experienced (apart from my previously stated reservations about jav's occupation). it was done with a realism and lack of self-consciousness that i liked. it's a very interesting book overall. quite a 'meaty' read. it has 'all the feels', and leaves you with a lot to think about. i may read it again in a year or so, and i think a second reading will be quite different.

title: ['The Fill-In Boyfriend']
cleaned_reviews: full review another thing that i'm finding i like about contemporary novels is i can easily finish them in a matter of hours, in one sitting. there's just something so satisfying about that. and this book is no exception. as cheesey as it might be, there's just something i really love about the whole "pretend to be in love and then accidentally catch feelings" trope. it's just so heartwarming and sweet, and it a bit early to say this (i haven't read too many contemporary novels) but i don't think i'll ever tire of it. this novel was just so sweet and cute. i was simultaneously both maddened and intrigued by the fact that we didn't learn the fill-in bradley's name until about a third of the way into the novel. i was satisfied with what his name ended up being though, it's a cute name (and no i'm not going to tell you what it is, you'll have to read it and find out for yourself). i didn't like gia at the start of the book, she was self centered and way to concerned with validation. her character arc was pleasing, and by the end of the story, i found myself liking her. i loved bec, she was just so real and sure of herself and want she wanted. i also, of course, loved fill-in bradley, who was slightly geeky, and adorable, and such a gentleman. his mom was also pretty awesome. of the rest of the side characters, the only one i found alright-ish was claire, though aside from being sweet she seemed a bit flat. gia's family look perfect from the outside, but they definitely aren't. and gia's friends, family, and most of the rest of the characters all shared two traits: shallow and judgemental.it sort of got to the point where i was like "ok is anyone not shallow and judgemental?" and i know that was part of the point, but it seemed a bit unbelievable that everyone could be like that. despite the sort of unrealistically shallow characters, this was a sweet heartwarming story.

title: ['Faking Faith']
cleaned_reviews: dylan's friends all warned her that blake was a jerk, but she didn't believe them until it was too late and he had already forwarded topless pictures of her to the whole school... completely ostracized by her classmates, dylan spends most of her time messing around on the internet, which is where she finds them - the blogs of homeschooled, fundamentalist christian teenage girls. dylan becomes fascinated by everything from their modest dress to their weird vocabulary, and quickly finds herself hooked. soon, just reading the posts isn't enough, so she creates a blogger alter-ego named faith, a devout maiden who lives on a farm in wisconsin. when she starts an online friendship with abigail, a girl who actually lives the life faith is pretending to live, it seems simple enough, but when abigail invites faith to visit her for two weeks, things get a lot more difficult. will dylan be able to convince people that she is faith, or will her lie be revealed? faking faith is a unique book that explores the pros and cons of both modern secular life and insular religious life. dylan and abigail are believable, fully-formed characters, and bloss doesn't take cheap shots or give easy answers to complex problems. this is a good read for girls who are interested in exploring religion or those who want a story of a girl triumphing over her past mistakes.

title: ['Magic Bleeds (Kate Daniels, #4)', 'Dreamfever (Fever, #4)', "Death's Mistress (Dorina Basarab, #2)", 'Black Night (Black Wings, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: magic bleeds is the fourth installment in the kate daniels series by writing duo ilona & gordan andrews. i started reading this series after winning a signed copy of this book. yes, amazing, i know! if you haven't read this series yet, don't start with magic bleeds. magic bites is book 1 and the series should be read in order. if i had to sum it up on 2 words, i would choose... genius & exciting! only pages in, i knew i would be addicted to this series. i read all four of these books in 3 days. i would have read them even faster, if it wasn't such a beautiful week! this whole series has an amazing fantasy tone that fits in so well with the urban setting. it has a bit of laurell k. hamilton's, anita blake series feel, but not too much. i find it has more of carrie vaughn's kitty norville feel to it, which i love. but, it still remains original and refreshing. if you are already a ilona andrews fan, than you know what to expect from her writing and i can tell you, you will not be disappointed. i want to add also, how much i like this book's cover art. it's fierce and pretty in one. very fantasy like. as always, everything seems to go wrong in kate daniels life. being a knight of the order of merciful aid, she doesn't have it easy. but, she's come a long way to where she is now, and i find from book 1, a lot has happened, and she's now fully coming to terms with the important things in her life. curran, the beast lord, and my favorite new man, stood her up after an agonizing wait. kate finally feels she might be ready to surrender her heart, but things always seem to stop her from being happy. now kate, fears that her family could be a major danger (stranger danger? jk) for curran and the other shape shifters. she's got a lot of her plate right now, but that's not all. saiman, a former god who likes to play with kate simply because she presents a challenge to him, decides to stir things up with kate and curran, and her professional career at the order is at crossroads. we also get to learn more about roland, and his past. but it's not all trials, and mystery. kate and curran finally get what they both want this time around, which made me get what i wanted! ilona really knows how to push you to the edge of your seat! i don't want to forget how hilarious ilona is. she writes amazing scenes, and her humor is always well put. i loved all of this series, but i think i have to say this one is my favorite, apart from magic strikes. each book brings more, interesting qualities and exciting scenes to the table, i cannot wait to see what's in store for the gang next. i highly recommend you start this series, and if you already have, this book rocked! don't you agree? ** spoiler alert ** karen marie moning is one of my favorite authors and the fever series is amazing. i've been hooked since the start, counting down the days for each new installment. and what an installment this was! it's a rollercoster of action and emotion. i couldn't put it down. mac was left off as pri-ya in horrible pain. she is fortunately some what saved by dani but that doesn't get her out of the hot water. only when barrons shows up and takes her away for weeks does she start to become herself again, and what a way i might add! their relationship takes a new path that we've wanted to see for a while, but is it how we want to see them? also, mac, barrons and v'lane have the usual triangle which leads to some great scenes. mackayla's murderer gives mac an invitation she can't refuse. he's kidnapped her parents and she has to go back home to save them. once she gets there it's not as easy as she thought. dreamfever is a very emotion filled and action packed story. it will make you think and put you on the edge of your seat. it's very hard to say this but i'd say it's my favorite installment of the series. i cannot wait for shadowfever in 2010. it will be the last of mac's adventures but i know it will be a winner! death's mistress is the second book in the dorina basarab series by karen chance. and like all chance's books, it was amazing. i'm a huge fan of chance's cassandra palmer series and dorina basarab is a branch off series of the palmer series. it's placed in the same world as cassie with some of the same characters such as mircea and louis-cesare.. this book has dorina helping her fey best friend clair with a fey problem. someone stold a precious fey relic that can help clair save her son from those who are trying to kill him because he is next for the fey throne. but dorina finds out it's much more bigger than just a few people. everyone who are powerful and sneeky want this relic and dorina doesn't know who is hner enemy and who she can trust. death's mistress was a powerful, fast paced book that keept me begging for more. i cannot wait to see what chance has for us next with dorina. she's a strong character that knows what she wants, when she wants it. i've been a fan from thne start and will be until the end. if you haven't read either the cassandra palmer series or the dorina basarb series by karen chance, you don't know what your missing. karen chance makes urban fantay. i highly recommend you read this! synopsis: dorina basarab is a dhampir-half-human, half-vampire. back home in brooklyn after the demise of her insane uncle dracula, dory's hoping her life is about to calm down. but soon dory realizes someone is killing vampire senate members, and if she can't stop the murderer, her friends may be next... another hit for christina henry! cleaned_reviews: wow i knew i liked aguirre's work, but now that she has teamed up with her husband there's an added level of awesomeness. in this new novel in a brand spankin new series about a steampunk novel a dynamic duo solve mysteries while dealing with potentially dangerous fae descendants. centuries before humans (invaders) found the land of faerie and war began. the war was so horrible that both sides suffered mass casualties until the summer queen and winter lord decided allying and missing their blood with the humans was preferable to dying off entirely. fast forward to present day and now there only remain certain houses that hold enough magic to be so powerful. the story starts with mikani and ritsuko being handed a very sensitive case. they are charged with finding a young lady, related to one of the major houses. after the young girl is found brutally burned to death it falls to their shoulders to then find the culprit and kill/arrest him. with pressure from the other houses the pair have to use all their wits and abilities (including mikani's rather fae-like gift of sensing) to solve these grizzly crimes. the characters and world building were just excellent. i thought the writing was just wonderful and though it's set in the most unrealistic world, i could definitely get behind the characters' credibility. throughout the story mikani and ritsuko's professional partnership starts becoming a little something more. i like how their romance is slowly blossoming and they end up realizing they need each other. cannot wait for the next one and this one barely came out! lol 4 stars

cleaned_reviews: hermann hesse's depiction of the spiritual journey has often been copied, usually badly by wanna-be new age writers. yet hesse's short novel will never be surpassed. it is an uplifting look at one man searching for the truth, loosely based on the buddha's own journey, that will remain a classic for all times. a must read. in my five-star review of the passage, i commented that cronin was one-thirds into writing a 21th century literary epic. now it's two-thirds finished as the twelve, the second installment of the author's passage trilogy, is as stellar a work as his first volume. the twelve goes back to the beginning of the apocalypse where we are introduced to new characters including a delusional female scientist and a janitor who is linked to the original viral carriers that make up what is known as the twelve. as in the first book, cronin covers a hundred years span and we are reintroduced to the characters from the first book who now have their own goals and agendas. the author weaves a complex tale where nothing is simple or obvious. this is a massive epic work that not only has an unique take on the vampire tale but has taken the post-apocalyptic novel to new heights. unlike the passage, this work has a clear ending yet does give us a big surprise and a good idea where the third and last installment will take us. this is one of the best novels of 2012 and hands down the best horror novel i've read this year.

title: ['Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (Harry Potter, #3)', 'Wires and Nerve, Volume 1 (Wires and Nerves, #1)', 'A Study in Charlotte (Charlotte Holmes, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: reread: november 2016 4 stars i really enjoyed that! it's a nice way to continue one of my all-time favorite series - by taking it to a new medium and shifting the focus to one of the side characters. it makes sense that after such an epic story, there are still many loose ends, and i like that we're getting a view of how the world pieces itself back together again. i will say that though the art is visually appealing, the characters didn't quite match my image of them. and that's kind of weird, when you've been attached to them for so long. and with the different format, their personalities seem a little off at times too. but maybe that's just because everyone's all happy in relationships and being lovey dovey and stuff. but honestly, that's nitpicking, because i will never let go of this series. 4 stars "modern sherlock retelling." at the moment, it doesn't take much more than that to get me salivating over a book. and i know that there is some skepticism if it could ever be done any better than the every series by ellie marney, and whether people should even bother trying anymore. well i absolutely loved cavallaro's take on the concept and i believe it's a retelling worth reading. there's one big thing that sets a study in charlotte apart from the rest - here, sherlock is female. charlotte is an actual descendant of sherlock holmes, and james is a descendant of john watson. the story is told from james's point of view, while charlotte is the oddball genius whose mind is on another level entirely. i loved that the characters sherlock and john were real in this world, because it creates such a colorful backstory for the main characters. it may seem a little convenient and forced at times because they resemble their ancestors so much - even charlotte's brother is a veritable mycroft who holds nuclear launch codes and stuff - but the storytelling absolutely worked for me. so charlotte and james end up at the same boarding school in the us, and though they had never met before, they are definitely aware of each other and their family histories. they meet and get off to a pretty rough start, but when a murder hits the campus and they are both the most likely suspects, they start to become friends. it's a slow build, but because they just understand each other so well and feel protective and defensive of each other, they end up best friends. are you awwing yet? because i was absolutely awwing. and my shippy feels were not far behind. i loved this story a lot for those characters and the way that relationship builds. probably my favorite part. i mean, they are not carbon copies of their ancestors. they do face modern day problems. and charlotte has a history that crushed my feels but made her so impressive and endearing. female sherlock ftw. she faces sexist views, family pressures, and one supreme douchebag at school, but she keeps being fiercely herself. (maybe the drug habit went a bit far at such a young age, but it's sherlock. didn't find it unbelievable.) and she and jamie have such a great rapport, some banter, some hilarity... they're a great team. but what also impressed me was the mystery part of it. first of all, the crimes that start occurring on their campus resemble old sherlock holmes stories. so it made it kind of like a fun scavenger hunt to discover who was framing them and why. second, my pet peeve of ya mysteries is when teens start investigating without the authorities, because they don't trust them, they're too stupid, yadda yadda yadda. a study in charlotte is not like that. they actually team up with the local detective and work together in a smart and (mostly) realistic way. that made it so much more fun and compulsively readable, because i wasn't continuously thinking about how far-fetched it was. the stakes do get rather high too. there were a couple moments when my heart leaped up in my throat and i clenched my fingers hoping they would be okay - which is precisely the perfect effect that a mystery should have. overall this was just a really well-rounded story, equal parts fun and thrilling. and that for a debut! wow. i can't wait to see what happens next. summing up: fans of sherlock holmes and ya mysteries take note: a study in charlotte is a book you must get your hands on. this female supersleuth, charlotte holmes, is a feminist powerhouse that you'll instantly fall in love with. and the combination of charlotte and jamie? completely aww-worthy. the mystery impressed me with its creativity and well-rounded backstory. and yeah, i just can't wait for more adventures with these characters. as soon as i finished reading this, i went online to pre-order a finished copy - it's that good. the combination of hilarity, wit, romance, thrills, and classic sherlock elements is extremely entertaining. gif it to me straight! recommended to: fans of sherlock - and, yes, the every series. *an electronic advance review copy was provided by the publisher in exchange for an honest review. this does not affect my opinion of the book or the contents of the review.

title: ['The Gods Themselves']
cleaned_reviews: the ideas and commentary make this an awesome book. asimov uses parallel universes to transfer energy and wraps the idea in mystery, crisis, and aliens. there are three stories with completely different perspectives that piece the entire story together. the second part that focuses on the aliens is slow and difficutlt to visualize at first but as it starts to make sense it gets interesting. i liked the commentaries on epistemic arrogance, social motivations, and sexuality. these commentaries occur in a way that strengthens the story instead of appearing as tangents for the author to insert speeches. as is typical for asimov, there isn't much action because the story revolves around the ideas. however, unlike his later addons to robots and foundation, this book doesn't devolve into a bunch of circuitous dialogue. the ideas drive the story. the far out sci-fi aspects can be supported by theories that are still current today. very well done. great science fiction.

title: ['Hild', 'Fahrenheit 451']
cleaned_reviews: this is some exquisite world-building--so impressive how griffith manages to evoke a time and place at the cusp of so many cultural transitions. i especially loved how carefully the novel is crafted to let readers see the world through hild's observant eyes. (the one difficulty i had with the book is the handful of occasions when it would switch perspective, seemingly without reason. those passages suddenly shifted the narrative so that readers end up looking at hild, rather than looking at the world through her. very disorienting.) now that i know a bit more about the historical person on which the book is based, i'm excited to read that griffith is planning to continue writing about hild. i'm curious to see how griffith will imagine hild's life as she moves into adulthood and toward a different role in the changing power dynamics of her world. it had been twenty years or more since i last read this, so i decided to listen to the audiobook on a long drive from iowa to oregon. there's nothing quite like tim robbins shouting denham's dentifrice into the prairie of eastern montana... except maybe hearing him tenderly recite "dover beach" in that same strange solitary landscape. as the crazy mountains appeared on the horizon, i realized i'd forgotten the entire final third of the book, which means i also forgot that at its heart (or at least, at its end), this is an anti-war novel. given what the book has to say about how closely linked forgetting and destruction are, i'm more than a little troubled at how much the years had erased. let's hope this time more of the sand stays in the sieve.

title: ['Thrawn (Star Wars: Thrawn, #1)', "Ender's Game (Ender's Saga, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: "is this what chiss do? see a trap, and just walk into it?" good science fiction--albeit a space opera--not just good star wars fiction. the reader need not have any previous exposure to star wars nor thrawn to enjoy this origins tale in which zahn skillfully weaves the many threads of existing stories into a fresh, original story. "there's no trust in politics. never has been. never will be." thrawn is there in all his glory, but he is also limited and occasionally tone deaf, so he's less superhuman. "all eli could see in his face was that maddening confidence of his." the two primary threads interweave convincingly. bad people see themselves as serving a greater good, just a good people are often blind to their own faults. good holmes-watson interchanges. understanding an opponent through his art is a constant with thrawn. "military leadership is a journey, not a destination." quibble: thrawn's voice, even his inner voice, is too childish. don't care for the cover art; inconsistent with other portrayals of thrawn. "a warrior may retreat. he does not flee. he may lie in ambush. he does not hide. he may experience victory or defeat. he does not cease to serve." ** spoiler alert ** yes, it's a good book. great pathos, but enormous improbabilities that kept knocking me out of the story. yes, ender's environment changed him from being a typical child, but we are more than the sum of our experiences. our innate qualities and tendencies form us also. not hard to believe a child might develop as ender did, but unlikely that he'd be so introspective so soon. and, in a way, isn't that what good literature is about: creating characters who--at some level--are us? not someone we identify, but someone who, were we not so lazy, limited and lackadaisical, we might be. (i've been thirteen for almost fifty years. how 'bout you?) card's view of future history still works thirty years after it was written. not that its what human society will look in seventy years, but that it's not jarringly wrong. note that the warsaw pact he discusses is the second such.) yes, he missed cell phones. asimov and heinlein missed microcomputers, but many of their stories still ring true. the end is maudlin, but as emotionally satisfying as it is unlikely. skipping the introduction was a good decision. i certainly didn't need all that biography and testimonials to enjoy the story. by telling me too much of the nuts and bolts of the book, card would have distracted me from the gestalt--the whole--of the story. but do read it later. a funny thing happened later: since ender's is a library book, i started to re-read it, and . . . i couldn't. i forced myself through the first couple of chapters but just couldn't get into the story again. isn't that strange? i used to say that a story is not good unless it's worth re-reading--i'm on my third time through the name of the wind--but it doesn't seem to work with ender. i don't blame the story. maybe the storytelling is too transparent. i thought that was good the first time through. now i'm not so sure.

title: ['A Most Wanted Man']
cleaned_reviews: how is it that no matter how the times, the locations, the methodologies, the patterns of thinking change, le carre always manages to stay relevant? this book, one of his most recent, is just as much a punch in the gut as any of his others, perhaps more so because i can still see it happening around me today, while his books on the cold war or the problems in latin america never seemed to as if they might have just happened yesterday. great story, great characters. i love how he makes a point with every book without ever seeming to moralize. but, boy, you can't put down one le carre and pick up another right after -- you'd turn into a suicidal depressive.

title: ['After I Do']
cleaned_reviews: 4.5 - 5 stars pretty darn amazing book. very realistic and not a glamorised romance novel. this is a life story. lauren and ryan have been together a long time. and like all long-term relationships problems become deeper and harder to deal with as time goes on, if left untreated. and that's what they've become--like an untreated wound. they reach breaking point and mull over other options, but end up on this life-changing decision: one year apart with no direct contact together. and so begins the story as we follow lauren on her way. i'd say (to people wondering about the style of this book) that it's a love story, but not a romance. lauren and her husband are apart for the book, but it doesn't mean this isn't about finding lauren at her core and what it means to be a person without ryan. after i do builds slowly, drawing a connection between the reader and lauren and her family. i must admit at times the book got pretty darn hard to take and it wasn't all pleasurable. but when everything comes to a complete circle by the end i was attached to lauren, and ryan, and the troughs and peaks that made it all worthwhile.

title: ['Frost Like Night (Snow Like Ashes, #3)']

title: ['Batman: The Black Mirror']
cleaned_reviews: this is the first comic i've read in quite a while that i put down and immediately wanted to read again. i finished the last few pages of this as slowly as possible, hoping to make it last a little longer. this may have become my favorite batman story of all time, and i've read a lot of batman. scott snyder has managed to lend a completely original voice to this, his run on detective comics. it floats somewhere between the serious, realistic christopher nolan films and the superheroics of stories like "hush," but that's just on the surface. underneath there is some harsh, sinister stuff going on in this story. i found myself genuinely shocked and revolted by parts of this story, and not just because of jock's intense artwork. snyder's character work is what did it. i was actually scared of something in batman for the first time since childhood. he made crazy crazy again. having read snyder's work on american vampire, i honestly didn't know what to expect. i find that series pretty predictable and middle-of-the-road. however, this book had been heavily hyped to me, so i was going in with high expectations. but he knocked it out of the park. expectations fulfilled and then some. it's amazing to me that a writer who's made his name on his own original series takes over a famous franchise like batman and kills it harder than his own thing. it feels like snyder was just born to write this. the stories come in 3-issue arcs, alternating artwork by jock and francisco francavilla. the styles and arcs complement each other perfectly, weaving in and out of each other, constantly surprising you with the elements that remain important and the ones that only stay within a given arc. i feel like i'm reaching a point where i'm gushing, so maybe i'll stop. but you have to read this. i require it.

title: ['The Little Stranger', 'Life As We Knew It (Last Survivors, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i've been eagerly anticipating this book and finally got it from the library, then devoured it. sarah waters returns to the post-ww2 england that she depicted so beautifully in the night watch for an uber-creepy ghost story set in a crumbling manor house. you get this sense of decay, not only from the house, but from the details of rationing, the collapse of the aristocracy, and the aftermath of the war effort. waters is a superlative historical novelist and is able to conjure up a time seemingly effortlessly with her use of language and detail. without spoiling it, i think there are parallels between the main relationship in the book and the smothering feeling you get from the house. although the themes of sexuality and gender aren't focused on as they are in most of her other work, it's there, and perhaps even more powerful because it's so subtle. i didn't think the book had scared me, but then i woke up in the middle of the night and couldn't stop thinking about it. i couldn't put it down, either. highly recommended, even if you generally don't like scary books. i really enjoyed this one; it reminded me a lot of in a perfect world, which i read a few months back. classic postapocalyptic fiction which begins with diary entries detailing the mundane suburban life of a teenage girl, which rapidly descends into darkness after a series of environmental catastrophes. pfeffer does a good job of portraying this scenario fairly realistically, and it's a fast read. one of the better ya postapocalyptic novels i've read lately.

title: ['On the Beach']
cleaned_reviews: on the beach, by nevil shute synopsis: they are the last generation, the innocent victims of an accidental war, living out their last days, making do with what they have, hoping for a miracle. as the deadly rain moves ever closer, the world as we know it winds toward an inevitable end... in a sentence: incredibly depressing but very thought-provoking. my thoughts: if the world was coming to an end in a few months' time, and there was nothing you could do to escape it, what would you do with your final days? that's the question i kept asking myself as i read this story. this book was very thought-provoking in that way, leading your thoughts into a deep dark hole where you don't want to go. it tackles a very difficult and uncomfortable issue: the end of mankind. this story has absolutely no action: just a character-driven plot. there is no moral to the story, not really. there is only a hopeless situation that nobody asked for, nor is there a thing that can be done about it, except wait. the story shows you how everyone reacts to the news and how they choose to spend the remaining time they have; do they look for a solution, a way to survive? do they drown themselves in drink? or would they go about their lives in complete denial? (i don't believe i'm giving away any spoilers here, all of this is pretty clear from the beginning). i found the whole thing extremely bleak and depressing, even terrifying. what's even worse is that the whole thing seems entirely plausible. it brings attention to the fact we are putting our trust in government leaders and officials who have complete control over an enormous amount of wmds. if one foolish leader decides to use them, the rest will follow, and we will destroy ourselves in the process, maybe not exactly in the way the book implies, but it would certainly be very similar. maybe there would be underground bunkers that could protect some people, but 99.9% of the world's population could be eradicated very easily, it seems. i don't know if anyone else finds that just a little bit scary, but i certainly do. some readers mentioned that certain scenarios were omitted that probably should have happened, but i think nevil implied that they already did happen. the people had known about what was coming for over a year, we're only just looking in during the last few months of it, and somehow that just makes the story even more gloomy than your usual novels. i wouldn't recommend this to everyone. it's a well-written, well-executed story, but it's also a very realistic, post-apocalyptic novel where no one survives. if you plan on reading this book be warned; abandon all hope, all ye who read this book, because you will not be a happy camper by the time the story's over.

title: ['The Last Dickens']
cleaned_reviews: 1870. charles dickens is dead. he leaves behind a struggling publisher, a bereaved public, and an unfinished novel. the mystery of edwin drood promised to be dickens' masterpiece, equally adored and misunderstood, and revolved around the question of whether the young hero was murdered or in hiding. now the mystery will never be solved; the novel is only half written. or is it? it falls to james osgood, dickens' american publisher, to find out the truth. along the way, he must fight opiate dealers, cutthroat publishers, and dickens' close friends' diverging opinions about the possible endings to drood. what he discovers is intriguing: could drood's missing ending hold the key to a real-life murder mystery? the novel is intriguing, a literary thriller written by a master of suspense. pearl does an excellent job of incorporating period details without ever slowing the pace. there were facts that i didn't know. did you know that dickens offered to tell queen victoria the ending of drood? or that dickens was stalked by a female admirer? or that an american tax collector blackmailed the dickens staff? the book is divided into six installments (the same number of installments as drood had at the time of dickens' death) and they flip from the present (after his death) and past (while dickens is on a book tour in america). at times, the structure can be confusing; after one or two of the flashbacks, i had difficulty remembering exactly what had happened in the previous section regarding the present day action. overall, though, that structure heightened the suspense and revealed dickens the man and how much the public craved his writings. i enjoyed the characters, especially dickens' publisher james osgood (a historical figure) and tom branagan (a fictional character) who acts as dickens porter on his last american tour. most of all, i enjoyed learning more about the time period and exploring the possibility of what might have been the ending of the author's last novel. edwin drood may be an unsolved mystery, but the last dickens' ending is satisfying.

title: ['We Were Liars']

"he was contemplation and enthusiasm. ambition and strong coffee. i could have looked at him forever." i could perfectly picture the liars even though i had a bit more trouble with the other cousins and uncles and aunts because the book is short and they are not really in the spotlight. i had expected a million things from this novel but certainly not this. it has a mysterious aura and is completely captivating. from the very beginning you know something wrong and twisted is coming and, of course, you try to take as many guesses as you possibly can but i never would have imagined the truth. it was such a surprise for me and it broke my heart. a lot of people say it was hard for them to get into the book at first but i didn't face the same problem. i totally loved the writing style and i am sure i would love more books from this author. i was fascinated by the sinclair family and all those luxurious places in which you can easily picture yourself thanks to the amazing descriptions. cadence is a very interesting character. she is very sick at the beginning of the book and it made me feel both bad and curious when you compare those chapters to the flashbacks in which she looks so happy and full of energy. i kept wondering what happened to make her so damaged. i had the urge to turn the pages quickly because i desperately needed to know the truth but i also didn't want to finish this book because i knew i was about to find out a horrible truth. when i got to the fifth part of the novel, i understood how much i had been lied to and i just couldn't get over it. i loved everything about this book and i would recommend reading it without knowing too much, first because it is really short and fast-paced (i read it in just three sittings), and second because there is so much suspense you don't want any spoilers. you need to find out the truth when you get there, just like cadence does. definitely a must-read for me.

title: ['Private Peaceful']
cleaned_reviews: beautifully written and deeply evocative, morpurgo has created what will undoubtedly become a classic in children's literature. besides its somewhat mature themes about war and life itself, 'private peaceful' is a delightfully original and lugubrious bildungsroman. first of all, while i do not believe that 'private peaceful' is a perfect book, i cannot stress enough times how i think that this is a book that should be read, especially by children. it is one of those must-reads. blending the best aspects from wilfred owen's poetic vision in the style and form suitable for children, morpurgo does not shy away from integrating a commentary on religion, life, relationships and war, while focusing on the injustice of it all, in his work. he has achieved his aim in the character of the protagonist, the everyman tommy, in his daily struggle of being in the light of, not, in his own words, in the shadow of, his older and beloved brother, charlie. tommy always had big boots to fill, especially in the absence of a father figure in his family and having a handicapped brother, big joe, to look after. charlie, being the eldest brother, makes it seem so effortless and natural that tommy couldn't help but feeling a little jealous sometimes. however, despite his family's unfortunate circumstances, they manage to make the best out of things. big joe's love of the nursery rhyme 'oranges and lemons', which he sings whenever he gets a chance to, is the 'good music' of the family, encouraging them when they are particularly troubled or despondent. molly is another integral character. tommy was always desirous of her attention since she was his boyhood crush. the outbreak of world war 1 changed their lives for ever. although, up till then, they always managed to be together through thick and thin, nobody expected it to have such lasting and wide-ranging effects. that is why men like siegfried sassoon criticized the insufficient imagination of the majority of people in those times. nobody had an idea of the ghastly horrors those poor souls in the army faced or what they had to endure. tommy and charlie get themselves enlisted, partly because of necessity and partly out of a sense of sibling camaraderie. tommy eventually asks why god could let hell let loose on earth, and learns that it is man who has created hell on earth. the change from tommy's and charlie's life in the country to their life in the army was skillfully handled by morpurgo. this brings us to the lugubrious second part of 'private peaceful'. many readers have expressed their opinions that they thought the ending was particularly heartbreaking. it is. injustice is the most poignant element about it though. ironically, it is their own army, and not the enemy's, which manages to break tommy and charlie apart. this was deliberate, as morpurgo carefully explains in the postscript. nevertheless, i do not find the degree of complicity morpurgo attributes to the british government to be fair. i am sure that court martial was absolutely a last resort, even in those circumstances. cases of lack of discipline, such as soldiers shooting their officers for being told off, were not uncommon, especially in the russian army. 'private peaceful' is one of those rare books that, no matter how many times you have read it, it still remains as beautiful, evocative and poignant as the day you grabbed the book in your hands. it truly is a stunning novel.
