title: ['The Red Knight (The Traitor Son Cycle, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: chivalry is oddly in vogue these days. the ideals of the code of chivalry are, sadly, not. the grim, dark nonsense of much high fantasy these days seems to take pleasure in eviscerating any lingering notions we might have that the ideals of honor, etc. were anything but cynical lies. martin loves to do this. anthony ryan did this so much that his books went from four star material to less than one star. even guy gavriel kay can't help but be a little cynical in his tale of troubadour love, a song for arbonne. then i stumbled on this series. oh, it's dark all right. the violence is almost clinical, it's so vivid. there's lots of swearing, lots of blasphemy, lots of darkness. but miles cameron is a true knight. he knows the middle ages, since he lives them (quite literally, the man is a professional reenactor) every day of his life. he can honestly see the brutality and the violence of the age, but he sees it in technicolor, not the drab browns of kristen stewart's offensive and idiotic snow white. and he is honest about that age being an age of faith. for the first time in a long time, i was actually swept away by the spectacle of grand writing nearly as effective as tolkien, and at least one scene was enough to nearly make we weep with pleasure at its grandness and its glimmer of ultimate truth. however. i have a feeling that miles cameron, the man, is setting me up for a big fall. through various characters' thoughts, i think the author is suggesting that there is nothing more to the metaphysical than the very dull ying-yang of competing powers being held in a kind of balance. personally, i find that unspeakably boring, but at this point it is merely a hint. so i will continue to enjoy the unironic and uncynical portrayal of medieval religion with as much pleasure as the grand spectacle of the battle scenes.

title: ['The Screaming Staircase (Lockwood & Co., #1)', "James Potter and the Hall of Elders' Crossing (James Potter, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: i honestly can't believe this book is packaged as a middle school novel. it must be because publishers stupidly believe that people only want to read books about people their own age. sure, the protagonists in this book are children, but the writing, language, plot, and world-building are at least on the level of a ya novel, and i would personally put on an adult level. it's fantastic. atmospheric, creepy, and genuinely frightening, and set in a brilliantly fascinating world. i can't wait for the next one! first of all, this is not about harry's dad (thankfully, because i am not a fan of him.) this is a direct continuation from the end of deathly hallows, and the story of harry's *son*. i'm naturally leery of fanfiction; i don't like stories that change the characters or plot of rowling's books. i don't like fanfiction that doesn't read exactly like it came from rowling's pen, and i'm particularly horrified by "slash" fanfic. but i'm also really feeling the loss of the wizarding world in my life. so, when hannah mentioned this series to me (i had actually forgotten i'd heard about it before) and explained that it was about james-the-son, not james-the-father, and since i now have a kindle and don't have to read the entire thing on a computer, i decided to give it a try. and it's good. surprisingly good. in fact, the opening was so good that i could have imagined rowling actually did write it. after the beginning though, there were a few parts that did ring wrong to me, and a few obvious errors where the author didn't quite remember his rowling canon, but overall? so good. i loved to pieces the "technomancy" classes and prof. jackson. (hickory wand...lol) it made me happy to be back at hogwarts. i just wish i could've turned off the part of my brain that had to keep weighing every sentence against rowling's books and judging how the writing and content matched hers, and just enjoyed it for what it was: an excellent companion to the rowling works. for when i'm feeling lonely for a little magic again. and yes. i will definitely be reading the rest of this series!

title: ['The Darkest Corners', 'The Fall of Five (Lorien Legacies, #4)']
cleaned_reviews: 3.5 stars the more i think about this book, the more i realize that there are many aspects of it that separate it from others. there is no romance and it focuses on the middle class rather than the upper class. these two facts alone separate it from many other thriller novels. the darkest corners follows tessa as she returns to her hometown to say goodbye to her dying father in prison. tessa is reluctant to return home because as a child she testified in a high profile serial killer case with her best friend. secrets are unearthed and memories become blurry as the past slowly starts to take place in the present. the main character tessa reminded me very much of a gillian flynn style character; meaning she's incredibly flawed and doesn't try to hide it. tessa isn't as evil as some of flynn's more notable characters, but there's a grittiness to her. this grittiness isn't just present in tessa's character, but within the entire story because of the writing style. every scene is vivid and the emotions of the characters leap off the pages. as i mentioned previously, there's no romance in this novel. tessa doesn't fall in love while she's investigating her past. she investigates her past with her ex-best friend callie, which creates an amusing dynamic between the two friends. it's awkward, tense, and hostile at times. their friendship is strained and is about to collapse. what made me ultimate rate the darkest corners 3.5 stars instead of something higher is the very slow pace of the book and its seemingly almost perfect conclusion. the book takes about 100 pages to get going, but even after it quickly returns to a slow pace. i think that if the pacing of the story was a little bit faster i would have enjoyed it much more. the conclusion at the end was interesting and i enjoyed reading how everything played out, but i wish the author had showed the ending rather than tell it. give us readers a little more credit; you don't have to directly tell us what happened in bullet point fashion so we understand. overall, the darkest corners was an interesting read that only becomes more interesting after you've sat and thought about it. the unique elements the author decided to include set this thriller apart from others and makes it worth the read. it's been a long time since i've read a pittacus lore book. i had the fall of five sitting on my tbr shelf since the day it came out, but never got around to it. until now. i cannot believe that i put off reading this book since i thought i grew out of it. i'm so glad i read it (and a friend pushed me to read it ;) because this series is one of the best of ever read. if you're unfamiliar with this series go read the first book, but i'm warning you now the first book isn't that great. continue to the second and third and be amazed by their awesomeness. one of the things i enjoy most about this series is the writing style. lore of a fantastic job of keeping the reader entertained with a light writing style filled with humour. for example: "it's fast." nine explains. "sandor outfitted all these in case we needed to move ass in a hurry" "does it have nitrous?" sarah asks. "what do you know about nitrous, sweetheart?" nine replies. sarah shrugs. "i've seen fast and furious. show me how it works. i've always wanted t drive something fast." this conversation not only shows the humorous side of the writing style and characters, but it also shows that these characters act and speak in a way that reflects their age as teenagers. they make bad decisions, they speak like teenagers, they have the priorities of teenagers, they are teenagers. and that's what i love about the writing style it's humorous and reflects the characters' ages. a quick note about the characters. the characters all stand on their own. they all have their own personalities, quicks, and movement that defines them so it's easy to separate them from each other. remembering who each of the characters were was a real concern of mine when diving back into this world. i thought i would forget who they were and not be able to differentiate between them. but i was wrong. lore did such a great job establishing each of the characters as their own person that it's very easy to distinguish who is who. this book is told from multiple perspectives and each of those perspectives are differentiated by a different font. in this book we have sam (loved his pov), john, and marina. these perspectives allow the reader to get a different view on each of the other characters as well as the mind set of the character with the pov. there is a particular scene in this book where the use of perspectives is handled beautifully. the characters are having a game of capture the flag an within that chapter the perspective constantly changes and give it a movie scene kind of feeling where the reader sees the all the action, not just the action from one character's perspective. the one thing i did not like about this book is that, although it does add to the overall plot line, this book's purpose was to build up tension and information for the next book. overall, this book was fantastic. i would definitely recommend this series to anyone since it's action packed with great characters. if you like good books, you'll love this

cleaned_reviews: this book was great - kristin has a great voice, is a wonderful character, and her story is interesting. gregorio does a great job of interweaving medical/science facts into the story without making it feel like you're reading a brochure. kristin's relationships with her dad, friends, and classmates feel realistic and i liked the slow development of new friendships in the face of the difficult situation she finds herself in. i think this is important for any reader struggling to come to terms with parts of their identity, but also for any reader that is trying to expand their understanding of the wide variety of possibilities in the human experience. also, good for any reader looking for a great story! for more, listen to the podcast: http://wp.me/p5zgv4-7z full review here: https://thebookmarkplace.com/2015/12/... diversity score: good effort a sff book with a person of color as a main character!!! very exciting! i thought there was a good mix of diversity - with mental illness, skin color, and economic class pretty well represented. two issues, though: that the mental illness can just "go away" once things are adjusted and the odd use of "type 1/2/3" for skin color description. i think this was to help show this isn't earth as we know it, but i think it would have been stronger without that device. i also noticed when the foreign name was "too hard" and sterling decided to shorten it; i think this could feel like a microaggression for readers that have this happen in their daily lives because people don't care to take the time to learn.

title: ['Everything I Left Unsaid (Everything I Left Unsaid, #1)', 'Reciprocity (Breach, #3)', 'Six of Hearts (Hearts, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: ~5 mind blown stars~ everything i left unsaid is like nothing i have ever read. it has an impeccable blend of sexiness, mystery, action, intrigue, and romance all wrapped up into one power punch of a read! as i feel it is imperative for every reader to go into this one blind, i will avoid spoilers at all cost in this review. "no one missed me. or worried. or wondered. i'd vanished and the world just kept spinning." annie is on the run and lands straight into a trailer park in the boonies of north carolina. in order to escape her abusive husband, she has abandoned everything in order to survive. moments after she has arrived in her new home (an rv trailer in the middle of a run down trailer park), she finds a phone. the phone rings and she meets dylan. "daniels was the beast. he was the bad guy in the stories. some other asshole could be the hero, save the day and get the girl." dylan is a recluse living in a mansion in the mountains. he has always had someone "watching" the old man living in the trailer park. when a new girl answers the phone, he realizes there is something different about her. dylan has scars (both emotionally and physically) that have caused him to want to hide away from the world. can annie be the angel he needs to drag him out of his hell? "the rules he was breaking were piling up around his feet like metal shavings, razor sharp and about to cut them both." honestly, this book was such a surprise. it was a bit of a slow starter for me because i was simply trying to gather my bearings. and yet, as the pieces began to fall into place, i could not put it down. with dylan's guidance, annie is discovering who she is. dylan awakens annie's sexual desires and once the temptation is awakened in her, she doesn't want to stop. the amount of passion and tension in this read is the driving force of the plot. it is silent but deadly throughout each beat of each moment. there are so many questions just desperately waiting to be answered. the secondary characters play a significant role in the story and thoroughly enhanced the plot. of course, i was dying to know what happened to dylan to make him 'the beast" that he has become? who is the old man in the trailer park? will annie finally be free from the demons of her past? is love really possible through so much pain? told in dual pov, ms. o'keefe keeps the intrigue building and the tension doesn't stop. not only is this a clever plot with well crafted execution but the sexy factor is off the charts. this book has something for everyone! "carefully, as if he were a live bomb, i wrapped my arms around his shoulders. i was struck with the very real fear that nothing was going to be enough with him. not ever." overall, i cannot rave enough about this read. however, be forewarned, you will want to have the next book handy as this one ends in a huge cliffhanger! thankfully, i was able to get the second book loaded on my kindle before i even finished this one. i highly recommend this read to anyone who enjoys a sexy romance story with action, suspense, and a story full of heart! i am so glad that i read this book and i cannot wait to read more from this author! ~arc graciously provided via netgalley in exchange for an honest review!~ for more reviews/reveals/giveaways visit: what an amazing ending to an amazing series! nathan and lila! these two are something else. this book has a formula of suspense, love, hotness, and amazing dialogue! i couldn't be more blown away by a series. definitely shelving this on the favorites...and will definitely re-read the series again! love!!!! looking for a little magic with your romance? six of hearts is the read for you! six of hearts doesn't wast any time putting the plot into action. the very beginning reveals everything you need to know to invest your heart into these characters. jay is an illusionist. he is built, sophisticated, sexy, and a man on a mission. jay needs legal council and he has decided to employ a local solicitor. it is there where he meets matilda. matilda is one of the most likable heroines of all time. she is transparent and full of heart. she is quirky, witty, and carries herself with a quiet confidence. when matilda meets jay for the first time she is enamored by his presence. matilda is a die hard romantic. "i want epic love, like you see in the movies. i want it so desperately that it fills my heart when i even think about the possibility of it." not only is jay looking for a solicitor but he is also looking for a place to live. surprising enough, matilda and her dad have a spare room. before you know it jay and matilda are spending time together. the sexual tension is unbelievable. their friendship continues to bloom and the romance is like a slow burning candle. it was quite a tender romance. jay lavishes matilda with time and attention. he is quite the charmer! "it makes my heart squeeze. he likes listening to me breathe. that's just so... romantic . yeah, i said it. it makes me get fanciful notions about the epic love i've always sought but never found."-mathilda while the romance is growing, jay's mad illusionist abilities are front and center. the man is amazing! jay has secrets. while he continues to wow the crowds, matilda is falling harder and faster in love with him! he doesn't want matilda to be with anyone else and yet he isn't quite ready to take the step to be with her the way she wants to be with him. the tension continues to build for quite a while in this read. you will need patience as you wait. jay has a reason for everything! when these two finally connect, the real magic happens! "his touch makes my brain go on holiday, a long, long holiday in a faraway country. and i want him more than i want to know what he's hiding."-matilda although all is revealed in the end, it was a bit frustrating at times. watching matilda long for jay. jay longing to be with matilda and yet he keeps her at a safe distance as all of the pieces fall into place! jay is a true alpha (my favorite trait in a book boyfriend) and the way he cares for matilda is just beauty! "these days it feels like i need his touch like i need air to breathe , and it's so seldom that i actually get it."-matilda i cannot possibly say anything else without revealing too much of the story. let's just say the characters are remarkable, the romance is sweet, the magic is amazing, the sex is steamy, and you will not be disappointed by diving into this book! "the sentiment, matilda, the sentiment. when i look at you, my head clears. most times there's a storm up in this brain of mine, but then you walk into a room and i can focus."-jay "he has this habit of making my heart sore, making my lungs feel like there's not enough air."-matilda overall, six of hearts has it all. even though the wait was long, it was worth it! i will definitely check out more from this author!

title: ['The Amulet of Samarkand (Bartimaeus, #1)', 'We Eat Our Own']
cleaned_reviews: this is taking me forever, but that's due to external circumstances! i am really enjoying it. i like the take on magic -- that human magicians have very limited power, really restricted to summoning magical beasts to do their work for them. and bartimaeus is hilarious. is this a flawless novel? no. does it have important things to say? hmmm, maybe not? but this was an obvious labor of love by a debut author who likes things i like (horror, movies, horror movies) and woman done her research. i was transported to 1980s colombia, small town and jungle, and an italian courtroom. i saw the flicker of film reels and the leathery hide of the corrupt hotel-keeper. i believed in the rebels and the film crew and the ridiculous actor, and even the 2nd person perspective worked -- do you know how rarely an author pulls that off? i am deeply envious of how much effort kea wilson put into this. it impressed upon me the importance and beauty of writing the story you want to read. and that is inspiring.

title: ['The Haunting of Hill House']

title: ['The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks']
cleaned_reviews: the immortal life of henrietta lacks by rebecca skloot synopsis: a poor black woman's cervical cancer cells were taken without patient knowledge by johns hopkin's hospital and her family was not paid nor informed of the issue. these cells later helped to discover how cells and cancer works, and to make practically every pharmaceutical drug out there that there is. impressions: this book made me kind of sad and pretty angry. it made me sad to think that at the time of publication, henrietta lacks was buried in an unmarked grave. (that may not be the case anymore.) it made me sad to know that this woman made such advances in science, and she didn't know basic cell biology. she didn't even read well! and of course, i was angry that johns hopkins refused to give them the money for the cells. i was angry because this wonderful woman with such a fascinating history was treated awfully in the hospital purely because of her skin color. and i was infuriated by the fact that before this book came out and became a bestseller, most scientists thought that hela (yes, that's what they called her cells) came from a woman named "helen lane". this isn't just a medical/science story, it's a story about sociology and psychology as well, with some history thrown into the mix. even though it's non-fiction, i felt like i was reading a novel. even though it's about science, i think i would have understood the basics of what was happening with cell biology even if i didn't do well in high school science. i can't say that for sure though, because i'm a nursing major with a passion for the biological sciences. needless to say, i never read much of a bad review about this book on goodreads, and i agree. it deserves every praise it gets. the only complaint i heard about was it's size, most because it's 370 pages and the type is rather small. it took me a month to read it, but i was kind of in a reading slump. i could have rushed this book, and you could too, but i wouldn't recommend it. this kind of book does not come around that often, so savor it. read it slowly and enjoy it. i think of it like chocolate cream pie. i don't eat chocolate cream pie fast because i never want my piece to end. it will end, but enjoy the moment. my favorite part of the book was reading about deborah and her difficulty grasping the history of her mother. i couldn't imagine living without my mother from a young age. the book wasn't just about henrietta lacks though, it was also about her daughter, deborah, and a little bit about the author, rebecca skloot. i nearly cried reading about deborah and her emotions about her mother. it was like the pain was jumping off the page at me. and to me, a book that makes me feel is a good book. so, in short, recommended highly from me. my mom also read it, and she liked it too. she finished it in three days, but she's a bit of a speed reader.

title: ['Elizabeth Is Missing']
cleaned_reviews: maud has alzheimer's disease and this is scary and confusing for her, and frustrating, upsetting and very exasperating for helen, her daughter. maud is convinced that her friend elizabeth is missing and goes on a quest to find her. alongside this we have a dual timeframe of maud's childhood, her older sister sukey and her husband and all these memories coalesce and become confused in her mind so we never know exactly who is missing, if anyone, and why. it was frustrating for the reader to keep reading "elizabeth is missing" and this is where the book got repetitive. what we didn't get to find out was helen's real perspective. we saw her getting upset and irritated and very weary with her mother, but how was it really for her? it really was an excellent debut novel and i am glad i read it.

title: ['Ignite Me (Shatter Me, #3)']
cleaned_reviews: this series was so freaking phenomenal that i'm really sad it's over. from the beginning, mafi's writing style captivated me and i'm not really one to appreciate poetic prose, but she somehow made it work for me and a few pages into the first book i was already sold. what i admire the most about this series is the way the characters are treated. the main characters and even most of the secondary ones are multi-dimensional, really rounded and authentic. juliette had such a unique voice, very easy to relate to and i really enjoyed watching everything through her eyes, because she was also new to the whole world setting and she was discovering all the things at the same time as the reader. i think that made her a really captivating narrator. now, as a character, juliette grows immensely from book one to three; at first she's this shy, afraid and broken little girl who's seeking protection and just wants to be loved. in book two, we see her taking her first steps towards greatness, she's still struggling to accept herself and what she can do, but she's aware that she can do amazing things and she's getting ready to fight and put her abilities to good use. in this final installment, juliette completely comes out of her shell, she finally understands the kind of power she has and is determined to use it to protect the ones she loves and to fight for justice. there's almost no signs of that girl who needs to be protected and now her fears are no longer holding her back, but fueling her determination of stopping the reestablishment once and for all. juliette is the kind of character that starts at a really low point and grows so much that by the end of the series she'd earned my absolute respect. the author did an amazing job at showing the subtle changes in juliette's personality, so all the changes went really smoothly and felt natural. the other character that impressed the crap out of me was warner. if you go back and read my previous reviews of this series, you'll see that i started off hating his guts with a burning passion. i was completely infatuated with adam and how nice he was to juliette, so warner was just really annoying for me and i just wanted him gone. but as the story progresses, we get little hints of his true self and just like that, little by little he started making his way into my heart. i completely switched teams in fracture me, when we get to see adam's true nature and i realized that if i did a fair comparison between him with warner, without juliette's kind of biased point of view, warner was clearly much more authentic and a better love interest overall. in ignite me, warner is in complete possession of my heart. everything he endures for juliette and just how much he cares about her is evident in this third book and it made me love him so much... the interesting thing is that i'm not really a person who can easily stop disliking a character when they make a bad first impression (like warner), and i know there's a lot of hardcore adam's fans who wouldn't switch teams to warner's in a million years, so i thought i would be one of them. but as with the poetic prose, this is just another exception to my rules. overall, i can say that i got everything i could've asked for in this series finale. i loved the whole series and i think this last book was the perfect conclusion to an amazing story. if you like romance and dystopian worlds, you have to give this one a try, because i'm telling you this series is one of the best in the genre.

title: ['Welcome to Sugartown (Sugartown, #1)', 'Dare to Run (The Sons of Steel Row, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: find this review and more at kimberlyfaye reads . "there's a mind-numbing restlessness that comes with living in small towns. the gossip, the people, and the unending monotony that makes you want to poke your eyes out with a fork." i grew up in a small town. it was *nothing* like the one carmen jenner created in welcome to sugartown. if it had been, i probably never would've left. ;) "you came strutting in here all cocky, with your dimples and your tattoos and your big brown eyes and expected us to swoon." "baby girl, if that's all it takes to make you swoon, then you just wait 'til you see what i do with my hands." man, did i enjoy this book. it was full of innuendos, smoking hot sexy times, great dialogue, intriguing character, some crazy action and plot twists. i loved ana belle. i could relate to her dissatisfaction in small-town life. until, you know, the walking-talking sex god elijah walked through the door to her pie shop and shook things up. elijah. just wow. hot. awkward. sexy. dangerous. far from perfect, but somehow wonderful because of that. he and ana had fantastic chemistry right off the bat and i just knew it was only a matter of time before they gave in and got it on. i was right. and when they did? day-yum. it was more than just lust, though. i cheered for them to get together and wanted to yell when they (inevitably) found a way to screw it up. "with all the shit i've done, the hurt i've caused people, some i barely knew and others i knew too well, for all the worthless hours i've spent wandering through this mess i call a life, looking at this girl before me - who is so perfect and innocent, and downright trusting in every way - i know that, somewhere along the line, i must have done something right for her to want to let me in." don't get me wrong, this book isn't all sweet and hot sexy times. the plot took some pretty interesting - and serious - twists that i didn't expect at all. some scenes were downright disturbing and more than a little uncomfortable, but somehow i still found myself unable to look away. the author's writing, my connection to the characters and the twists and turns kept me fully engaged until the end. even then, it left me wanting more. "come on, ana, would it really kill you to go out with mr i'm so freaking hot even my mother would sell her soul to get a piece of this? would it kill you to have a little fun for once?" welcome to sugartown does a really good job portraying life in a small town: the gossip, the scandals and the characters who were just quirky enough to be interesting without being unbelievable. ana's best friend holly was always good for a laugh or advice. sometimes both. her little brother sammy was absolutely freaking adorable and i loved the relationship between them. ana's dad is a trip, too. i loved him. it was particularly fun to read his interactions with elijah. not all the characters were good. you'll find that out for yourself. if i'm being honest, this book wasn't at all what i was expecting, but that is far from a bad thing. i thought it would be a sexy, fluffy story with a hea. it was sexy. i'm not telling you anything about the ending. :) but damn, the action in this book. mind-blowing. it was exhausting - in the best way possible! i laughed, i swooned, i cried, i freaked the hell out. what a ride. i can't wait to see what happens in the next book, enjoy your stay. it's holly's story. :) find this review and more at kimberlyfaye reads. several months ago, jen contacted me and asked if i would be interested in beta reading part of her new anti-hero novel. i jumped at the chance. (an author i love writing something totally different? an anti-hero? yes.) it was only a few chapters, but it was enough for me to realize i had to have the book. when i got my hands on a review copy, i wanted to do cartwheels. i couldn't wait to see how the story turned out for lucas, heidi and everyone involved. i didn't get to jump into dare to run as early as i wanted to, but once i did? i couldn't stop reading. i was totally wrapped up in this new-to-me side of boston that jen created. the characters and their interactions truly drove this novel for me. i loved the complexity of lucas. here's this tough, ex con who has done a ton of unspeakable things, but there's something totally different underneath. there's a lot happening beneath the surface of his tough exterior in this book. first, someone is trying to kill him. given his line of work, this isn't really something new... but this time the threat seems to come from the inside. then he saves local bartender/owner heidi from being raped by a group of men, leading them to believe he's her man, so you can add a fake relationship on top of everything else. so now he has more enemies and a fake "girlfriend" who is inspiring some very real feelings in him. just what he needed, right? but yes, heidi was exactly what lucas needed. i can't imagine either of them paired up with another character. she was a wonderful, feisty, tough heroine. i love finding a woman this strong in romantic suspense. she'd spent some time on the streets and dealt with a world of crap in her past, so it was no wonder she didn't exactly back done from a fight. it didn't take long for these two to begin to really feel something for each other and it was real and hot and i loved them together. they complemented each other perfectly and made one hell of a team. everything wasn't as it seemed in this book, so prepare for some twists along the way. there's a hefty dose of action and suspense along with the smokin' hot romance in dare to run. lucas and heidi's story ends in this book, but the series continues and, i gotta tell you, i cannot wait to get the next book in the series. dare to stay is chris' book. it's gonna be an interesting one! i'll be sitting over here in the corner with grabby hands until august. ;) i received a copy of this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review. favorite quotes: "your halo may be tarnished, yet you still saved me. that means more than if you were the hero type." "i told you, i'm not fucking 'nice.' don't call me that. i'm the villain in the fairy tale, not the hero." he was this hardened, jaded soul, but with me... well, he wasn't. and it was only with me, so that meant something. he made me feel as if i was the only person on earth that mattered to him. the only one he showed this soft, sweet, lovable side to. it made what we had, no matter how temporary it might be, all the more special. it was useless. around her, i'd always be breathless. and i wouldn't have it any other way.

title: ['The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender', '1984', "Quiet: The Power of Introverts in a World That Can't Stop Talking"]
cleaned_reviews: this writing reminded me of alice hoffman so much, so you know i fell in love so quickly! this strange story has been one of my favorite reads this year. ava lavendar's family history was so intriguing to me and i honestly couldn't put this book down (sorry, work). i borrowed it from the library but will definitely buy a copy in the future when i need a re-read! "to many, i was myth incarnate, the embodiment of a most superb legend, a fairy tale. some considered me a monster, a mutation. to my great misfortune, i was once mistaken for an angel. to my mother, i was everything. to my father, nothing at all. to my grandmother, i was a daily reminder of loves long lost. but i knew the truth--deep down, i always did. i was just a girl." 'if you want a picture of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face--forever.' this book is more important than ever- i highly recommend reading it. "aggressive power beats you up; soft power wins you over." "there's zero correlation between being the best talker and having the best ideas." from the history of the switch from the culture of character to the culture of personality, to groupthink opinions, to biology, to trips and tricks, and to different cultures around the world, this book was just what i hoped it would be. as an ambivert (mostly introverted), i was so intrigued when i first heard of this book. introverts, you say- who wants to read about introverts?! well, as 1/3-1/2 of the world are introverts, it's quite a lot. this book has gained so much attention that i finally had to see what the fuss was about for myself, and i'm so glad i did. cain structured this book beautifully- i was worried she'd focus on her own stories for the majority of the book or leave out hotly debated topics, but she didn't let me down. the only reason i can't give it 5 stars is because i feel like she "got back" every extrovert who ever made her feel inadequate or invited her to a party, meeting, etc. i know my fair share of extroverts and love them for who they are. i don't expect them to judge me so harshly on being mostly introverted, so i won't judge them for their gregariousness. cain didn't have a lot of positive things to say about extroverts and at one point it seemed like she was just downright calling them out for not being good enough. overall, however, this book was fantastic.

title: ['Undone (Fiery Tales, #2)', 'The Last Wicked Scoundrel (Scoundrels of St. James, #5)']
cleaned_reviews: as with all the lila dipasqua books i have read, undone is filled with compelling characters, sizzling love scenes, suspense and a passionate romance. simon is the sort of tormented hero i love. he is full of self-condemnation having realised that, in blindly pursuing his own driving ambitions to rise above his lowly origins, he had closed his eyes to what was happening to his own people.... 'the destruction and devastation'. his life is a mess and he feels tainted by his association with the corrupt superintendent of finances, fouquet. everything he'd done for his country and king, everything he'd worked for was now tainted. in blood. simon is an honourable man, willing to sacrifice his dream in order to save his men and bring fouquet to account for his actions. his compassion shows in his condemnation of slavery and the way he has provided a home and work for so many desperate people. he'd brought many families to marguerite, at first only the crewmen's families, then later, anyone who was in dire straits. he gave them employ in the fields. he gave us an opportunity to survive rather than to die in france." he is also just and fair when judging complaints brought before him. i love how cleverly he resolves the charge brought against angelica by pere crotteau. anglica is gentle and compassionate but also strong and courageous. it is that inner strength that enabled her to escape her loathsome step-father's clutches ten years ago and find sanctuary within the walls of a convent. she still bears deep emotional scars and a belief that no man could ever want someone like her. she has never been able to share her dark, shameful secret with anyone, even her close friend, gabrielle. i love how angelica demonstrates not only her compassion but also her bravery when she confronts the schoolmaster she sees brutally beating a young boy. instinctively, she swung around and struck him with an open palm across his face. "don't touch me! i am not one of these helpless children you enjoy mistreating." the sexual tension between these two is definitely explosive. angelica finds simon exciting and his mere touch stirs her senses while simon is drawn to angelica's beauty, decency and bravery but their journey to a happy ever after is strewn with obstacles, not least their own closely guarded secrets. it was rewarding to watch simon gradually demolish the walls angelica has built around herself with his compassion, acceptance and understanding, inspiring her to take risks and find happiness and how angelica makes simon see the noble man he truly is. "...you have sought to gain nobility, but you are noble. you don't want to be ordinary, but you never have been. you wish to be exalted, but in the eyes of so many, you are." be warned! the love scenes are very graphic and the language explicit and, if i have one complaint, it's that they seem rather repetitive in content. i really like robert d'arles, the nobleman who saved simon from the streets and has always treated him like a son. he is an honourable man, willing to offer angelica the protection of his name. i couldn't help but feel heart-broken for simon and angelica when circumstances conspire to keep them apart but neither of them is willing to betray robert. his word to simon really touched my heart. "you were my only family...you have made me proud...raising you into the man you are today has given me a sense of purpose and fulfilment in my life...simon...there is no limit to what a man can achieve except the limits he places on himself..." fouquet is a formidable enemy but his downfall rests with his sheer arrogance in underestimating the young king louis. although i love the regency era, the setting of 17th century france was refreshingly different. ms dipasqua brings to life all decadence and political intrigue of the royal court and the inclusion of real-life figures like fouquet and louis xiv adds an extra level of authenticity to the story. the epilogue gathers everyone together on marguerite island for a charming happy ever after. my verdict: if you enjoy a compelling story, fascinating characters and a lushly erotic romance, then i can definitely recommend undone. review rating: 4.5/5 stars fiery tales series to date (click on the covers for more details): this review is also posted on my rakes and rascals blog : https://rakesandrascals.wordpress.com... i loved this conclusion to one of my all-time favourite series. the scoundrels of st. james series (obviously inspired by dickens's oliver twist) tells the story of five child thieves lucian, jack, frannie, james and william, all members of feagan's merry little band of ne'er-do-wells. their lives are irrevocably changed when it is discovered that lucian is the lost heir to the earl of claybourne. william was a constant presence throughout the other books and i am so pleased that he finally gets his own happy ending in this novella. in the first book, in bed with the devil , winnie is the dearest friend of lady catherine mabry, the heroine of that book. she is married to the duke of avendale, a brute of a man who abuses his wife both physically and sexually. when catherine discovers winnie after a particularly severe beating, she fears for winnie's life and sends for william. he not only nurses winnie back to health but also provides sanctuary in his home for her and her son, whit. shortly afterwards, the duke of avendale dies in a fire at his estate leaving winnie free from his tyranny and free to explore her growing feelings for william. william is drawn to winnie but keeps a respectful distance because he believes he doesn't deserve someone like her. he knows he has kept a terrible secret from her and fears that, if she discovers the truth, it will destroy any feelings she has for him. but when past deeds come back to haunt him, william must risk everything to protect the woman he loves. william is such a wonderful hero. he has risen above his humble origins to become a renowned doctor but, he can never quite forget his past and the guilt he feels over his mother's death. he has tried to make amends by helping others. i love how he treats winnie with such tenderness and sensitivity. he sees her vulnerability but also her hidden strength. he makes cleaned_reviews: i always love the hate-to-love trope and this version had such a personality to it. i wish it had alternative viewpoints because i would have killed to get a peek inside of josh's mind. but lucy was so much fun. delilah marlow goes to a traveling circus that features cryptids: half-human, half-animal creatures that have been systematically rounded up after a major fae disaster called "the reaping." the cryptids are treated brutally, made to perform for human entertainment. delilah is horrified when a carnival worker abuses a young werewolf girl in front of her but something other than human comes out of delilah in response. suddenly, she is locked up, all rights, liberty and property taken away since she is no longer human and she is sold to the very menagerie that so horrified her in the first place. poetic justice is the driving force behind this novel. it's dark and gruesome and fascinating. each chapter shifts between the different perspectives, sometimes randomly, but the majority focuses on delilah's experience. i tried really hard not to read the end. the mystery of what delilah is as well as the poor experience of the cryptids kept in the menagerie and how much worse their treatment could have been in other places was strangely fascinating. it's like a show that you can't watch unless you are peeking through your fingers. delilah is strong and purposeful and bows to no man. my only complaint was how quickly it wrapped up. the novel spends so much time building the suspense but the end was like, oh that's it? but i guess there are more to come, so we will see what happens next. inventive retelling of jane austen's persuasion. ** spoiler alert ** genre: graphic novel, racism, fitting in, summary: the book has three plotlines that eventually tie up together at the end of the novel. one follows the adventures of the monkey king, a legend that is very popular in china and other parts of asia. the monkey king wants to be accepted by the other gods and goddesses, and when he isn't, he tries to change himself, becomes something that he is not, and learns to serve others with the talents he has. another storyline follows jin wang, an american born of immigrant parents who suffers prejudice and racism growing up. the last storyline follows an all-american white boy, danny, who has a chinese cousin, chin kee, who is depicted as the ultimate chinese stereotype, in looks and behavior. the three tie nicely together at the end of the novel when jin (as the reader finds out at the end of the book, changed himself into danny) learns from the monkey king (who turned out to be chin kee in disguise) that it is useless to run away from the person you really are and that you need to be proud of where you come from and help others in return. response: this was an amazing book, and i really wish that i could have given it a half star more. i loved the format of the novel, i think that it couldn't have been portrayed in a better way. i loved how seamlessly the three plotlines tied together. however, the subject of racism that the book deals with was a little harsh at times, a little uncomfortable at others. it definitely makes you reevaluate how you treat others. stereotypes hurt, even if they may seem harmless. it would be a great book to tie into other classic novels that deal with racism, mythical archetypes or cultural diversity in the classroom.

title: ['Extra Yarn', 'One Moment', 'No Mercy (Dark-Hunter #18, Were-Hunter, #5)', "Spider's Bite (Elemental Assassin, #1)"]
cleaned_reviews: my girls (4 & 6) loved this and so did i. such a very sweet story of a selfless little girl named annabelle who discovers a bottomless box of yarn. she then takes it upon herself to turn her drab environment into something bright and colorful. the illustrations are stunning. this is a story that will leave you all warm and fuzzy. i think i smell a future classic children's book here! loved! loved! loved! *sniffle* this book *sniffle* one moment was not a novel i could devour in one sitting. it took me the better part of two weeks to plow through this story with tear filled eyes. this is a book that had me breaking out the "ugly cry" (don't pretend you don't know what i'm talking about). having lost a close friend to a car accident while i was a sophomore in high school, i found i connected with one moment on a very personal level. this may also be one of the reasons i had to read in moderate doses. the author does a beautiful job of capturing the voices of teens struggling with a devastating loss and it all just felt so real. the plot was paced perfectly with a mystery that makes you want to keep reading. i enjoyed getting to know maggie as she discovered the secrets joey was hiding, as well as tried to process the grief and guilt she was struggling to contain. the secondary characters added a nice element. i loved the idea of childhood friends growing up together and was fascinated by the author's take on how they would react when a member of their close-knit group was suddenly taken from them. this was one intense read and can still easily conjure residual emotions even weeks after i finished reading. it isn't often i encounter books that have such staying power. one moment isn't a book i'll forget anytime soon (if ever). oh contemporary genre, how i love you and loathe you almost equally. you make me want to read even as you break my heart into tiny little pieces. this is not a genre i venture into often, but i'd do it again with no hesitation if kristina mcbride's name was on the cover. if you haven't read this talented author's work you really must! the dark-hunters series is one that i'm always saying i'll catch up on. i read the first, and fell in love with sherrilyn kenyon's story telling. when the opportunity to review the newest addition to this much loved series arose, i said sure because according to most readers this is a series you don't have to read in order. thank goodness they were telling the truth. i had no problems figuring out the workings of the world in which the dark-hunters and were-hunters reside, and suffered only mild confusion when it came to boss guy acheron and the peculiar nick. i'm not sure if reading previous books would help clear that up or not because both guys seem to harbor many secrets along with a mutual dislike of each other. i was immediately engrossed by the story of dev and sam. dev is a shapeshifter who works at his family owned bar as a bouncer. he has experienced more than his fair share of grief during his longer than average life. sam is a former amazonian warrior (very cool!) who made a deal that she'd get to take revenge on those that killed her family in exchange for becoming a dark-hunter. living with the constant pain of the loss she felt so many years ago, she never expected to be happy again. unable to even touch others because of her empath abilities coupled with her dark-hunter responsibilities, she has resigned to living the life of a loner. then she meets dev who is a closed book to her, and she can't seem to fight the attraction. she is falling for him and he for her, but unfortunately this is against the rules. that isn't enough to stop these two from a few forbidden kisses and more. of course a paranormal romance isn't complete without bad guys trying to stir up trouble. there is plenty of trouble making, along with a healthy dose of romance and sizzling chemistry between the two main characters. after finishing no mercy the first thought that occurred was why the heck haven't i read books 2-18. author, sherrilyn kenyon, has such an amazing ability to create fascinating plots weaved with greek mythology, and super hot couples. i've also found my newest book boyfriend, ethon. i truly hope he is featured more prominently in future novels because i think i might be in love dev is a super sweet and likable guy. he has lost so many people that are close to him, but isn't nearly as jaded as one would expect. sam comes off all kick your ass biker chick in leather, but has a kind heart under the tough exterior. they are a perfect match. things progress quickly between the lovely couple this book focuses on, but this is something i've come to expect and accept in this genre. only complaint was the ending seemed rush. we spent all this time building up to this super battle only to have it over before this reader was ready. no mercy is still a fascinating and enjoyable read, but the execution of the ending could have been paced better. this is a series all paranormal romance fans need to check out. of course i might just be the last pnr fan to experience the fabulousness that is sherrilyn kenyon. gin blanco was left to fend for herself after her family was brutally murdered by a fire wielding elemental. living on her own on the rough streets of ashland, and eating out of dumpsters to survive all while still a child. then fletcher lane took her in, served as a father figure, and eventually introduced her to the life of an assassin. now gin is all grown up, and has quite a reputation as the paid killer known as "the spider". her most recent assignment is supposed to be a quick and straightforward kill. after gin planned to take a much needed vacation. imagine her surprise when the person who ordered the hit decides to double cross the spider by hiring another assassin to take her out, murdering her handler, and torturing a man close to her. gin puts the vacation on hold while she seeks revenge for those she loves. this was an exciting start to a new series. i never thought i'd sympathize with an assassin until i met gin. the poor girl has had a rough life, and now focuses on taking the law into her own hands. most of the people she is hired to kill are pretty sleazy folk so that makes the whole hitman thing a little easier to forgive. she is very skilled in hand to hand combat as well as the use of knives. as an elemental she also has the power of stone and ice to fall back on. she is the epitome of badass chick, and a great addition to the urban fantasy genre! i enjoyed the world the author created, but i wish she would have given a little more background on the elementals and how it all worked. i also wasn't feeling the chemistry between gin and detective caine. i was secretly rooting for finn to sweep her off of her feet, but the references to him being like family dashed most of my hopes of a gin and finn hookup. still a really strong start to the series. i'm currently devouring the second book, web of lies.

cleaned_reviews: "your fate is not yet sealed. even in the darkest night a star will shine, a bell will chime, a path will be revealed." ryan's book is certainly thought provoking and emotional. when you get to the point where all seems despairing, when darkness appears to overcome the valiant efforts of remarkable young people forging a solution out of the terrible circumstances of their lives, remember this quote and don't put the book down! she has captured the way life can bring hopeful resolutions at our darkest hours, hinting at the importance of never giving up on hope. the ability of music to transcend such delineations as race and circumstance, and to bring people together is represented in the magical harmonica that travels across time and borders. it spotlights the lives and minds of three children experiencing hitler's oppressive rise to dictatorship, orphanhood during the american depression, and the prejudice against migrant farmers and removal of japanese americans from the west during wwii. each of these children face monumental challenges and develop plans to escape catastrophe. each is slammed with tragedy that is out of their control. ryan's structure leads you to a point of despair about continuing, but i'm glad i didn't put the book down. this definitely merits a second reading to ferret out further implications and reconsider interweaving themes of music, relationships, community, youthful determination, adult complicity, an inescapable larger world, and more.

cleaned_reviews: i recently finished listening to the audiobook of a discovery of witches, which i enjoyed so much i went straight to audible for shadow of night. i am pleased to say this novel is even better. there are plenty of good reviews for these books, a fair few not so positive, too, so i will be brief. if you read charlaine harris' southern vampire series and wondered what on earth a 1,000+ year old viking vampire found interesting about sookie stackhouse, and why eric northman never actually comes across like a creature who has lived through never mind knows anything about history, well this trilogy might be just what you are looking for, sookie stackhouse for grownups. diana is a professional historian, an academic, as is deborah harkness, and it shows. there is romance, and very satisfying it is too, but i loved all the period detail and scene-setting other reviewers found boring, and the alchemy and historical science. i adore vampires, especially good-looking, adult male ones with a droll sense of humour, so i was pretty much guaranteed to fall for matthew. i like that we meet his family, too. the large part of this novel set in elizabethan london was thoroughly enjoyable. reading about how a 21st c woman must adapt to daily life 400 years ago felt surprisingly real to me, due to the subtle underpinning of historical research that makes the past vivid. i now eagerly, impatiently, await the final book in this marvelous series. i didn't know much about this novel going in other than its booker long list nomination. my interest was grabbed instantly by the setting, 19th century applecross, an area of outstanding beauty, and even today, remoteness from the hourly burly of modern life. what a brilliant read, an utterly convincing recreation of a bloody historical crime so well done i had to double check to make sure the story it tells really is fiction not true crime! literary fiction is not always my thing, but this novel deserves its booker nomination, and the wide readership that will bring. the writing is top notch and the structure of the book perfectly suited to the nature of the story, giving multiple perspectives on the murders of three members of the mackenzie family by 17 year old roddy macrae in 1869. take my advice and don't read too much about the novel before you start reading. you will certainly want to read more about it and seek out reader discussion afterwards. this is the kind of book you tell friends and family about so you will have others to share the experience with, to speculate and debate the issues it raises. historical crime fiction at its best that shows an unromanticised portrait of highland life in the nineteenth century, a grim picture of poverty, low expectations, ill health, rudimentary living conditions, calvinist acceptance, exploitation and indifference on the part of landowners. i fell in behind the two well-dressed gentlemen and eavesdropped on their conversation. the first declared in a loud voice, "it is easy to forget that such primitives still exist in our country." his companion nodded solemnly and wondered aloud whether more might be done for us. the first gentleman then expressed the view that it was difficult to assist people who were so incapable of doing anything for themselves. those who have enjoyed the likes of the serial podcasts and making a murderer will find a similar 'feel' about this book, setting out as it does the pov of the young man charged with a terrible crime, bringing to bear witnesses, local residents, experts from the legal and medical professions. that roddy is guilty is never in question. whether we believe justice was served at the end is what the novel is about. some of the expert testimony wouldn't be out of place in nazi germany, quite shocking to modern sensibilities, but we should remember future generations will be similarly appalled by what we regard as acceptable and just. only john murdoch departed from the notion that the verdict was a foregone conclusion. his southern colleagues, he explained,overlooked the empathy the jurymen might feel towards an ill-used crofter. the resentment caused by centuries of ill treatment of the highlander was keenly felt, and in roderick macrae, they might see an individual who had revolted against the vindictiveness of the powers-that-be. above all the novel is about roddy macrae, what we make of him from his own account written in gaol that forms a big part of the novel. to that impression others add their perspectives through witness statements and observations. it's a complicated and fascinating story. tragic and indicting of the system of land ownership and governance in place at the time, not so far removed from today as you might think, though, obviously, living conditions have been transformed and remoteness ameliorated by modern infrastructure and technology.

cleaned_reviews: this book reads like a blend of american tall tales and european faerie talkes along with a style of magic realism that puts me in mind of gabriel garcia marquez. hatfields and mccoys meet midsummer night's dream. it's a haunting story that is not afraid to string the reader along with hints and guesses of what is truly happening and what we might be just imagining. it's a story about homecoming, trauma, and finding out who you are within and outside of your family. it's hard to say more without giving too much away, but if you like any of the above, i encourage you to read this book. i'll definitely be continuing in the series. so after marathoning through the last two hundred pages, i'm finally done. i feel like i've run an actual marathon whilst some one was occasionally punching me in the head. i got really excited about this book and tried to explain it to people, but then had to stop because of course there is no way at all to summarize this book. the dust jacket does a terrible job of it, and i ended up with a very different book than i expected. the only other stephenson book that i've read is "anathem" which is such a slow burn i have a hard time believing these are the same authors (other than the intense attention to seemingly minor details). i expected a lot more sci-fi and gaming elements, but really the game is only one very small piece and a massive 3d puzzle. i don't normally read a lot of thrillers because they stress me out, and boy did this one stress me out. stephenson is a master of, "how could this possibly get any worse?" these poor characters catch not a single damn break until the final show down. and you, the reader, like these characters. you like cool calculating sokolov and nerd master marlon and enterprising zula and really the whole cast of "good guys." there's a million points when you think, "ah, so this is how they will finally escape and be okay," but nope! there's still 600 pages of horrible, horrible things, so strap in. stephenson did a helluva lot of research for this book, and i can't speak to the accuracy of any of it since i have approximately zero experience with russian mafia, islamic terrorists, guns, mmorgs, or mountain lions. that said, i feel pretty damn well educated now. that said, i sometimes felt a little too educated, especially when getting into the details of t'rain. i might have made it through this book in decent time without the in depth look at t'rain's geology, politics, and economics, but then the whole thing might have felt a bit more like a cheap plot device. if i have a criticism, it might be that the ending is a little too pat. (view spoiler)[the various couples hooking up, especially sokolov and olivia whom i appreciated more as a james bond one time deal than a long term thing and the only good guy death being dear sacrificial lamb uncle john. like other books with super happy endings though, i'm just so relieved everyone is okay that i would likely feel upset and angry if they didn't get a happy ending. (hide spoiler)] this book is in no way for the faint of heart, but if you have a *lot* of time on your hand and don't mind wrapping your brain around some of the cruelest plot twists in fiction, give this one a go.

title: ['This Raging Light']
cleaned_reviews: i was given an arc copy by the publisher through netgalley in exchange for an honest review. this raging light proves that the main character doesn't have to be an assassin, a vigilante, nor a queen to be badass. lucille's dad was admitted to a mental facility when she was younger, and ever since then her mother has never been the same. now, even her mom is gone. on top of that, she has a baby sister to take care of, bills to pay, a best friend to worry about, and worse of all, a boy who has a girlfriend to fall in love with. i gotta tell you, i felt like the tone and the way that this book was written felt different for me. it took me a while to get used to it, but once i did it didn't take me long to fall in love with the story. i can't ever imagine being put into lucille's shoes, but i must tell you that she is the most badass main character i've read. like what fred said, lucille is someone who jumps and takes actions; who doesn't wait for things to happen. she's strong and brave at the same time, but she's also vulnerable because after all, she's just human. i'm glad that she learned to let others helped her in the novel, and that's one more thing that made her stronger. i loved how this book was also about hidden angels. i loved the way that things progressed - how the characters grew as time passed. even wren, as little as 10, really stepped up. i loved how honest to book is, and how it made me feel. i didn't like how things ended though. (view spoiler)[i want to know what happened to her mom, and what happens to her dad later on. who will take care of them. what happened with digby and elain? (hide spoiler)] i felt like there were just to many things left unexplained. maybe the author meant for it to be that way, but i definitely wasn't satisfied by it. still, i recommend this book. this raging light is definitely an amazing book about a teen who had to grow up too soon. a must-read.

title: ['Lockdown (Escape from Furnace, #1)', 'The Glass Arrow']

ashley, of macmillan children's publishing, for providing me with an arc in exchange for an honest review. from the minute i read the synopsis of this book i knew i was going to love it. this was one more evidence is brought to light, readers will become unsure of who actually did it. i really liked the characters in this novel. it is written from the pov of twin sisters, joy and grace. joy is rash and loud and always says what's on her mind while grace is quiet and shy and devotes all her time to studying. both characters are very complex. joy is unsure of whether or not she actually killed adam for what he did to grace, but she knows that she very well could have because of the hate she has for him. and now she is getting blackmailed for it. grace just wants everything to go cleaned_reviews: i have now read pride and prejudice at least three times. i am not one to pick up books over and over, even ones i love, because there are just so many other books to read. but sometimes, i make an exception, especially when i think i'll get more out of it on another go around. such is the case with this book. my esteem for it grows and grows each time i read it. last time i read it, i gave this book four stars. today? five solid stars. pride and prejudice has everything. breathtaking drama. fairy tale romance. laugh out loud humour. the characters are both endearing and embarrassing. sometimes it is hard to step out of our comfort zone and read something that uses different sentence structure and word choice. sometimes it can be confusing when we live in a completely different culture than a story is set in. but if we allow ourselves to simply be swept away by austen's words, pride and prejudice is a page turner. i'm sorry it is over. i will definitely be reading this again.

title: ['Unwind (Unwind, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: okay...so i liked this book, but it took me a bit to get into it. i was not truly invested in the first 75-100 pages. but that could have been because at that point i had a very strong aversion to lev. i couldn't stand him and had no desire to read about him. i loved connor, though didn't really connect with risa for a while...anyway slowly my opinion changed. i was wavering between 3 stars or 4 and in the end decided on 4, because it has been quite a while since a book shocked me, horrified me...and there was definitely one if not more places this book did that. it surprised me, and it was raw. my mouth dropped and my head has still not wrapped around the events. this book leaves the reader wondering how society/humanity can end up like it does...because truly for pages my mind was screaming at characters. are you for real?? how can you call yourself human?? at first the concept of unwinding an adolescent is awful, but in my head i took it for what it was, not condoning it, but saying okay but this is how this particular society works. but that was before we went inside those doors, (those of you who have read this, know the doors i'm talking about)...after those doors were open, there was no accepting...it was incomprehensible, and yet, i was reading it... i think that this book speaks of a dark dark side of society...but a side of society that actually does exist - maybe not in reality, but in thought. this book takes it to the extreme and forces the reader to face it themselves.

title: ['Reconstructing Amelia']
cleaned_reviews: private schools, hierarchy and classification based on what neighborhood you're from or how much money you have, cliques and cliches...this is exactly the type of environment i try to steer clear of. looking past all that, though, the story was a pretty good one. amelia's mom, kate, gets a phone call from the school in the middle of an important business meeting, saying that she needs to pick amelia up immediately. amelia, who has never cheated in her life, supposedly plagiarized most of the english paper she turned in about her favorite author. kate arrives late to discover that her daughter is dead, having leapt from the roof of the school. the entire book is basically an investigation of what happened in amelia's life leading up to this event. the chapters jump between past and present, kate and amelia, facebook and an anonymous blog that keeps up with the drama at this particular school. amelia is a likable character, a typical confused teenager trying to fit in, an athletic straight "a" student who has never really had an interest in boys. the people she is closest to are her mom and her best friend. amelia has never known her father, and her mom is a lawyer. after amelia insists that kate get rid of the nanny, amelia is left to fend for herself most of the time, but kate does the best she can as a single working mom. she's much more down to earth than a lot of the other parents. after amelia's death, kate receives a mysterious text, and this is where the investigation begins. she desperately tries to put together the pieces of amelia's life, so she can learn what happened the day she died. in the process, she discovers a lot about amelia that she didn't know and secrets that the school has been hiding. when we finally get some answers, it isn't what is expected. that's always a plus in my book. i enjoy surprises.

title: ['Behind the Scenes at the Museum']
cleaned_reviews: this was a really good book--likely my best of 2017 so far. if you're a kate atkinson fan, do not be dissuaded by the fear that this was her first. in the first twenty pages or so, i was nervous that the work was a little rough around the edges, but i soon fell into a familiar rhythm, catching the cozy beats of an atkinson novel. when we were in nice wandering around the chegall museum, nathan remarked, "well, he was consistent." it can be easy to fault artists for creating work that feels similar, drawn from the same palate. in atkinson's case this usually involves struggling relationships, complex characters, stoic and/or depressed women, a death or two, a mystery, and a pinch of the otherworldly. i love her writing, i love her consistency, and i don't fault her for finding her niche. if you love atkinson, this isn't a novel to miss. if you've never read atkinson, start with life after life and work backwards.

title: ['All the Light We Cannot See', 'Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2 (Harry Potter, #8)']
cleaned_reviews: i had to pick this up after seeing it top so many best lists. it's a beautiful and heart breaking look at wwii told from the perspective of two teenagers on opposite sides of the conflict. on the occupied france side is blind marie-laure and on the german side is the somewhat reluctant nazi protege werner. the story shifts back and forth in time between events at the end of the book and the time leading up to their eventual meeting. the story of the two teenagers is framed by the mystery of a lost diamond. the book balanced such sweet moments with ones that break your heart. all of the horrors of wwii are touched upon here. my take away from this particular book is not only how much the invaded people suffered at the hands of the germans but how brutal they could be to anyone they perceived as weak even if it was their own people. i found this story to be very touching and even if you have read a stack of wwii stories this one still feels fresh and inventive. i started reading the harry potter series when my daughter was born. when she was just an infant i read it out loud to her and then when she grew older she read the series on her own. now with the release of the cursed child, harry and i both find ourselves with teenagers who we don't understand and who don't understand us. if the boy who lived can't control his teenager, albus severus potter what hope is there for us mere muggles? the story begins with a misunderstanding between harry and his son in which a regrettable utterance is made by harry in anger. i really felt for harry in that moment. i think all parents have spoken in anger to our teenagers who seem especially able to push our buttons and they are not very gracious about forgiving and letting us live it down. at least that's been my experience. in any case albus uses his anger to defy harry, steal a time turner, and along with his best friend scorpius, he goes back in time to save cedric diggory in order to impress his new crush delphi. if you have ever read a time travel book then you know messing with the past is not advisable. the trips to the past cause unwelcome changes to the present. will things be set right again? is lord voldemort back? will harry ever get along with his teenage son? these and other burning questions are answered in the cursed child. i am a huge harry potter fan. reading this was like visiting old friends. the chocolate frogs, moaning myrtle, bane, even professor trelawney gets a mention. this is not the place to start the series with. you need to have read the complete series especially goblet of fire in order to appreciate this book. in addition to all of the loved characters of the past we get the addition of scorpius, draco malfoy's son who is destined to be a fan favorite. and speaking of draco, i loved his softer side, especially as it related to his love for his wife and child. harry is still heroic, hermione clever, and ron goofy. it was so much fun to spend time with them again. this play is a great addition to the harry potter canon and i hope to see it performed one day. i read this book as my second entry in the r.eaders i.mbibing p.eril xi. challenge held every fall at http://www.stainlesssteeldroppings.co...

title: ['Daughter of Smoke & Bone (Daughter of Smoke & Bone, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: i first read this book last year. i don't know why, but ending left me confused and little bit disappointed back then. maybe it was the outcome of the story and promise of another war (which i don't like in fantasy books, because they seem all the same to me) i didn't like, i don't know anymore. the point is - i remember how i loved this book and how i kept talking about it to my friend - how she has to read it, how amazing it is. so i read it again. and i fell in love with it again. characters in dos&b are just amazing. so likable and real. i really would love to have friends like karou and zuzana. and i would really love to punch kaz - on behalf of the humanity. i don't actually like it when the characters are overly perfect - too beautiful, too smart, too everything. but here i didn't mind. i loved karou because she was independent. she wasn't naive, she knew how to take care of herself, but she wasn't arrogant either. she was caring and loyal. her decisions and thoughts actually made sense (which isn't very commong in ya fantasy). she was real. and what got me most (after the writing, of course) - is probably that it wasn't the same old "i am a normal (lonely) girl which falls in love with supernatural amazing (arrogant) guy". karou was living supernatural her whole life. and she wasn't even hiding it (too much) or making big deal out of it. it was her life and even though it got on her nerves time to time, she loved it and enjoyed it. almost as much as i enjoyed reading this book. :) favorite quotes: " 'all you need in this life is ignorance and confidence; then success is sure.' mark twain, you know. he had a fine mustache. men of wisdom so often do." "have you ever asked yourself - do monster make war or does was make mosters?" (this one actually got me thinking a lot.)
