title: ['Warm Bodies (Warm Bodies, #1)', 'The Rosie Project (Don Tillman, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: so for the past year ...or maybe two... i've been sneering at this book and rolling my eyes: "a zombie love story...yes, we've gone there..." as with most ridiculously popular things i don't get, i start wondering what the fuss is about - why is it so popular? how the heck is it a zombie eats a guy, falls for the guy's girlfriend, and this is somehow supposed to work?? i watched the movie trailer. it was kind of funny... alright... fine, i'll just read it and find out. i read it, really liked it, and now have to admit it after allllll that snickering and eye rolling. when am i ever going to learn? stop making fun of things, because it's going to come back (haha) to haunt you (hardy har har). there's a few things about the book that don't work at all...maybe by my weird rules of logic, maybe by others'. i found i didn't care. what do you mean you can eat someone's brain and while it's working its way down your gullet to your not-working stomach, you somehow absorb its thoughts and memories? how is that... oh who cares. if a vampire can suck someone's blood and "feel" their feelings and life essence, then i guess a zombie can eat a brain and have a thought. it's surprisingly well written by way of atmosphere, character and ideas expressed. i liked the overall "moral of the story" and the feeling of irony in many elements of it. i wasn't too bothered by the romeo/juliet parallel (or "rip off" as one friend said) -so many stories draw from romeo and juliet or other shakespearean that this isn't really a negative, to me. better shakespeare than tom green. i could have done with a bit less perry-nattering. speaking of dead who won't stay dead... i liked the quote: "shit happens and it's a shitty world, but you don't have to bathe in shit." a bit blunt, maybe, but a good point. (view spoiler)[ - where was he going with the anatomy book? i thought we were going to reveal something extra interesting about r's past. - what is the scoop on the gold eyes? so he did transmit the virus to her with a kiss but she was cured by love sort of thing? but why gold? - wait till your wife wakes up, r... - did perry deliberately sacrifice himself on the basis of a theory? - the dad ending more or less sucked, imo. (hide spoiler)] in all, i wouldn't say i'm converted on the undead romance element, but i enjoyed the overall story and characters. it was a good - weird - read. galley copy in ebook format. the short & sweet: i really enjoyed it - it feels like a light read, but there's more depth to it (or perhaps i inserted my own) when reading between the lines and taking in the implications of don's reactions and observations of the world around him. reading between the lines, i found it quite poignant. many are comparing don to sheldon of big bang theory: i started the book with that in mind, but found don to be a more endearing character. he doesn't have the egotistical pomposity of sheldon (well, bar the "fish" episode) and seems to be trying harder to fit in and understand social cues. edit: actually, i was reminded less of sheldon and more of data (the poetic android of star trek: tng) on his path to explore and understand the human experience and emotion. don's language is very "android-esque" in some ways as he talks about "rebooting" his brain, etc. to clarify, i'm not comparing someone with asperger's to an android in the sense of "they're robots," but rather *this* character's journey to understand emotion is reminiscent of *that* character's journey. and perhaps the people around him, as well. aspergers: there's a little controversy in other reviews i've read, as to how accurate a representation this is of aspergers. i think the primary concern is centered on don's seeming lack of feeling: will the take-away from this novel be the assumption that people on the autism spectrum do not have feelings and therefore cannot have their feelings hurt? i think it is a valid concern. this is light reading and not meant to be a primer on aspergers, however because of growing public awareness, people are (wonderfully) hungry for more understanding and perspective. while the intent is a light hearted romantic comedy that appeals to, and is "safe," for guys to read, the author can expect that aspergers will a the primary discussion point about the book. i have to say that i didn't find don emotionless, myself, but rather, simply disconnected from being able to identify and name the emotions he was having. that said, the aspergers talk he gives at the beginning of the novel could have been be fleshed out a bit to clarify a couple of those questions, if the author had this feedback earlier on. because i think it might be a bit late for that sort of revision, i would like to see clarification from the author on what his experiences are with aspergers and autism - what kind of research he did or if there are personal experiences that tie into this. or a disclaimer, if necessary. i feel it'll be a question raised over and over again, so an faq of sorts will probably save him some time down the road. comments on the story itself: (view spoiler)[ given don's personality and need for efficiency, i'm surprised that the father project did not immediately start with testing phil. but, then, it'd be a short book & it's roughly understood that don launches into this grand project as a way of spending more time with rosie, who intrigues him, rather than in the interests of being absolutely clinically accurate and efficient. it was odd that no one bothered to say to him: hey don, i think you might have aspergers. it struck me as a weird revelation to have at the end of the novel. that said, not having that information on the table at the beginning of the novel gave the author a chance to be more organic about the process rather than having to stand off to the side in don's shoes and explain details about aspergers here and there: i'm like this because i'm like this... etc. still, back in the world of the story: if gene was educated enough on the subject to be the one who was initially supposed to give a talk on it, he'd know that blunt "get straight to the point" communication would be the way to approach don (rather than the roundabout way kate - if i remember her name correctly - approaches the topic). so why say nothing? that, more than anything, felt like making don the butt of a joke - but then, gene is a bit self-involved and unaware of himself in crucial ways, too. i love love loved the one liner in there about traveling with the geneticist halfway around the world only to use the internet... lol the "class clown" part i wondered about. class clown implies deliberately using humor as a coping device through high school, but don has little understanding of humor and is often oblivious to how he, himself, is funny to others. he also clearly dislikes humor at his own expense. with that in mind, how did he deliberately make himself a class clown as a teen? this doesn't "click" for me. i could see people calling him class clown, not realizing his humor was inadvertent rather than deliberate. the way the question of gene as a father came up, i had a secret lurking fear that rosie was one of his conquests and she was going to find out it was her father after the fact. her anger and disgust with gene seemed to lead that direction. i'm glad we didn't end up there!! despite the questions raised, i didn't take the book too seriously. i really liked don and wanted him to - if not get the girl - be happy. there were a couple times i thought: "... is that true to what aspergers is?" and i will go check those questions out for myself. other things were dead on the nose. the "i woke up in the chair the next morning" scene was particularly poignant. his lack of hangover - well that just made me bitter. ;) i did not feel that don was "emotionless" despite his own lack of understanding of emotions. just unable to identify and articulate what it was he was feeling. title: ['American Psycho']
cleaned_reviews: oh heck. never have my feelings about a book been quite so conflicted. i think i appreciate what bret easton ellis was trying to do with this novel; i think he succeeded, to a large extent. it's just that i don't think i've ever enjoyed a book less. for a start, there's the violence. be warned: you need a strong stomach for this one. as in, a very strong stomach. it's true that there's a definite suggestion that the murders only take place in the protagonist's mind, rather than in reality, but still - they're vividly imagined. and while i'm not very easy to shock, and don't object to violence in fiction per se, this is something else. if you're a delicate soul who faints at the sight of blood, give this one a miss. please. i mean it. weirdly, though, what's most agonising about american psycho is not the gore, but the bits in between. when blood isn't spurting every which way, it's really sort of dull. patrick bateman has absolutely no moral compass, no finer feelings, no pity; in his glassy-eyed vacuity, he only values what he wears, where he goes, what he has, and the mind-numbing, soul-stifling pap that he watches on tv. it is in fact a little like listening to the dead-of-eye office bore droning on and on about the minutiae of his/her life until you want to scream. there's no joy, no sorrow, no rage, no acceptance, no fear. there's no hope, and there's no despair either - there's just hollowness, which is far, far worse. and of course, this being a comment on the empty heart of hyper-capitalism, that's probably the whole point. but it's painful. and at the same time, i sort of couldn't put it down. which is probably also the whole point. i get the feeling i've stopped making much sense here, and since i generally value lucidity that's also an indication of the effect american psycho has on me. i honestly didn't know whether to give it 1 star or 5, and so i've decided to err on the side of generosity and give it 4. it's really sort of brilliant; it's just that i absolutely hated it.

title: ['Crazy Cool (Steele Street, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: after reading the first one in the steele street series i was jumping right into crazy cool, because i wanted, no, i needed, to know about this man they called superman. what sort of woman was going to unhinge this guy who was so deep undercover it was hard to tell whether or not he was still working for the good guys. well, hard to tell unless you're sdf, special defense force, down at steele street with the rest of the former chop shop boys and their crew. christian is the guy who you're attracted to because he's a beautiful man but yet there's that edge where you're not sure how dark he'll go. oh, he's plenty dark. christian served two years in prison for a murder he didn't commit. the girl he'd been wrapped up in at the time, the one he thought dropped him like a bad habit, but who went through her own hell, is suddenly back on the map and there's literal fireworks. this is one that christian can't fight, because this is the girl, bad luck as he likes to call her, that he gave his heart to and never got back. christian is badass, katya is poise that comes apart for the man with angel wings tattooed on his back. i will say i wanted more from katya, and she buckled so quickly under pressure, which was just so opposite of superman. i understood her charm, in a way, but still. for a guy who was so much, his counterpart should have had a bit more cojones. seeing everyone's place in steele street, getting so much of christian, the emotions you'll feel for certain member's heartache, and the combustible force that is nikki and kid chaos makes this one a stellar sequel.

title: ['Hourglass (Hourglass, #1)', 'Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art', 'Bossypants', 'The Sky Is Everywhere', 'Sunny Side Up']
cleaned_reviews: this page turner is an original combination of sci-fi and romance genres. emerson is a fully drawn character that is worth rooting for, and although parts of the teenage love triangle caused my adult self a few eye rolls, i don't think teens will bat an eye. mccloud uses comics to explain comics in this smart, original, well-researched study of the history, vocabulary, and artistic merit of sequential art. recommended for all comics readers and anyone who has a hard time "getting" graphic novels. i am not even a tina fey fan, but this book is laugh out loud funny and highly entertaining. nelson really excels at portraying authentic family relationships. the writing is lovely and the scattered poems are an effective tool to showcase lennie's grief over the death of her sister. with so many similarities in theme and motif (sky/sun, music/art, sisters/twins) to nelson's second printz-winning novel, i'll give you the sun, this seems like a warm-up for what is ultimately the better book, though it is still excellent. while the underlying theme is talking about and dealing with family members who are struggling with substance abuse, this upbeat story is really a story about relationships. holm manages to take a dark theme and make it appropriate for the age group. plus, it's funny!

title: ['The Night Circus']
cleaned_reviews: this is a beautiful work of art. reading the night circus feels like a dream, for lack of a better way to put it. it's that foggy immersive feeling that you get. i have been racing though books all break, but this one i took slow. it was like i had no choice. reading it felt like i was trying to walk though a pool or the caramel the the circus smells of. it just lasted. but it wasn't a bad slow. the pace was just right. reading this book too quickly would make you lose the magic of it, i think. like many people have said the back cover is very deceiving. it does not describe the book at all. what you get is not a fast paced action packed love story, but a dreamy take about a magical circus, that happens to also contain some characters, a competition, and a little love story. there are so many time lines and story lines and character arcs and points of view going on that it can seem a little chaotic and difficult, but all of that adds to the dreamlike experience. the circle of dreams is magical.

title: ['The Orphan Queen (The Orphan Queen, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: more amazing then i thought possible. jodi has done it again! review to come @ please feed the bookworm i'll admit it. i blindly had loved the orphan queen from the moment the gorgeous cover was revealed. the fact that jodi meadows wrote it seemed like icing on the proverbial cake. while not without a few faults, this book was definitely a favorite read of mine thus far in life...in life! if i was give a non ya obsessed friend the brief run down of the orphan queen, it could end up sounding rather generic. the lost princess becomes vicious, tough, & dangerous she will do anything and be anyone to infiltrate the enemies palace to get the info needed to regain her kingdom from those who stole it from her. i mean the name the orphan queen sounds pretty self explanatory, a queen who is an orphan therefore must have gone through something god-awful. photo im waiting_zpskox4zlad.gif while it is all those things i described above, it is also so much more. a fiercely loyal and determined band of noble orphans called the ospreys, take on not only revenge for the lost kingdom of aecor, but a curse called the wraith that threatens to wipe out all of the indigo kingdom, just as it has done to surrounding lands. wraith is a pollution that grows every time magic is used which is the reason it was outlawed years ago. it also has a direct correlation to the cause of wil & the other osprey's orphaning. that magic caused pollutant is tearing across their land causing horrid beast and complete devastation in it's wake. the plan is take back the kingdom then find a way to stop the wraith however what wil & melanie find after infiltrating the castle are unlikely allies and even more unlikely motives. after posing as royal refugees from the wraith infested kingdom of liadia, the ospreys are both closer and farther from the answers they seek all at once. power struggles and conflicting interests cause the group to choose sides and then things go horribly awry. photo storming the castle_zpsssoghkw0.gif i didn't grasp the seriousness of the wraith until wil took a journey to wraith infested land to find some answers. i thought "oh no big deal! so some evil beasts come into town every now and then and eat some people. wow, was i underestimating. there is also a horrible side affect from using the wraith for the gain of strength. it corrupts & mutates men into beings know as "glowmen", super strong, unfeeling, giants who have a taste for violence and a thirst for blood. the scenes in this waste land were just disturbing. there are mice as big as cats, trees that begin to nibble on the inhabitants of its branches, even if you happen to be a sleeping human, and the ever present threat of wraith beast & glowmen alike. as if this is not enough, wil encounters a town with the inhabitants of the building still frozen inside clearly trying to escape but forever frozen in their last moments unable to live or truly die... you think that is bad just wait till she sees a lady blink! photo am-i-going-mad-gif-vizzini-pri-pnc3_zpsbclr3xti.gif the world building is decent enough but, the thing that solidified this as a 5 'shroom book for me, was the interactions between the black knife, a vigilante with a hidden identity & wilhelmina. masked man i thrived on this relationship and was happily sustained throughout the entire book. the cat and mouse things they did was fun and before you know they truly were the only ones each other could rely on. it was a really cool progression to see how they built up that mutual trust and respect in each other. as a matter of face, all of the relationships were well thought and calculated, even the soul crushing end. photo 72920-inconceivable-gif-princess-bri-z2av_zpsaptgwwzw.gif jodi meadows has to have great things in store for the next book for her to leave the ending as she did. i won't hold it against her (maybe a little) but i know she has some magic up those sleeves of hers! if you love some nasty court politics, magic gone wrong, and the awaiting of a triumphant return....read this one. even if you don't like those things... read this anyway!

title: ['French Milk']
cleaned_reviews: finally, a good "graphic novel" (that's in quotations because, french milk is more of an illustrated journal). this was a sort of travel book but knisley also discusses her fears about being 22 and taking on all the responsibilities of adulthood. being 22 myself, i could completely relate to her worries. however, what made me fall in love was this book was its focus on the art and food of paris. as a foodie,i loved her appreciation and description of the delicious meals she had. (i now want to go to a french restaurant and drink some white wine and eat foie gras). and the art. as if i didn't love french art and culture enough, this book just made me want to save up and go on a month long tour of france (mainly paris). i would definitely recommend this book to those who enojoy travel autobiographies, food, and/or art.

title: ['Nightshade (Nightshade #1; Nightshade World #4)']
cleaned_reviews: first of all, i love the original cover of this series and i don't know why they changed it because now it looks bad! even though my covers won't match, i just had to get the original because it's so pretty. anyways, i really enjoyed reading this one. maybe because i don't read a lot of werewolf stories, but i liked andrea's take on it, how it's more spiritual and magical, rather than painful and obligatory. the characters don't even consider themselves as "werewolves" but call themselves "guardians", sworn protectors of the "keepers" who are basically witches and warlocks. their relationship has a very mysterious and questionable history that calla and shay, the human boy, slowly uncover. my favorite parts would have to be anything with ren in it, as i'm pretty much team ren. he's the typical pretty boy, alpha male kind of guy, but he's just so sexy and smooth, i can't help but smile when i think of him. i mean, andrea wrote some pretty steamy scenes between ren and calla that i just devoured. shay is the typical nice guy who does have his moments, but i'm rooting for ren. luckily, calla isn't an annoying female lead and she's very determined and strong-willed, which is important because she's the leader of her pack. i think andrea did a great job at taking the werewolf folklore and turning it into her own and i can't wait to see where she goes with it and she was able to balance the paranormal with the romance just right. granted, i was more interested in the romance than the paranormal parts and i flipped pages hoping to see more of ren, but overall, i really liked it. you'll definitely want to try this series if you like werewolves and hot, steamy scenes with sexy guys. can't wait to read wolfsbane!

title: ['What We Saw']
cleaned_reviews: this is one of those books that i almost don't want to rate, because it just doesn't feel right. enjoyed is definitely the wrong word for this book. this book was hard and painful and full of tough truths that are not to be enjoyed. but it is important and beautiful in its honesty. we all knew a "stacey" in high school to some extent. the girl who would maybe not be taken seriously if she accused someone of forcing themselves on her, because she was "asking for it". i hate that these phrases exist and that in reading this, i immediately could tell you who in my school i could have pictured in this situation. i hate that a book like this needs to exist because it is based on a true case. and i hate that many more cases like this exist that don't make the front page news, and that don't get reported at all. this was heart-breaking and made me so angry while i was reading it. not just at the rapists, but at the people who make excuses for them, either through the guise of religion or sticking together or to save face, or whatever other lame reason they give for trying to make it okay.

title: ['The House of the Scorpion (Matteo Alacran, #1)', 'Gone with the Wind', 'Eragon (The Inheritance Cycle, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: started this book to discuss it with my ninth grader. she had read it previously, but was looking forward to analyzing it this time. i, on the other hand, had never heard of it, which surprises me. anyone who is familiar with the science fiction idea of cloning probably has a good idea of what matt's intended destiny is, though i admit i thought it would be more serious than it was. however, the idea of raising someone the way matt was raised did strike me as surprising; far easier to lock it up and throw away the key. in retrospect, the conclusion should not have come as a surprise, and it makes the reality of parading life in front of your clone more understandable. i really enjoyed the pacing of the novel. it was a true page turner, and i wrapped it up in one day, rushing my kids out of the room when they bugged me. there have been few novels lately i've been that into, though whether that says something about what i'm reading versus my growing, err, maturity is another discussion. but i think some of the other reviews nailed the problems with this book. the characters seemed realistic, but at the same time often came off as flat. did celia raise the previous clones? if so, what made matt different to her? and why was she selected - simply because el patron wanted his clones to hear the accent of his youth? at what point in the during of clones food she and tan lin meet? even those who were horrid - why did the doctor not do more when he saw how rosa treated matt? if he lived her, he would have wanted her protected, not thrown get under the bus. i could see the logic but there's no intimation that he is that cold. then too i wonder about maria's mother. so many unanswered questions! at the same time, the novel acts as an interesting probe into morality, and how our voices shape who we become. but that isn't necessarily permanent, as tan lin demonstrates; people can change. it's an excellent jumping off point for a young reader, and though it could suffer more development, i still enjoyed the ride. this has always been one of my favorite books. i read it for the first time in 7th grade and i think it only took me 2 or 3 days to finish it. my initial impulse was to give this 4 stars, but let's be honest. once i got past the introduction (which was a bit dry for me), i stayed up all night reading the book. that should make it auto-receive 5 stars. this was a great book, and i'm eager to read the rest of the series, which of course i don't have because i'm traveling. it was interesting and captivating. it's hard to believe this was written by a teenager (well, in some respects, anyway; there were points that were clearly very standardized, like the typical hangover and some of the relationship angst. at the same time, check out the description of a sunrise. i was just listening to someone point out how sunsets have become cliche, but paolini manages to snag a new yet exact take on them. well done.) one of the biggest complaints i have is that we don't learn how old eragon is until roughly 2/3 of the way through the novel. he could be 12 or 18. that's a pretty big gap, and something odd to leave hanging. the closest guess we have comes from his cousin, who is a few years older and about to be married. but hey, maybe the kid is a late bloomer. this is key in terms of timeline, like the fact that bronn showed up 15 years ago. was that before or after eragon was born? (about the same time, it turns out.) i also found eragon's reaction to death a bit blase. probably standard for fantasy, but still we're missing a basic human reaction. true, he is willing to slice and dice the human-like monsters, but the only insight we get is when he pukes a bit on seeing a massacre. yet given the state of it, that seemed a bit weak; this was serious carnage. he does struggle a bit with ideals versus reality when his friend kills an unconscious man who had threatened them, and that's good, but mostly he feels idealized. that said, this book has a lot of depth for a ya novel, and is definitely one i would recommend to my kids, if my daughter hadn't already beaten me too it. i'm eager to read the rest of the series. it left me with a few lingering suspicions on eragon's parentage that i'm anxious to see resolved.

"hell you don't. you shuffle, peabody clomps, mcnab prances." also, eve strides and roarke prowls. each of their walking styles is indicative of their personalities. which is why i love mcnab. plus he says stuff like this: he's a magnificent prancing man! just when you think the smut can't get much hotter, they crank it up a notch! holy apocalypse, batman! that is some hot stuff! in this book, we get a threesome couple and let's just say the girl who gets to be the cream filling in this oreo is one lucky chick! that's right, stuff your face with this smutty oreo goodness! so freaking good! this hr is about two rival clans in ye old scotland that are forced by the king to join one of the chieftains to the other chieftain's daughter in marriage. the hope is that this will stop all of the crazy killing between the clans. neither clan is happy about it at all. these were some unhappy clams clans. but then, oh it was so awesome! the hero, graem, is a total sweetie pie. yes, an alpha sweetie pie, but still. and, the heroine, eveline, is so amazing. ugh! the cute-o-meter goes through the roof! i think the damn thing broke! yes, this much cuteness! and, best of all: no too stupid to live moments. no idiotic reasons they have to break-up and get back together. the sex was actually reasonable. he even waited a few days after she lost her virginity to give her time to heal, like a considerate guy. even the bad guy, who could have been considered a bit over the top, had a good plan as to why he does what he does. it made sense. weird! i actually have no complaints about anything that happened in this book. none! my only complaint is that i don't get to complain. it was just too awesome. i guess i'll always have that if constant bloody battles against disgusting monsters is your thing, this is the book for you. duece, the 16 yr old girl who has the name of 60 year old two-bit male alcoholic magician in vegas, is desperately trying to put together an army to fight the horde of monsters. for some strange reasons, not many grown men are willing to enlist in an army run by a 16 year old girl whose name is what they say they need to drop when heading for the bathroom. so, she and her small band of men use guerrilla tactics to build a reputation and start doing some damage. but, eventually, she knows a big war is coming, and the horde outnumbers the humans in a big way. the book is an exciting conclusion to the series and very satisfying for those whom have come to love duece and fade.

title: ['Lucas (Preston Brothers, #1)', 'One', 'Wardrobe Malfunction']
cleaned_reviews: yet again, jay mclean has delivered an absolutely brilliant rollercoaster of a book, packed full of so many different emotions throughout you can't help but keep turning those pages. i went through so many emotions and feelings whilst reading this book. i'm going to say it, i didn't like lucas much to start with. and honestly, started off really liking cooper (although that did change pretty quickly once you got to know him!!!!). throughout the book he made me really cross, but i think that was also the beauty of it. some of the decisions he made were rather questionable and it made me angry. laney was a great character and i really liked her. at times she came across a little weak and naive, but she is extremely loyal to lucas and the rest of the preston family. i loved her relationship with all the brothers and how much you could see the love and respect they all had for one another. lucas and laney's friendship throughout this book was epic. you just really hope they can move past all of their issues, pasts, sadness and devastation in their lives. so much happens in this book is brilliant. it's hugely fast paced with a lot of excitement and action throughout. some extremely funny moments with the rest of the preston family, and also some immensely serious and difficult times too. a wonderful friends to lovers story (but with a little more than that...), that will leave you experiencing all the emotions and more! it was heartbreaking, breathtaking, and in a way, it was kind of beautiful. lucas preston was beautiful. i love jay mclean's books and she will always be an immediate one-click author for me! i can't wait to see what the rest of the preston brothers bring! **** 4.5 loyalty and love stars **** wow, this book just blew me out of the water!! i have only recently discovered jewel's books, decided to read the 'jack and jill' series first, then was fortunate enough to read this arc. i didn't just read it, i devoured it, and really felt like i was experiencing the story right alongside the characters. this book is a standalone, but i honestly would recommend you read the jack and jill series first. not just because one contains some rather big spoilers, but because that is an awesome series in itself! when realising that one was going to be a book for cage and lake, i was so so happy!! they are amazing characters on their own, so this story which takes them on a new journey was always going to be something special! lake jones met cage monaghan in the past (we read about this meeting in the jack and jill series), and ever since then she's never been able to forget him. i knew him for a few hours. one day. one kiss. one moment. one unforgettable memory. yet she's had to, she's moved on, she's living her life following an accident she had which left her in a coma, with an amputated leg and without her boyfriend who died (don't worry, these aren't really spoilers and nothing you wouldn't know from very early on!). yet when a chance encounter (you could call it fate...) at her new neighbour everson banks aka "kong's" house, means they meet again, everything changes! this book has it all! it's a really lighthearted, sweet read, mixed with some beautiful touching moments, and some wonderful heat and chemistry which keeps the pages turning and your attention peaked throughout! so many times when i should have been doing other things, i though 'just one more page'! plus the humour - jewel has a really superb knack of including so many funny moments into this story! so many moments i was laughing out loud whilst reading the book. cage and lake's connection in this story in very intense. there is a lot of depth to their story, with both characters struggling with some issues from their pasts, their losses, their grief and guilt in different ways. and although this story to an extent is a romantic comedy, there is actually so much more to it. jewel has woven lots of little twists, turns and hurdles which get in the way of the characters, which as a reader keeps you guessing throughout right up to the very end of the book! i went through so many feels and emotions reading this book and even shed a little tear! the secondary characters were brilliant! i loved everson and his little side story, the quirkiness of thad and also flint (i'm a little bit hopeful we may see more of him in the future?). overall a superb 5 star "f*eur# gravity" read that i would highly recommend!! [?][?][?][?][?] brilliant!! i really enjoyed this book from samantha towle. i love her books anyway, but found this to be really refreshing and different. i devoured it in less than a day and thoroughly enjoyed it from start to finish. charly and vaughn are simply pure romance book perfection. i didn't even read the blurb for this, just went in blind and loved it all. from the very start i had a soft spot for vaughn, when we are introduced to him on a chat show with his girlfriend and best-friend who have all recently starred in a movie together. when a revelation is made live on air, immediately i felt for him! and charly is a brilliant female character, full of life, laughter and quirkiness. everything about the story line for these two characters simply worked... from their less than ideal start, to friends, to lovers, everything came together in a wonderful little package. with the perfect amount of emotion and angst, this book had everything i wanted. this whole book had a air of comedy and humour running thorough it which really made the book. and lets be honest the scene where charly earns her nickname of 'pins' - one of the funniest scenes i've read in a book for a long time! and of course there was plenty of build up in this story line. it wasn't exactly an insta-connection, but there were definitely sparks. and when those sparks finally ignite, boy it was hot! a fast paced, really well written story which flows perfectly. the characters were all superb, especially vaughn's gran - we all wish we had a gran like that!! and the banter between the characters is just wonderful! i thoroughly enjoyed this book from start to finish, with plenty to make you laugh swoon, and maybe even shed a tear or 2. 4.5 'pins' stars! lou 4tloreading blog

title: ['White Hot (Hidden Legacy, #2)', 'Out of Turn (Kathleen Turner, #4)', 'Needing Her (From Ashes, #1.5)', 'Magic Rises (Kate Daniels, #6)']
cleaned_reviews: yes, yes, yes! review to come... 4.5 stars this is a series that gets better with each book! so glad connor got his hea! dislike when the last 30% of a book though is previews for other books. :-/ katie daniels returns with a gripping new adventure that will hold you captive well past the last page! the pack is in desperate need of panacea, a magical herb compound that drastically decreases the chance of loupism in shifter youths. when a chance to obtain barrels of the medicine is offered in exchange for guarding a pregnant wolf shifter until she gives birth kate and curran know that they can't refuse. not only is the life of young maddie on the line without more panacea, but also the life of any future children of kate and curran. however, they know this is a trap. who the trap is for though is the big question. magic rises is without a doubt, my favorite book of the series so far. with unsurpassed creativity, ilona andrews takes the world we already know across the ocean and opens it up to a whole new realm of trials, lore, danger, and heavy-hitting players. adding depth to the already well-bonded series arc, keeping it fresh and exciting. kate handles being thrown in a castle full of shifters that look down on her because of her mere human status in her usual tough-talking, straight-shooting manner, but when the man-beast she loves pushes their relationship to the near breaking point, all of those old fears and doubt return to the forefront. the feels in this book gripped my heart with an iron fist. not to mention all of the inner blubbering i did at different intervals while griping my chest in empathized pained. kate stands behind curran and her belief in their love for as long as she can, but when certain situations are brought to light without enough answers she goes through a bitter spiral of fear, doubt, disbelief, fury, and heartbreak. and as a reader you are sucked into every tumultuous moment. gah! i don't to get too spoilery so i won't expand on that much more, but there were times that i seriously wanted to drop a boulder on curran's head and then strangle him for good measure. i was also a little miffed at the lack of remorse in curran when reasons were at last, aired out. the whole situation left me floundering and questioning the longevity of their relationship. i'll definitely be picking up the next book in the series, magic breaks, and diving in as soon as humanly possible just to reassure myself. bottom line; magic rises was a story packed with white-knuckle suspense of all flavors, i could not put this book down! i love the continual growth of the series; the plot was well paced and flowed from page to page and the world building was superb as usual. each and every character from the story is enrapturing, from the most vile to the most beloved. five stars coming from a reader who usually sticks to the straight-up romance side of literature, should tell you just how blown away i was by this urban fantasy and the authors ability as writers!

title: ['The Archived (The Archived, #1)', 'Time Between Us (Time Between Us, #1)', 'Every Move (Every, #3)']
cleaned_reviews: 4.5 stars - wesley ayers you guys!!! full review to come! 4.5 stars!! i can admit it... i haven't really read a lot of time travel books, so i was a bit leery going into this. i don't know what i was thinking. i absolutely loved it. anna lives in 1995 in chicago. bennett lives in 2012 in san francisco. they were never supposed to meet. bennett has an incredible ability to travel through time. there are a few catches to the whole process, but as long as he stays within the years he's been alive, he's never had any trouble, and i thought this was a wonderful twist to the story. he shows up in chicago in 1995, seemingly out of nowhere. anna first encounters him on the bleachers while she runs one morning, only bennett says it wasn't him. the bulk of the story takes place during this time period and it was wonderful to relive all the things that were going on back then... the music references and concerts! after something happens that forces bennett to spill his secrets to anna, they grow closer. i couldn't help but feel nervous for these two, simply because bennett was somewhere he wasn't supposed to be and anna was falling for him completely. i'm not sure what i'm supposed to do with this information. tell him to leave? tell him to stay? but i don't have time to consider any other alternatives, because he scoots in closer and brings his hands to my face, and i fall back into the bookcase as he kisses me with this intensity-like he wants to be here, and if he kisses me just long enough, deeply enough, none of what he just said will actually be true. and as much as i know it's all true and that it's incredibly stupid to feel this way about someone who doesn't belong here-who, when he leaves, will hardly be a plane ride away-my hands leave the berber carpet, find his back, and pull him toward me until i'm flat against the shelves. because he's here now. and because i'm pretty certain i don't want this to stop. ever. after something happens and both bennett and anna test his abilities by changing the past and breaking his personal rules for his ability, i swear i read with a ball of nerves resting in my stomach, waiting for something to happen. i mean, they are messing with fate and i've seen that movie the butterfly effect. just saying. i really enjoyed the characters - definitely anna, while i found myself a bit angry with her a few times, i thought she was written really well. i did find myself emotionally attached to her and her feelings so she obviously worked for me. bennett, once we got to know him was sweet and protective and caring and while their relationship wasn't born of the normal, he made the effort to try and give her the normal as well as the spectacularly grand and unbelievable. one thing i would have liked to know more about is the manifestation of his ability. we get a brief explanation, which works for the book, but being naturally curious you wonder if there is anyone else like him, who has this talent as well ... where did it come from, why him... those kinds of things. i myself would have a hard time accepting the ability without doing tons of digging and trying to find out why me. i also would have liked to know what happened with anna in her previous life... why in the prologue does she give him the letter and what made her first choice not the right one for her. i think what is most intriguing about this book is the idea of time travel itself and changing history... 'what if' ... what if you could have made a different choice in life, what if you could change the outcome of an event. all these things are intriguing and can't help but make you as a reader think of the way things might be different in your life if only... once i started this book it was hard to put down, like i said, i turned page after page nervous for these two while reading. if you're looking for a sweet contemporary ya romance than this is just the thing for you. this review can be found on my blog, fic fare: my love for this series is complete. of course being incredibly impatient about series books, i ordered my copy of every move from australia on its release day there and then waited with baited breath for it to arrive in my mailbox... it only took about 2.5 weeks. amazingly i survived. i will try not to spoil a single thing about this book since it is the final installment, but i will say that i absolutely adored everything about it. i know, i know. there are going to be some people who are going to be mad about a few things... (view spoiler)[1. another boy is introduced here and while i was a little concerned at certain points, i realized that there really was no reason to be because while mycroft & watts are a bit shaky at the beginning of this story, they find that solid connection that endeared me to them so much in the first two books. 2. rachel does something that is a bit questionable and i normally wouldn't agree with in some situations, but to be honest it really didn't bother me as much in this situation. i will leave it at that. (hide spoiler)] so, about this other boy. harris derwent is an old family friend who has come back to melbourne with her and mike and he actually works with rachel on some self-defense techniques and really helps her get her confidence back. i found myself really enjoying his story... i think i heard that he's going to have his own book and this makes me incredibly happy. it will be nice to see where his life goes from here. the story itself is exactly what i had hoped for in a conclusion. the mystery and suspense around who mr. wild is and mycroft's parent's death was excellently done and riveting. marney keeps the pace of the story moving quickly and it's full of action. there is of course the romance and the reconnecting between james & rachel, and i'm not exaggerating when i say swoon. "come here," he says softly. he takes my hand and steps towards the wall, puts his back to it. he drops my hand once i'm standing in front of him. "kiss me again." his voice is so low and rough that i melt a little. i blink at him. "and you're just going to stand there?" "yes." my lips quirk up. "so... why the wall? is that some sort of - " "it's been a while," he says. "i don't know how my legs will go." i mean seriously. i adore this boy so much. his struggle with needing to find out what happened to his parents yet, his desire to shelter and keep rachel safe is just the best. and just seeing how the loss of his parents has affected him in ways he hasn't fully realized yet was heartbreaking. but i think that my favorite part was rachel's story... to see her growth from book 1 to where she is now was truly gratifying. i loved that when she returned to five mile, she had all these amazing memories but was able to see how her life has changed for the better since leaving. i really enjoyed seeing her reconnect with her mom and of course loved seeing the strength her character grew into. if you haven't picked up this series, please make a point to do so. this series is definitely at the top of my all-time favorites list and while i'm sad to see it come to an end, i'm excited to see what marney has in the works!

title: ['Incarnate (Newsoul, #1)', 'Dead Silence (The Body Finder, #4)']
cleaned_reviews: i absolutely loved this book. it kept me going from beginning to end, and i can't remember the last time i loved a heroine so very much. even more than the hero! the book cover caught my eye, admittedly, but like most aesthetically pleasing covers i thought it might be a dud. i gave it go anyway and i am glad i did. this story follows ana, a new soul born into a world of reincarnated souls that actually remember each and every single one of their lives, and what they don't remember they can look up in meticulously kept library archives. since ana replaced a soul that should have been reborn and since she is the first of her kind, she is an outcast. her father abandons her and her mother treats her terribly. i ached for ana. she had been so programmed to think she was worthless and to not expect anyone to be kind to her that when someone was, she didn't know how to deal with it. this book starts with ana deciding to enter the city of heart after her mother had taken her away from there so no one could associate with the "nosoul" as her mother referred to her. along the way she runs into trouble with slyphs and sam, our hero, rescues her. i absolutely adored sam. he was so good and patient with ana. he knew how broken she was after her what her mother had done to her. but ana is no meek miss. she is strong and capable and works hard to carve out a life for herself, never knowing if this will be her only life or if she will also be reincarnated. i loved this book and i am so glad that this will be a series! i just love this series. the build up to the climax is enjoyable without feeling like it's dragging. there is a lot going on with these characters to keep one riveted. i can't wait for the next one!

title: ['Life As We Knew It (Last Survivors, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: this is an interesting apocalyptic ya novel. it's not amazing, but i really enjoyed it. it's a simpler plot than most ya novels, but i liked it better because of it. it's really just about the characters surviving the "end of the world" and how they're trying to keep it together. it's not about the main character saving anything or anyone, it's just about her trying to live her life. it's really more of a drama than an action/adventure, which is what you get with most ya novels.

title: ['Allegiant (Divergent, #3)']

title: ['On Demon Wings (Experiment in Terror, #5)', 'Play It Safe']

cleaned_reviews: (this review can be found on my blog the (mis)adventures of a twenty-something year old girl). i'd been wanting to read this book for awhile now, but due to other commitments, i just never got around to it until now. i'm so glad i did get a chance to read this book because it was really interesting! i think the title suits the book well. the book is about the main character, sia. plus, amnesia can't be spelled without "sia." i'm not sure if the author did that deliberately or not. i'm not usually one for just putting a person on a cover and leaving it at that, but it does work for this cover. i love the soft colors used as well for the cover. i only had a few complaints about the world building, and these could just be personal opinion. firstly, i was just wondering why sia's parents didn't get sia some therapy after she returned home. if it was my child that that had happened to, therapy would've been one of my top priorities. the second problem i had was how accepting everyone was at school about sia's amnesia. i've been to high school; it's a very cruel place. i was very surprised that sia didn't get made fun of because of her amnesia, especially by her former friends. maybe i'm just being too cynical. i don't know. i can't really comment about fugue amnesia and if sia actually did have the symptoms of it as described in the book because i don't really know too much about it. anyway, besides those few things, i did enjoy the world building very much! i thought the pacing of this book was really good. i never became bored with this book, and once i started reading it, it was hard to stop. the plot line about a popular mean girl having amnesia and then turning into a nice girl was rather interesting. i wanted to know what would happen when sia got her memories back. i guessed what would happen, and i was right though. there's no big plot twists, and it works for this book. there's no cliff hanger ending either. i thought all the characters were written very well. sia is a very likable character, and it was easy to feel her frustration that came with having amnesia. i liked the way she tried to make a difference. kyle was a great guy, and i totally understood why he was so apprehensive when it came to sia. amber was a great mean girl, and stacey was likable even if her social status meant too much. in fact, this book kind of reminded me of the film mean girls in a lot of places. the dialogue flowed very smoothly and fit in well with a young adult novel. the character interactions never felt forced either. there's only one scene that has violence in it although it's not graphic. i don't remember any swearing in this book either. overall, sia is a fantastic novel with a great plot and likable characters. it also sends out a positive message throughout. i'd recommend this book to those aged 15+ who are fans of the movie mean girls and those who love sweet books. title: ['The Lake House', 'A Monster Calls']
cleaned_reviews: loved. loved this book. i thought it was a bit long and could have been edited down a bit but i loved the mystery of it and the ending. i think i still liked the forgotten garden better but still one of my favorite books. 'i have had as many names as there are years to time itself! roared the monster. i am herne the hunter! i am cernunnos! i am the eternal green man!' 'stories are wild creatures, the monster said. when you let them loose, who knows what havoc they might wreck?' 'you do not write your life with words, the monster said. you write it with actions. what you think is not important. it is the only important you do.' read this review and more on my blog.the book return blog the story behind the writing of 'a monster calls' is one of grief and loss. irish author siobhan dowd originally conceived of the idea of 'a monster calls'. tragically she passed away from breast cancer before she could write the story. patrick ness later wrote the novel based on her ideas. this novel focuses on the most painful issues a young adult can experience, death, divorce, abandonment, and bullying. 'a monster calls' is the story of conor o'malley. he is a thirteen year old boy whose mother is dying of cancer. his father has left the family, remarried, and moved to america. as if this wasn't enough, conor is also bullied violently at school. his grandmother (who helps care for him while his mother is ill) is uptight and very ungrandmotherly towards him. not surprisingly, as a result of all this conor is plagued by nightmares. one night a monster begins visiting him. he is not, however, the monster conor expected. the monster tells conor he will tell him three stories. then conor will then have to tell the monster his own story. this book has all the magic and fantasy of a classic fairy tale. the story itself is both deep and poignant. the distress and guilt conor feels about his mother's impending death is clear from the beginning and plays a significant part of the story line. reality and fantasy are woven so intricately into this novel that it becomes believable that the monster visits conor every night. 'a monster calls' is a wonderful complex story that i absolutely loved. the plot was amazing, the characters were real, and the pace kept me turning pages. the illustrations were amazing and added a gothic feel to the story. 'a monster calls 'is destined to become an instant classic and i foresee it as required reading for many english lit classes to come. this novel is also a vital resource for anyone who is grieving. i am not sure if the upcoming film adaptation will do justice to the story but i can't wait to find out. plus, i can't wait to hear liam neeson, as 'the monster'.this review was originally posted on the book return...

title: ['Killers of the Flower Moon: The Osage Murders and the Birth of the FBI']
cleaned_reviews: killers of the flower moon offers a look at osage murders and the conspiracy behind what happened, and the process that investigators went through to find out who was behind it all. david grann takes the reader on a wild ride as her chronicles the events leading up to the first murder of an osage woman, and the horrendous and mysterious slayings of several others over time. the fact that this is not a part of american consciousness is indicative of the erasure of the histories of native americans. with the plot thickening and no solution in sight, j. edgar hoover tasks some agents with investigating these mysterious events. thus, the fbi was born. this is non-fiction that reads just like any great piece of fiction, except the implications have real world consequences. narratively, the story of the murders and the birth of the fbi reads quite well. it's easy for a reader to get into it, and if you're a fan of true crime, this might do it for you. grann does more than simply tell the story up until the final reveal; by inserting himself into the narrative and thus the investigation. he searches for closure for the descendants, and makes some startling discoveries. for an exciting true crime story, check out killers of the flower moon.

title: ['Embassytown', 'Norwegian Wood']
cleaned_reviews: i'm still not totally sure how to categorize this book. it is definitely one of the strangest and most confusing books i've ever read- but by far one of the most unique, and mieville's prose is incredible. it's hard to describe embassytown at all, but it is essentially about the relationship that humans have on a specific planet, arieka, with the native species, the ariekei or "hosts." the hosts speak a certain "language" where there are no signs or signifieds- everything they say is true and literal. they also speak with two mouths simultaneously and cannot comprehend artificial forms of language, so the only way humans can communicate with them is with ambassadors, sets of twins that can communicate simultaneously with one sentient mind. kind of. i have to commend mieville for writing something so unbelievably difficult. the kind of creativity involved in crafting a story like this seems almost impossible, and his writing style is perfect to tell it. it was fascinating to read a sci-fi book entirely centered on language and semiotic theories, and to try to imagine the linguistic concepts he mentions. my main problem with embassytown is that it felt like the author was trying to shoehorn in a ton of interesting, but extremely confusing, concepts that weren't really relevant to the story. for example, the immer, which is a sort of universe that's been consistent throughout all three iterations of the universe where arieka and embassytown are located. cool, but insanely hard to comprehend and not all that relevant to the story. the same goes for ehrsul and the turingware, "floaking," and other concepts. they play a tangential role in the story, but they mostly just distract from the plot itself, which is confusing enough on its own! i would probably give this 3.5 stars- closer to 4 for complete originality and ingenuity, closer to 3 because the book felt very jumbled, which made it even more difficult to read and understand. one of the best books i've read in a long time. murakami is one of the best living authors, and it's incredible to see how deftly he can master another genre- i'm used to his stories in the magical realism genre, like hard-boiled wonderland and the end of the world and the wind-up bird chronicle, but this is much more reminiscent of on seeing the 100% perfect girl one beautiful april morning or the ice man, some of his incredible short stories. norwegian wood follows the life of a young student, toru watanabe, and his relationships with those around him, particularly with naoko, the former girlfriend of his best friend kizuki prior to kizuki's suicide, and midori, a vivacious fellow student. i was struck at several points by just how well murakami describes the human condition- being lonely, loving someone, all feelings that everyone has experienced, but only murakami can describe so poetically. is it realistic? not really. is it touching? absolutely.

title: ['A Man Called Ove']
cleaned_reviews: hit my reading goal for the year, and i wanted to highlight this book in particular, because it's one of only two books that i gave a full five stars to, and this one was probably my favorite. if you get the chance, definitely check it out. this is my original review. *** i have a story to tell you. it's a little long, but i really feel like i need to share this. as i sit here writing this review, i'm honestly not sure why the book i just read affected me so much. i don't normally read a lot of regular contemporary fiction - i keep it mostly to fantasy and sci-fi. but this book caught my attention. it made me think - more than any other book has made me think in a very long time, and it reminded me of something i learned over a year ago that has really stuck with me. i work as an insurance salesman at a state farm agency in queens, ny. my job being the kind of job that it is, i deal with hundreds of people a week, from sales calls, to service calls, to whatever else in between. one of the things i hate the most about my job is dealing with angry customers, but that kind of comes with the territory. on this one particular day, an elderly woman (she looked to be in her early seventies) walked into the office, clearly upset. she had a russian accent that made it a little hard for me to understand everything she was saying, but she still spoke excellent english. and when i say she was upset, i mean she was livid - like really livid. she demanded that i open her and her husband's car policy, because supposedly we raised her rates unjustly, and she said that i had better help her fix it or else she was going to cancel her policy right then and there. "i am an elderly woman!" she said. "i barely even drive my car, and i've never had an accident in my life!" i was already frustrated, because *i* was not the one who raised her rates, i just happened to work for the insurance company that did. i felt like she was being extremely rude to me. i couldn't understand for the life of me why somebody would walk into an office and think that they had the right to treat somebody the way that she was treating me. and in any case, she was paying probably half of what the average person in queens pays for their car insurance, and in my mind, she shouldn't be complaining. i'm not even saying this in a prideful way, but like... i try to be a nice person. i've always felt like i was a reasonably nice guy, even to people who didn't particularly like me. for whatever reason though, on that particular day, i'm ashamed to admit that i responded to her by being rude in return. i was having a bad day as it was, and i was stressed trying to plan my wedding, and i didn't feel like i deserved her poor treatment and accusations. i ignored all of her claims, quickly told her that it was out of my hands, and explained there was nothing i could do. i made it as clear as possible that i could not help her. anything, i thought, to get this woman away from my desk. i was shocked to see that she gave up almost immediately. when people are upset about their price, they almost never quit right away, but she dropped it almost before the words were even out of my mouth. "well, alright," she said. "that's not what i came in here for, anyways." she started to reach into her bag, and it looked like she was removing some kind of document. i assumed it was something typical, like a driving course certificate or an inspection form, because i deal with that stuff literally all the time. she placed the document on my desk, and turned to the side, almost like she didn't even want to look at me. she seemed anxious, all of a sudden. i was confused at this point, so i looked down at the piece of paper she put on my desk. it was a death certificate. she had come to remove her husband from the policy. he died roughly two months ago. my heart sank, and i looked up. she was sitting sideways on the chair, looking away from me; but i could already see there were tears in her eyes, even as she started to speak again. "we were together for almost 40 years," she said, and her voice was shaking. "they send so much mail... i just need to get his name off of it." and a single tear started to fall down her cheek, her eyes filled with sadness, where before i could only see anger and rage. the woman who i could only see as a problem to get rid of, all of a sudden, became human right in front of me. and i didn't know what to do. "i am so sorry," i said, even though it felt cheap after the exchange that we just had. i didn't know what to say. in that moment, i swear to you, it was like god brought directly to the surface of my mind every time i had been rude, or insulting, or even impolite to somebody who i thought was bothering me. and he reminded me that everybody has a story. everybody has a hundred things that make them broken, in little ways, and probably a handful of things that have broken them in big ones. this woman in front of me was dealing with so much grief, and the only thing that i could think about was that i was being mistreated, i was being insulted, i did not deserve her harsh words. and i realized how self-centered i was. it made me want to cry, because that is not who i ever wanted to be. why mention this? this book tells the story of a man we've all met. he is the guy giving you a hard time at your retail job. the man who is so strict and on top of the rules it's infuriating. he is the old man next door that scares everybody in the neighborhood. a man who most of us are usually tempted to disregard. a man that most of us see as a problem. he is the woman who walked into my job, raging about the price of her insurance. and he is the man who has a story. a story that most of us will probably never take the time to know. more than anything, to me, this book was a powerful reminder that everybody we come in contact with is more than meets the eye. even more than this, it reminded me that we have the power to truly make a difference in the lives of the people who we only ever see as a problem. and that's something we can never take for granted and wow i loved it. powerful story. beautiful writing. there are some books that are just more than books to me, and this is one of them. a lifelong favorite, for sure. read it if you can =]. *** friends.... read. this. book. easily in my top ten favorites of all time. it's been sitting in my audible library for over a year, so i decided to just pick it up, and i can't even tell you how pleasantly surprised i was. i have so much to say and write. i'll post a full review tomorrow.

and a war veteran. now, back living at the house where he grew up and hayley spent her first few years, she attempts to attend a mainstream high school and deal with her fellow classmates and teachers, who she considers nothing more than "zombies." this is the first novel i've read that's dealt with the issue of veterans and ptsd. hayley is accused by her friends of taking care of her father more than he takes care of her, but she is only trying to do the best that she can in this unfortunate situation. and she can take care of herself. hayley was such an awesome main character. i really identified with her independent nature, willingness to learn, and snarky attitude towards following the rules. she's constantly in trouble because, even though she's obviously very smart, she has trouble applying herself in school while she's dealing with more important things in her home life. and then there's finn. hayley's best (and only) friend grace gives her the idea that she and finn would be perfect together...as they're both "anti-zombie" and a little weird. finn has a similarly rough situation at home, so they really are kind of perfect for each other, and it's so sweet when they realize that, too. i really loved reading their conversations. the back-and-forth teasing was adorable, and neither of them knew quite how to be in a typical high school relationship, so it was cute to watch them figure it out as they went along. this novel also deals with the theme of memory. hayley's father's memories of the war and hayley's childhood memories are both importance parts of this novel, and those random sections throughout the book don't really click into place until the last chapter. while i thought that what anderson was trying to accomplish with the memory sections was cool, i didn't feel like it was done as well as it could've been. it was kind of confusing and i wasn't really sure what the point of it all was. there wasn't really that big "ah hah" moment that i'd expected. it all came together, but it was jumbled up and wasn't that shocking or surprising. it seemed like we were supposed to think that there was this big mystery, when there really wasn't. and i wanted the issue of memory to have more to do with the ending of the book than it really did, because it seemed like it was going to be really important and then it wasn't. i also had this weird feeling throughout the whole book of not really getting what the novel was all about. like this sense of not understanding where the author was going. usually when you read a novel, you kind of know what the "end game" is. the main character is going to fall in love, escape from a bad situation, finally break out of her shell...whatever it may be, you usually see it coming. but this novel meandered around and didn't have a clear direction, and that was kind of annoying. it wasn't just that i couldn't figure out where it was going, or it was supposed to be a mystery...it just wasn't really going anywhere. there was kind of a big climax at the end, but it just felt strange that the whole novel was leading up to that point. i guess i was expecting something else to happen, mostly with the memory stuff, and i didn't really get the payoff that i was hoping for, or any understanding of why the novel seemed so pointless for so long. but even though it did seem a little directionless for the majority of it, i was still totally sucked in. i read half of the book, woke up and read the next half. i did not want to stop reading. i really came to care about the characters, and i wanted to know what was going to happen to hayley, her father, and finn. i think that the author did a really good job in ending the book, as well. although some of the issues in the cleaned_reviews: beware the death's head fez in this is weird, mystery adventure in brief, heraclix & pomp is a fun, well-constructed fairy tale that will appeal to fans of historical and speculative fiction. mystery adventure: as the book summary indicates (copied below), heraclix & pomp tracks an undead man (recently raised) and a magical sprite as they hunt down a necromancer. the amnesiac, frankenstein-like-golem 'heraclix' rediscovers himself (and the history of his subparts which maintain their own volition) while the mischievous, chronologically-challenged fairy 'pomp' learns human concepts. as the title suggests, this book is really about their plight, but they serve well as proxies for any introspective reader who questions "who am i?" and "where is my life going?" don't worry, the adventure is more comedic than philosophical. the unique duo navigates the austrian & ottoman empires of 18th century europe (with sorties into hell); the below dialogue excerpt captures their collective voice. with a story that hinges on two characters not knowing where they are going, or who they are, the reader should expect dealing with some uncertainty. there is also an implicit promise that heraclix's mysterious history will be explained, and it is. whereas the dosing of information seemed spot on for the first half, the latter suffers from some disjointed/unexpected transitions and reveals. in all, aguirre artfully unveils heraclix's past(s) well enough, even if his geographical trajectory cannot be predicted. the real strength of aguirre's writing is his weird style and eye for design: weird style: aguirre's prose is steeped with entertaining weirdness (see weird excerpt), but could hardly be classified as horror despite the key word "necromancy" tagging it. as done for the novella swans over the moon, aguirre's meticulous character design is again brilliant. foremost, the appearance of the death's-head-fez caps must be highlighted. the juxtaposition of skull-and-crossbones on the timely headpiece (popular in the 18th century) represents the necromancer, indeed the entire book, well. if this was a sword & sorcery tale, we'd expect to encounter a grimmer skull helmet akin to the head of frazetta's deathdealer; but this book is more of historical fantasy that delivers weird myth under more inviting flare. the elegant cover (credit artist claudia noble) and introductory quote from the esteemed alchemist hermes trismegistus, promise readers an intellectual narrative. my knowledge of history is terrible, so i undoubtedly missed many historical references, but the inclusions of real curiosities are enjoyable: for instance, the winged hussar cavalry units that appeared in angelic-costume on the battlefield make a cameo here. historical and speculative fiction fans will enjoy this unique tale. weird excerpt: "around, above, and through--yes, even through them--flowed a gathering of spectral beings, close to a hundred strong, their ecto-plasmic strands in tatters behind them as they floated up and down the stone stairway and the great, empty, circular shaft around which it spiraled. the specters were loathsome, every one of them crippled in some way. many were missing limbs, several sported gunshot wounds, a few were altogether decapitated. but the mere sight of the apparitions, strangely, did little to affect heraclix who was himself, after all, caught in some kind of state between life and death. rather, it was the soft crying and plaintive weeping (of those who still had mouths, tongues, and heads with which to weep), the faintly echoed pleas that caused him to shiver..." dialogue excerpt "what do you see?" pomp asks. "the past. or at least a part of it." "what is 'past'?" "it's what happened before now." pomp looks up at heraclix with a skeptical squint. "i met you in mowler's apartment. you came there in a jar. before, you were free. and i have a hunch that i might have once been free." "but mowler pushes you around." "that's precisely it. what did i have to fear from him? i am physically superior to him in every way: stronger, faster. yet i didn't fight back." "you should." "but i didn't. something held me back." "what holds you back?" "guilt." "what is 'guilt'?" "'guilt' is feeling bad for something you've done." "why do you have guilt?" pomp asks. "i don't know, exactly. but i think it might have something to do with . . ." heraclix stops. "with what?" "with whatever happened to me before i awoke in the cauldron of blood." book summary: heraclix was dead and pomp was immortal. that was before heraclix's reanimation (along with the sewn-together pieces and parts of many other dead people) and pomp's near murder at the hands of an evil necromancer. as they travel from vienna to prague to istanbul and back again (with a side-trip to hell), they struggle to understand who and what they are: heraclix seeks to know the life he had before his death and rebirth, and pomp wrestles with the language and meaning of mortality. as they journey across a land rife with revolution and unrest, they discover that the evil necromancer they thought dead might not be so dead after all. in fact, he might be making a pact to ensure his own immortality . . .

title: ['Ash']
cleaned_reviews: loved it! most fantasy authors seem to baulk at the idea of making "historical" settings have values anything other than modern conservatism draped over some medievalist's nostalgic wet dream about chivalry. lo breaks this convention really naturally, presenting a fantastic world where queerness is visible and thankfully lacking some intense coming out/struggling with "am i gayyyyyyyy???!" storyline (not that those story lines aren't important, but they are sometimes such a staple of queer lit [esp. ya fiction] that it's a fucking breath of fresh air to not have that). it is a nice cinderella, with enough familiarity to remain a retelling, but enough changed that the story doesn't feel predictable (i was still guessing how it would end up until like the last few pages). it is written with an enjoyable awareness of its intertextual-ness which doesn't fall into smug overly referential and unnecessary parts. it does contain a lot of really cool reimaginings of classic folk tales and, potentially some originals (i don't know though, because there are definitely a butt tonne of folk tales i don't know!) i also love some of the reviews i was reading before which were really indignant that cinderella might be queer, and it gave me life and joy that at least one person was genuinely upset by this one version ruining everything

title: ['The Perks of Being a Wallflower']
cleaned_reviews: "...reading the perks of being a wallflower. it's a very peculiar-esque book, in a very charlie-esque way." ~me the perks of being a wallflower was such a quick read. chbosky sucked me into this book and i'm not sure i expected it. i've been eyeballing the book since i was in high school. what finally made me pick it up? probably the fact that it was being made into a movie coupled with the fact the book kept staring me down at work (yes, i work in a bookstore, and oh, what wonderful books i encounter there). so, i bought it. like i said, i'd been eyeballing it an i figured, why not? what made me unable to put it down? good god, there are quite a few things, but they primarily fall into one category: the epistolary format of the book. chbosky could have chosen to tell charlie's story via first person narration or third. frankly, it just wouldn't have produced the same results. there is such a brutal honesty that charlie pours into his "friend" who "listens and understands and didn't try to sleep with that person at the party even though [s/he] could have." through his letters, charlie is able to freely let his thoughts flow. that is the whole advantage to writing to a "friend" he doesn't know--he can be as candid as he'd like to be, which seems essential to who charlie is. charlie, at his heart, is a good person; he tends to over-think things and put others needs and wants before his own. i am confident that charlie has always been this way, and that these natural character traits have been dramatized by the events of his childhood: (view spoiler)[essentially, the fact that charlie was molested by his favorite aunt defined the way he reacted to certain events (ie. watching a girl being forced to have sex in his bedroom, his sister getting hit from her boyfriend and then witnessing them having sex only days after, etc). (hide spoiler)] in these scenarios, it is hard for charlie to respond to any of these situations because he was unable to respond to them himself, and i get the impression that if he were able to respond, he wouldn't feel as if he knew how to do it. i think what his english teacher, bill, had said struck a cord with charlie, "we accept the love we think we deserve." charlie never forced his way into any relationship, but received openly the love his family/friends gave him and he accepted--only occasionally over-thinking it. charlie's character was very dynamic; his honesty and innocence sucked me into his life, and i always wanted to know more. i realize that this book has become another piece of pop-culture with the production of the film, and i also realize that there were quite of few people who sort of bashed charlie and the way he told his story of growing up. charlie, like us, is different. maybe he is a little bit more different than the rest of us, but i think that if you can see past his differences, you can pick out the similarities. there are probably more similarities between charlie and ourselves than there are differences. my biggest similarity? i think it centers around one of charlie's favorite sentiments: the concept of being "infinite". "and in that moment, i swear we were infinite." there is something philosophical to me about charlie. he thinks about life, realizes things that i don't know [if] many of us realize. a prime example is when charlie is looking at his parent's pictures. charlie gets that not only were they happy in the picture, but in that moment they were happy beyond what the camera showed. he understood that by taking the photo, the happiness of the people in the photo would always be infinite because it was being remembered. i suppose i can identify with charlie's thought process, so maybe he doesn't seem so hard for me to understand. whatever the case maybe, it was a pleasure to read charlie's letters. he told me his story, it was relevant, and i got it. charlie's story is anything but typical, but then, if it were, it wouldn't cause such a stir. so, the only question that really matters is what will you make of charlie? (for anyone who has read it, there are questions at the back of the book. i don't think i am ready to be done with charlie yet...anyone else not ready to be done with charlie?) my rating: 4.5 stars out of 5. it may actually be a 5, but i'm not sure yet...i'm still mulling over charlie and his letters.
