title: ['Broken Harbor (Dublin Murder Squad #4)']
cleaned_reviews: tana french is a literary crack dealer. i've tried referencing her books for tips in my writing and never can stop at one sentence, paragraph, or chapter--even if i've read the book before. she is the master of the page turner. you sink into her stories and characters like diving into a deep, warm pool with lots of interesting things to find at the bottom. sounds from the real world fade, you don't want to come up, even to breathe. while i still like the likeness best, broken harbor is very good, but i'm torn between 3 and 4 stars. the likeness is an exception to what has become french's formula: lead detective works a case that goes very badly, in a place with deep meaning from his childhood. broken harbor fits this to a t. the coincidences are getting to be a bit much. but, still, i couldn't put it down. halfway through, the case seems solved, so you know something's go to go terribly wrong. i kept trying to follow along, with my own theories--french is good about this because you feel like you are getting all the clues along with scorcher. but, like in the other books, he's not a very reliable narrator. can you trust him? worse, can you trust french, because toward the end, she throws in a curve from out of the blue that made me lose faith. she managed to bring it around by the end, and i very much enjoyed the end--in that kind of "there's not good outcome" way she has mastered. as for the others who want rob/cassie back? i want cassie back and wonder who's left in the murder squad to continue the next installment. the place has a hell of a turnover. quigley? that'd be a hard sell! how about sam? but he's not in this one.

title: ['Storm Ravaged (Storm Damages, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: great story!!! i absolutely loved this continuation of elizabeth's and gabe's story. gabe has lost his memory and elizabeth is pregnant with his child. gabe wants elizabeth to marry him so that his child will be legitimate and can be his heir, that's the only reason...at least at first. the loss of memory was interesting point to the story. gabriel didn't really want anyone to know so instead of elizabeth and gabriel relearning things together, gabriel tried to fake it for long enough and then told elizabeth. i really enjoyed the way that elizabeth tried to stick to her guns. she was in a tough spot because of the situation and danger that she was in. i admired her wanting to stay independent but also being able to compromise for the relationship. gabriel pretty much pissed me off the whole time. i was not pleased with the way that he acted and manipulated elizabeth. he is going to have to wake up and learn to compromise in the next one, that's for sure. i was proud of elizabeth in the end for doing what she had to do because she was right and hopefully it's the wake up call that gabriel needs. the characters are definitely expanded on in this story and you get to know them better and see different sides of them. the story is nice and smooth and of course draws you in from the beginning. you do need to read the first story to really enjoy this one and to know what's going on. without it, certain events and reactions just won't make enough sense. the pace is great and allows for a greater connection with the characters. once i started i couldn't put it down. i still want more of the secondary characters, especially brianna and jake. there is another cliff hanger, just fyi, and i can't wait for the next one to come out so that i can find out what's going to happen next and how everything can be fixed. hopefully i won't have to wait too long lol.

title: ['Stardust']
cleaned_reviews: *warning: this review probably makes no sense* buddy read with asha! i've been putting off this review because i'm not 100% sure how to rate stardust.. so, you know how the grandpa reads the princess bride to his sick grandchild? stardust is that book for me. neil gaiman's writing is pure magic. before i read stardust i thought that i had read a fairytale but i was wrong. i've read lots of fantasies but never a fairytale. there is something so different about them and i just can't quite put my finger on it.. i think it might have to do with the flow of the story and the way the magic is perceived. i loved that the magic wasn't over the top. it was found in small things like dreams that could be heard aloud, glass flowers, the flame of a candle. neil gaiman spun his words in a way that made everything seem almost delicate. i loved the concept that the stars are alive and watch over the human world and that if a star just so happens to fall on the right side of the wall, it's really so much more. the characters are silly and shallow and cruel in their own way and every one of them has a lesson to learn. as i said before i've alway adored stardust, but up until now i had only ever seen the movie. the movie is way i'm having a heard time rating the book. i love them both equally but differently. i love the book for it's subtle magic and beautiful prose while i love the movie for it's adventure and action. though i was very, very disappointed that captain shakespeare did not make an appearance in the book. he is by far my favorite character. though the movie is based on the book i feel like they are very different and each have there pros and cons yet they compliment each other. the endings are so vastly different that you get the best of both worlds. in the end, i will read this book forever. when i'm sick, when it's rainy and i need an adventure, at the beach. *sorry this review is so shitty, ha! i just feel like i can't put into words how i feel about this book. maybe one day i'll be able to.

title: ['Origin (Lux, #4)', 'He Will be My Ruin']
cleaned_reviews: i'm wavering on how many stars i think origin should get, because it really could be between a 3 and a 4 for me, but it held my attention enough that i will give it a 4. for me the beginning of this was not interesting. i thought daemon immediately (view spoiler)[ giving himself up to daedalus was too predictable, and it wasn't interesting. (hide spoiler)] so for a little while i wasn't sure where it was going until the (view spoiler)[ origins were revealed. (hide spoiler)] now that i found to be super interesting. it was a great twist to the story, and it made daedalus even more creepy and intimidating. from then on it got better. there were still a lot of corny moments, and predictable moments. i'm not 100% happy with the end, the last few sentenced were kind of strange, but i liked the premise behind it. it's a good cliffhanger for the next book. 4 stars from me. looking forward to the next book, but i'm glad she'll be wrapping it up. to me the 5th book seems like it might be pushing it. actual rating: 3.5 he will be my ruin is among one of the few suspense/thriller novels that i have read, when you compare it to all the other novels i've digested throughout the years. when k.a. tucker announced the synopsis behind her newest novel, i was intrigued by the shift from her previous works. her first murder mystery! (that i know of.) i'm a big fan of her work, and recently even met her at an author event in chicago. no matter the plot, i would be bound and determined to read this. one of the reasons why i haven't read many suspense/thriller novels is because for the most part, they don't hold my attention. it sounds crazy, but the twists and turns easily become too much for me, and if i'm going to read about corrupt people and violence, it can just as easily come from the pages of a fantasy or sci-fi thank you very much. in any case, i dove into this head first without any of my usual reservations. i will start by saying that overall i liked the experience of reading he will be my ruin. tucker had me on a wild goose chase and my suspicions were all over the place. of course, this was by design, but all the same my heart was pounding in the last few chapters. with that being said, for the first half of this book i had to push my way through. it didn't feel like a chore, i just wasn't completely enamored with the story and the cast of characters. besides being a suspense/thriller, he will be my ruin is also tagged as a romance. i'm quite familiar with tucker's romance and so i was expecting something pretty typical, but boy was i wrong. i don't want to spoil anything for anyone, so i won't say too much. it was not what i expected, and i'm disappointed by that. i didn't find this to be quite as, er, sexy as her other novels. my let down is due 100% to my own prior expectations and predictions. i do applaud her for doing something out of the ordinary and there are plenty of readers who will love it. tucker managed to tackle quite a bit in this novel that was out of the ordinary. she's well-known for writing deeply complicated and flawed characters (also known as humans). no cardboard cutouts here, folks. how far would these characters go for the people they care about? to seek the truth? pretty far, apparently. and the result is a spiral into some pretty deep and dark things society regards as taboo: prostitution, depression, and prescription drug use. i think tucker did a fantastic job shining a light on the prostitution industry. it is too easy for us to sit on our high horses and look down on the men and women who sell their bodies and sex for money. we don't stop to think about what pushed them into this. instead we label them as whores, sluts, skanks. we ridicule them and we don't rub elbows with them willingly. tucker's portrayal of prostitution puts the reader inside the head of not just the woman doing the act, but the best friend who has to deal with the consequences after discovering her murdered friend's secret. i will say that i do not condone prostitution, and i especially do not condone the people who pay for it and perpetuate it's existence. but i am happy that tucker took this subject and did something good with it. she made us feel for the woman. i was not disgusted by her actions, i was sad for her and with her. tucker understands the importance of not belittling the women who choose to do this, while also letting the reader know that it is still not okay. it's precarious ground, and she handled it very well. i would not trust many authors to write on this subject and keep their heads above water. after hitting the halfway mark of this book, the story picked up considerably. we learned more about celine, the murdered woman, and followed maggie's journey at uncovering the truth. once it started moving at a faster clip, i enjoyed reading this more than i had been before. the twists towards the end certainly did lend to my overall enjoyment, for awhile there i was afraid i would be left disappointed. a pretty solid murder mystery. as always, i'm excited for what k.a. tucker will do next!

title: ['Never Knowing', 'We Are Called to Rise']
cleaned_reviews: i'm becoming a huge chevy stevens fan! never knowing was a book that kept me on the edge of my seat. i read all day long today, accomplishing nothing because i couldn't put it down. the story was absolutely chilling. can you imagine going on a hunt to find your biological parents and discovering your mother wants nothing to do with you because your birth was the result of an attack by a serial killer? i literally could not put this book down and the suspense had my foot moving a mile a minute. i did wonder why sara's adoptive father showed such animosity toward her and i'd hoped it would be resolved. i also wondered why this story was told through sessions with sara's therapist. this scenario made perfect sense in her last novel as the story was slowly revealed in still missing, but didn't seem necessary to this story. i still enjoyed it immensely and gave this novel five stars. go, chevy stevens! i highly recommend this book (and do not miss her other book, still missing!). this was a terribly sad and heartbreaking story, but it was incredibly well written. i enjoyed the setting in las vegas, portraying the city as a place where real people live and raise families. i loved bashkim's character and felt mcbride captured his voice so well in the wake of his experiences. i was also very taken with mcbride's writing when avis realized she was actually accepted by others in her life as a suburban mom and no longer felt like an imposter after her rough upbringing. all of the characters in this novel were compelling and i couldn't put the book down! that's the mark of a great book.

title: ["The Handmaid's Tale", 'Allegiant (Divergent, #3)']
cleaned_reviews: i've read a few horrors in my time, and this book is scarier than any of them simply because of how easily our own world could turn into a situation such as the one described by offred, a handmaid who is placed within a family because of her capacity to breed. this or similar is the world we could live in, if we stop valuing people's diversity; something that seems to be happening at a staggering rate in a variety of contexts in our current political contexts. in this book the details matter and there are a lot of them. this leads to some moments that are fairly explicit, both in terms of violence and sexuality. but it is because, not despite of this, that i feel this should be a necessary read to share with the mature young women in our lives, combined with in depth discussion of the things that somehow seem more possible in the world's current climate than less than they did twenty years ago. things like religion, sex, conformity, education, authority, government intervention, feminism, patriarchies... the list goes on. i recently read an article of atwood's reflecting on this book and she said "back in 1984 the main premise seemed--even to me--fairly outrageous. would i be able to persuade readers that the united states had suffered a coup that had transformed an erstwhile liberal democracy into a literal-minded theocratic dictatorship?" in 2017, with a simple-minded, authoritarian president holding the reins of government in washington, dc, and all manner of intolerant extremists in the wings, that premise no longer seems preposterous. atwood's prose, is impeccable. she writes with urgency, purpose, and humanity--and delivers an ending more brilliant and deliberate than i thought was coming. then finally in a post script, we zoom out to a place of academia, where the calm eye of history in review sees offred story as a blip, or an inconvenience as "she could have told us much about the workings of the gileadean empire, had she had the instincts of a reporter or a spy." offred's tale of captivity is reduced to how much information she gave about her male captor. how often do we do this already? looking at first hand accounts of atrocities that have happened in our own history with no empathy for the victim, but rather bemoaning the details we aren't able to glean in the name of research? how easy is it to forget the faces we even now see every night on the news, victims of atrocities being carried out in our own back yards? this novel is too powerful and relevant to dismiss because of the more unpleasant aspects portrayed within its pages. instead it is a startling prediction about the direction our lives could be taking. it challenged and startled me as i was reading it, and i suspect it will continue to do so in years to come. this last installment in the divergent series is a lot more political, helping us gain a view into why this dystopic world is the way it is. we once again see tris asserting herself as an independent and strong woman, while it is four, the male lead, who is the one lead astray by his emotions as an interesting twist. it does move a little slower than the others, but this again serves the aforementioned purpose of giving us a bit of perspective and letting us into the history of the compound. and the ending... well... i can't say i didn't suspect, but i was still surprised when ti actually happened. read it, you'll see.

title: ['The Book of the Unnamed Midwife (The Road to Nowhere #1)', 'Uprooted']
cleaned_reviews: ** spoiler alert ** this one grew on me slowly. it starts out kind of weak with a few random side characters who end up going nowhere. about halfway through, it hits its stride when the protagonist leaves the grim streets of la and stumbles upon a group of mormons in utah, where things really start to get interesting. the beginning is like 28 days later because protagonist wakes up after recovering from a sickness and finds the world is ending. this sickness kills 98% of men and an even greater percentage of women. even worse, every pregnant woman dies. i hated this because it was so inconsistent and poorly explained! some of the women have miscarriage after miscarriage. the majority of them carry seemingly healthy babies to term and then hemorrhage out at birth. the babies always die too. some real diseases do affect fertility. zika causes birth defects, so does german measles; mumps can cause men to become infertile; i'm sure there are many more examples. but this disease just really, really didn't seem realistic to me. how is it spread? does it just lie dormant until birth? if so, what about giving birth brings it on--a hormone or something? the way the babies and women die sounds most similar to the rh factor, but that's genetic, not viral. women who have survived the disease and women who have never contracted it end up losing their babies in exactly the same way. that irritated me the most. someone who survived the fever would gain a natural immunity. provided enough time had passed between the illness and the pregnancy, it wouldn't make any sense for there to be a relapse right at birth. and why does the same thing happen to women who never got sick in the first place? if they're immune going in, or somehow avoided exposure, you'd think they'd be the only ones who could still get pregnant. natural selection ensures that diseases that rip through a population quickly and fatally don't survive past that first wave--they can't, because they don't have new people to spread to. but that's exactly what this disease does. the author also throws in some weird and seemingly random hints here and there about the nature of the fever. she refers to the bloody mess that happens when a woman gives birth in the post-fever world, and seems to imply that there's more... tearing and ripping, somehow? like these are all twilight-esque demon babies? i just. don't. buy it. arrrghh. lots of books have used the "there's no more babies" apocalypse. children of men and the handmaid's tale are the most obvious examples. also, there are so many zombie dystopias and ones about others diseases, like my most recent favorite, station eleven. i'm willing to buy the premise in general because diseases are scary, and i can suspend my disbelief for the sake of artistic expression. but what i really need is internal logic, and this book just doesn't have it. all the other examples i've given have clear parameters about what the disease does and doesn't do, or similarity to real diseases. they theorize about what caused the illness and how it's spread in a way that makes sense. here, it seems random and nonsensical, and it's just too clearly a plot device used to get at the themes of gender and power that the author really wants to talk about. on that note, i also don't think the majority of men would just start raping and literally buying and selling female slaves as soon as the dust of the apocalypse has cleared, shortage of women be damned. the book does include some good men, but also kind of implies that most men are basically just one world-ending virus away from becoming slavers and rapist monsters. call me naive, but i do have a little more faith in humanity than that. finally, the protagonist is a prickly narrator and hard to get to know. i liked her ballsiness, adaptability, and grit. i liked her sarcasm. but, aside from the tiniest hints about her background, she's a blank slate. and her diary entries were annoying, totally hard to read and punctuated with "=" signs for some reason. so why does it have 4 stars despite that? it kept me reading. it has some cool modern shoutouts to lgbtq people and forms of relationships other than monogamy, but it reads more like a good old fashioned western adventure than sci-fi dystopia. the book this reminded me most of is actually world war z. both books are terse and to-the-point. there isn't much time wasted on sentimentality, or even philosophy--it's about survival. and both books create a world i want to read more about. i don't know about this book, guys. i've read a lot of great books, but i can't remember the last time i read one that had me reading addictively, obsessively, in every spare moment; pining for it when i couldn't sit down and read it all in one gulp. all i knew before starting it was, "it's a retelling of 'beauty and the beast'," which was enough to make me want to read it; i love fairy tales and reinterpretations. but i hesitated to check it out from the library and then hesitated to start it. my issue with "beauty" has always been the icky stockholm syndrome at the heart of its "love" story. every retelling, and the original tale, start by necessity on troubling footing--how can true, fairy-tale love develop from keeping someone prisoner, without that love being corrupted at its core? but upon starting uprooted, i was spellbound; naomi novik neatly sidestepped the problematic elements of the original tale and wove it into something beautiful instead. this is because her "beauty," agnieszka, does not have physical beauty (or a beautiful name). what she has, instead, is power, and agency. princesses in other stories gather their power slowly, through many trials (wooing a beast who is keeping you prisoner, for instance), or are given it by a fairy godmother. they always have that power only until they end up in love with a prince, at which point it becomes useless to them; it's a given that they won't need it any longer. agnieszka, on the other hand, stumbles upon her power and just does stuff with it, as wild as a lightning bolt. how can this still be a "beauty and the beast" story? you'll have to read it to find out. that's far from all that i loved about this book, though. it's fast-paced--novik paced the story so that as soon as one trial is completed, a new one starts, and each has been caused by the one before it, like falling dominoes. the characterization of magic is rich and scary and wonderful. there are only, like, 1.5 sex scenes, but they're perfectly placed within the story and well written (yay for enthusiastic consent!). the whole thing had a feeling, for me, that was greater than the sum of its parts. i included the miyazaki gifs because it reminded me of those movies. you could summarize any one of them--a wizard, a house on stilts, a fire; a forest, a princess, a warrior; a girl who enters an alternate universe of witches and dragons and spirits--and it would only hint at the beautiful, heartbreaking, almost spiritual vibe of those movies. i'm sure you could find complaints about the book, but i was so swept up in the story, i refused to look for them. you know a book is really, really, really good when you feel the sadness that it's over as a physical ache in your chest. 10/10, would read again. ***edit based on 2017 re-read - spoilers ahead*** you know what? this time, i did see the flaws. although fast-paced in the sense that action keeps happening, the book is actually slow too. it could have used some editing--especially during the part where agnieszka is in the capital getting invited to all the parties. boring! also, i don't buy the whole central conceit of the book. these villagers have just been putting up with their lord abducting a random girl every 10 years? and then when she comes back completely different they don't have any questions? the huh? also, the love story. eh. meh. he's old and weird; she's young and clumsy... oh my god is this twilight. no, no, it's all good, it's not twilight... even if it is uncomfortably twilight-ish. there are some key differences. mostly: they're not obsessed with each other, he's not sparkly, he doesn't watch her while she's sleeping, losing her virginity isn't this weird uncomfortable rape-y event, she doesn't have to choose between him and literally everyone else in her life, and she doesn't lose her mind every time she's near him or throw herself in harm's way because of him. despite the fact that all of their conversations are basically him criticizing her and despite the massive age difference, which i'm sure some people rightly find problematic, i totally loved their relationship. they learn from each other and grow together and omg so cute. basically guys: my mind sees the flaws; my heart loves the book. some things can't be helped.

cleaned_reviews: *warning - review contains mild spoilers* pretty girl 13 is not a fun and light read, instead its one gritty and unsettling physiological thriller that deals with some very tough issues. angie disappeared while on a camping trip with the girl scouts when she was thirteen years old. now, three years later she shows up at her parent's house with no memory of how she got there, where she's been or who she's been with. angie is taken to the hospital for a physical examination. after the exam the doctor tells her parents that not only has she been physical abused but she has been sexually abused as well. when angie goes to a psychologist to try and remember what happened, she learns that she has what is called dissociative identity disorder (did), which basically means multiple personalities. in angie's case her mind created alternative personalities (alters) in order to help her deal with the things she was going through while angie remained dormant. this is the first book that i have read that deals with multiple personalities and i was amazed how different each alter was. angie is a very complex character to say the least. in her mind she is still thirteen years old but in reality she is a sixteen year old girl that has suffered for the past three years. angie is a lot stronger than she realizes, instead of hiding she faces her alters head on so she can try to get her life back. overall, pretty girl 13 isn't a light read but it was a fast one. this book is raw, emotional and so jam-packed with suspense and mystery that it will keep you flipping the pages wondering what will happen next. i honestly wasn't expecting to love this book as much as i did; i will definitely be reading more by this author. find this review at http://christysbookaddiction.blogspot... this review was originally posted on novel inkwow, i'm just speechless right now. i admit that i've loved pretty much all of coho's books and she has now became an auto buy author for me so i pretty much figured that i would like it, but this book, it blew me away. so fair warning, this review may be a rambling mess. lily is a character that was very easy for me to connect with, she was smart, strong and by the end of this book, i really admired her and her courage. she has been through so much and she could have easily let her circumstances destroy her and everything she had came to believe in, but she stood strong and she had faith in herself and i really loved that about her. i also really loved how this book alternated between present and the past (in the form of lily's old journal entries). i really think it added something extra to the story and it made me understand lily better. we get to see a glimpse of the things she had to witness and endure in her past. to me, this let me understand and connect with lily better in the present. lily's story isn't an easy one to read, there are a lot of tough subjects in this book and i'm sure this book won't be for everyone. however, coho handles these tough subjects very well and i feel like the overall message of the book is so important. i can't go into details due to spoilers but let me just say that i was happy with the way things ended. it ends with us is an heartbreaking, emotional rollercoaster that i did not want to get off. lily's story, while at times was hard to read, is a very important book to read.

what is up with aries being on the radar of the baggers? so many questions that i need book three. i received this book via netgalley to give an honest review. very good mystery book. you have the main character tracy who has been obsessed with wanting to find out what happened to her sister sarah twenty years ago. she is so involved with it that her relationships with others have gone down the drain, her main focus on anything is sarah. tracy is a detective and even though she does her job on her free time it is all about looking over the case files, figuring out if witnesses are telling the truth and questioning the man convicted of killing her sister edmund house. edmund seems to be the perfect fit for killing sarah especially since he almost murdered one girl who he raped, so this should be a slam dunk, open shut case. for tracy things just don't seem to pan out when she ends up getting the call that her sister has been found in a grave tracy is more than determined to find out the truth behind what happened to her. is this the closure she needs? or will she even get the answers? we read through the trial that edmond receives, we find out what secrets that certain people are trying to hide and when it all comes together you can understand even if you don't agree why it was done. i enjoyed how we went between what happened twenty years ago via tracy's p.o.v. to the present and then at the end to sarah's p.o.v., i think the author did a great job with that. the characters were well written and i do wonder if tracy and dan (the lawyer but friend) will have a romance going on. it seems to hint around but it never is definite! the short chapters made it easier to read and get through rather quickly which i enjoyed. i do like long chapters but sometimes it is just nice to have chapters that are shorter. i would love to write more but i don't want to give away spoilers at all. overall very enjoyable once i started i couldn't put it down at all. if you like thrillers or mysteries then this is one you should read.

title: ['Thoughtless (Thoughtless, #1)']
cleaned_reviews: it was so wrong...yet it was so right. 3.5 - 4 stars at times i loved this book, and at times i hated it. kiera had me rating it at 3.5 stars, kellan however, had me bumping it up to 4 stars (after he got over being a complete arsehole) so i'm stuck in the middle somewhere. i found myself saying over and over again "no, stop doing that, you are both horribly hurting each other. stop being stupid." kiera, for me, was easily dislikeable at first; being uptight and slightly prudish which personally i don't like in a leading female. however, as the story progressed i found myself torn between hating what she was doing and feeling incredibly sorry for her having to make such an awful decision. in one corner she had denny; her amazing boyfriend. and in the other she had kellan; sexy, alluring and obviously madly in love with her. let's face it, cheating on denny was just so horribly wrong, but ignoring her true feelings and desire for kellan would have been harder and in hindsight maybe even more wrong. so, do i blame kiera?...no. should she have ended it with denny first?...yes, of course she should have. but, remember this is a fictional story based on real life possibilities, and remember in the fictional world we do tend to allow ourselves to cheer for what we wouldn't normally in real life...i guess that's one of the things i love about a good of book; detaching myself from reality and not feeling guilty about it. i did really enjoy this book in the end. it was well written and took me on an emotional roller coaster. while reading this book i not only fell in love with kellan, but also a good cup of coffee again. mmmm, looking forward to picking up effortless next.

cleaned_reviews: i'm 31 years old, and this is my first stephen king novel. i know, shame. especially since people have been telling me to read it for about a decade. the gunslinger is the first volume in the dark tower saga and is now found as a novel, but it is actually a collection of novellas and short stories originally published between 1979 and 1981. it is a remarkably fast read, probably because it was originally written for literary magazines, and each of its five parts stands alone to some extent, although they clearly follow. it is quite probably that the same could be said for the rest of the dark tower, but i'll find out for sure when i get there. i will freely admit that my impetus to read this now is the impending dark tower film, which is scheduled for release 30 days from this writing. that being said, the gunslinger was not what i was expecting in the best possible meaning of that phrase. the book opens with the enigmatic gunslinger. "the man in black fled across the desert, and the gunslinger followed." from this opening line, which i hear quoted almost as often as that of a wrinkle in time, the gunslinger develops into something which i never thought i would find in stephen king, a knight in the chivalric tradition of king arthur, siegfried, and roland, nephew of charlemagne. when i was an undergrad, we read selections from le morte d'arthur: king arthur and the legends of the round table in my medieval literature course, and a lot of that content came roaring back on this read. the gunslinger is a very american idea of a knight, the heroic figure of the old west, standing against bandits, indians, and unscrupulous land holders and businessmen, and mr king has melded the two archetypes beautifully. the gunslingers are very recognizable as knights as well as cowboys, and i would go so far as to say that, in their heyday, they must have followed the laws of chivalry scrupulously. in case you don't know what those are, here ya go. http://www.nobility.org/2011/05/09/th... in keeping with the religious nature of chivalry, (that's right, it's not just holding doors for ladies, see link) i found the gunslinger to be suffused with the sense of the divine. again, not really something i was expecting from mr king, but a pleasant surprise. it comes out in the course of the narrative that the gunslinger himself may be the only living person who has ever seen a bible and the implication is that part of his mission is to defend the truth of the scriptures. in addition to this, there are certain parallels in the gunslinger's backstory with the arthurian legends which firmly ground him as a knight of a camelot type society. the novel reminded me quite a bit of the vampire hunter d novels by hideyuki kikuchi, or i should say that the d novels kind of reminded me of this as vampire hunter d was published several years later. both seem to take place in the far future of our world where occasional artifacts of our time crop up. in addition, both the gunslinger and d travel across the frontiers of their respective worlds seeking a final confrontation. as a kind of an aside, i found that the gunslinger was super successful at portraying a chivalrous knight, even as the pursuit of his quarry leads him to moral quandry and assault on his nobility. this was portrayed much better than i think any king arthur film of the last 10 or 15 years, and i think it might be kind of fun to try and capture the magic of the dark tower's world in an arthur movie. either that, or i find the idea of lancelot, gawain, geharis, percival, and tristan running around with six guns hilarious. to sum up, i am extremely excited to read the rest of the dark tower and i'm hoping to finish it before the movie comes out. mr king has stated that the dark tower was inspired by childe roland to the dark tower came by robert browning. while this is a victorian poem, it solidly draws from the chivalrous tradition and the first volume of the dark tower is unmistakably cut from the same cloth as the song of roland and king arthur. my only hope is that it carries through the rest.

title: ['The Association of Small Bombs']
cleaned_reviews: a crisp, interesting look at terrorism and its effects on the victims and the perpetrators. the interesting part about the book is how it is structured--it starts with the bomb and only afterwards do we see the shattered remnants of people's lives. mahajan's prose hammers in the theme of being like the bomb on multiple levels (at times this can get a little heavy-handed, but for the most part, is really heartbreakingly clever). the story starts with three boys--the khurana brothers and their muslim best friend, mansoor--going to pick up the khuranas' television at the electronics repair stand. the brothers perish in the blast, but mansoor survives the blast, running away in the confusion, sustaining a serious wrist injury that comes back to haunt him in adulthood. we see the khuranas cope in their own way, and how the ahmeds deal with the blast. mansoor eventually studies abroad in the us and returns to india once his wrists start acting up again, and the memories still haunt the two families. for mansoor's part, he tries to get involved in an activist group challenging harmful attitudes against muslims and advocating rights for suspected terrorists. there he meets ayub, a young man of a more humble background who initially is the most vocal advocate for nonviolent resistance. but human emotions get the better of ayub, who becomes involved in a seedy world, and brings those issues out into the open. i really enjoyed this book, and i can see why it's getting rave reviews. i'd rate this a 4.5 (a half star off because i think the ending is a little rushed). mahajan is a gifted writer, and i hope to read more of his future works (and now i'm off to hunt for his previous novel).

rating: 4.25* of five the publisher says: one of beirut's most celebrated voices, rabih alameddine follows his international bestseller, the hakawati, with a heartrending novel that celebrates the singular life of an obsessive introvert, revealing beirut's beauties and horrors along the way. aaliya sohbi lives alone in her beirut apartment, surrounded by stockpiles of books. godless, fatherless, divorced, and childless, aaliya is her family's "unnecessary appendage." every year, she translates a new favorite book into arabic, then stows it away. the thirty-seven books that aaliya has translated have never been read--by anyone. after overhearing her neighbors, "the three witches," discussing her too-white hair, aaliya accidentally dyes her hair too blue. in this breathtaking portrait of a reclusive woman's late-life crisis, readers follow aaliya's digressive mind as it ricochets across visions of past and present beirut. insightful musings on literature, philosophy, and art are invaded by memories of the lebanese civil war and aaliya's volatile past. as she tries to overcome her aging body and spontaneous emotional upwellings, aaliya is faced with an unthinkable disaster that threatens to shatter the little life she has left. a love letter to literature and its power to define who we are, the gifted rabih alameddine has given us a nuanced rendering of a single woman's reclusive life in the middle east. my review: the doubleday uk meme, a book a day for july 2014, is the goad i'm using to get through my snit-based unwritten reviews. today's prompt is to discuss your favorite novel in translation. so far this year, this is my hands-down favorite novel translated from the furrin. **correction** the novel was written in english, but it's so beautiful i don't want to take it down! what does it mean to be invisible? if you choose not to interact with the world, become a recluse, divest yourself of close relationships and divorce yourself from the life of the boudoir, and seal yourself away in a capsule formed of books and words, you are a freak. aaliya's neighbors think she's a ruined woman. aaliya's customers at the bookstore she works at, intellectuals all, don't notice her enough to form an opinion, and her family (absent the dearest companion of her life, her *true* family, a departed friend) hasn't given her much attention at all. she lives in beirut, that once-fabulous once-gorgeous ruin on the mediterranean, an early victim of the endless idiotic religious wars of the region. aaliya represents beirut's decline from a world-class cultural center to a shuttered mass of broken buildings holding wary, angry people. aaliya is an angry woman, or at least i see her as such, and has walled herself in to avoid the nasty consequences of being angry amid armed and angry men. she would not be isolated if beirut wasn't what it is, i think, because she is a reflection of the energy of that wounded and dying place. she preserves her sanity by translating her beloved books, the beauties of which she renders into the sinuous sonorous rhythms of arabic. and then, like she does with her self, she packages them up and puts them away. they are safe. they are invisible. this is tragic. this is a sin. a woman, a mere woman, cannot be her full self; a book, a useless object, cannot spread its beauties for fear that it will not be appreciated or will be used as a weapon by the religious idiots. and this is the reason i give this book over four stars. alameddine has created a literary person's most deeply felt example of why the world appears to be headed directly for the bottom of the septic tank: aaliya reads and thinks on and renders the majesty and magic of words into the language of her people, and then cannot, will not, dare not allow them out of her keeping. this book should have made me feel claustrophobic. it appears to be a scream from within the coffin that anti-intellectual religious idiots are all but nailing shut around the world. (creation science?! really?!) instead i felt...uplifted in a curious way, heartened, encouraged. alameddine sees it too! he created this most marginal of marginal beings, the unmarried childless woman intellectual in an islamic society, and set her to singing. aaliya sings her thoughts, sings her translations, warbles her precious quotes to herself, her best and only audience. she makes beauty from beauty as she sits and rots in the cesspool of gawd. i don't know if this is a cautionary tale, an elegy, or the quietest jeremiad of all time. i do know that i can't, and don't wish to, forget aaliya. this work is licensed under a creative commons attribution-noncommercial-sharealike 3.0 unported license.

on her way home with her mother, their car crashed and libby was presumed dead. this is a terrible turning point in may's life. not only has she just lost her best friend, but her parents divorce shortly afterwards. three years later, may is visiting her father when she sees a sticker in a window for princess x. immediately she begins hoping that maybe libby didn't die in the car accident. maybe she's still alive after all. as may starts to follow the trail of princess x, she realizes that what happened in the past is not quite how she remembers. princess x started out really bittersweet. you immediately feel bad for may and her loss. the heartache she still feels three years later from losing one of the most important people in her life. then, may finds princess x and the story turns into a gooniesesque search for treasure at the end of the trail (so to speak). i loved the sense of adventure. since libby's death, may kind of just got by. she's made new friends, despite always having been shy, but none as significant as libby. but with the discovery of the princess and what that might mean in the end, you see may really coming alive. i liked that princess x was solely focused on the friendship between libby and may and didn't try to include any kind of romantic entanglement (as if may needed to add anything else to think about while she's searching for clues, right?) i appreciated the addition of the pincess x artwork within the story. it helped me to understand what may was looking at because, obviously, i got to visually see it too. kind of pulls the reader in, but past a certain point in the story, it kind of drops off but i kept expecting to turn the page and see another panel. i understand that the artwork coincided with what may found as she searched online for the princess x story, but i almost feel like the book itself was too hyped up with being labeled a kind of hybrid graphic novel, but to me, didn't really turn out that way. still, it was a pretty good read. 3.5 bay of sighs picks up right where stars of fortune left off. our six guardians found the fire star and now all signs point to the island of capri as being where they will be able to find the next star (the water star). so sawyer, with his handy compass, transports everyone. again, the guardians make preparations to protect the house they're staying at from attack. they know it's only a matter of time before nerezza finds them. this time, sasha has predicted nerezza will pull someone else in to aid her in her quest to obtain the stars from the guardians. it's clear that with this second book the romance will center around traveler sawyer and mermaid annika, and as the search progresses it's clear that annika, being a mermaid will be essential in locating and finding this star as it apparent she's the only one who can hear the bay of sighs. this was kind of a difficult book to rate. i love nora roberts, i really do. but as i think of how to review this book, there are so many glaringly obvious holes in the story, or just things that irked me. but for everything i found unsatisfying, the story as a whole entertained and kept my attention. i'll say that i liked bay of sighs more than the first book. in the first book there was just too much coincidence in the way all the guardians came together "hey you happen to be staying at the same hotel as me and we're both looking for these long-lost legendary stars. cool." since characters and story is established already, i was happy to leave all the coincidence behind. there are still a few moments where things seem a bit too easy, but these moments didn't overwhelm the story. i really liked how roberts links the three goddesses who originally created the stars with our three female guardians. i don't know if this was done in start of fortune, if so i missed it, but i caught it this go around, and i like that connection. annika, being one half of our focus in this book, was a great character. she comes from a completely different world than our other guardians in that she's a mermaid. i loved her sweetness and her sometimes-naivete, and never once did it come off as hokey. all of her interactions with other characters and actions come across as very genuine instead of gimmicky. i also really liked continuing to get to know more about our first couple sasha and bran. sasha mainly because her powers as a seer are still growing. obviously since our characters share such close quarters to completely block the previous couple out would be silly, but i like that the characters we've already seen still continue to surprise and grow even when they're not the main focus of the story. the same goes for riley and doyle who, as it's easy to guess at this point, are our next couple up. another thing done really well in the book is the scenery. i descriptions of the villa where our guardians take up residence, that of the sea, sasha's paintings, the search for the star, etc. are presented very vividly. really makes me want to take a vacation now! something that didn't work well here is the addition of another "baddie". or more specifically the lack of character building for said "baddie". i want to feel more for my characters - whether good or bad - so i want some emotion. i felt like the addition of another foil to the guardians' search for the stars didn't have as big of an impact as it could have because the character was so underdeveloped. now, maybe i'll be singing a different tune come the third book, but as of now, it feels just kind of meh. also, it's pretty easy to spot who our next, and last, couple will be in this trilogy. however, i don't feel like there's been much, or enough, build up for their impending relationship. i want a little bit more tension between my potential couples. i want to feel their chemistry jump off the page book after book until their own book comes. roberts did a great job with this for her characters branna and fin from the cousins o'dwyer trilogy, who are featured in blood magick. again, this may be a feeling that changes for me as the final book is released. these are just my thoughts up to and including this book. overall, nora roberts pretty much always delivers in the entertainment department. her stories are always an escape for me, and bay of sighs is no different. i'm definitely looking forward cleaned_reviews: rating: 3.5 stars i read my first jennifer echols book, forget you, a few years ago, and although i enjoyed it, it failed to "wow" me in any manner. perhaps that's why i haven't read anything else by echols till now. going too far was also just as enjoyable, if not more, than forget you, yet the way in which its subject matter was tackled managed to utterly impress me. meg refuses to be tied down to anything - her home, her family, and literally even handcuffs, seat belts and locked cars. john refuses to leave anything behind - the place where he grew up, his police job, and literally his haunting memories. when meg is caught trespassing a bridge one night, all officer after wants to do is teach her a lesson. little does he realize that she may teach him a few lessons about his own life too... going too far seems like your usual light, contemporary romance read. in many ways it is. the banter between meg and john is witty and entertaining, their romance is beautifully written and slow to grow, and - my favorite - meg doesn't even realize that she's truly in love with him until nearly the end of the novel. yet, going too far manages to cover some very serious subject matter. both meg and john have hidden pasts and their inability to move on past them causes them misery and pain. throughout the novel, meg challenges john to move on past his grief just as john challenges meg to embrace the life she was given. it is impossible to describe their interactions without giving away too much of the plot, but rest assured that it is utterly compelling, slow moving, and believable. i loved the pacing of this book and the way everything came together was realistic and a perfect fit. i have very few qualms with this book, the major one being the rushed ending. to me, it felt as if meg and john's "curing" or moving on from their pasts happened in the span of a day or even a night. it was the only aspect of the book in which the pacing, which i loved, was off. i wish echols had extended the novel just a little bit more so that we could see how these characters were coping with their lives after their past tragedies. either than that, the only other area that some readers might find problematic is the dialogue. it is definitely very flirty at times and meg's character can even be said to be portrayed as slutty very often. yet, what i loved about echols' writing was that even though meg wore flimsy clothes and showed off her cleavage, she herself never came off as being a slut and the reader never felt that way either. i thought it was extremely clever and unique to portray the main character in such a light. going too far is really a hard book to review. it looks deceptively like a typical contemporary romance - and the romance was amazingly written mind you - but its so much deeper, tragic, and important than that. i thoroughly enjoyed reading this novel and i'm definitely more inclined to check out echols' other novels after seeing how superbly she wrote this one! :)

cleaned_reviews: a gay country song once more, lucy lennox takes an often used trope and gives it some fresh life. jude is a country singer and has stayed in the closet, mostly for that reason. also because he was shattered by a past lover. derek has been jude's bodyguard for six months. he's also gay but is so far in the closet, he's with the dust bunnies. mostly because he has a homophobic family and he was in the marines, where he wasn't comfortable being out, either. when he and jude finally get together, the catalyst is the old boyfriend, who seems too eager to spend sometime with jude. there's also a drunken stalker and a few incidents making derek into a live-in bodyguard. they start as friends with bennies of course and the sex is scorching in the first half. if it had stayed at that level and followed a cleaner plot line, it might have even made five stars. alas, the book had some issues, including being a little too long, with too many attempts at creating suspense over threats and blackmail. there was a lot of detail that seemed to be headed for misleading the reader for a surprise finish. well, it was a surprise but only because all the detail fizzled out into nothing. it was replaced by some relationship drama, which was a bit too cliche as well. it did have some of the banter and humor of the prior books but i could do without the inappropriate old ladies. yuck. not a bad book by any means, it just needed more focus and tying up the plot threads more neatly. it's still in the same vein as the first two of the series; romance, erotica, low-level drama and minor angst. satisfying as a lighter read and sexy entertainment. i was utterly enthralled sci-fi stories were my favorite reading choice for a very long time starting in high school. i devoured heinlein, clarke and asimov, among others. so, of course i had to read this when i saw it and i'm so glad i did. this is not an ordinary romance, and for the majority of the book, our mc's are connected only by voice. curt, now 40, is the mission commander of the hermes 1. he's nasa's bad-boy: hot-tempered, hard-drinking, brash and an unapologetic straight talker. he was a wunderkind and the youngest astronaut to go into space. patrick is a 27 yr old engineer, brought in to handle communications through the system he developed, between houston and the spacecraft. he monitors information and talks with crew members frequently. he's that voice you hear on news reports, waking the crew and piping in music. patrick can see curt on monitors, but curt can only hear him. patrick can tell when bp and heart rates show curt is awake during sleep schedules and they begin to converse, as it's also how the crew stays connected with "home". this is how their romance begins, through exchanges of information, both personal and professional. their exchanges range from describing cheeseburgers and take-out orders from space, to the feelings they share about star-gazing and the lure of space. i wasn't sure if i was going to like a day by day narrative, but kay simone did a great job of keeping it flowing and interesting. there's a news interview interspersed through part of it, detailing how curt was the catalyst that revived nasa's manned space program, after the 2012 budget cuts. i do think the political reasons were oversimplified here (but that's just me). there are very thinly veiled celebrity names used in the interviews, that i thought were quite amusing. the premise is highly improbable but i loved that the crew was so diverse. patrick had come out as bisexual in the 90's, two members are a lesbian couple, one of whom is trans, the pilot is female and pansexual and there's one token straight guy! there's almost no sex in this book and the couple doesn't even meet until about 75%. but their first kiss is just awesome! there isn't a great deal of technical jargon but much of the story does include activities on the ship, of the crew and ground crew. mostly though, it's about people and the strange intimacy that develops between the crew members themselves and between them and those on the ground, who they depend upon to get them there and back. there are wonderful secondary characters and their friendships and support develop beautifully. i didn't buy the rather quick way they both decided they loved each other. this was after only two weeks, although they didn't say it to each other. i could accept a strong connection and attraction through conversation alone but "love" was too much to believe. it was pretty damned romantic though. this was not technically perfect writing and it had some editing issues. it did not detract at all from the story as far as i was concerned. it was a little long but was just thoroughly enjoyable and fascinating with very much an hea!

title: ['The Night Gwen Stacy Died']
cleaned_reviews: sarah bruni's "the night gwen stacy died" is a powerful coming of age novel and love story between 17 year old sheila gower and a taxi driver in his 20s who calls himself peter parker. both feel trapped in their small nebraska town. sheila plans to move to france, to eat croissants and speak french and be sophisticated and awesome and totally unlike her high school self. her parents don't understand her (of course) and her french teacher tries to caution her that france-the-reality is a lot different from france-the-cultural-icon, and warns her that running away doesn't solve anything. enter peter parker, with a gun, at the gas station she works at. they empty the till and fake her kidnapping, heading out to chicago in pursuit of a horrific dream he's convinced he can prevent. bruni does a fantastic job covering what it's like to be a teen girl in a small town, to want something more, to not fit in. she also does an incredible job depicting chicago. she mixes a very grounded real-feeling story with fantastic elements (dreams that come true, coyotes invading the city on some secret mission of their own). sheila and peter are both searching for something both within and without themselves, and bruni takes us on a wonderful journey.

title: ['We Have Always Lived in the Castle']
cleaned_reviews: we have always lived in the castle was such a surprising read for me. i had heard great things about this short novel and for some reason, i was just drawn to it from the beginning. it was one of those novels i just had to read sooner rather than later despite knowing very little about it. i am so glad i picked it up and as it was my first read of 2016, if it is any indication of my reading year to come, i am certainly in for a great year. my favorite thing about we have always lived in the castle, was unsurprisingly, mary katherine - also referred to as merricat in the novel. merricat's innocent yet harrowingly dark and sometimes shockingly violent narrative voice really set the tone for the novel. her feelings and thoughts were so strong that you couldn't help but be affected by them when reading. merricat's narration made the atmosphere of this novel come alive and really made this novel haunting. despite having guessed the 'twist' early on, i still loved every moment of this novel and would highly recommend it.

title: ['Civil War: A Marvel Comics Event']
cleaned_reviews: when i set out to read the civil war comic event, i hadn't realized it was so big. i wanted to read more than just the central story, but there was no way i was reading everything. had to pick and choose. in the end, i'm glad i decided to read the event and not just mark millar's central conflict. the big, epic scope lends itself well to the main story, especially the front line, spider-man, and captain america comics. i enjoyed mark millar's civil war book. there's some cool action, interesting twists, and really good art. i guess i'll never know if it works as well without the tie-ins, but as one big package it's highly enjoyable. the concept of a registration act leading to civil war amongst the costumed ranks is a cool idea for marvel to do, and they handled the event with style. i liked that it was a more political marvel story, sometimes with knowing nods to events in our history, now played out with capes and masks. and you know, seeing heroes fight each other is cool because it gives fans a bit of something new, instead of just having them beat up on doctor doom all the time. i enjoyed the event and millar's central story really works to hold it all together. i do think this particular story could've come to a more satisfying conclusion, though. while the final moments do hit home the ideas central to the story, it's still a bit of a letdown. like, it was all building to that? still, the comic does forever alter the marvel universe, so maybe i shouldn't be surprised that they limited the death toll in the final battle and pulled some punches. these are the heroes, after all. but overall, i enjoyed myself. i haven't read this many marvel comics in years. it was fun. with the marvel cinematic universe heading in the direction of civil war, i'll be curious to see how much has been altered and how much remains the same.

title: ['The Ship Beyond Time (The Girl From Everywhere, #2)']
cleaned_reviews: the good: i just love the whole premise of this series. time-traveling ships? existential questions? complex characters? it's so unique and i'm eating it right up. i love nix's character because she's so grumpy and serious but damn can you root for her! and kashmir . . . just, more kashmir, always. characters surprised me in many ways in this book and i loved the deep ethical and existential questions that were brought up without it becoming a total drag. i wish more people read these book because there's so much to talk about! the bad: perhaps this is a side-effect of my reading experience (i couldn't sit and read through the way i wanted to), but it felt very fragmented right until the end. lots of threads and plot points that seemed a bit confusing. it all came together in the end, but it was a bit tough to follow at times and made the reading just a little frustrating. the supporting cast of the crew wasn't as prominent in this book as in the last, and i kind of missed them, though i understand the need to reduce their role. some characters didn't feel totally fulfilled, like gwen, but there was enough going on that it didn't bother me too much. representation: this is an #ownvoices book, and representation is really well done. the main character is biracial and much of the supporting cast are poc, as well. the villains are white. this book also approaches mental illness and addiction with care and nuance, just as the first book in the series did. there's one lesbian character who was also present in the first book, though she had a slightly reduced role in this book. i wish more fantasy books were as well-represented as this series is! favorite line: "my love is a curse, kashmir!" "i'd rather be cursed with it than damned without it." rating: 4/5!

cleaned_reviews: i love everything mariana zapata writes, but this one was so amazing. i loved it from beginning to end. her writing is addictive and you can't help falling in love with all her characters. iris was an amazing character, his innocence was refreshing and funny. dex is a sexy tattooed bad boy who has his world rocked when iris comes to work for him. they were a great match. this book is a lot sexier, funnier, and steamier than her other books. set in texas behind the doors of a tattoo parlor and a close knit family of mc members, this book had all the things i love to read about, including mariana's infamous slow burn romance that builds between her main characters. under locke is just amazing. acutal rating 4.5 i read this book in one day and i loved it. i absolutely loved it and works fail to describe how this book made me feel. i am at a loss for words. it had me feeling so many emotions. this book has so much depth. even though when i really thought about it, this book a sorta instalove feel, it pretty much has you forgetting that's what actually happening. why? because olly makes maddy want to live. maddy suffers from skid and is unable to leave her house. she lives through her books and by spying on the people in her neighborhood through her window. that is until olly moves in and makes her think about all the things she could do in the outside world with him. maddy was content to live out her existence inside her home until she started talking to olly. she wanted to experience normal teenage things, like kissing, touching, and knowing what the ocean feels like. i wanted that for her so much. olly was such a sweet boy and was understanding of her sickness. but this book is much for than both these things combined. i really loved this book and it has a very unexpected turn that will have your head spinning. there is so much to love about this book. it just gives me all the feels and i would throw this book on any person who would dare admit they have never read it. it that good. i'm so happy i finally read it because its such a beautiful story with lovable characters. i want to read it all over again. i am always blown away at how amazing colleen hoover is as a writer. the stories that shape and form in her head are simply beautiful. i love how her books make you think and reexamine how you view your way of thinking and views. her characters have so much depth and carry their own painful pasts. their flaws make them human and their story stays with you for a long time. i will confess that i don't fall in love with colleen hoover books like others do. i definitely enjoy them and will continue to run out and read her books. but the thing that makes her love her as a author that will always have me picking up her books are the life lessons in her books. the writing is absolutely beautiful and i seriously fall in love with her books. its no different when it comes to owen and auburn.

understand, some marking scenes i just adored, most marking scenes, words, gesticulations and gnomes that left me hugely amused. i did find myself left with issues relating to eddie's story arc, with his friends reactions to his choices, but that was a small rile-ment in a story that i loved for it's descriptions of food, world of comic-detail (comic as in comic, comic as in hilarious- la!), characters who were there for each other in a friendship pact that i admired and loved, and for the tale of australia in the apocolypse. i didn't expect to love legend, but- to cut a rather long story involving my love of dystopian to my inability to find dystopian novels i felt like i hadn't read before- i did. i wasn't all out willing to take chances with it, which led me to read the graphic novel first, and i'm really glad i made that choice because the graphic novel was so good. the art was lovely and i feel for june well and truly. legend is what i wasn't able to find in dystopia for years. it was captivating and vivid and original, the characters were hard, at times, desperate, but they were still human. they were vulnerable and they made mistakes- and they knew it- and it made the story just so much more believable for me, knowing those characters had to grow and change and seeing it happen, seeing their development play out before me. it was interesting and there's enough that isn't included in the graphic novel, or that is developed further, that made me not mind that i knew how things panned out, or that i was reading the same plot. i also fell for june a lot more than i already had, getting more of her thoughts and feelings over the novel than i had in the gn, and i really love her as a character. i'm more lukewarm to day, at the moment, my feelings neither here nor there, but i don't mind hugely. june steals the show for me, well and truly. i enjoyed both throughly, and i would (and hope to) repeat the process with prodigy, when i get to it.
